top10_weekly.title: Neuronal cell-cycle re-entry stratifies clinical trajectories in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
top10_weekly.abstract: The clinical heterogeneity of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) remains a fundamental barrier to effective therapy. While cell cycle re-entry in post-mitotic neurons is a known precursor to neurodegeneration, its role in defining patient-specific outcomes has never been established. Here, we integrate large-scale transcriptomic profiling from the AnswerALS cohort with mechanistic studies in human iPSC-derived spinal motor neurons to define how cell-cycle re-entry shapes disease heterogeneity in ALS. We identify a transcriptionally distinct patient subgroup with the highest expression of G1 or G2-phase cyclins that exhibit significantly slower functional decline (ALSFRS-R), whereas the engagement of S-phase markers correlates with accelerated disease progression. Nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction, a hallmark of ALS and related disorders, disrupts the spatial distribution of key regulatory proteins and may contribute to maladaptive cell-cycle activation. Our recent evidence suggests that impaired nuclear import may initiate, rather than merely accompany, neuronal cell-cycle re-entry. Using iPSC-derived motor neurons, we show that impaired nuclear import initiates TDP-43 pathology and global nuclear/cytoplasmic mis-localization of key ALS-related proteins. This nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction triggers a transient wave of cell-cycle activity immediately preceding neuronal cell death. Crucially, we show that DNA-replication initiation is a pathological inflection point of no return, as neurons entering S-phase accumulate replication-associated DNA damage and undergo cell death. Selective inhibition of CDK4/6 prevents S-phase entry and confers potent neuroprotection. Our findings demonstrate that impaired nuclear import drives maladaptive cell-cycle reactivation in ALS and that the depth of cell-cycle engagement stratifies neuronal fate and patient trajectories.

top10_weekly.title: The Cxcl14 chemokine defines pioneer axon guidance and early circuit assembly in the inner ear.
top10_weekly.abstract: The nervous system wiring requires the precise coordination of axon guidance, neuronal migration, and target cell recognition. Here, we show that inner ear circuit formation relies on pioneer cells extending an axonal scaffold that selectively targets early-born hair cells. High spatiotemporal imaging of pioneer axons reveals how they navigate through the cranial environment, establishing dynamic cell-cell contacts with other axons to finally stabilize in target cells. These pioneer axons are required not only for follower axon growth but also for coordinated migration of follower neurons, revealing a cellular hierarchy underlying circuit assembly. We identify the chemokine Cxcl14 as a novel instructive guidance cue regulating pioneer axon extension, turning, and fasciculation at discrete cellular decision points. Loss of Cxcl14 disrupts axonal navigation, compromises synaptic organization in hair cells, and impairs mechanosensory-based behavior. Together, our findings establish a new chemokine-based mechanism linking pioneer axon guidance to early sensory circuit assembly necessary for building mechanosensory networks.

top10_weekly.title: Antisense oligonucleotide silencing rescues neurodevelopmental deficits in AMPA receptor gain-of-function mice.
top10_weekly.abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are essential for neuronal development and brain function. We investigated the role of a recurrent AMPAR GluA1 variant (GRIA1 p.A636T) identified in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using a Gria1-A636T knock-in mouse model, we show that this variant is sufficient to produce core ASD/ID-like behaviors and cause selective hippocampal vulnerability characterized by progressive dendritic atrophy and neuronal loss. Despite a reduction in GluA1-containing complexes, synaptic AMPARs exhibit hyperexcitability and fail to transition from calcium-permeable to calcium-impermeable AMPARs during development, resulting in persistent excitotoxicity. To explore potential therapeutic interventions, we developed an allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to selectively silence the mutant transcript. A single neonatal ASO dose prevents hippocampal pathology and rescues behavioral deficits. These findings define a mechanism of developmental excitotoxicity driven by a GRIA1 gain-of-function channelopathy and support RNA-targeted precision therapy for AMPAR-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

top10_weekly.title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
top10_weekly.abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

top10_weekly.title: Amyloid and tau display distinct patterns across Alzheimer's in anterior caudate.
top10_weekly.abstract: The anterior caudate shows a pattern of Alzheimer's disease pathology that differs from the more extensively studied cortex. Across 41 donors, we found mostly diffuse amyloid beta plaques in gray matter and phosphorylated tau threads associated with white matter. Combining digital pathology with single-nucleus and spatial gene expression data, we detected no significant loss or gain in neuronal cell-type abundance with increasing pathology. However, we did observe increases in an FLT1+/IL1B+ microglial population with tau burden. Fast-spiking PTHLH-PVALB interneurons showed changes in genes related to ion channels, cellular trafficking, and phosphorylation. These findings offer a cellular-resolution reference for investigating how Alzheimer's disease affects subcortical brain regions.

top10_weekly.title: Live-cell imaging of inter-organelle contacts using an integrated dimerization-dependent fluorescent protein reporter.
top10_weekly.abstract: Organelles communicate with each other by building membrane contact sites (MCSs) via specialized protein-protein and/or protein-membrane interactions. Conventional light microscopy cannot distinguish organelles connected by MCSs from those merely juxtaposed. In addition, organelle contacts are dynamic, yet only a limited number of tools are available to monitor MCSs in living cells. In this study, we developed a series of reporters based on dimerization-dependent fluorescent proteins (ddFP) to visualize, quantify and follow inter-organelle contacts. We first generated an integrated system specifically designed to study contacts between late endocytic compartments (late endosomes and lysosomes) and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). This system utilizes a single plasmid coding for the two complementary ddFP components: green A (GA) and green B (GB) targeted to the ER and late endosomes and lysosomes (LE/Lys), respectively. This construct enabled the generation of a stable reporter cell line suitable for semi-quantitative imaging. The ddFP reporter, which we called ddFP LELYS-ER, did not perturb endogenous LE/Lys-ER contacts in stable cells, and detected changes in the number of LE/Lys-ER contacts, for example, upon downregulation of the ER-resident VAP tether protein family, or under conditions of lysosomal damage. Moreover, live-cell imaging revealed that LE/Lys-ER contacts have distinct shapes, mobilities and lifetimes. Finally, using the same vector design, we generated two additional integrated reporter systems adapted to the study of contacts between the ER and the plasma membrane, and between the ER and mitochondria.

top10_weekly.title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals molecular organization of human and nonhuman primate basal ganglia.
top10_weekly.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are interconnected subcortical nuclei with a complex topographical organization that orchestrate goal-directed behaviors and are implicated in neurodegenerative movement disorders. We generated a cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the BG in human, rhesus macaque, and common marmoset, sampling over one million cells in each species. By integrating spatial data with a cross-species consensus single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cell-type taxonomy, this atlas reveals principles of molecular organization within and across structures. Extensive spatial sampling across the rostral-caudal axis illuminates complex, yet highly stereotyped, multi-axis gene expression gradients superimposed onto discrete compartments of the striatum. Additionally, we identify core-shell organization of the internal globus pallidus. This unified, cross-species spatial transcriptomics atlas will be a foundational resource for characterizing the molecular and functional organization of the BG and their roles in health and disease.

top10_weekly.title: NeuroBase: A Web-Based Transcriptomic Resource and R Package for Cross-Disorder Analysis of Neurodegenerative and Neuropsychiatric Diseases.
top10_weekly.abstract: Neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia, are highly prevalent and biologically complex conditions that remain difficult to diagnose and treat. This study aimed to develop NeuroBase, a web-based transcriptomic resource that supports exploratory comparison of shared and disorder-specific gene expression features across these disorders. Fourteen human brain bulk RNA sequencing datasets (262 total samples) were processed using a standardized pipeline, followed by differential gene expression analysis with DESeq2, edgeR and limma-voom for broad exploratory discovery, complemented by a multi-method sensitivity analysis to define a method-concordant core gene set, protein-protein interaction network analysis using STRING with downstream exploration in Cytoscape, and functional enrichment analysis. Principal component analysis and clustering-based visualizations were used to summarize similarities and differences in transcriptomic patterns among disorders. Differential expression analysis identified dataset-level significant genes within each disorder using DESeq2 for one dataset per disorder (FDR ≤ 0.05), including 38 genes in Alzheimer's disease, 6,704 in autism spectrum disorder, 3,559 in bipolar disorder, 687 in Parkinson's disease, and 2,750 in schizophrenia; a stricter multi-method intersection analysis yielded method-concordant Core Intersection sets in the most informative datasets (983 core DEGs in autism spectrum disorder, 505 in bipolar disorder, 281 in schizophrenia, and 234 and 151 in two Parkinson's disease datasets; only two core genes (SPP1 and CHST3) were found in Alzheimer's disease). A unified strict-threshold reanalysis (FDR ≤ 0.05, |log₂FC|≥ 1) revealed disorder-level DEG burdens ranging from 34 (Alzheimer's disease) to 2,812 (autism) deduplicated genes, but only 24 genes were reproducible across independent cohorts of the same disorder, highlighting the limited cross-cohort reproducibility characteristic of bulk brain transcriptomics. Enrichment analyses identified significantly enriched signaling pathways in autism spectrum disorder and nominally enriched synapse-related pathways in Alzheimer's disease. Representative high-signal genes included SPP1 in Alzheimer's disease, NRGN in one Parkinson's disease dataset, and BEST1 in autism spectrum disorder. Cross-disorder comparison identified 465 differentially expressed genes shared between the neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorder groups, and principal component analysis showed that sample variation was dominated by dataset and tissue of origin. NeuroBase is a publicly accessible, web-based transcriptomic database and companion R package (neurobaseR) that enables standardized, cross-disorder exploration of bulk brain gene expression profiles across neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, supporting comparative analysis, programmatic data access, and hypothesis generation through interactive visualization and pathway-level summaries.

top10_weekly.title: The people behind the papers - Pavel Tomancak and Jean-Yves Tinevez.
top10_weekly.abstract: Segmenting cells and tracking their internal structures remains a complex image-analysis challenge in cell and developmental biology. In their work, Johannes Girstmair, Tobias Pietzsch, Pavel Tomancak, Jean-Yves Tinevez and colleagues demonstrate how Mastodon, an existing Fiji/ImageJ plugin, can visualise and analyse cell lineages and track cells in 3D within large microscopy datasets. To learn more about their work, we talked to the two corresponding authors, Pavel Tomancak, Principal Investigator at the Max Planck Institute of Molecular Cell Biology and Genetics, Germany, and director of the Central European Institute of Technology, Czech Republic, as well as Jean-Yves Tinevez, founder and leader of the Image Analysis Facility, Institute Pasteur, France.

top10_weekly.title: iPSC-based Approaches to Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: from Drug Screening to Regenerative Medicine in Early Clinical Translation.
top10_weekly.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterised by progressive loss of upper and lower motor neurons (MNs), with limited therapeutic options and modest benefit from currently approved drugs. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have emerged as a versatile platform for ALS research, enabling both regenerative medicine and phenotypic drug screening. iPSC-based transplantation strategies aim to replace lost cells or deliver neuroprotective support, while iPSC-derived MNs support drug discovery and repositioning. In the two decades since their discovery, iPSC technologies have progressed from concept to clinical translation, with both cell therapy products such as AstroRx and XS-228 entering trials and three screened drug candidates, Ropinirole, Bosutinib, and Ezogabine, advancing into clinical trials, underscoring their translational potential. In this review, we summarise iPSC-based approaches to ALS, focusing on cell therapies and drug discovery, highlight factors influencing transplantation success, and discuss ongoing clinical trials. We further discuss constraints that impede clinical trial progress, including limited understanding of ALS pathogenesis, absence of robust biomarkers to guide patient stratification and evaluate treatment response, and technical challenges related to the maturation of iPSC-derived neural cells. Finally, we advocate that advancing iPSC approaches requires both deeper understanding of ALS biology and technical innovation. Key priorities are refining iPSC differentiation protocols to improve neuronal maturity and implementing trial designs with adequate duration and rigorous patient stratification.

primary.title: Insights into how JIP3 and JIP4 adaptor proteins relieve the auto-inhibited form of the kinesin-1 motor.
primary.abstract: While our understanding of kinesin autoinhibition mechanisms is advancing, key insights into kinesin activation, especially autoinhibition relieved by cargo-motor adaptors, remain unclear. JIP3 and JIP4 are adaptors that activate kinesin-1 and dynein-dynactin motors, enabling bidirectional transport along microtubules. Here, we characterized the interaction between the kinesin-1 heavy chain, KIF5B, and both JIP3 and JIP4 (JIP3/4), using mutagenesis and binding experiments associated with modelling. We identified the minimal regions of JIP3/4 and KIF5B required for interaction. JIP3/4 binds to the CC4 coiled-coil domain of KIF5B, with no significant interaction detected with the distal tail. Conversely, KIF5B-CC4 binds to the RH1 domain of JIP3/4, with the preceding disordered N-terminus modulating the force of the binding. Notably, JIP3 and JIP4 exhibit ∼40-fold differences in affinity for KIF5B. We performed extensive site-directed mutagenesis on KIF5B-binding regions of JIP3/JIP4 targeting accessible charged residues and sequence differences between JIP3 and JIP4. This revealed multiple weak-affinity binding sites that collectively define an extensive KIF5B-binding surface on the RH1 domain of JIP3. Importantly, the KIF5B-binding surface on JIP3 differs from that of the DLIC (dynein light intermediate chain), confirming no competition between the two motors. Altogether, the fragment and mutant mapping of KIF5B binding to JIP3 and JIP4 presented here provides insights into how the auto-inhibited form of kinesin-1 might be relieved, with the CC4 region playing a central role.

primary.title: Ultrastructural studies reveal a new role for JIP3/MAPK8IP3 in endo-lysosomal maturation within the neuronal cell body.
primary.abstract: In recent years, substantial heterogeneity in lysosomes, in terms of their composition, function, and positioning, has come to be recognized. Despite this, there are gaps in knowledge of our understanding of the molecular basis of lysosome heterogeneity, especially in neurons. To this end, we used electron microscopy to define endolysosomal organelles of human iPSC-derived neurons at the ultrastructural level. Through this, we identify endolysosomal maturation defects within neuronal cell bodies of iNeurons lacking JNK-Interacting Protein 3 (JIP3), a lysosome adaptor previously known to primarily regulate axonal lysosome movement. Loss of JIP3 results in an expansion of immature lysosomes within neuronal soma, along with a concomitant decrease in mature lysosomes. JIP3 loss also leads to delayed trafficking of endocytic cargo through these compartments, implicating JIP3 in the regulation of endolysosomal maturation within neuronal cell bodies. Our studies highlight the utility of electron microscopy in understanding neuronal lysosomal heterogeneity. Additionally, given recent links between JIP3 and a neurodevelopmental disorder, our findings here could provide new insight into mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental pathology.

primary.title: JIP4 and RILPL1 utilize opposing motor force to dynamically regulate lysosomal tubulation.
primary.abstract: Lysosomes are dynamic organelles that remodel their membrane in response to stimuli. We previously uncovered a process we term LYsosomal Tubulation/sorting driven by LRRK2 (LYTL), wherein damaged lysosomes generate tubules sorted into vesicles. LYTL is orchestrated by the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2 that recruits the motor adaptor protein and RHD family member JIP4 to lysosomes. JIP4 enhances LYTL tubule extension toward the plus-end of microtubules. To identify new players involved in LYTL, we mapped the lysosomal proteome after LRRK2 kinase inhibition. We found that RILPL1 is recruited to dysfunctional lysosomes in an LRRK2 kinase activity-dependent manner, facilitated by pRAB proteins. Unlike JIP4, RILPL1 induces retraction of LYTL tubules by binding to p150Glued, thereby moving lysosomal tubules toward the minus-end of microtubules. Our findings emphasize the dynamic regulation of LYTL tubules by two distinct RHD proteins and pRAB effectors, acting as opposing motor adaptor proteins. These opposing forces create a metastable lysosomal membrane deformation, enabling dynamic tubulation events.

primary.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
primary.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

secondary.title: Characterization of a novel inherited splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3 expands the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: The MAPK8IP3 gene encodes JIP3, a kinesin-1 adapter protein crucial for axonal transport and JNK signaling pathway regulation. This gene exhibits extreme intolerance to loss-of-function variants. Heterozygous pathogenic MAPK8IP3 variants are linked to a neurodevelopmental disorder with or without variable brain abnormalities (NEDBA). This study characterizes a novel inherited canonical splice-site variant identified in a three-generation family. METHODS: Exome sequencing was performed on three affected individuals from a single non-consanguineous family with presenting neurological abnormalities. The molecular consequences of the identified variant were evaluated by RNA analysis. Clinical features of the variant carriers were evaluated in detail. RESULTS: We identified a heterozygous dinucleotide deletion (c.2630-2_2630-1del) at the canonical acceptor splice site of MAPK8IP3. This variant co-segregated with the neurological phenotype in an affected mother and her two children. RNA analysis demonstrated that this variant leads to a partial deletion of exon 22 (r.2630_2673del), which is predicted to cause a frameshift and introduce a premature termination codon (p.Gly877Valfs∗36). Notably, despite carrying an identical genotype, the three affected individuals exhibited marked interindividual variability in clinical severity, ranging from mild specific learning difficulties to global developmental delay with severe intellectual disability and autism. CONCLUSION: This represents the first report of a familial, autosomal dominantly inherited pathogenic splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3, extending the established inheritance pattern beyond previously described de novo events. Our findings expand both the mutational and phenotypic spectrum of MAPK8IP3-related disorders, highlighting the complexity of genotype-phenotype correlations and underscoring the necessity of functional assays for accurate variant interpretation.

limitations: Future studies involving larger cohorts and integrated functional assays are essential to establish more accurate genotype-phenotype correlations.

secondary.title: A toxic gain-of-function variant in MAPK8IP3 provides insights into JIP3 cellular roles.
secondary.abstract: Mitogen-activated protein kinase 8 interacting protein 3 (MAPK8IP3) gene encoding a protein called JIP3 is an adaption protein of the kinesin-1 complex known to play a role in axonal transport of cargo. Mutations in the gene have been linked to severe neurodevelopmental disorders, resulting in developmental delay, intellectual disability, ataxia, tremor, autism, seizures, and visual impairment. A patient who has a missense mutation in the MAPK8IP3 gene (c. 1714 C>T, Arg578Cys) (R578C) manifests dystonia, gross motor delay, and developmental delay. Here, we showed that the mutation was a toxic gain-of-function mutation that altered the interactome of JIP3; disrupted axonal transport of late endosomes; increased signaling via c-Jun N-terminal kinase, resulting in apoptosis; and disrupted dopamine receptor 1 signaling while not affecting dopamine receptor 2 signaling. Furthermore, in the presence of the mutant protein, we showed that an 80% reduction of mutant JIP3 and a 60% reduction of WT JIP3 by non-allele-selective phosphorothioate-modified antisense oligonucleotides was well tolerated by several types of cells in vitro. Our study identifies what we believe to be several important new roles for JIP3 and provides important insights for therapeutic approaches, including antisense oligonucleotide reduction of JIP3.

best.title: Insights into how JIP3 and JIP4 adaptor proteins relieve the auto-inhibited form of the kinesin-1 motor.
best.abstract: While our understanding of kinesin autoinhibition mechanisms is advancing, key insights into kinesin activation, especially autoinhibition relieved by cargo-motor adaptors, remain unclear. JIP3 and JIP4 are adaptors that activate kinesin-1 and dynein-dynactin motors, enabling bidirectional transport along microtubules. Here, we characterized the interaction between the kinesin-1 heavy chain, KIF5B, and both JIP3 and JIP4 (JIP3/4), using mutagenesis and binding experiments associated with modelling. We identified the minimal regions of JIP3/4 and KIF5B required for interaction. JIP3/4 binds to the CC4 coiled-coil domain of KIF5B, with no significant interaction detected with the distal tail. Conversely, KIF5B-CC4 binds to the RH1 domain of JIP3/4, with the preceding disordered N-terminus modulating the force of the binding. Notably, JIP3 and JIP4 exhibit ∼40-fold differences in affinity for KIF5B. We performed extensive site-directed mutagenesis on KIF5B-binding regions of JIP3/JIP4 targeting accessible charged residues and sequence differences between JIP3 and JIP4. This revealed multiple weak-affinity binding sites that collectively define an extensive KIF5B-binding surface on the RH1 domain of JIP3. Importantly, the KIF5B-binding surface on JIP3 differs from that of the DLIC (dynein light intermediate chain), confirming no competition between the two motors. Altogether, the fragment and mutant mapping of KIF5B binding to JIP3 and JIP4 presented here provides insights into how the auto-inhibited form of kinesin-1 might be relieved, with the CC4 region playing a central role.

best.title: Ultrastructural studies reveal a new role for JIP3/MAPK8IP3 in endo-lysosomal maturation within the neuronal cell body.
best.abstract: In recent years, substantial heterogeneity in lysosomes, in terms of their composition, function, and positioning, has come to be recognized. Despite this, there are gaps in knowledge of our understanding of the molecular basis of lysosome heterogeneity, especially in neurons. To this end, we used electron microscopy to define endolysosomal organelles of human iPSC-derived neurons at the ultrastructural level. Through this, we identify endolysosomal maturation defects within neuronal cell bodies of iNeurons lacking JNK-Interacting Protein 3 (JIP3), a lysosome adaptor previously known to primarily regulate axonal lysosome movement. Loss of JIP3 results in an expansion of immature lysosomes within neuronal soma, along with a concomitant decrease in mature lysosomes. JIP3 loss also leads to delayed trafficking of endocytic cargo through these compartments, implicating JIP3 in the regulation of endolysosomal maturation within neuronal cell bodies. Our studies highlight the utility of electron microscopy in understanding neuronal lysosomal heterogeneity. Additionally, given recent links between JIP3 and a neurodevelopmental disorder, our findings here could provide new insight into mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental pathology.

best.title: Characterization of a novel inherited splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3 expands the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: The MAPK8IP3 gene encodes JIP3, a kinesin-1 adapter protein crucial for axonal transport and JNK signaling pathway regulation. This gene exhibits extreme intolerance to loss-of-function variants. Heterozygous pathogenic MAPK8IP3 variants are linked to a neurodevelopmental disorder with or without variable brain abnormalities (NEDBA). This study characterizes a novel inherited canonical splice-site variant identified in a three-generation family. METHODS: Exome sequencing was performed on three affected individuals from a single non-consanguineous family with presenting neurological abnormalities. The molecular consequences of the identified variant were evaluated by RNA analysis. Clinical features of the variant carriers were evaluated in detail. RESULTS: We identified a heterozygous dinucleotide deletion (c.2630-2_2630-1del) at the canonical acceptor splice site of MAPK8IP3. This variant co-segregated with the neurological phenotype in an affected mother and her two children. RNA analysis demonstrated that this variant leads to a partial deletion of exon 22 (r.2630_2673del), which is predicted to cause a frameshift and introduce a premature termination codon (p.Gly877Valfs∗36). Notably, despite carrying an identical genotype, the three affected individuals exhibited marked interindividual variability in clinical severity, ranging from mild specific learning difficulties to global developmental delay with severe intellectual disability and autism. CONCLUSION: This represents the first report of a familial, autosomal dominantly inherited pathogenic splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3, extending the established inheritance pattern beyond previously described de novo events. Our findings expand both the mutational and phenotypic spectrum of MAPK8IP3-related disorders, highlighting the complexity of genotype-phenotype correlations and underscoring the necessity of functional assays for accurate variant interpretation.

best.title: A toxic gain-of-function variant in MAPK8IP3 provides insights into JIP3 cellular roles.
best.abstract: Mitogen-activated protein kinase 8 interacting protein 3 (MAPK8IP3) gene encoding a protein called JIP3 is an adaption protein of the kinesin-1 complex known to play a role in axonal transport of cargo. Mutations in the gene have been linked to severe neurodevelopmental disorders, resulting in developmental delay, intellectual disability, ataxia, tremor, autism, seizures, and visual impairment. A patient who has a missense mutation in the MAPK8IP3 gene (c. 1714 C>T, Arg578Cys) (R578C) manifests dystonia, gross motor delay, and developmental delay. Here, we showed that the mutation was a toxic gain-of-function mutation that altered the interactome of JIP3; disrupted axonal transport of late endosomes; increased signaling via c-Jun N-terminal kinase, resulting in apoptosis; and disrupted dopamine receptor 1 signaling while not affecting dopamine receptor 2 signaling. Furthermore, in the presence of the mutant protein, we showed that an 80% reduction of mutant JIP3 and a 60% reduction of WT JIP3 by non-allele-selective phosphorothioate-modified antisense oligonucleotides was well tolerated by several types of cells in vitro. Our study identifies what we believe to be several important new roles for JIP3 and provides important insights for therapeutic approaches, including antisense oligonucleotide reduction of JIP3.

best.title: JIP4 and RILPL1 utilize opposing motor force to dynamically regulate lysosomal tubulation.
best.abstract: Lysosomes are dynamic organelles that remodel their membrane in response to stimuli. We previously uncovered a process we term LYsosomal Tubulation/sorting driven by LRRK2 (LYTL), wherein damaged lysosomes generate tubules sorted into vesicles. LYTL is orchestrated by the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2 that recruits the motor adaptor protein and RHD family member JIP4 to lysosomes. JIP4 enhances LYTL tubule extension toward the plus-end of microtubules. To identify new players involved in LYTL, we mapped the lysosomal proteome after LRRK2 kinase inhibition. We found that RILPL1 is recruited to dysfunctional lysosomes in an LRRK2 kinase activity-dependent manner, facilitated by pRAB proteins. Unlike JIP4, RILPL1 induces retraction of LYTL tubules by binding to p150Glued, thereby moving lysosomal tubules toward the minus-end of microtubules. Our findings emphasize the dynamic regulation of LYTL tubules by two distinct RHD proteins and pRAB effectors, acting as opposing motor adaptor proteins. These opposing forces create a metastable lysosomal membrane deformation, enabling dynamic tubulation events.

best.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
best.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. primary.title: The Cxcl14 chemokine defines pioneer axon guidance and early circuit assembly in the inner ear.
primary.abstract: The nervous system wiring requires the precise coordination of axon guidance, neuronal migration, and target cell recognition. Here, we show that inner ear circuit formation relies on pioneer cells extending an axonal scaffold that selectively targets early-born hair cells. High spatiotemporal imaging of pioneer axons reveals how they navigate through the cranial environment, establishing dynamic cell-cell contacts with other axons to finally stabilize in target cells. These pioneer axons are required not only for follower axon growth but also for coordinated migration of follower neurons, revealing a cellular hierarchy underlying circuit assembly. We identify the chemokine Cxcl14 as a novel instructive guidance cue regulating pioneer axon extension, turning, and fasciculation at discrete cellular decision points. Loss of Cxcl14 disrupts axonal navigation, compromises synaptic organization in hair cells, and impairs mechanosensory-based behavior. Together, our findings establish a new chemokine-based mechanism linking pioneer axon guidance to early sensory circuit assembly necessary for building mechanosensory networks.

primary.title: Antisense oligonucleotide silencing rescues neurodevelopmental deficits in AMPA receptor gain-of-function mice.
primary.abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are essential for neuronal development and brain function. We investigated the role of a recurrent AMPAR GluA1 variant (GRIA1 p.A636T) identified in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using a Gria1-A636T knock-in mouse model, we show that this variant is sufficient to produce core ASD/ID-like behaviors and cause selective hippocampal vulnerability characterized by progressive dendritic atrophy and neuronal loss. Despite a reduction in GluA1-containing complexes, synaptic AMPARs exhibit hyperexcitability and fail to transition from calcium-permeable to calcium-impermeable AMPARs during development, resulting in persistent excitotoxicity. To explore potential therapeutic interventions, we developed an allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to selectively silence the mutant transcript. A single neonatal ASO dose prevents hippocampal pathology and rescues behavioral deficits. These findings define a mechanism of developmental excitotoxicity driven by a GRIA1 gain-of-function channelopathy and support RNA-targeted precision therapy for AMPAR-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

primary.title: Disruption of cell-type-specific molecular programs of striatal spiny projection neurons in autism.
primary.abstract: Rare genetic variants contribute substantially to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet the regulatory logic of vulnerable subcortical cells is poorly understood. In a 16p11.2 deletion mouse model, lineage tracing across five brain regions revealed prominent striatal changes. In the human putamen from ASD and neurotypical donors, single-nucleus multi-omics showed transcriptional alterations concentrated in D1 striosome spiny projection neurons (SPNs), affecting synaptic and energy metabolism genes, with altered synapse-supporting programs in astrocytes. Gene regulatory network analysis integrating chromatin accessibility and expression identified EGR1 and EGR3 as key regulators of these programs, with reduced activity in D1 striosome SPNs. Deleting EGR1 or EGR3 in human striatal organoids produced partially overlapping transcriptional changes. These findings establish the striatum as a site of molecular convergence in ASD and provide a multi-omic resource for dissecting subcortical mechanisms.

primary.title: RBM42 couples alternative splicing to cytoskeletal organization to direct cortical development.
primary.abstract: Alternative splicing coordinates gene expression programs that shape the developing cerebral cortex. Here, we used nervous system-specific Rbm42 conditional knockout mice, RBM42-depleted human SH-SY5Y cells, RNA sequencing, RIP-seq, proteomics, and splice-switching rescue to define how the spliceosomal RNA-binding protein RBM42 supports cortical development. Rbm42 loss caused perinatal lethality, cortical thinning, defective lamination, reduced progenitor proliferation, increased apoptosis, and disrupted neuronal cytoskeletal organization. RBM42 bound and regulated cytoskeleton-associated transcripts, including NIN/Nin and NUMA1/Numa1, and its loss altered their splicing in human cells and mouse cortex. Restoring RBM42 corrected these splicing defects and improved proliferation and neurite growth. Selective correction of NIN exon 18 mis-splicing partially restored βIII-tubulin organization and proliferation but did not rescue apoptosis. These findings connect spliceosome-dependent isoform control with cytoskeletal remodeling during cortical development and provide a mechanistic framework for RBM42-associated neurodevelopmental disease.

primary.title: Overexpression of endoplasmic reticulum acetyl-CoA transporter AT-1 alters neuronal metabolism, growth, and synaptic activity.
primary.abstract: Acetyl-CoA is a molecule central to cellular metabolic homeostasis. As part of the secretory pathway, acetyl-CoA is imported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by a membrane-bound transporter AT-1 (SLC33A1). AT-1 mutations have been linked to peripheral neuropathy, developmental delay with premature death, and intellectual disability with progeria. Here, we show that AT-1 overexpression impacts diverse phenotypes related to neuronal function and plasticity. Differences in ribosomal, synaptic processing, and metabolic pathways were identified at transcriptomic and proteomic levels. Metabolic adaptations included changes in mitochondrial membrane potential, architecture, and respiration, and tracing experiments revealed changes in the fate of glucose favoring glycogen storage over the pentose phosphate pathway. Altered redox was linked to NAD-dependent proteins SIRT1 and CtBP2. Depletion of lipid stores was associated with greater plasticity in fuel substrate utilization. Metabolic adaptation was coincident with decreased synaptic activity, indicating that neuronal communication is coordinated, in part, through acetyl-CoA metabolism.

primary.title: Genomic landscape of rare variants in a Chinese autism cohort and discovery of novel risk genes.
primary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a genetically complex neurodevelopmental condition with a high heritability. However, genomic studies of ASD have been underrepresented in East Asian populations, and the molecular yield in ASD cohorts remains modest. Here, we present a whole-genome sequencing analysis of 3109 samples across 1033 Chinese ASD families. By examining a wide spectrum of genetic variation, we identified rare ASD-associated variants in 19.2% of affected individuals, providing a population-specific view of the genetic architecture of ASD. We identify significant enrichment of de novo variants in probands, nominate or strengthen candidate risk genes (e.g., NCL, SPPL3, ADGRB1, SLC9A3, KIF1B) through mutational burden, evolutionary constraint, recurrent missense site, and functional assays, and implicate convergent pathways including protein palmitoylation. By integrating over 40,000 ASD cases across unpublished and published global cohorts, we identify 245 ASD risk genes, including 45 with limited prior evidence and 32 with no prior association. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the developing human cortex reveals that ASD risk genes exhibit widespread yet heterogeneous expression across all major cell types, with peak expression in excitatory neurons, particularly intratelencephalic neurons, and enriched expression in microglia (e.g., C1QC, CARD11, SNX13, MEF2C, FOXP2, TCF12, MED13L), suggesting convergent involvement of both synaptic and neuroimmune mechanisms. Together, our findings expand the ASD genetic landscape and suggest convergent pathogenic axes involving transcriptional regulation, synaptic signaling and plasticity, and neuroimmune interactions. This work supports the development of inclusive diagnostic strategies and provides a foundation for mechanistic and intervention exploration in ASD.

secondary.title: Expression of the neurodevelopmental disease susceptibility genes CADM1 and CADM2 in the early human fetal forebrain.
secondary.abstract: CADM1 and CADM2 are cell-adhesion molecules with likely roles in cell migration, axon guidance and synapse formation. Both are considered potential susceptibility genes for various neurodevelopmental disorders. However, their expression patterns in early human brain development have not been explored. Here we employed transcriptomics, RNAScope in situ hybridisation (ISH) and immunofluorescence (IF) to determine the time course and location of expression in the human cerebral cortex and thalamus between 7.5-17 postconceptional weeks (PCW). In the cerebral cortex, tissue RNAseq revealed both to be highly expressed throughout this period. CADM1 exhibited very high expression which declined slightly with age. CADM2 exhibited high expression which increased over time. Single-cell RNA-seq and ISH revealed that both genes were co-expressed in most cells; however, IF revealed different patterns of cellular localisation. At 8 PCW, expression for both CADMs was similar throughout the cortex and predominantly located in the cytoplasm/cell surface in the cortical plate (CP) but with stronger expression of CADM1 in the subventricular zone. However, from 10 PCW onwards, the strongest immunoreactivity for CADM1 was in the cell nucleus with weak cytoplasmic localisation, whereas CADM2 was expressed on the cell surface and increasingly in axons with age. By 17 PCW, CADM2 exhibited strong immunoreactivity in the thalamocortical and callosal corticocortical axons but was weakly expressed in corticofugal pathways. In the thalamus, CADM2 expression in posterior and lateral projection neurons contributing to thalamocortical pathways was confirmed. CADM1 and CADM2 show differential expression in the thalamus and associated nuclei, suggesting a role in their segregation; CADM1 favouring anterior and medial thalamic nuclei and the ventromedial subthalamus, CADM2 the lateral habenula, lateral and posterior thalamus and dorsolateral subthalamus. CADM1 and CADM2 may play important and varied roles in early fetal human forebrain development, guiding cell migration and aggregation, and axon guidance and fasciculation.

secondary.title: SHANK3 drives abnormal neurodevelopment in iPSC-derived 2D and 3D brain models of Phelan-McDermid Syndrome.
secondary.abstract: Phelan-McDermid Syndrome (PMDS) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by 22q13.3 deletion involving SHANK3. While SHANK3 is critical for synapses, its role in early human neurodevelopment remains elusive. Here, we generated induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived 2D neuronal cultures and 3D cerebral organoids from two twin Phelan-McDermid syndrome patients with a 1.7 Mb 22q13 deletion encompassing SHANK3 gene. PMDS organoids showed reduced volume due to impaired neural progenitor cells (NPCs) proliferation. PMDS NPCs exhibited biased differentiation with decreased excitatory neurons but increased GFAP+ astroglia and GABAergic neurons. PMDS neurons displayed simplified morphology, reduced synapse density and diminished excitability. Importantly, lentiviral-mediated SHANK3 overexpression largely rescued these defects. Our findings identify SHANK3 as a key regulator of early neurodevelopment and provide mechanistic insights into PMDS pathogenesis.

secondary.title: Transdiagnostic variation in age-related patterns of rich-club organization across neurodevelopmental and related mental health conditions.
secondary.abstract: Rich-club organization is a topographical property of functional brain networks where highly connected regions are more densely interconnected. The rich-club has been shown to be vital for supporting cognitive functioning, and differences have been associated with a wide range of mental health and developmental conditions. This type of organization undergoes complex changes across development, and we have previously shown that males and females have strikingly distinct age-related changes. While disruptions in its development have been related to neurodevelopmental conditions and related mental health conditions such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), the diagnostic- and sex-specific age-related patterns remain unexplored. These conditions also have heterogeneous and overlapping neurobiology and phenotype, and thus transdiagnostic approaches may be most suitable for addressing the complexities. Here, we combine the temporal advantages of magnetoencephalography (MEG) with a data-driven, transdiagnostic approach to parse the heterogeneity of age-related variation in rich-club organization in 386 neurodivergent (116 ADHD, 231 autism, 39 OCD) and 231 neurotypical children and youth, stratified by biological sex. In males and females, subgroups with distinct age-related patterns of rich-club organization did not align cleanly with the diagnostic categories. These patterns were frequency specific, separating the female subgroups in the alpha and gamma bands and the male subgroups in the theta, alpha, beta, and high gamma bands. While the female subgroups differed in their proportions of autistic and neurotypical individuals, all diagnostic categories were represented across the subgroups. The female subgroups also differed in intelligence, while the male subgroups differed in hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms. Together, our findings indicate that frequency-specific, age-related variation in rich-club organization is largely shared across neurotypical and neurodivergent children and youth, rather than delineating diagnostic categories, and highlight the importance of considering sex when studying the biological constructs underlying neurodivergence.

secondary.title: Altered dynamic brain states and potential transcriptomic correlates in autism spectrum disorder.
secondary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is associated with widespread alterations in functional brain networks, but its transient dynamic brain states and potential transcriptomic correlates remain unclear. We applied Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis (LEiDA) to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 110 individuals with ASD and 110 healthy controls (HCs) from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange I (ABIDE I) dataset. Five recurrent phase-locking states were identified, and dynamic brain state metrics were compared between groups. Compared with HCs, individuals with ASD showed reduced fractional occupancy (FO) of State 5, which was predominantly characterized by the visual network with additional involvement of the sensorimotor network. Exploratory analyses within the ASD group revealed nominal negative associations between State 4 FO and ADOS total and social scores. To investigate potential transcriptomic correlates, we derived an ROI-wise ASD-HC State 5 weighted beta map and related it to Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) gene expression data and SFARI ASD risk gene sets. SFARI ASD risk gene sets showed a consistent pattern of negative spatial associations with the ASD-related State 5 imaging phenotype, but these associations did not reach statistical significance after BrainSMASH testing and FDR correction. Exploratory rank-based Gene Ontology (GO) analysis implicated biological functions related to neuronal structure, synaptic function, and the regulation of neuronal excitability. These findings identify alterations in dynamic brain state organization in ASD and provide exploratory transcriptomic clues to their potential biological context.

secondary.title: Disruption of GAD1 protein architecture by a novel missense variant in a consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intellectual disability represents a heterogeneous group of neurodevelopmental disorders marked by significant impairments in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior. Among the various causes, genetic factors play a major role, with autosomal recessive intellectual disability (ARID) constituting a genetically diverse subgroup. ARID is prevalent in consanguineous families and arises from homozygous mutations that disrupt critical genes involved in brain development and function. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to identify disease-causing genetic variants responsible for ARID in a consanguineous Pakistani family and to evaluate the structural and functional impact of a novel variant identified in GAD1 through protein modeling. METHODS: A consanguineous family affected with intellectual disability was enrolled. Whole-exome sequencing was performed on an affected individual, followed by bioinformatics analysis including alignment to the GRCh38 reference genome, variant calling, and annotation. Variants were filtered based on rarity, predicted functional impact, and autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Candidate variants were validated and assessed by Sanger sequencing and segregation analysis. Protein modeling was performed to evaluate the structural impact of the identified variant. RESULTS: A novel homozygous missense variant NM_000817:c.1700G>A;p.Arg567Gln in GAD1 was identified. Segregation analysis confirmed co-segregation of the variant with the affected phenotype. Protein modeling suggested that the variant may disrupt GAD1 enzymatic function involved in gamma-aminobutyric acid synthesis. CONCLUSION: This study emphasizes the significance of genetic investigation in familial cases and the crucial role that GAD1 mutations play in neurodevelopmental disorders with intellectual disability. The results advance the knowledge of molecular causes of ARID and broaden the mutational range.

secondary.title: Transcriptional boosting and buffering during neurodevelopment by shifts in mRNA instability.
secondary.abstract: The contribution of mRNA half-life is commonly overlooked when examining changes in mRNA abundance during development. mRNA levels are regulated by transcription rate or mRNA half-life, but combinations of both could boost or buffer the final steady-state. We measured transcription rate and mRNA half-life changes during human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neuronal development using RATE-seq. The most prevalent mode of gene regulation during transitions to neuronal progenitors and neurons was transcriptional buffering. Less prevalent modes consisted of transcriptional boosting events, transcription rate only shifts, or mRNA half-life only shifts. Buffered and novel boosted gene sets were enriched in RNA-binding protein (RBP) motifs and microRNA sites. Global mRNA half-life decreased two-fold in neurons. microRNA copy number per cell increased during neurodevelopment coincident with destabilization of a subset of short isoforms that contributed to increased average 3'UTR length. Our findings identify mRNA instability mechanisms that regulate transcript levels and 3'UTR isoform abundance, and provide a precedent for transcriptional boosting or buffering during development of other human tissues.

secondary.title: Digital twin control framework uncovers individualized cross-scale links between functional connectivity deviations, communication impairment, and molecular mechanisms in autism.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is hallmarked by pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity in brain function and clinical manifestations. Conventional neuroimaging studies yield highly inconsistent findings, as extrinsic confounding factors and intrinsic disease heterogeneity mask ASD-specific functional connectivity (FC) signatures, hampering the identification of individualized neural mechanisms linked to symptom severity. METHODS: We developed a digital twin control analytical framework based on deep contrastive learning. By comparing each ASD participant with their matched digital twin control, we quantified individual-specific FC deviations. Principal component analysis was applied to extract the core aberrant pattern, followed by multi-dimensional analyzes and validation including clinical correlation, transcriptomic decoding, neurotransmitter and mitochondrial co-localization, as well as disease and cognitive enrichment. RESULTS: The model effectively disentangled disease‑related from non‑disease‑related variations. The identified dominant aberrant FC pattern was significantly associated with Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) communication scores, suggesting it is associated with to communication impairment. This pattern showed convergent associations with synaptic pathways, excitatory/inhibitory neuronal signatures, critical developmental windows and subcortical structures, and exhibited negative spatial association with multiple neurotransmitter systems and mitochondrial respiratory complexes. Biological validation further supported its ASD specificity and communication‑related cognitive relevance. CONCLUSIONS: Leveraging the twin control analytical framework, this study provides an exploratory cross-scale framework linking individualized FC deviations with clinical, transcriptomic, neurochemical, and mitochondrial maps. The findings indicate that communication difficulties in ASD may partly arise from multi-scale disturbances in neural integration, social-perceptual processing and activity-dependent cellular energy regulation.

secondary.title: Disrupted neuronal expression of autism risk genes and white matter micro-organization after infant Zika infection.
secondary.abstract: Congenital and early-life Zika virus (ZIKV) infection can result in neurologic deficits. Precise mechanisms of injury, especially in the more subtle presentation of postnatal infection, are not fully elucidated. Here, we defined the effects of ZIKV on the developing brain using single-cell transcriptomics, histopathology, design-based stereology, diffusion MRI, and neurobehavioral assessments in infant rhesus macaques. ZIKV upregulated interferon-stimulated genes in activated microglia and cell death pathways in neurons and downregulated metabolism and differentiation genes in mature oligodendrocytes. Abnormal micro-organization of the corpus callosum and limbic white matter tracts was seen on diffusion-weighted imaging. A curated gene set associated with autism spectrum disorder risk was negatively enriched in inhibitory and excitatory neurons from ZIKV-infected infants, with increased emotional reactivity already evident 2 weeks after infection. From single cells to organism-level behaviors, these results define the pathways and processes disrupted by early-life ZIKV infection.

secondary.title: Differential frontostriatal ΔFosB dynamics and behavioral flexibility in autism like VPA-exposed mice.
secondary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) involves social impairments, repetitive behaviors, and behavioral inflexibility, defined as an inability to adapt behavior to changing contingencies, and is linked to frontostriatal dysfunction. How behavioral training modulates these circuits is unclear, but ΔFosB, a marker of sustained neural activity, may be useful to establish their relationship. The aim was to evaluate frontostriatal ΔFosB expression following prenatal exposure to valproic acid (VPA) and to determine how experience in the midsession reversal (MSR) task modulates posterior ΔFosB expression. CD-1 mice were prenatally exposed to VPA (500 mg/kg) or vehicle. Brains from postnatal day (PND) 30 mice were analyzed to quantify baseline ΔFosB + cells in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), dorsal striatum (DS), and ventral striatum (VS). In the second experiment, mice performed the MSR task for 13 days. Then, ΔFosB was re-evaluated at PND43 to assess experience-dependent changes. At PND30, VPA-exposed mice showed a significant increase in ΔFosB + cells in mPFC, OFC, DS, and VS, suggesting sustained activity-dependent engagement of the frontostriatal circuit. In the MSR task, mice adapted to contingency shifts using mixed strategies, including win-stay/lose-shift behavior and temporal estimation, whereas VPA mice showed less consistent strategy selection after reversal. After MSR, ΔFosB expression in the OFC and striatum of VPA mice normalized to control levels and remained persistently elevated in the mPFC at PND43. Thus, prenatal VPA induces long-term increases in neuronal transcriptional changes, suggesting activity-dependent plasticity in the frontostriatal circuit. Despite these neural alterations, behavioral flexibility was preserved, suggesting circuit-level adaptations underlying ASD-related strategies. Future studies could broaden these results by examining sex differences and characterizing the cellular and molecular changes dependent on frontostriatal ΔFosB dynamics.

best.title: The Cxcl14 chemokine defines pioneer axon guidance and early circuit assembly in the inner ear.
best.abstract: The nervous system wiring requires the precise coordination of axon guidance, neuronal migration, and target cell recognition. Here, we show that inner ear circuit formation relies on pioneer cells extending an axonal scaffold that selectively targets early-born hair cells. High spatiotemporal imaging of pioneer axons reveals how they navigate through the cranial environment, establishing dynamic cell-cell contacts with other axons to finally stabilize in target cells. These pioneer axons are required not only for follower axon growth but also for coordinated migration of follower neurons, revealing a cellular hierarchy underlying circuit assembly. We identify the chemokine Cxcl14 as a novel instructive guidance cue regulating pioneer axon extension, turning, and fasciculation at discrete cellular decision points. Loss of Cxcl14 disrupts axonal navigation, compromises synaptic organization in hair cells, and impairs mechanosensory-based behavior. Together, our findings establish a new chemokine-based mechanism linking pioneer axon guidance to early sensory circuit assembly necessary for building mechanosensory networks.

best.title: Antisense oligonucleotide silencing rescues neurodevelopmental deficits in AMPA receptor gain-of-function mice.
best.abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are essential for neuronal development and brain function. We investigated the role of a recurrent AMPAR GluA1 variant (GRIA1 p.A636T) identified in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using a Gria1-A636T knock-in mouse model, we show that this variant is sufficient to produce core ASD/ID-like behaviors and cause selective hippocampal vulnerability characterized by progressive dendritic atrophy and neuronal loss. Despite a reduction in GluA1-containing complexes, synaptic AMPARs exhibit hyperexcitability and fail to transition from calcium-permeable to calcium-impermeable AMPARs during development, resulting in persistent excitotoxicity. To explore potential therapeutic interventions, we developed an allele-specific antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) to selectively silence the mutant transcript. A single neonatal ASO dose prevents hippocampal pathology and rescues behavioral deficits. These findings define a mechanism of developmental excitotoxicity driven by a GRIA1 gain-of-function channelopathy and support RNA-targeted precision therapy for AMPAR-related neurodevelopmental disorders.

best.title: Disruption of cell-type-specific molecular programs of striatal spiny projection neurons in autism.
best.abstract: Rare genetic variants contribute substantially to autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet the regulatory logic of vulnerable subcortical cells is poorly understood. In a 16p11.2 deletion mouse model, lineage tracing across five brain regions revealed prominent striatal changes. In the human putamen from ASD and neurotypical donors, single-nucleus multi-omics showed transcriptional alterations concentrated in D1 striosome spiny projection neurons (SPNs), affecting synaptic and energy metabolism genes, with altered synapse-supporting programs in astrocytes. Gene regulatory network analysis integrating chromatin accessibility and expression identified EGR1 and EGR3 as key regulators of these programs, with reduced activity in D1 striosome SPNs. Deleting EGR1 or EGR3 in human striatal organoids produced partially overlapping transcriptional changes. These findings establish the striatum as a site of molecular convergence in ASD and provide a multi-omic resource for dissecting subcortical mechanisms.

best.title: RBM42 couples alternative splicing to cytoskeletal organization to direct cortical development.
best.abstract: Alternative splicing coordinates gene expression programs that shape the developing cerebral cortex. Here, we used nervous system-specific Rbm42 conditional knockout mice, RBM42-depleted human SH-SY5Y cells, RNA sequencing, RIP-seq, proteomics, and splice-switching rescue to define how the spliceosomal RNA-binding protein RBM42 supports cortical development. Rbm42 loss caused perinatal lethality, cortical thinning, defective lamination, reduced progenitor proliferation, increased apoptosis, and disrupted neuronal cytoskeletal organization. RBM42 bound and regulated cytoskeleton-associated transcripts, including NIN/Nin and NUMA1/Numa1, and its loss altered their splicing in human cells and mouse cortex. Restoring RBM42 corrected these splicing defects and improved proliferation and neurite growth. Selective correction of NIN exon 18 mis-splicing partially restored βIII-tubulin organization and proliferation but did not rescue apoptosis. These findings connect spliceosome-dependent isoform control with cytoskeletal remodeling during cortical development and provide a mechanistic framework for RBM42-associated neurodevelopmental disease.

best.title: Expression of the neurodevelopmental disease susceptibility genes CADM1 and CADM2 in the early human fetal forebrain.
best.abstract: CADM1 and CADM2 are cell-adhesion molecules with likely roles in cell migration, axon guidance and synapse formation. Both are considered potential susceptibility genes for various neurodevelopmental disorders. However, their expression patterns in early human brain development have not been explored. Here we employed transcriptomics, RNAScope in situ hybridisation (ISH) and immunofluorescence (IF) to determine the time course and location of expression in the human cerebral cortex and thalamus between 7.5-17 postconceptional weeks (PCW). In the cerebral cortex, tissue RNAseq revealed both to be highly expressed throughout this period. CADM1 exhibited very high expression which declined slightly with age. CADM2 exhibited high expression which increased over time. Single-cell RNA-seq and ISH revealed that both genes were co-expressed in most cells; however, IF revealed different patterns of cellular localisation. At 8 PCW, expression for both CADMs was similar throughout the cortex and predominantly located in the cytoplasm/cell surface in the cortical plate (CP) but with stronger expression of CADM1 in the subventricular zone. However, from 10 PCW onwards, the strongest immunoreactivity for CADM1 was in the cell nucleus with weak cytoplasmic localisation, whereas CADM2 was expressed on the cell surface and increasingly in axons with age. By 17 PCW, CADM2 exhibited strong immunoreactivity in the thalamocortical and callosal corticocortical axons but was weakly expressed in corticofugal pathways. In the thalamus, CADM2 expression in posterior and lateral projection neurons contributing to thalamocortical pathways was confirmed. CADM1 and CADM2 show differential expression in the thalamus and associated nuclei, suggesting a role in their segregation; CADM1 favouring anterior and medial thalamic nuclei and the ventromedial subthalamus, CADM2 the lateral habenula, lateral and posterior thalamus and dorsolateral subthalamus. CADM1 and CADM2 may play important and varied roles in early fetal human forebrain development, guiding cell migration and aggregation, and axon guidance and fasciculation.

best.title: Overexpression of endoplasmic reticulum acetyl-CoA transporter AT-1 alters neuronal metabolism, growth, and synaptic activity.
best.abstract: Acetyl-CoA is a molecule central to cellular metabolic homeostasis. As part of the secretory pathway, acetyl-CoA is imported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by a membrane-bound transporter AT-1 (SLC33A1). AT-1 mutations have been linked to peripheral neuropathy, developmental delay with premature death, and intellectual disability with progeria. Here, we show that AT-1 overexpression impacts diverse phenotypes related to neuronal function and plasticity. Differences in ribosomal, synaptic processing, and metabolic pathways were identified at transcriptomic and proteomic levels. Metabolic adaptations included changes in mitochondrial membrane potential, architecture, and respiration, and tracing experiments revealed changes in the fate of glucose favoring glycogen storage over the pentose phosphate pathway. Altered redox was linked to NAD-dependent proteins SIRT1 and CtBP2. Depletion of lipid stores was associated with greater plasticity in fuel substrate utilization. Metabolic adaptation was coincident with decreased synaptic activity, indicating that neuronal communication is coordinated, in part, through acetyl-CoA metabolism.

best.title: Genomic landscape of rare variants in a Chinese autism cohort and discovery of novel risk genes.
best.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a genetically complex neurodevelopmental condition with a high heritability. However, genomic studies of ASD have been underrepresented in East Asian populations, and the molecular yield in ASD cohorts remains modest. Here, we present a whole-genome sequencing analysis of 3109 samples across 1033 Chinese ASD families. By examining a wide spectrum of genetic variation, we identified rare ASD-associated variants in 19.2% of affected individuals, providing a population-specific view of the genetic architecture of ASD. We identify significant enrichment of de novo variants in probands, nominate or strengthen candidate risk genes (e.g., NCL, SPPL3, ADGRB1, SLC9A3, KIF1B) through mutational burden, evolutionary constraint, recurrent missense site, and functional assays, and implicate convergent pathways including protein palmitoylation. By integrating over 40,000 ASD cases across unpublished and published global cohorts, we identify 245 ASD risk genes, including 45 with limited prior evidence and 32 with no prior association. Single-cell transcriptomic profiling of the developing human cortex reveals that ASD risk genes exhibit widespread yet heterogeneous expression across all major cell types, with peak expression in excitatory neurons, particularly intratelencephalic neurons, and enriched expression in microglia (e.g., C1QC, CARD11, SNX13, MEF2C, FOXP2, TCF12, MED13L), suggesting convergent involvement of both synaptic and neuroimmune mechanisms. Together, our findings expand the ASD genetic landscape and suggest convergent pathogenic axes involving transcriptional regulation, synaptic signaling and plasticity, and neuroimmune interactions. This work supports the development of inclusive diagnostic strategies and provides a foundation for mechanistic and intervention exploration in ASD.

best.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
best.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

best.title: Altered dynamic brain states and potential transcriptomic correlates in autism spectrum disorder.
best.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is associated with widespread alterations in functional brain networks, but its transient dynamic brain states and potential transcriptomic correlates remain unclear. We applied Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis (LEiDA) to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 110 individuals with ASD and 110 healthy controls (HCs) from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange I (ABIDE I) dataset. Five recurrent phase-locking states were identified, and dynamic brain state metrics were compared between groups. Compared with HCs, individuals with ASD showed reduced fractional occupancy (FO) of State 5, which was predominantly characterized by the visual network with additional involvement of the sensorimotor network. Exploratory analyses within the ASD group revealed nominal negative associations between State 4 FO and ADOS total and social scores. To investigate potential transcriptomic correlates, we derived an ROI-wise ASD-HC State 5 weighted beta map and related it to Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) gene expression data and SFARI ASD risk gene sets. SFARI ASD risk gene sets showed a consistent pattern of negative spatial associations with the ASD-related State 5 imaging phenotype, but these associations did not reach statistical significance after BrainSMASH testing and FDR correction. Exploratory rank-based Gene Ontology (GO) analysis implicated biological functions related to neuronal structure, synaptic function, and the regulation of neuronal excitability. These findings identify alterations in dynamic brain state organization in ASD and provide exploratory transcriptomic clues to their potential biological context.

best.title: Disruption of GAD1 protein architecture by a novel missense variant in a consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intellectual disability represents a heterogeneous group of neurodevelopmental disorders marked by significant impairments in intellectual functioning and adaptive behavior. Among the various causes, genetic factors play a major role, with autosomal recessive intellectual disability (ARID) constituting a genetically diverse subgroup. ARID is prevalent in consanguineous families and arises from homozygous mutations that disrupt critical genes involved in brain development and function. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to identify disease-causing genetic variants responsible for ARID in a consanguineous Pakistani family and to evaluate the structural and functional impact of a novel variant identified in GAD1 through protein modeling. METHODS: A consanguineous family affected with intellectual disability was enrolled. Whole-exome sequencing was performed on an affected individual, followed by bioinformatics analysis including alignment to the GRCh38 reference genome, variant calling, and annotation. Variants were filtered based on rarity, predicted functional impact, and autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Candidate variants were validated and assessed by Sanger sequencing and segregation analysis. Protein modeling was performed to evaluate the structural impact of the identified variant. RESULTS: A novel homozygous missense variant NM_000817:c.1700G>A;p.Arg567Gln in GAD1 was identified. Segregation analysis confirmed co-segregation of the variant with the affected phenotype. Protein modeling suggested that the variant may disrupt GAD1 enzymatic function involved in gamma-aminobutyric acid synthesis. CONCLUSION: This study emphasizes the significance of genetic investigation in familial cases and the crucial role that GAD1 mutations play in neurodevelopmental disorders with intellectual disability. The results advance the knowledge of molecular causes of ARID and broaden the mutational range.

best.title: Transcriptional boosting and buffering during neurodevelopment by shifts in mRNA instability.
best.abstract: The contribution of mRNA half-life is commonly overlooked when examining changes in mRNA abundance during development. mRNA levels are regulated by transcription rate or mRNA half-life, but combinations of both could boost or buffer the final steady-state. We measured transcription rate and mRNA half-life changes during human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neuronal development using RATE-seq. The most prevalent mode of gene regulation during transitions to neuronal progenitors and neurons was transcriptional buffering. Less prevalent modes consisted of transcriptional boosting events, transcription rate only shifts, or mRNA half-life only shifts. Buffered and novel boosted gene sets were enriched in RNA-binding protein (RBP) motifs and microRNA sites. Global mRNA half-life decreased two-fold in neurons. microRNA copy number per cell increased during neurodevelopment coincident with destabilization of a subset of short isoforms that contributed to increased average 3'UTR length. Our findings identify mRNA instability mechanisms that regulate transcript levels and 3'UTR isoform abundance, and provide a precedent for transcriptional boosting or buffering during development of other human tissues.

best.title: Digital twin control framework uncovers individualized cross-scale links between functional connectivity deviations, communication impairment, and molecular mechanisms in autism.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is hallmarked by pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity in brain function and clinical manifestations. Conventional neuroimaging studies yield highly inconsistent findings, as extrinsic confounding factors and intrinsic disease heterogeneity mask ASD-specific functional connectivity (FC) signatures, hampering the identification of individualized neural mechanisms linked to symptom severity. METHODS: We developed a digital twin control analytical framework based on deep contrastive learning. By comparing each ASD participant with their matched digital twin control, we quantified individual-specific FC deviations. Principal component analysis was applied to extract the core aberrant pattern, followed by multi-dimensional analyzes and validation including clinical correlation, transcriptomic decoding, neurotransmitter and mitochondrial co-localization, as well as disease and cognitive enrichment. RESULTS: The model effectively disentangled disease‑related from non‑disease‑related variations. The identified dominant aberrant FC pattern was significantly associated with Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) communication scores, suggesting it is associated with to communication impairment. This pattern showed convergent associations with synaptic pathways, excitatory/inhibitory neuronal signatures, critical developmental windows and subcortical structures, and exhibited negative spatial association with multiple neurotransmitter systems and mitochondrial respiratory complexes. Biological validation further supported its ASD specificity and communication‑related cognitive relevance. CONCLUSIONS: Leveraging the twin control analytical framework, this study provides an exploratory cross-scale framework linking individualized FC deviations with clinical, transcriptomic, neurochemical, and mitochondrial maps. The findings indicate that communication difficulties in ASD may partly arise from multi-scale disturbances in neural integration, social-perceptual processing and activity-dependent cellular energy regulation.
