best.title: Genetic evidence for a functional association between Parkinson's disease proteins leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 and α-synuclein during axonal transport.
best.abstract: Mutations in α-synuclein (α-syn) and LRRK2 cause familial Parkinson's disease (fPD), yet how these proteins functionally interact remain ambiguous. We previously showed that α-syn undergoes bi-directional transport within axons and influences mitochondrial health, while other studies suggested that LRRK2-G2019S disrupts the axonal transport of autophagic vesicles and mitochondria. Here we tested the hypothesis that α-syn and LRRK2 are functionally linked during axonal transport. Expression of human LRRK2-WT in Drosophila larval nerves caused modest CSP-containing axonal blockages whereas no defects were seen in LRRK2 loss of function mutants in contrast to other proteins directly involved in axonal transport. Surprisingly, fPD mutations in the GTPase (LRRK2-Y1699C) and WD40 (LRRK2-G2385R) domains suppressed axonal blocks compared to LRRK2-WT, while kinase-domain mutant G2019S enhanced them. Reducing kinesin-1 had no effect with LRRK2-WT, but increased axonal transport defects with LRRK2-G2385R suggesting a functional interaction between the LRRK2 WD40 domain and the anterograde transport machinery. Further, co-expression of α-syn with either the GTPase domain or WD40 domain LRRK2 fPD mutants significantly suppressed α-syn-mediated axonal transport defects, decreased stalled α-syn-vesicles, but did not alter α-syn-mediated neuronal cell death. Taken together, these results suggest that while LRRK2 itself may not play an independent role in axonal transport, its GTPase and WD40 domains likely associate functionally with α-syn during transport within axons.

primary.title: Tubulin autoregulation factors recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MTOCs for neuronal microtubule nucleation.
primary.abstract: Neuronal function and survival depend on stereotyped non-centrosomal microtubule (MT) arrays. How these arrays form remains poorly understood. Here, we found that two factors previously implicated in tubulin mRNA turnover control neuronal MT content through γ-tubulin-dependent nucleation. In C. elegans neurons, loss of scaper, ttc5, or both reduced MT numbers to a similar degree as depletion of γ-tubulin, the main MT nucleator. Using conditional single-cell degradation alleles and endogenous tagging, we find that scaper and ttc5 are required to recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MT organizing centers (MTOCs). SCAPER is also instructive, as its overexpression raises γ-tubulin levels at nucleation sites and increases MT density. SCAPER, TTC5, and γ-tubulin are dispensable for developmental axon growth but play essential roles during regeneration, where SCAPER recruits γ-tubulin to a growth-cone-localized MTOC to orient MT nucleation. Last, SCAPER is required for activity-dependent MT nucleation in rat hippocampal neurons, suggesting a conserved role. These findings reveal mechanisms governing neuronal cytoskeleton assembly and function and suggest potential crosstalk between tubulin autoregulation and MT nucleation.

primary.title: Tubulin polyglutamylation modulates Golgi morphodynamics and neurite branching during neuronal morphogenesis.
primary.abstract: Neurons establish functional networks through morphological remodeling during neuronal differentiation. Microtubule polyglutamylation is a key microtubule post-translational modification that is highly enriched during this process and plays an important role in differentiation. However, how remodeling of organelle features such as morphology, distribution and interactions depends on tubulin polyglutamylation during neuronal differentiation remains unclear. Here, we employed multispectral imaging combined with quantitative three-dimensional organelle analysis to comprehensively profile eight organelles simultaneously in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons. We discovered that depletion of tubulin polyglutamylation induces pronounced alterations in somatic Golgi morphology and associated organelle interactions. In addition, Golgi-derived compartments in proximal neurites exhibited altered morphology and dynamics, namely, decreased anterograde transport together with less efficient movement. These changes were accompanied by increased neurite branching and tortuosity. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for tubulin polyglutamylation in coordinating organelle organization with neurite architecture, providing a mechanistic link between tubulin post-translational modifications, Golgi morphology, dynamics and neuronal morphogenesis.

primary.title: The N-Ank protein Ankrd24 shapes neurons and couples to syndapin and the F-actin promoter Cobl-like.
primary.abstract: Proper neuromorphogenesis is pivotal for neuronal network formation and brain function. The underlying cell biological tasks are complex, as they include both remodeling of membrane topologies and of cytoskeletal structures. Yet, mechanisms coordinating these two different cell biological functions are largely unknown. Here, we molecularly and functionally characterize ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 24 (Ankrd24) and demonstrate that this ankyrin-repeat protein is able to interact with and bend membranes and mechanistically and functionally belongs to the recently proposed N-Ank superfamily. Mutational analyses revealed that the N-Ank functions of Ankrd24 are indispensable for Ankrd24's role in neuromorphogenesis. Ankrd24 furthermore physically cooperated with the F-BAR domain protein syndapin I (PACSIN1) and with Cobl-like (Cobll1), a protein promoting actin filament formation, by ternary complex formation. Both partners were critical for Ankrd24-mediated dendritic arborization. This identified Ankrd24 as critical part of a larger, coordinated effort in inducing new dendritic branches. Our work thereby sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying the complex task of proper neuronal arbor development.

primary.title: Tubulin autoregulation mediator TTC5 regulates neuronal morphology and migration.
primary.abstract: Microtubule dynamics are essential for neuronal development, yet how neurons regulate tubulin levels remains poorly understood. Tetratricopeptide repeat domain 5 (TTC5) mediates tubulin autoregulation, the co-translational degradation of tubulin transcripts in response to excess soluble tubulin, and TTC5 mutations cause cerebral atrophy with speech and motor impairment. Here, we show that tubulin autoregulation is active in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and depends on TTC5. TTC5 loss, or structure-guided mutations that disable autoregulation suppress microtubule polymerization, axonal outgrowth, and arborization, while enhancing cellular motility. Motility changes extend to non-neuronal cells, where they alter focal adhesion dynamics and can be rescued by manipulating soluble tubulin levels. Furthermore, downregulation of TTC5 interactor and autoregulation mediator S-phase cyclin A-associated protein in the endoplasmic reticulum (SCAPER) also suppresses neurite outgrowth and enhances motility. In vivo, TTC5 loss in mouse cortical projection neurons disrupts axon and dendrite arborization and causes hypermigration, recapitulating the cellular phenotypes observed in vitro. Patient-derived TTC5 disease mutants phenocopy this motility dysregulation, directly linking loss of TTC5 function to neurological deficits seen in patients. Together, these findings establish TTC5 as an essential regulator of neuronal morphogenesis and connectivity, with direct implications for TTC5-associated neurodevelopmental disease.

primary.title: Extracellular neuroligin-ICAM5 coupling drives dendritic growth via actin remodeling.
primary.abstract: Neuroligins (NLGNs) organize neuronal connectivity by engaging a diverse set of interaction partners, yet how extracellular recognition couples to intracellular growth programs remains unclear. Using affinity proteomics, we identify intercellular adhesion molecule-5 (ICAM5), a cell-surface protein localized to dendritic filopodia, as a NLGN interactor. Surface plasmon resonance and cell-based assays demonstrate direct binding between the ICAM5 and NLGN3 extracellular domains and reveal that ICAM5 engages all NLGN isoforms. In neurons, NLGN3 and ICAM5 preferentially colocalize at extrasynaptic, F-actin-positive dendritic sites, linking this interaction to regions of active cytoskeletal reorganization and growth. Accordingly, ICAM5 strongly enhances NLGN-induced dendritic outgrowth, but the NLGN3-ICAM5 complex does not detectably contribute to synaptogenesis. Mechanistically, ICAM5 sustains PAK-cofilin signaling and F-actin organization in growth cones, positioning it as a modulator linking NLGN engagement to actin remodeling. Together, these findings define a NLGN-ICAM5 axis that couples extracellular recognition to intracellular cytoskeletal remodeling to control neuronal structural development.

primary.title: Cofilin hyperphosphorylation triggers TDP-43 pathology in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
primary.abstract: Pathological forms of TAR-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), involving its aberrant mislocalization to the cytoplasm, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, are present in ∼45%-50% frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease individuals and most (97%) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Hence, identifying mechanisms that induce TDP-43 pathology are central to neurodegeneration and developing new therapeutic targets in these conditions. Cofilin is a multifunctional protein with a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Actin has important neuronal-specific activities in dendritic spines, axonal growth cones and synapses and it is in constant equilibrium between two forms: monomeric globular actin (G-actin) and polymeric filamentous actin (F-actin). Cofilin controls actin dynamics by depolymerizing and severing actin filaments. When cofilin is phosphorylated (at serine-3, Ser3) by LIM kinase1 (LIMK1), it becomes inactive, leading to production of more F-actin. Defects in cofilin are well described in other neurodegenerative disorders, unlike in ALS. We examined phosphorylation of cofilin and actin dynamics in post-mortem spinal cord tissue from sporadic ALS (SALS) patients, the TDP-43 rNLS8 transgenic mouse model and NSC-34 motor neuronal cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. F-actin was pharmacologically stabilized to mimic cofilin hyperphosphorylation and TDP-43 pathology was assessed. Neuronal cells were treated with a non-phosphorylatable cofilin S3A peptide (MAAGVAVSDGVIKVFN) and TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis were evaluated. Here, we show that cofilin is hyperphosphorylated in human ALS and disease models compared to controls. This was detected in spinal motor neurons from SALS patients and a TDP-43 mouse model (rNLS8) displaying key ALS phenotypes, and in motor neuronal NSC-34 cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. Supporting this observation, more F-actin relative to G-actin was present in cortical/spinal cord lysates from SALS patients and TDP-43 rNLS8 mice, and NSC-34 cells expressing TDP-43. We also show that mimicking cofilin hyperphosphorylation by pharmacological stabilization of F-actin induced TDP-43 pathology: cytoplasmic mislocalization, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, and promoted its recruitment into stress granules (SGs). Furthermore, we detected increased levels of LIMK1 phosphorylation and tropomyosin isoforms 4.1 and 4.2 in SALS patients. These findings reveal aberrant cofilin hyperphosphorylation disrupts actin dynamics, triggering TDP-43 pathology and SG recruitment in SALS. They imply that preventing cofilin phosphorylation is a novel therapeutic strategy applicable to most ALS cases. Treatment of neuronal cells with the S3A peptide prevented features of TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis compared to control peptides. These findings thus describe a novel pathogenic mechanism producing TDP-43 pathology, applicable to most ALS cases and other neurodegenerative diseases.

primary.title: The Path to Kinesin and Beyond.
primary.abstract: The recognition that the components of the axon and synapse originated in the neuronal cell body and were transported to their final destinations was recognized as early as Ramon y Cajal's pioneering studies on regeneration. However, mechanisms by which this transport was accomplished remained a mystery even as information accumulated about the rates and the composition of material being transported. The challenge was a lack of knowledge about molecular motors. In the early 1980's, advances in live cell imaging in combination with a novel model for study of vesicle transport in the axon led to the discovery of a new family of molecular motors, the kinesins.

primary.title: RBM42 couples alternative splicing to cytoskeletal organization to direct cortical development.
primary.abstract: Alternative splicing coordinates gene expression programs that shape the developing cerebral cortex. Here, we used nervous system-specific Rbm42 conditional knockout mice, RBM42-depleted human SH-SY5Y cells, RNA sequencing, RIP-seq, proteomics, and splice-switching rescue to define how the spliceosomal RNA-binding protein RBM42 supports cortical development. Rbm42 loss caused perinatal lethality, cortical thinning, defective lamination, reduced progenitor proliferation, increased apoptosis, and disrupted neuronal cytoskeletal organization. RBM42 bound and regulated cytoskeleton-associated transcripts, including NIN/Nin and NUMA1/Numa1, and its loss altered their splicing in human cells and mouse cortex. Restoring RBM42 corrected these splicing defects and improved proliferation and neurite growth. Selective correction of NIN exon 18 mis-splicing partially restored βIII-tubulin organization and proliferation but did not rescue apoptosis. These findings connect spliceosome-dependent isoform control with cytoskeletal remodeling during cortical development and provide a mechanistic framework for RBM42-associated neurodevelopmental disease.

primary.title: Cell adhesion molecule-related proteins signal to promote cytoneme elongation from Sonic Hedgehog-producing cells.
primary.abstract: Tissue morphogenesis and postdevelopmental homeostasis rely on efficient information exchange between communicating cells. Cytonemes are actin-based protrusions that contribute to precise information flow by facilitating contact-mediated directional transport of diverse signaling cargoes. How pathway-specific cytonemes are formed is poorly understood, as are the molecular mechanisms promoting actin organization for elongation and stability of the dynamic cellular extensions. We investigated biogenesis of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) cytonemes, revealing functional repurposing of cell adhesion molecule-related proteins Brother of CDON (BOC) and Cell adhesion molecule-related, Down-regulated by Oncogenes (CDON) into recruiters of actin regulators FARP1 and Cdc42 for cytoneme elongation. Loss of BOC and CDON function blunts protrusion-localized Cdc42 activity, reducing cytoneme lengths and occurrence in SHH-expressing cells. Live imaging of developing murine spinal cords reveals that CDON loss in SHH-expressing cells reduces the frequency of neuroepithelial cytonemes and alters neuronal cell fate specification. These results inform a model whereby SHH-binding proteins promote ligand transport through stimulating formation of long cytonemes.

primary.title: A chemomechanical bifurcation landscape unifies sustained growth, length homeostasis, and regenerative collapse in axons.
primary.abstract: Axonal growth machinery is largely shared across neurons, but axons exhibit strikingly different fates depending on developmental and environmental context: sustained elongation in peripheral neurons under permissive conditions, length homeostasis in cortical neurons after target innervation, and pathological collapse into dystrophic endbulbs in injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons. These divergent outcomes have resisted explanation by length-sensing and biomechanical models that treat long-range transport and local force generation as separate problems. We unify these phenomena through a mechanochemical model that couples bidirectional motor transport and intracellular signaling to growth-cone balance of axonal tension, actomyosin contraction, and adhesion within a single feedback loop: The lengthening axon uses its own growing transport delay to establish self-limiting mechanical feedback, as the accumulating delay reshapes signaling waveforms to progressively elevate myosin contractility against actin-driven protrusion. Two physical parameters, the transport delay and the signaling feedback strength, organize axon fate into a unified state-space landscape spanning sustained growth, length homeostasis, and pathological collapse. Reduced feedback strength weakens this self-limiting mechanical feedback by simultaneously enhancing protrusion and suppressing contractility, providing a mechanistic interpretation of axon lengthening under partial reduction of retrograde transport. Bistability in the inhibitory regime explains why mature CNS tracts persist where nascent sprouts collapse, recasting regenerative failure as a state-dependent gate rather than a capacity limit. The framework predicts that partial rather than complete inhibition of retrograde transport could shift collapsed axons across the bifurcation into a growth-permissive regime, identifying a class of interventions complementary to existing capacity-restoration strategies for nerve injury.

primary.title: Microglial Cofilin-1 Regulates Neuroinflammatory Responses and Behavioral Outcomes Following Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
primary.abstract: Cofilin-1, an actin-binding protein, modulates cytoskeletal dynamics and cellular motility. Although its role in conditional neuron knockout (KO) and neuronal injury has been well studied, the specific deletion of cofilin-1 in microglia and its role in neuroinflammation after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) remains unknown. This study aimed to characterize the effects of microglia-specific cofilin-1 deficiency on microglial morphology, homeostasis, behavioral phenotypes, and neurobehavioral and neuroinflammatory outcomes following ICH in male and female mice. A conditional KO mouse model was generated by crossing cofilinfl/fl (Flx) mice with CX3CR1-Cre drivers to achieve microglia-specific deletion. Baseline behavioral performance, microglial morphology, and homeostatic markers were evaluated in both sexes. ICH was then induced by intra-striatal collagenase injection, and neurobehavioral function, brain edema, hematoma volume, microglial activation, and peripheral immune responses were evaluated three days post-injury. Microglial deletion of cofilin-1 was associated with reduced TMEM119 expression, increased IBA1 immunoreactivity, and morphological transformation toward an activated phenotype. Female KO mice showed pronounced hyperlocomotion and decreased anxiety-like behavior, whereas both sexes exhibited impaired neuromuscular performance in the wire hang test. After ICH, KO mice had significantly larger hematoma volumes, enhanced microglial activation, and increased peripheral leukocyte counts compared with Flx controls. Notably, these changes were more severe in female KO mice, indicating a sex-dependent vulnerability. Our findings establish cofilin-1 as a key regulator of microglial homeostasis and immune balance within the brain. Deficiency of microglial cofilin-1 predisposes to worse secondary brain injury after ICH in a sex-dependent manner.

primary.title: Kinesin-3 KIF1A functions as a diligent worker and its functionality is regulated by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
primary.abstract: Long-distance intracellular transport is driven by motor proteins that walk along microtubule tracks. The fate of the motor protein after transport is unclear. Classically, motor proteins have been thought to function as Diligent Workers (DW) that remain attached to cargo during the entire transport event and are degraded at the end of the journey. In contrast, previous work suggests that kinesin-1 transport can be described by a Loose Bucket Brigade (LBB) model in which individual motor proteins participate in multiple rounds of transport. Here, we used live-cell imaging in iNeurons to test whether the kinesin-3 KIF1A functions as a DW during axonal transport. We demonstrate that the fluorescence intensity of KIF1A on particles undergoing axonal transport does not change over time, suggesting that KIF1A remains attached to its cargo for the entire transport event. We determined that KIF1A has a relatively short protein half-life, consistent with KIF1A being degraded at the end of the journey. Moreover, protein turnover appears to be tightly controlled in iNeurons, as treating cells with inhibitors of the ubiquitin/proteasome system results in a cessation of KIF1A-driven transport, the appearance of KIF1A aggregates in the cell body, and their subsequent degradation through aggrephagy. These results suggest that KIF1A transport fits the DW model and that KIF1A protein levels may play a role in signaling proteostatic stress in neuronal cells.

primary.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
primary.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

primary.title: Isozyme-Specific Inhibition of GSK-3 Reveals Distinct Cellular Responses in Huntington's Disease Fibroblasts.
primary.abstract: Inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) has been implicated in alleviating Huntington's disease (HD)-associated phenotypes. However, the mechanisms linking GSK-3 to HD pathogenesis, and particularly the distinct roles of GSK-3 isozymes in regulating HD-associated cellular dysfunction, remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the cellular responses of patient-derived HD fibroblasts to selective inhibition of GSK-3α or GSK-3β using isozyme-specific inhibitors, focusing on metabolic and bioenergetic pathways. Although inhibition of either isozyme suppressed mTORC1 signaling, selective GSK-3β inhibition elicited broader cellular responses, including altered oxidative stress signaling, increased expression of proteins associated with mitochondrial fission, enhanced lysosomal activity, and mitophagy, together with lysosomal redistribution and increased α-tubulin acetylation, suggesting improved microtubule-dependent intracellular trafficking. Quantitative proteomic analysis of four independent patient-derived HD fibroblasts corroborated these findings: GSK-3β inhibition elicited a broad set of proteins involved in cytoskeletal organization, adhesion signaling, and metabolic adaptation, whereas GSK-3α inhibition produced a more restricted and heterogeneous response. Collectively, these findings identify distinct cellular responses to selective GSK-3 isozyme inhibition and reveal GSK-3β as a predominant regulator of intracellular trafficking and mitochondrial and cytoskeletal dynamics in HD fibroblasts. Thus, inhibition of GSK-3β may represent a potential therapeutic approach for modulating HD-associated cellular dysfunction.

primary.title: APC regulates NSLIT2-induced internalization and signaling of the chemorepellent receptor, ROBO1.
primary.abstract: The SLIT-Roundabout signaling pathway regulates axon guidance and cell migration, and ROBO1 is a receptor for SLIT ligands. ROBO1 undergoes constitutive endocytosis, which is enhanced upon NSLIT2 binding, but the molecular mechanisms and functional consequences of this process are not well understood. Using pharmacologic inhibitors and molecular techniques, we found that clathrin-mediated endocytosis is necessary for NSLIT2-induced inhibition of cell spreading. To explore the underlying mechanisms, we performed proximity-dependent biotin identification to identify ROBO1-interacting proteins whose association with the cytoplasmic domain of ROBO1 is differentially regulated by NSLIT2. We discovered that adenomatous polyposis coli, a multifunctional tumor suppressor, is in close proximity to ROBO1 but dissociates upon binding of NSLIT2 and that this dissociation is necessary for clathrin-mediated endocytosis of ROBO1 and subsequent effects on cell morphology. These findings provide new insights into the functional mechanisms by which NSLIT2 binding to ROBO1 affects changes in actin cytoskeletal architecture.

primary.title: Cross-species molecular mapping of the photoreceptor sensory cilium and periciliary structures identifies conserved and species-specific architectural features.
primary.abstract: Photoreceptor sensory cilia comprise a microtubule-based structural core and the phototransductive outer segment. The microtubule-based ciliary axoneme extends from the basal body through the connecting cilium into the outer segment, thereby linking the inner and outer segments. Around this central axis, specialized periciliary structures are distributed across the apical inner segment and basal outer segment. Yet how these ciliary and periciliary structures differ between rods and cones and across mammals remains incompletely defined. Using ultrastructure expansion microscopy, we compared their nanoscale molecular organization across canine, non-human primate and human retinas. Key rod-cone differences in ciliary organization were broadly conserved among all three species, whereas the scale and morphology of individual ciliary subcompartments differed between species. Periciliary structures showed even greater species-specific diversification, particularly in rods. Human photoreceptors shared several structural features with non-human primate photoreceptors but also displayed inter-individual variability in accessory inner segment-like structure. These findings refine current understanding of photoreceptor sensory cilia and associated periciliary structures in large mammals, revealing that conserved rod-cone differences co-exist with pronounced species-specific structural and molecular specializations.

primary.title: The postsynaptic scaffold protein ABLIM1 regulates seizure susceptibility by maintaining GluA2 membrane localization in chronic epilepsy.
primary.abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), the most common form of drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) in adults, is a frequent chronic neurological disorder. Nevertheless, the precise pathophysiological mechanisms underlying TLE remain largely undefined. Our findings demonstrate that Actin-binding LIM protein 1 (ABLIM1) is broadly expressed in the adult mouse brain, with high expression in the hippocampus. The protein is primarily localized to neurons, enriched in the postsynaptic density (PSD), colocalizes with the scaffold protein PSD95, and directly binds to F-actin. Co-IP experiments confirmed that ABLIM1 interacts with the α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) subunits GluA1 and GluA2. Following hippocampal stereotaxic injection of adeno-associated virus (AAV) to specifically knock down ABLIM1 expression, we observed reduced F-actin polymerization, decreased dendritic spine density, and thinning of the PSD in the mouse hippocampus. In the chronic epilepsy models induced by kainic acid (KA), ABLIM1 knockdown significantly exacerbated seizure severity and increased seizure susceptibility. Further mechanistic studies revealed that ABLIM1 knockdown specifically reduces membrane expression of GluA2 without altering its total protein levels. Collectively, ABLIM1 may regulate epileptogenesis and disease progression by maintaining postsynaptic structural integrity and GluA2 membrane homeostasis. Thus, the ABLIM1-GluA2 signaling axis represents a potential therapeutic target for DRE.

primary.title: Pathogenic KIF1A variants differentially disrupt axonal trafficking and impede synaptic development.
primary.abstract: The nervous system relies on billions of neurons connected through trillions of synapses to support vital functions. Despite the importance of this synaptic network, cellular mechanisms dictating synapse formation during human neurodevelopment remain unclear. Long-distance trafficking by the microtubule motor KIF1A is crucial for synaptogenesis and downstream synapse maintenance. Mutations in KIF1A cause KIF1A-associated neurological disorder (KAND). We employed isogenic gene-edited human-induced pluripotent stem cell -derived neurons to assess the effects of disparate pathogenic mutations in KIF1A on synaptic trafficking and function. Null (p.C92*) and hypoactive (p.P305L) mutations delay neurite outgrowth, mislocalize synaptic cargoes, and decrease synapse density. Conversely, a hyperactive (p.R350G) mutation supports neurite outgrowth but causes aberrant motility of synaptic vesicle precursors and deficits in microtubule-dependent presynaptic patterning. Functional analysis of neuronal activity reveals delayed synaptic maturation in loss-of-function mutations (p.P305L, p.C92*) and precocious activity in the hyperactive p.R350G mutation. These data provide insights into how KIF1A mutations with distinct molecular-level impacts lead to significant downstream synaptic deficits in human neurons.

primary.title: EGR1 mediates neuronal damage via suppressing HIF1A-induced mitophagy following traumatic brain injury.
primary.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a leading cause of neurological morbidity and mortality, characterized by complex pathophysiological cascades. Here, we investigate the role of the transcription factor EGR1 (early growth response 1) in modulating mitochondrial homeostasis via the HIF1A (hypoxia inducible factor 1, alpha subunit)-BNIP3 (BCL2/adenovirus E1B interacting protein 3) axis following TBI. Using integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic analyses, we identified EGR1 as a critical regulator of TBI pathology, with its expression acutely upregulated in neurons post-injury. Genetic ablation of Egr1 in mice significantly reduced neuronal apoptosis, preserved dendritic integrity, and ameliorated cognitive and sensorimotor deficits. Mechanistically, chromatin immunoprecipitation and luciferase assays revealed that EGR1 directly binds to the Hif1a promoter, repressing its transcription. Loss of EGR1 enhanced HIF1A-BNIP3-mediated mitophagy, reducing mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress both in vitro and in vivo. Conversely, silencing HIF1A or BNIP3 abrogated the neuroprotective effects of EGR1 deficiency. secondary.title: Caltubin regulates microtubule stability through tubulin interaction favouring neurite regrowth.
secondary.abstract: Microtubule regulation is highly controlled in nerve regeneration. Caltubin, a novel Lymnaea stagnalis protein, contains putative EF-hand calcium-binding motifs and promotes neuronal outgrowth in Lymnaea and mouse. Here, we generated cell-permeable caltubin proteins to investigate mechanisms underlying this effect. We observed increased neurite extension and regrowth following acute neurite injury in CaT-Tat-treated embryonic mouse cortical neurons compared to vehicle controls. Purified caltubin bound the L391-V405 region of α-tubulin, promoting microtubule assembly. Caltubin reduced the association of tubulin tyrosine ligase with tubulin, which catalyzes tubulin retyrosination, and increased the ratio of detyrosinated to tyrosinated tubulin. Crystal structure analysis confirmed that caltubin has a calmodulin-like fold with four EF-hand motifs which also coordinate Sr2+. These findings identify caltubin as a direct modulator of tubulin assembly and tubulin tyrosination state. While this may represent an essential mechanism of axonal regulation, the present functional assays were performed in embryonic neuronal cultures and do not directly test calcium dependence or in vivo regeneration, and future studies should evaluate CaT-Tat in mature neuronal and in vivo injury models.

secondary.title: Postsynaptic remodeling and F-actin dysregulation in the Dctn1Δ2-4 mouse model of motor neuron disease.
secondary.abstract: The microtubule motor dynein and its co-adaptor dynactin govern organelle positioning within highly polarized neurons. The dynactin subunit p150Glued, encoded by DCTN1, is associated with motor neuron disease. The p150Glued G59S mutation disrupts the microtubule-binding domain and drives selective motor neuron degeneration in patients and animal models. The p150Glued microtubule-binding domain mediates the initiation of retrograde transport at axonal terminals and stabilizes presynaptic sites at neuromuscular junctions. Nevertheless, the key functions of p150Glued and its microtubule-binding domain within postsynaptic compartments remain poorly defined. Using Dctn1Δ2-4 mice, in which exons 2-4 of Dctn1 encoding the microtubule-binding domain are deleted, we performed morphological, biochemical, and cellular physiological analyses, together with genetic manipulation and pharmacological intervention, to investigate how loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function affects excitatory postsynaptic organization and neuronal vulnerability. We found that excitatory postsynaptic remodeling occurred before overt dendritic degeneration and motor neuron loss in Dctn1Δ2-4 mice. We further demonstrated that p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction induced early remodeling of excitatory postsynaptic densities, leading to increased postsynaptic accumulation of N-methyl- D-aspartate receptors, dysregulated Ca2+ homeostasis, and heightened susceptibility to glutamate-induced excitotoxicity. Mechanistically, p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction promoted the postsynaptic accumulation of endosomes and the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog complex, resulting in excessive F-actin assembly and pathological enhancement of postsynaptic density architecture. Furthermore, these postsynaptic abnormalities were rescued by re-expression of wild-type p150Glued, but not the disease-associated G59S mutant. Pharmacological inhibition of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, in turn, attenuated excitotoxic injury and neurodegeneration. Our findings identify a previously unrecognized postsynaptic pathogenic mechanism in DCTN1-associated motor neuron disease. We propose that loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function disrupts postsynaptic endosome positioning, leading to aberrant Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog-mediated F-actin remodeling, pathological enhancement of excitatory postsynaptic densities, excessive N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor targeting, and increased vulnerability to excitotoxicity.

secondary.title: Microtubule-associated protein 1S phosphorylation regulates dynein-driven transport and synaptogenesis in neurons.
secondary.abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase like 5 (CDKL5) is a serine-threonine kinase enriched in the mammalian brain whose loss of function causes a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy named CDKL5 Deficiency Disorder. We previously showed that CDKL5 phosphorylates the microtubule-associated protein MAP1S, but how this regulates microtubule-dependent functions is not well understood. To address this question, we generated MAP1S phosphomutant mice in which the CDKL5 phosphorylation sites S786 and S812 were mutated to alanine (MAP1S S786/812A; MAP1S SA). Using a microtubule cosedimentation assay, we found that dynein binding to microtubules was reduced in MAP1S SA and CDKL5 knockout (KO) brain lysates, and time-lapse imaging showed impaired dynein motility in dendrites from both genotypes. MAP1S SA mice also exhibited reduced AMPA receptor transport, dendritic spine density, and excitatory synapses, accompanied by anxiety-like behavior and motor, social, and memory deficits relevant to CDD. Mechanistically, MAP1S SA and CDKL5 KO neurons showed increased microtubule stability and reduced tubulin tyrosination, consistent with excessive MAP1S-mediated stabilization. Restoring tubulin tyrosination by expressing tubulin-tyrosine ligase rescued dynein transport defects. Together, these findings identify MAP1S phosphorylation as a critical regulator of microtubule dynamics and dynein-dependent transport.

secondary.title: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6)-mediated α-tubulin (K40) deacetylation and microtubule destabilization disrupt autophagosome-lysosome fusion in PBDE-47-induced neurotoxicity.
secondary.abstract: 2,2',4,4'-tetrabromodiphenyl ether (PBDE-47) is a pervasive environmental brominated flame retardant that accumulates in nervous tissues and induces persistent neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates that PBDE-47 perturbs neuronal autophagy, yet the definitive upstream molecular mechanism remains uncharacterized, hindering the development of effective protective strategies. This study was performed to clarify the toxic regulatory cascade and explore feasible pharmacological interventions using in vivo neonatal rat hippocampal tissue and in vitro PC12 neuronal cell models. Animals were neonatally exposed to PBDE-47 (0.1, 1.0, 10.0 mg/kg·bw), and PC12 cells were treated with PBDE-47 (1, 10, 20 µM) for mechanistic exploration. Results showed that PBDE-47 dose-dependently upregulated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), decreased α-tubulin (K40) acetylation, and destabilized neuronal microtubules. Such microtubule structural damage impaired autophagosome retrograde trafficking, blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and eventually caused neuronal loss, synaptic protein reduction, and cognitive impairment. For mechanism validation and rescue experiments, 1 mg/kg·bw paclitaxel (PTX) and 1 mg/kg·bw tubastatin A (TBA) were administered to neonatal rats, whereas 12.5 nmol/L PTX and 10 µmol/L TBA were used for PC12 cell treatment to stabilize microtubules and selectively inhibit HDAC6, respectively. Both pharmacological interventions effectively restored tubulin acetylation, rescued defective autophagic flux, and mitigated PBDE-47-induced neuronal injury, with TBA showing better applicability due to its high blood-brain barrier permeability and biosafety. Behavioral tests in vivo verified that PTX and TBA treatment significantly ameliorated PBDE-47-elicited learning and memory deficits. Collectively, these findings define the HDAC6/microtubule acetylation axis as a core upstream pathway responsible for PBDE-47-triggered autophagic transport failure and neurotoxicity, providing robust experimental evidence and a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of PBDEs-mediated neurological disorders.

secondary.title: Elevation of the mechanically-sensitive e protein emerin links nuclear mechanotransduction to tau-induced cytoskeletal remodeling in neurons.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease, are neuropathologically defined by pathological tau deposition. While tau drives neurotoxicity by disrupting cytoskeletal, nucleoskeletal, and genomic architecture, cellular mechanisms mediating tau-induced dysfunction of the cytoskeleton and nucleoskeleton are incompletely understood. Here, we identify proteins with differing abundance in a cellular tauopathy model, iTau. Building upon previous findings that pathogenic tau reduces nuclear tension, we find elevated levels of emerin, a central regulator of nuclear mechanotransduction, in iTau neurons and tau mutant iPSC-derived neurons. Neuronal emerin overexpression drives neurotoxicity, increases filamentous actin (F-actin), and induces nuclear invagination, mimicking cellular phenotypes of tauopathy. Alterations in emerin binding partners reflect its cytosolic relocalization in iTau neurons, suggesting that pathogenic tau may impact nuclear mechanotransduction by altering emerin levels and localization. Overall, we identify emerin as a potential mediator of cytoskeletal and nucleoskeletal remodeling in tauopathy and provide a foundation for future studies of emerin function in neurons.

best.title: Tubulin autoregulation factors recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MTOCs for neuronal microtubule nucleation.
best.abstract: Neuronal function and survival depend on stereotyped non-centrosomal microtubule (MT) arrays. How these arrays form remains poorly understood. Here, we found that two factors previously implicated in tubulin mRNA turnover control neuronal MT content through γ-tubulin-dependent nucleation. In C. elegans neurons, loss of scaper, ttc5, or both reduced MT numbers to a similar degree as depletion of γ-tubulin, the main MT nucleator. Using conditional single-cell degradation alleles and endogenous tagging, we find that scaper and ttc5 are required to recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MT organizing centers (MTOCs). SCAPER is also instructive, as its overexpression raises γ-tubulin levels at nucleation sites and increases MT density. SCAPER, TTC5, and γ-tubulin are dispensable for developmental axon growth but play essential roles during regeneration, where SCAPER recruits γ-tubulin to a growth-cone-localized MTOC to orient MT nucleation. Last, SCAPER is required for activity-dependent MT nucleation in rat hippocampal neurons, suggesting a conserved role. These findings reveal mechanisms governing neuronal cytoskeleton assembly and function and suggest potential crosstalk between tubulin autoregulation and MT nucleation.

best.title: Tubulin polyglutamylation modulates Golgi morphodynamics and neurite branching during neuronal morphogenesis.
best.abstract: Neurons establish functional networks through morphological remodeling during neuronal differentiation. Microtubule polyglutamylation is a key microtubule post-translational modification that is highly enriched during this process and plays an important role in differentiation. However, how remodeling of organelle features such as morphology, distribution and interactions depends on tubulin polyglutamylation during neuronal differentiation remains unclear. Here, we employed multispectral imaging combined with quantitative three-dimensional organelle analysis to comprehensively profile eight organelles simultaneously in human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons. We discovered that depletion of tubulin polyglutamylation induces pronounced alterations in somatic Golgi morphology and associated organelle interactions. In addition, Golgi-derived compartments in proximal neurites exhibited altered morphology and dynamics, namely, decreased anterograde transport together with less efficient movement. These changes were accompanied by increased neurite branching and tortuosity. Together, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role for tubulin polyglutamylation in coordinating organelle organization with neurite architecture, providing a mechanistic link between tubulin post-translational modifications, Golgi morphology, dynamics and neuronal morphogenesis.

best.title: The N-Ank protein Ankrd24 shapes neurons and couples to syndapin and the F-actin promoter Cobl-like.
best.abstract: Proper neuromorphogenesis is pivotal for neuronal network formation and brain function. The underlying cell biological tasks are complex, as they include both remodeling of membrane topologies and of cytoskeletal structures. Yet, mechanisms coordinating these two different cell biological functions are largely unknown. Here, we molecularly and functionally characterize ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 24 (Ankrd24) and demonstrate that this ankyrin-repeat protein is able to interact with and bend membranes and mechanistically and functionally belongs to the recently proposed N-Ank superfamily. Mutational analyses revealed that the N-Ank functions of Ankrd24 are indispensable for Ankrd24's role in neuromorphogenesis. Ankrd24 furthermore physically cooperated with the F-BAR domain protein syndapin I (PACSIN1) and with Cobl-like (Cobll1), a protein promoting actin filament formation, by ternary complex formation. Both partners were critical for Ankrd24-mediated dendritic arborization. This identified Ankrd24 as critical part of a larger, coordinated effort in inducing new dendritic branches. Our work thereby sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying the complex task of proper neuronal arbor development.

best.title: Tubulin autoregulation mediator TTC5 regulates neuronal morphology and migration.
best.abstract: Microtubule dynamics are essential for neuronal development, yet how neurons regulate tubulin levels remains poorly understood. Tetratricopeptide repeat domain 5 (TTC5) mediates tubulin autoregulation, the co-translational degradation of tubulin transcripts in response to excess soluble tubulin, and TTC5 mutations cause cerebral atrophy with speech and motor impairment. Here, we show that tubulin autoregulation is active in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and depends on TTC5. TTC5 loss, or structure-guided mutations that disable autoregulation suppress microtubule polymerization, axonal outgrowth, and arborization, while enhancing cellular motility. Motility changes extend to non-neuronal cells, where they alter focal adhesion dynamics and can be rescued by manipulating soluble tubulin levels. Furthermore, downregulation of TTC5 interactor and autoregulation mediator S-phase cyclin A-associated protein in the endoplasmic reticulum (SCAPER) also suppresses neurite outgrowth and enhances motility. In vivo, TTC5 loss in mouse cortical projection neurons disrupts axon and dendrite arborization and causes hypermigration, recapitulating the cellular phenotypes observed in vitro. Patient-derived TTC5 disease mutants phenocopy this motility dysregulation, directly linking loss of TTC5 function to neurological deficits seen in patients. Together, these findings establish TTC5 as an essential regulator of neuronal morphogenesis and connectivity, with direct implications for TTC5-associated neurodevelopmental disease.

These findings identify caltubin as a direct modulator of tubulin assembly and tubulin tyrosination state. best.title: Extracellular neuroligin-ICAM5 coupling drives dendritic growth via actin remodeling.
best.abstract: Neuroligins (NLGNs) organize neuronal connectivity by engaging a diverse set of interaction partners, yet how extracellular recognition couples to intracellular growth programs remains unclear. Using affinity proteomics, we identify intercellular adhesion molecule-5 (ICAM5), a cell-surface protein localized to dendritic filopodia, as a NLGN interactor. Surface plasmon resonance and cell-based assays demonstrate direct binding between the ICAM5 and NLGN3 extracellular domains and reveal that ICAM5 engages all NLGN isoforms. In neurons, NLGN3 and ICAM5 preferentially colocalize at extrasynaptic, F-actin-positive dendritic sites, linking this interaction to regions of active cytoskeletal reorganization and growth. Accordingly, ICAM5 strongly enhances NLGN-induced dendritic outgrowth, but the NLGN3-ICAM5 complex does not detectably contribute to synaptogenesis. Mechanistically, ICAM5 sustains PAK-cofilin signaling and F-actin organization in growth cones, positioning it as a modulator linking NLGN engagement to actin remodeling. Together, these findings define a NLGN-ICAM5 axis that couples extracellular recognition to intracellular cytoskeletal remodeling to control neuronal structural development.

best.title: Cofilin hyperphosphorylation triggers TDP-43 pathology in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
best.abstract: Pathological forms of TAR-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), involving its aberrant mislocalization to the cytoplasm, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, are present in ∼45%-50% frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease individuals and most (97%) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Hence, identifying mechanisms that induce TDP-43 pathology are central to neurodegeneration and developing new therapeutic targets in these conditions. Cofilin is a multifunctional protein with a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Actin has important neuronal-specific activities in dendritic spines, axonal growth cones and synapses and it is in constant equilibrium between two forms: monomeric globular actin (G-actin) and polymeric filamentous actin (F-actin). Cofilin controls actin dynamics by depolymerizing and severing actin filaments. When cofilin is phosphorylated (at serine-3, Ser3) by LIM kinase1 (LIMK1), it becomes inactive, leading to production of more F-actin. Defects in cofilin are well described in other neurodegenerative disorders, unlike in ALS. We examined phosphorylation of cofilin and actin dynamics in post-mortem spinal cord tissue from sporadic ALS (SALS) patients, the TDP-43 rNLS8 transgenic mouse model and NSC-34 motor neuronal cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. F-actin was pharmacologically stabilized to mimic cofilin hyperphosphorylation and TDP-43 pathology was assessed. Neuronal cells were treated with a non-phosphorylatable cofilin S3A peptide (MAAGVAVSDGVIKVFN) and TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis were evaluated. Here, we show that cofilin is hyperphosphorylated in human ALS and disease models compared to controls. This was detected in spinal motor neurons from SALS patients and a TDP-43 mouse model (rNLS8) displaying key ALS phenotypes, and in motor neuronal NSC-34 cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. Supporting this observation, more F-actin relative to G-actin was present in cortical/spinal cord lysates from SALS patients and TDP-43 rNLS8 mice, and NSC-34 cells expressing TDP-43. We also show that mimicking cofilin hyperphosphorylation by pharmacological stabilization of F-actin induced TDP-43 pathology: cytoplasmic mislocalization, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, and promoted its recruitment into stress granules (SGs). Furthermore, we detected increased levels of LIMK1 phosphorylation and tropomyosin isoforms 4.1 and 4.2 in SALS patients. These findings reveal aberrant cofilin hyperphosphorylation disrupts actin dynamics, triggering TDP-43 pathology and SG recruitment in SALS. They imply that preventing cofilin phosphorylation is a novel therapeutic strategy applicable to most ALS cases. Treatment of neuronal cells with the S3A peptide prevented features of TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis compared to control peptides. These findings thus describe a novel pathogenic mechanism producing TDP-43 pathology, applicable to most ALS cases and other neurodegenerative diseases.

best.title: The Path to Kinesin and Beyond.
best.abstract: The recognition that the components of the axon and synapse originated in the neuronal cell body and were transported to their final destinations was recognized as early as Ramon y Cajal's pioneering studies on regeneration. However, mechanisms by which this transport was accomplished remained a mystery even as information accumulated about the rates and the composition of material being transported. The challenge was a lack of knowledge about molecular motors. In the early 1980's, advances in live cell imaging in combination with a novel model for study of vesicle transport in the axon led to the discovery of a new family of molecular motors, the kinesins.

best.title: RBM42 couples alternative splicing to cytoskeletal organization to direct cortical development.
best.abstract: Alternative splicing coordinates gene expression programs that shape the developing cerebral cortex. Here, we used nervous system-specific Rbm42 conditional knockout mice, RBM42-depleted human SH-SY5Y cells, RNA sequencing, RIP-seq, proteomics, and splice-switching rescue to define how the spliceosomal RNA-binding protein RBM42 supports cortical development. Rbm42 loss caused perinatal lethality, cortical thinning, defective lamination, reduced progenitor proliferation, increased apoptosis, and disrupted neuronal cytoskeletal organization. RBM42 bound and regulated cytoskeleton-associated transcripts, including NIN/Nin and NUMA1/Numa1, and its loss altered their splicing in human cells and mouse cortex. Restoring RBM42 corrected these splicing defects and improved proliferation and neurite growth. Selective correction of NIN exon 18 mis-splicing partially restored βIII-tubulin organization and proliferation but did not rescue apoptosis. These findings connect spliceosome-dependent isoform control with cytoskeletal remodeling during cortical development and provide a mechanistic framework for RBM42-associated neurodevelopmental disease.

best.title: Cell adhesion molecule-related proteins signal to promote cytoneme elongation from Sonic Hedgehog-producing cells.
best.abstract: Tissue morphogenesis and postdevelopmental homeostasis rely on efficient information exchange between communicating cells. Cytonemes are actin-based protrusions that contribute to precise information flow by facilitating contact-mediated directional transport of diverse signaling cargoes. How pathway-specific cytonemes are formed is poorly understood, as are the molecular mechanisms promoting actin organization for elongation and stability of the dynamic cellular extensions. We investigated biogenesis of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) cytonemes, revealing functional repurposing of cell adhesion molecule-related proteins Brother of CDON (BOC) and Cell adhesion molecule-related, Down-regulated by Oncogenes (CDON) into recruiters of actin regulators FARP1 and Cdc42 for cytoneme elongation. Loss of BOC and CDON function blunts protrusion-localized Cdc42 activity, reducing cytoneme lengths and occurrence in SHH-expressing cells. Live imaging of developing murine spinal cords reveals that CDON loss in SHH-expressing cells reduces the frequency of neuroepithelial cytonemes and alters neuronal cell fate specification. These results inform a model whereby SHH-binding proteins promote ligand transport through stimulating formation of long cytonemes.

best.title: A chemomechanical bifurcation landscape unifies sustained growth, length homeostasis, and regenerative collapse in axons.
best.abstract: Axonal growth machinery is largely shared across neurons, but axons exhibit strikingly different fates depending on developmental and environmental context: sustained elongation in peripheral neurons under permissive conditions, length homeostasis in cortical neurons after target innervation, and pathological collapse into dystrophic endbulbs in injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons. These divergent outcomes have resisted explanation by length-sensing and biomechanical models that treat long-range transport and local force generation as separate problems. We unify these phenomena through a mechanochemical model that couples bidirectional motor transport and intracellular signaling to growth-cone balance of axonal tension, actomyosin contraction, and adhesion within a single feedback loop: The lengthening axon uses its own growing transport delay to establish self-limiting mechanical feedback, as the accumulating delay reshapes signaling waveforms to progressively elevate myosin contractility against actin-driven protrusion. Two physical parameters, the transport delay and the signaling feedback strength, organize axon fate into a unified state-space landscape spanning sustained growth, length homeostasis, and pathological collapse. Reduced feedback strength weakens this self-limiting mechanical feedback by simultaneously enhancing protrusion and suppressing contractility, providing a mechanistic interpretation of axon lengthening under partial reduction of retrograde transport. Bistability in the inhibitory regime explains why mature CNS tracts persist where nascent sprouts collapse, recasting regenerative failure as a state-dependent gate rather than a capacity limit. The framework predicts that partial rather than complete inhibition of retrograde transport could shift collapsed axons across the bifurcation into a growth-permissive regime, identifying a class of interventions complementary to existing capacity-restoration strategies for nerve injury.

best.title: Microglial Cofilin-1 Regulates Neuroinflammatory Responses and Behavioral Outcomes Following Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
best.abstract: Cofilin-1, an actin-binding protein, modulates cytoskeletal dynamics and cellular motility. Although its role in conditional neuron knockout (KO) and neuronal injury has been well studied, the specific deletion of cofilin-1 in microglia and its role in neuroinflammation after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) remains unknown. This study aimed to characterize the effects of microglia-specific cofilin-1 deficiency on microglial morphology, homeostasis, behavioral phenotypes, and neurobehavioral and neuroinflammatory outcomes following ICH in male and female mice. A conditional KO mouse model was generated by crossing cofilinfl/fl (Flx) mice with CX3CR1-Cre drivers to achieve microglia-specific deletion. Baseline behavioral performance, microglial morphology, and homeostatic markers were evaluated in both sexes. ICH was then induced by intra-striatal collagenase injection, and neurobehavioral function, brain edema, hematoma volume, microglial activation, and peripheral immune responses were evaluated three days post-injury. Microglial deletion of cofilin-1 was associated with reduced TMEM119 expression, increased IBA1 immunoreactivity, and morphological transformation toward an activated phenotype. Female KO mice showed pronounced hyperlocomotion and decreased anxiety-like behavior, whereas both sexes exhibited impaired neuromuscular performance in the wire hang test. After ICH, KO mice had significantly larger hematoma volumes, enhanced microglial activation, and increased peripheral leukocyte counts compared with Flx controls. Notably, these changes were more severe in female KO mice, indicating a sex-dependent vulnerability. Our findings establish cofilin-1 as a key regulator of microglial homeostasis and immune balance within the brain. Deficiency of microglial cofilin-1 predisposes to worse secondary brain injury after ICH in a sex-dependent manner.

best.title: Postsynaptic remodeling and F-actin dysregulation in the Dctn1Δ2-4 mouse model of motor neuron disease.
best.abstract: The microtubule motor dynein and its co-adaptor dynactin govern organelle positioning within highly polarized neurons. The dynactin subunit p150Glued, encoded by DCTN1, is associated with motor neuron disease. The p150Glued G59S mutation disrupts the microtubule-binding domain and drives selective motor neuron degeneration in patients and animal models. The p150Glued microtubule-binding domain mediates the initiation of retrograde transport at axonal terminals and stabilizes presynaptic sites at neuromuscular junctions. Nevertheless, the key functions of p150Glued and its microtubule-binding domain within postsynaptic compartments remain poorly defined. Using Dctn1Δ2-4 mice, in which exons 2-4 of Dctn1 encoding the microtubule-binding domain are deleted, we performed morphological, biochemical, and cellular physiological analyses, together with genetic manipulation and pharmacological intervention, to investigate how loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function affects excitatory postsynaptic organization and neuronal vulnerability. We found that excitatory postsynaptic remodeling occurred before overt dendritic degeneration and motor neuron loss in Dctn1Δ2-4 mice. We further demonstrated that p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction induced early remodeling of excitatory postsynaptic densities, leading to increased postsynaptic accumulation of N-methyl- D-aspartate receptors, dysregulated Ca2+ homeostasis, and heightened susceptibility to glutamate-induced excitotoxicity. Mechanistically, p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction promoted the postsynaptic accumulation of endosomes and the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog complex, resulting in excessive F-actin assembly and pathological enhancement of postsynaptic density architecture. Furthermore, these postsynaptic abnormalities were rescued by re-expression of wild-type p150Glued, but not the disease-associated G59S mutant. Pharmacological inhibition of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, in turn, attenuated excitotoxic injury and neurodegeneration. Our findings identify a previously unrecognized postsynaptic pathogenic mechanism in DCTN1-associated motor neuron disease. We propose that loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function disrupts postsynaptic endosome positioning, leading to aberrant Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog-mediated F-actin remodeling, pathological enhancement of excitatory postsynaptic densities, excessive N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor targeting, and increased vulnerability to excitotoxicity.

best.title: Kinesin-3 KIF1A functions as a diligent worker and its functionality is regulated by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
best.abstract: Long-distance intracellular transport is driven by motor proteins that walk along microtubule tracks. The fate of the motor protein after transport is unclear. Classically, motor proteins have been thought to function as Diligent Workers (DW) that remain attached to cargo during the entire transport event and are degraded at the end of the journey. In contrast, previous work suggests that kinesin-1 transport can be described by a Loose Bucket Brigade (LBB) model in which individual motor proteins participate in multiple rounds of transport. Here, we used live-cell imaging in iNeurons to test whether the kinesin-3 KIF1A functions as a DW during axonal transport. We demonstrate that the fluorescence intensity of KIF1A on particles undergoing axonal transport does not change over time, suggesting that KIF1A remains attached to its cargo for the entire transport event. We determined that KIF1A has a relatively short protein half-life, consistent with KIF1A being degraded at the end of the journey. Moreover, protein turnover appears to be tightly controlled in iNeurons, as treating cells with inhibitors of the ubiquitin/proteasome system results in a cessation of KIF1A-driven transport, the appearance of KIF1A aggregates in the cell body, and their subsequent degradation through aggrephagy. These results suggest that KIF1A transport fits the DW model and that KIF1A protein levels may play a role in signaling proteostatic stress in neuronal cells.

best.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
best.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

best.title: Isozyme-Specific Inhibition of GSK-3 Reveals Distinct Cellular Responses in Huntington's Disease Fibroblasts.
best.abstract: Inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) has been implicated in alleviating Huntington's disease (HD)-associated phenotypes. However, the mechanisms linking GSK-3 to HD pathogenesis, and particularly the distinct roles of GSK-3 isozymes in regulating HD-associated cellular dysfunction, remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the cellular responses of patient-derived HD fibroblasts to selective inhibition of GSK-3α or GSK-3β using isozyme-specific inhibitors, focusing on metabolic and bioenergetic pathways. Although inhibition of either isozyme suppressed mTORC1 signaling, selective GSK-3β inhibition elicited broader cellular responses, including altered oxidative stress signaling, increased expression of proteins associated with mitochondrial fission, enhanced lysosomal activity, and mitophagy, together with lysosomal redistribution and increased α-tubulin acetylation, suggesting improved microtubule-dependent intracellular trafficking. Quantitative proteomic analysis of four independent patient-derived HD fibroblasts corroborated these findings: GSK-3β inhibition elicited a broad set of proteins involved in cytoskeletal organization, adhesion signaling, and metabolic adaptation, whereas GSK-3α inhibition produced a more restricted and heterogeneous response. Collectively, these findings identify distinct cellular responses to selective GSK-3 isozyme inhibition and reveal GSK-3β as a predominant regulator of intracellular trafficking and mitochondrial and cytoskeletal dynamics in HD fibroblasts. Thus, inhibition of GSK-3β may represent a potential therapeutic approach for modulating HD-associated cellular dysfunction.

best.title: Microtubule-associated protein 1S phosphorylation regulates dynein-driven transport and synaptogenesis in neurons.
best.abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase like 5 (CDKL5) is a serine-threonine kinase enriched in the mammalian brain whose loss of function causes a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy named CDKL5 Deficiency Disorder. We previously showed that CDKL5 phosphorylates the microtubule-associated protein MAP1S, but how this regulates microtubule-dependent functions is not well understood. To address this question, we generated MAP1S phosphomutant mice in which the CDKL5 phosphorylation sites S786 and S812 were mutated to alanine (MAP1S S786/812A; MAP1S SA). Using a microtubule cosedimentation assay, we found that dynein binding to microtubules was reduced in MAP1S SA and CDKL5 knockout (KO) brain lysates, and time-lapse imaging showed impaired dynein motility in dendrites from both genotypes. MAP1S SA mice also exhibited reduced AMPA receptor transport, dendritic spine density, and excitatory synapses, accompanied by anxiety-like behavior and motor, social, and memory deficits relevant to CDD. Mechanistically, MAP1S SA and CDKL5 KO neurons showed increased microtubule stability and reduced tubulin tyrosination, consistent with excessive MAP1S-mediated stabilization. Restoring tubulin tyrosination by expressing tubulin-tyrosine ligase rescued dynein transport defects. Together, these findings identify MAP1S phosphorylation as a critical regulator of microtubule dynamics and dynein-dependent transport.

These findings provide new insights into the functional mechanisms by which NSLIT2 binding to ROBO1 affects changes in actin cytoskeletal architecture.

best.title: Cross-species molecular mapping of the photoreceptor sensory cilium and periciliary structures identifies conserved and species-specific architectural features.
best.abstract: Photoreceptor sensory cilia comprise a microtubule-based structural core and the phototransductive outer segment. The microtubule-based ciliary axoneme extends from the basal body through the connecting cilium into the outer segment, thereby linking the inner and outer segments. Around this central axis, specialized periciliary structures are distributed across the apical inner segment and basal outer segment. Yet how these ciliary and periciliary structures differ between rods and cones and across mammals remains incompletely defined. Using ultrastructure expansion microscopy, we compared their nanoscale molecular organization across canine, non-human primate and human retinas. Key rod-cone differences in ciliary organization were broadly conserved among all three species, whereas the scale and morphology of individual ciliary subcompartments differed between species. Periciliary structures showed even greater species-specific diversification, particularly in rods. Human photoreceptors shared several structural features with non-human primate photoreceptors but also displayed inter-individual variability in accessory inner segment-like structure. These findings refine current understanding of photoreceptor sensory cilia and associated periciliary structures in large mammals, revealing that conserved rod-cone differences co-exist with pronounced species-specific structural and molecular specializations.

best.title: The postsynaptic scaffold protein ABLIM1 regulates seizure susceptibility by maintaining GluA2 membrane localization in chronic epilepsy.
best.abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), the most common form of drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) in adults, is a frequent chronic neurological disorder. Nevertheless, the precise pathophysiological mechanisms underlying TLE remain largely undefined. Our findings demonstrate that Actin-binding LIM protein 1 (ABLIM1) is broadly expressed in the adult mouse brain, with high expression in the hippocampus. The protein is primarily localized to neurons, enriched in the postsynaptic density (PSD), colocalizes with the scaffold protein PSD95, and directly binds to F-actin. Co-IP experiments confirmed that ABLIM1 interacts with the α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) subunits GluA1 and GluA2. Following hippocampal stereotaxic injection of adeno-associated virus (AAV) to specifically knock down ABLIM1 expression, we observed reduced F-actin polymerization, decreased dendritic spine density, and thinning of the PSD in the mouse hippocampus. In the chronic epilepsy models induced by kainic acid (KA), ABLIM1 knockdown significantly exacerbated seizure severity and increased seizure susceptibility. Further mechanistic studies revealed that ABLIM1 knockdown specifically reduces membrane expression of GluA2 without altering its total protein levels. Collectively, ABLIM1 may regulate epileptogenesis and disease progression by maintaining postsynaptic structural integrity and GluA2 membrane homeostasis. Thus, the ABLIM1-GluA2 signaling axis represents a potential therapeutic target for DRE.

best.title: Pathogenic KIF1A variants differentially disrupt axonal trafficking and impede synaptic development.
best.abstract: The nervous system relies on billions of neurons connected through trillions of synapses to support vital functions. Despite the importance of this synaptic network, cellular mechanisms dictating synapse formation during human neurodevelopment remain unclear. Long-distance trafficking by the microtubule motor KIF1A is crucial for synaptogenesis and downstream synapse maintenance. Mutations in KIF1A cause KIF1A-associated neurological disorder (KAND). We employed isogenic gene-edited human-induced pluripotent stem cell -derived neurons to assess the effects of disparate pathogenic mutations in KIF1A on synaptic trafficking and function. Null (p.C92*) and hypoactive (p.P305L) mutations delay neurite outgrowth, mislocalize synaptic cargoes, and decrease synapse density. Conversely, a hyperactive (p.R350G) mutation supports neurite outgrowth but causes aberrant motility of synaptic vesicle precursors and deficits in microtubule-dependent presynaptic patterning. Functional analysis of neuronal activity reveals delayed synaptic maturation in loss-of-function mutations (p.P305L, p.C92*) and precocious activity in the hyperactive p.R350G mutation. These data provide insights into how KIF1A mutations with distinct molecular-level impacts lead to significant downstream synaptic deficits in human neurons.

best.title: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6)-mediated α-tubulin (K40) deacetylation and microtubule destabilization disrupt autophagosome-lysosome fusion in PBDE-47-induced neurotoxicity.
best.abstract: 2,2',4,4'-tetrabromodiphenyl ether (PBDE-47) is a pervasive environmental brominated flame retardant that accumulates in nervous tissues and induces persistent neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates that PBDE-47 perturbs neuronal autophagy, yet the definitive upstream molecular mechanism remains uncharacterized, hindering the development of effective protective strategies. This study was performed to clarify the toxic regulatory cascade and explore feasible pharmacological interventions using in vivo neonatal rat hippocampal tissue and in vitro PC12 neuronal cell models. Animals were neonatally exposed to PBDE-47 (0.1, 1.0, 10.0 mg/kg·bw), and PC12 cells were treated with PBDE-47 (1, 10, 20 µM) for mechanistic exploration. Results showed that PBDE-47 dose-dependently upregulated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), decreased α-tubulin (K40) acetylation, and destabilized neuronal microtubules. Such microtubule structural damage impaired autophagosome retrograde trafficking, blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and eventually caused neuronal loss, synaptic protein reduction, and cognitive impairment. For mechanism validation and rescue experiments, 1 mg/kg·bw paclitaxel (PTX) and 1 mg/kg·bw tubastatin A (TBA) were administered to neonatal rats, whereas 12.5 nmol/L PTX and 10 µmol/L TBA were used for PC12 cell treatment to stabilize microtubules and selectively inhibit HDAC6, respectively. Both pharmacological interventions effectively restored tubulin acetylation, rescued defective autophagic flux, and mitigated PBDE-47-induced neuronal injury, with TBA showing better applicability due to its high blood-brain barrier permeability and biosafety. Behavioral tests in vivo verified that PTX and TBA treatment significantly ameliorated PBDE-47-elicited learning and memory deficits. Collectively, these findings define the HDAC6/microtubule acetylation axis as a core upstream pathway responsible for PBDE-47-triggered autophagic transport failure and neurotoxicity, providing robust experimental evidence and a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of PBDEs-mediated neurological disorders.

best.title: EGR1 mediates neuronal damage via suppressing HIF1A-induced mitophagy following traumatic brain injury.
best.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a leading cause of neurological morbidity and mortality, characterized by complex pathophysiological cascades. Here, we investigate the role of the transcription factor EGR1 (early growth response 1) in modulating mitochondrial homeostasis via the HIF1A (hypoxia inducible factor 1, alpha subunit)-BNIP3 (BCL2/adenovirus E1B interacting protein 3) axis following TBI. Using integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic analyses, we identified EGR1 as a critical regulator of TBI pathology, with its expression acutely upregulated in neurons post-injury. Genetic ablation of Egr1 in mice significantly reduced neuronal apoptosis, preserved dendritic integrity, and ameliorated cognitive and sensorimotor deficits. Mechanistically, chromatin immunoprecipitation and luciferase assays revealed that EGR1 directly binds to the Hif1a promoter, repressing its transcription. Loss of EGR1 enhanced HIF1A-BNIP3-mediated mitophagy, reducing mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress both in vitro and in vivo. Conversely, silencing HIF1A or BNIP3 abrogated the neuroprotective effects of EGR1 deficiency. best.title: Elevation of the mechanically-sensitive e protein emerin links nuclear mechanotransduction to tau-induced cytoskeletal remodeling in neurons.
best.abstract: Neurodegenerative tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease, are neuropathologically defined by pathological tau deposition. While tau drives neurotoxicity by disrupting cytoskeletal, nucleoskeletal, and genomic architecture, cellular mechanisms mediating tau-induced dysfunction of the cytoskeleton and nucleoskeleton are incompletely understood. Here, we identify proteins with differing abundance in a cellular tauopathy model, iTau. Building upon previous findings that pathogenic tau reduces nuclear tension, we find elevated levels of emerin, a central regulator of nuclear mechanotransduction, in iTau neurons and tau mutant iPSC-derived neurons. Neuronal emerin overexpression drives neurotoxicity, increases filamentous actin (F-actin), and induces nuclear invagination, mimicking cellular phenotypes of tauopathy. Alterations in emerin binding partners reflect its cytosolic relocalization in iTau neurons, suggesting that pathogenic tau may impact nuclear mechanotransduction by altering emerin levels and localization. Overall, we identify emerin as a potential mediator of cytoskeletal and nucleoskeletal remodeling in tauopathy and provide a foundation for future studies of emerin function in neurons.
