primary.title: iPSC-based Approaches to Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: from Drug Screening to Regenerative Medicine in Early Clinical Translation.
primary.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterised by progressive loss of upper and lower motor neurons (MNs), with limited therapeutic options and modest benefit from currently approved drugs. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have emerged as a versatile platform for ALS research, enabling both regenerative medicine and phenotypic drug screening. iPSC-based transplantation strategies aim to replace lost cells or deliver neuroprotective support, while iPSC-derived MNs support drug discovery and repositioning. In the two decades since their discovery, iPSC technologies have progressed from concept to clinical translation, with both cell therapy products such as AstroRx and XS-228 entering trials and three screened drug candidates, Ropinirole, Bosutinib, and Ezogabine, advancing into clinical trials, underscoring their translational potential. In this review, we summarise iPSC-based approaches to ALS, focusing on cell therapies and drug discovery, highlight factors influencing transplantation success, and discuss ongoing clinical trials. We further discuss constraints that impede clinical trial progress, including limited understanding of ALS pathogenesis, absence of robust biomarkers to guide patient stratification and evaluate treatment response, and technical challenges related to the maturation of iPSC-derived neural cells. Finally, we advocate that advancing iPSC approaches requires both deeper understanding of ALS biology and technical innovation. Key priorities are refining iPSC differentiation protocols to improve neuronal maturity and implementing trial designs with adequate duration and rigorous patient stratification.

primary.title: Neuronal and mitochondrial phenotypes in iPSC-derived bipolar disorder models with and without a family history of mitochondrial disease.
primary.abstract: Psychiatric disorders frequently accompany primary mitochondrial diseases (PMDs), suggesting shared biological pathways between mitochondrial function and psychiatric vulnerability. In this exploratory study, we investigated whether bipolar disorder (BD) occurring in the context of a family history of primary mitochondrial disease is associated with differences in neuronal and mitochondrial phenotypes. We generated induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), neural progenitor cells (NPCs), and cortical neurons (CNs) from three non-psychiatric controls, three individuals with BD without a family history of mitochondrial disease, and three individuals with BD who did not themselves have mitochondrial disease but had relatives with clinically diagnosed mitochondrial (BD-FHMD). Our primary endpoints were distinguished network activity and cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ dynamics, complemented by measurements of mitochondrial and cellular function and metabolomic profiles across differentiation. Across neurodifferentiation, we assessed neuronal network activity, calcium dynamics, mitochondrial and cellular health, and metabolomic signatures. BD neurons exhibited sustained hyperexcitability with increased firing and burst activity. In contrast, BD-FHMD neurons showed lower network activity with enhanced cytosolic calcium responses and prolonged mitochondrial calcium transients. BD-FHMD also exhibited stage-dependent mitochondrial alterations, while BD and BD-FHMD showed distinct developmental metabolic signatures. Together, these findings identify two distinct mitochondrial-associated phenotypes within BD. BD is characterized by a hyperexcitable neuronal phenotype associated with altered developmental metabolic programming, whereas BD-FHMD exhibits calcium dysregulation and altered mitochondrial developmental trajectories consistent with increased bioenergetic vulnerability. These findings suggest that BD occurring in the context of a family history of primary mitochondrial disease may be characterized by a distinct pattern of neuronal and mitochondrial dysfunction. Replication in larger, independently characterized cohorts will be important to determine whether this family-history-defined phenotype can contribute to biologically informed subtyping and therapeutic approaches in BD.

primary.title: Female iPSC X chromosome inactivation erosion and its transcriptomic effects during CRISPR gene editing and neural differentiation.
primary.abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), together with CRISPR editing, are commonly used for studying neurodevelopmental disorders. Female iPSCs gradually lose the expression of the noncoding X chromosome inactive-specific transcript (XIST), leading to random X chromosome inactivation (XCI) erosion that affects both X-linked and autosomal gene expression. However, the effects of CRISPR editing and neural differentiation on XCI erosion and how this may confound a real-world analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are poorly understood. Here, we analyzed hundreds of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) samples of CRISPR-edited iPSC lines for 66 genes and the matched single-neuron RNA-seq data. We found variable XCI in CRISPR-edited female iPSCs, which was largely preserved in iPSC-derived neurons and predominantly influenced X-linked genes. Mechanistically, XIST mediates allele-specific epigenetic regulation of both X-linked and autosomal genes, with the former showing stronger allele-specific expression (ASE) bias that affects neurodevelopmental genes. These results have significant implications in hiPSC-based modeling of neurodevelopmental disorders.

primary.title: Characterization of structural variants in KOLF2.1J iPSCs and their potential impact on forebrain organoid differentiation.
primary.abstract: The KOLF2.1J human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) line was created as a reference for neurological disease modeling. Previous genotyping efforts identified several large structural variants (SVs), raising questions about their potential impact on neuronal differentiation. Here, we identified 37 additional SVs using long-read sequencing and optical genome mapping. Additionally, we found that one of the known SVs contained a previously undetected overlap with RYBP, a neurodevelopmental gene. To assess the functional consequences of these SVs, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of day 90 forebrain organoids derived from KOLF2.1J and two independent control iPSC lines. While cell-type composition was preserved, multiple SV-affected genes were differentially expressed and cell-cell adhesion and synapse-related processes were enriched in KOLF2.1J organoids. These findings highlight the importance of robust genetic characterization and multi-line validation for reliable iPSC-based modeling.

primary.title: Neuronal cell-cycle re-entry stratifies clinical trajectories in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
primary.abstract: The clinical heterogeneity of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) remains a fundamental barrier to effective therapy. While cell cycle re-entry in post-mitotic neurons is a known precursor to neurodegeneration, its role in defining patient-specific outcomes has never been established. Here, we integrate large-scale transcriptomic profiling from the AnswerALS cohort with mechanistic studies in human iPSC-derived spinal motor neurons to define how cell-cycle re-entry shapes disease heterogeneity in ALS. We identify a transcriptionally distinct patient subgroup with the highest expression of G1 or G2-phase cyclins that exhibit significantly slower functional decline (ALSFRS-R), whereas the engagement of S-phase markers correlates with accelerated disease progression. Nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction, a hallmark of ALS and related disorders, disrupts the spatial distribution of key regulatory proteins and may contribute to maladaptive cell-cycle activation. Our recent evidence suggests that impaired nuclear import may initiate, rather than merely accompany, neuronal cell-cycle re-entry. Using iPSC-derived motor neurons, we show that impaired nuclear import initiates TDP-43 pathology and global nuclear/cytoplasmic mis-localization of key ALS-related proteins. This nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction triggers a transient wave of cell-cycle activity immediately preceding neuronal cell death. Crucially, we show that DNA-replication initiation is a pathological inflection point of no return, as neurons entering S-phase accumulate replication-associated DNA damage and undergo cell death. Selective inhibition of CDK4/6 prevents S-phase entry and confers potent neuroprotection. Our findings demonstrate that impaired nuclear import drives maladaptive cell-cycle reactivation in ALS and that the depth of cell-cycle engagement stratifies neuronal fate and patient trajectories.

primary.title: A coronavirus protease activates sensory neurons via TRPA1 to drive sneeze, cough, and pain.
primary.abstract: Sneezing, coughing, and pain are common symptoms of respiratory viral infection. These responses are initiated by airway-innervating nociceptors that detect noxious stimuli, but how SARS-CoV-2 activates these neurons remains unclear. Here, we show that the coronavirus papain-like protease (PLpro) directly activates airway-innervating nociceptors in mice and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived nociceptors. PLpro triggers sneezing, coughing, acute pain, and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) release in the airways. Both the proteolytic activity of PLpro and the host ion channel transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) are required for neuronal activation and sneezing. Infection with the mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 or the murine coronavirus MHV-A59 also induces sneezing in mice, and MHV-A59-evoked sneezing is TRPA1-dependent. SARS-CoV-2 infection of the trigeminal ganglia altered transcriptional programs associated with nociception, including upregulation of the TRPA1-CGRP signaling pathway activated by PLpro. Together, these findings reveal a direct mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 triggers pain and airway reflexes and identify PLpro and TRPA1 as potential therapeutic targets for COVID-19.

primary.title: iPSC-derived RPE and retinal organoids from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients show differences in ABCA4 function.
primary.abstract: Stargardt disease is a phenotypically heterogeneous disease caused by bi-allelic mutations in the ABCA4 gene. We generated retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, photoreceptor precursors (PhRPs), and retinal organoids (ROs) from two induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell lines derived from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients. We observed that RPE cells from the patient with peripheral affectation showed reduced ABCA4 expression, reduced phagocytosis and digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POSs), and accumulation of lipid byproducts. ROs from both patients show stunted segments, more rods, caspase-3 activation, and lipofuscin accumulation at week 45 of maturation. Phenotypical differences seen in Stargardt disease patients are caused by their specific ABCA4 variants, but cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the process of photoreceptor degeneration are still poorly understood. Here, we suggest that peripheral phenotypes associated with these macular dystrophies can be linked to poor clearance of POSs by RPE cells, giving these cells a higher role in the pathogenesis of the disease.

primary.title: KIF1A-Mediated Axonal Transport of Netrin-1 in iPSC-Derived Human Forebrain Neurons.
primary.abstract: Netrin-1 is a secreted laminin-like protein that functions as a guidance cue for axon pathfinding in development. Netrin-1 also modulates synapse formation in developing neurons and long-term potentiation in mature neurons. Netrin-1 is expressed in human neurons; however, its intracellular distribution and trafficking have not been assessed. Moreover, there is a genetic association in Caenorhabditis elegans between UNC-6/netrin-1 and UNC-104/KIF1A, a kinesin-3 motor protein required for axonal transport. We characterized the endogenous expression of netrin-1 via immunocytochemistry and demonstrated it is localized to both the axon and dendrites of induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived human forebrain neurons. Next, live-cell imaging of netrin-1-mRFP revealed rapid, bidirectional axonal transport, comparable to that of other cargos undergoing microtubule-based trafficking in vertebrate neurons. To identify the netrin-1 vesicle population, co-localization analyses demonstrated that netrin-1 puncta overlap with the dense-core vesicle marker Chromogranin A. Netrin-1-mRFP and Chromogranin A-eGFP also undergo co-transport within the axon. Finally, we demonstrated a role for the kinesin-3 motor protein, KIF1A, in Netrin-1 transport by demonstrating that KIF1A-associated neurological disease (KAND) patient variants significantly reduce netrin-1 axonal transport.

primary.title: OGT regulates RNA-binding protein nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, but this fails in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
primary.abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

primary.title: Time-dependent effects of rapid-acting antidepressants in iPSC-derived neurons from treatment-resistant depression and healthy volunteers.
primary.abstract: Rapid-acting antidepressants like ketamine and serotonergic psychedelics show promise for treatment-resistant depression (TRD), but the molecular mechanisms that contribute to their therapeutic effects remain unclear. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offer a platform to model human cortical neurons and investigate drug effects in a human-relevant system. Here, iPSCs from individuals with TRD and healthy volunteers (HVs) were differentiated into mature cortical-like neurons and treated for six and 24 h with agents being investigated as rapid-acting antidepressants, including (2 R,6 R)-hydroxynorketamine (HNK), psilocybin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and 2,5-Dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine (DOI). Bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing assessed global and cell-type-specific transcriptomic responses. Synaptic proteins were evaluated via Western blotting and immunocytochemistry. To validate translational relevance, transcriptomic results were compared to CSF proteomics from ketamine-treated HVs. Despite differing initial pharmacological targets, overall gene expression across all compounds was highly correlated at matched timepoints compared to vehicle control, suggesting shared downstream effects. Both glutamatergic and serotonergic drugs converged on pathways involving inflammation, mTORC1 signaling, and cellular growth. At the single-cell level, (2 R,6 R)-HNK showed distinct cell-type specific alterations: upregulation in excitatory neurons and concomitant downregulation of inhibitory neuron populations. Differentially expressed genes from (2 R,6 R)-HNK-treated neurons also overlapped with CSF proteomic signatures from ketamine-treated individuals, supporting the model's translational relevance. This study is the first to assess multiple putative rapid-acting antidepressants in parallel using an iPSC-derived neuron model. Both convergent and drug-specific changes in gene expression and pathway enrichment were observed across diverse compounds, supporting the use of human iPSC-derived neurons in antidepressant drug discovery. primary.title: Convergent neuroimmune signaling underlying rapid antidepressant response to ketamine and psychedelics.
primary.abstract: Despite distinct receptor targets, both ketamine and serotonergic psychedelics produce a rapid clinical response and share biological signatures that suggest convergence on common downstream molecular mediators. To identify shared biomarkers of rapid antidepressant response, this study integrated CSF proteomics from healthy volunteers (HVs) who received intravenous ketamine with transcriptomic analyses from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from participants with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) and HVs; iPSCs were treated with ketamine, its metabolite (2 R,6 R)-hydroxynorketamine, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), or psilocybin. Multimodal clinical characterization (transcriptomics (n = 16 TRD; 11 HV), magnetoencephalography (MEG) (n = 30 TRD; 25 HV), and plasma cytokines (n = 39 TRD; 25 HV) were also performed on TRD and HV participants who received a single dose of intravenous ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) or placebo. Conserved immune pathways were identified across CSF and iPSC neurons with interleukin-15 (IL)-15 and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) emerging as key regulatory hubs. Transcriptomically, in whole blood, ketamine responders exhibited decreased IL-15 and elevated B-cell signaling pathways at baseline that were reversed post-treatment. At the protein level, plasma IL-7 levels (primary B-cell driver) correlated with baseline MEG gamma power, reaching brain-wide significance across all participants (main effect pFDR < 0.05). The association was most pronounced in the TRD participants across subcortical regions (diagnosis x IL-7 pFDR < 10-14). Post-ketamine, the TRD IL-7-gamma relationship inverted, paralleling widespread gamma power reductions throughout default-mode network regions (session x IL-7 pclc < 0.05). In mixed-effects models, cytokine ratios linked to IL-7/IL-15 signaling predicted antidepressant response (IL-4/interferon gamma (IFN-γ) pFDR < 0.041) and non-response (MCP-1/IL-7 pFDR < 0.009), suggesting that rebalancing within the IL-7/IL-15 axis may contribute to therapeutic efficacy. secondary.title: SHANK3 drives abnormal neurodevelopment in iPSC-derived 2D and 3D brain models of Phelan-McDermid Syndrome.
secondary.abstract: Phelan-McDermid Syndrome (PMDS) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by 22q13.3 deletion involving SHANK3. secondary.title: Base editing rescues a hereditary motor neuron disease in mouse and patient-derived iPSC organoid models.
secondary.abstract: In hereditary motor neuron diseases (MNDs), including forms of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) caused by single-nucleotide variants, effective therapeutic strategies need to address both gain- and loss-of-function mechanisms. Genome editing-based gene therapy represents a promising approach for simultaneously targeting these mechanisms. To establish proof-of-concept for base editing in a hereditary MND, we targeted the P285L variant in the TRK-fused gene (TFG), which causes hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy with proximal dominant involvement (HMSN-P), a disorder that shares clinical and histopathological features with ALS. We identified the optimal adenine base editor by comparing candidate editors in HMSN-P patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). We then generated a transgenic mouse model expressing human TFG P285L and evaluated the selected editor by subpial delivery of adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors to the spinal cord. AAV-mediated base editing prolonged survival, preserved motor neurons, and attenuated axon loss in ventral nerve roots. Treatment with the selected base editing vector reduced TFG aggregation and suppressed neuronal death in HMSN-P iPSC-derived neuromuscular organoids. Collectively, these findings support the therapeutic potential of base editing for hereditary MNDs.

secondary.title: Restoration of BDNF/TrkB signaling rescues presynaptic dysfunction in GM1 gangliosidosis iPSC-derived neurons.
secondary.abstract: GM1 gangliosidosis is a lysosomal storage disease characterized by progressive neurodegeneration and severe central nervous system (CNS) dysfunction. Although the abnormal intracellular accumulation of GM1 ganglioside is recognized as a major pathological feature, the molecular mechanisms underlying neuronal dysfunction remain unclear. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) plays essential roles in CNS development and the maintenance of synaptic function and plasticity; however, its contribution to the pathology of lysosomal storage diseases remains unclear. We previously identified a marked impairment of neurotransmitter release in GM1 gangliosidosis neurons, accompanied by reduced expression of synapse-related molecules. In this study, we investigated the potential involvement of endogenous BDNF signaling in synaptic dysfunction using human iPSC-derived neurons. We found that endogenous BDNF expression was significantly reduced in GM1 gangliosidosis neurons, accompanied by a marked decrease in full-length tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), a key mediator of BDNF signaling. Further, the gene expression of synapse-related molecules involved in neurotransmitter release, including SNAP25 and VAMP2, was reduced. Importantly, exogenous BDNF supplementation ameliorated presynaptic dysfunction and substantially restored the expression of synapse-related molecules, which were reduced in disease neurons. Furthermore, 7,8-dihydroxyflavone (7,8-DHF), a selective TrkB agonist, markedly reversed presynaptic dysfunction. These findings suggest that impaired BDNF/TrkB signaling contributes to presynaptic dysfunction in GM1 gangliosidosis and identify the enhancement of this pathway as a potential therapeutic strategy.

secondary.title: High-resolution genomic architecture of a 1.71-Mb inverted SNCA triplication in a patient-derived PARK4 model.
secondary.abstract: PARK4, caused by SNCA locus multiplications, is a severe, early-onset form of autosomal dominant parkinsonism. However, the precise structural topography of these massive genomic rearrangements remains inadequately resolved. In this study, we resolved the nucleotide-level architecture of a novel 1.71-Mb PARK4 triplication lineage (PARK4-4) and elucidated its early-stage biochemical consequences in a patient-derived cortical model. By integrating Optical Genome Mapping (OGM) and Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read sequencing, we mapped a complex 1.71-Mb inverted triplication spanning the HERC6 to CCSER1 loci. This rearrangement is organized in a Forward-Inverted-Forward (F-I-F) architecture, punctuated by precisely defined Head-to-Head (H2H) and Tail-to-Tail (T2T) junctions. Using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) differentiated into forebrain cortical neurons, targeted RT-qPCR and automated capillary western blotting demonstrated SNCA gene-dosage-associated α-synuclein overexpression, with a robust ∼2.3-fold increase. Furthermore, exploratory transcriptomic profiling (RNA-seq) revealed candidate synchronized upregulation of co-triplicated neighboring genes (PIGY, FAM13A, and TIGD2), supporting a regional gene-dosage effect. To our knowledge, this is the first structural characterization of a 1.71-Mb F-I-F inverted SNCA triplication at nucleotide resolution, revealing a complex architecture distinct from previously reported tandem triplications. While future isogenic and functional studies are required to establish mature disease-relevant pathology, this precisely mapped model provides an invaluable platform for studying dosage-dependent early biochemical phenotypes and evaluating targeted therapeutics.

best.title: iPSC-based Approaches to Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: from Drug Screening to Regenerative Medicine in Early Clinical Translation.
best.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder characterised by progressive loss of upper and lower motor neurons (MNs), with limited therapeutic options and modest benefit from currently approved drugs. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) have emerged as a versatile platform for ALS research, enabling both regenerative medicine and phenotypic drug screening. iPSC-based transplantation strategies aim to replace lost cells or deliver neuroprotective support, while iPSC-derived MNs support drug discovery and repositioning. In the two decades since their discovery, iPSC technologies have progressed from concept to clinical translation, with both cell therapy products such as AstroRx and XS-228 entering trials and three screened drug candidates, Ropinirole, Bosutinib, and Ezogabine, advancing into clinical trials, underscoring their translational potential. In this review, we summarise iPSC-based approaches to ALS, focusing on cell therapies and drug discovery, highlight factors influencing transplantation success, and discuss ongoing clinical trials. We further discuss constraints that impede clinical trial progress, including limited understanding of ALS pathogenesis, absence of robust biomarkers to guide patient stratification and evaluate treatment response, and technical challenges related to the maturation of iPSC-derived neural cells. Finally, we advocate that advancing iPSC approaches requires both deeper understanding of ALS biology and technical innovation. Key priorities are refining iPSC differentiation protocols to improve neuronal maturity and implementing trial designs with adequate duration and rigorous patient stratification.

best.title: Neuronal and mitochondrial phenotypes in iPSC-derived bipolar disorder models with and without a family history of mitochondrial disease.
best.abstract: Psychiatric disorders frequently accompany primary mitochondrial diseases (PMDs), suggesting shared biological pathways between mitochondrial function and psychiatric vulnerability. In this exploratory study, we investigated whether bipolar disorder (BD) occurring in the context of a family history of primary mitochondrial disease is associated with differences in neuronal and mitochondrial phenotypes. We generated induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), neural progenitor cells (NPCs), and cortical neurons (CNs) from three non-psychiatric controls, three individuals with BD without a family history of mitochondrial disease, and three individuals with BD who did not themselves have mitochondrial disease but had relatives with clinically diagnosed mitochondrial (BD-FHMD). Our primary endpoints were distinguished network activity and cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ dynamics, complemented by measurements of mitochondrial and cellular function and metabolomic profiles across differentiation. Across neurodifferentiation, we assessed neuronal network activity, calcium dynamics, mitochondrial and cellular health, and metabolomic signatures. BD neurons exhibited sustained hyperexcitability with increased firing and burst activity. In contrast, BD-FHMD neurons showed lower network activity with enhanced cytosolic calcium responses and prolonged mitochondrial calcium transients. BD-FHMD also exhibited stage-dependent mitochondrial alterations, while BD and BD-FHMD showed distinct developmental metabolic signatures. Together, these findings identify two distinct mitochondrial-associated phenotypes within BD. BD is characterized by a hyperexcitable neuronal phenotype associated with altered developmental metabolic programming, whereas BD-FHMD exhibits calcium dysregulation and altered mitochondrial developmental trajectories consistent with increased bioenergetic vulnerability. These findings suggest that BD occurring in the context of a family history of primary mitochondrial disease may be characterized by a distinct pattern of neuronal and mitochondrial dysfunction. Replication in larger, independently characterized cohorts will be important to determine whether this family-history-defined phenotype can contribute to biologically informed subtyping and therapeutic approaches in BD.

best.title: Female iPSC X chromosome inactivation erosion and its transcriptomic effects during CRISPR gene editing and neural differentiation.
best.abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), together with CRISPR editing, are commonly used for studying neurodevelopmental disorders. Female iPSCs gradually lose the expression of the noncoding X chromosome inactive-specific transcript (XIST), leading to random X chromosome inactivation (XCI) erosion that affects both X-linked and autosomal gene expression. However, the effects of CRISPR editing and neural differentiation on XCI erosion and how this may confound a real-world analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are poorly understood. Here, we analyzed hundreds of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) samples of CRISPR-edited iPSC lines for 66 genes and the matched single-neuron RNA-seq data. We found variable XCI in CRISPR-edited female iPSCs, which was largely preserved in iPSC-derived neurons and predominantly influenced X-linked genes. Mechanistically, XIST mediates allele-specific epigenetic regulation of both X-linked and autosomal genes, with the former showing stronger allele-specific expression (ASE) bias that affects neurodevelopmental genes. These results have significant implications in hiPSC-based modeling of neurodevelopmental disorders.

best.title: Characterization of structural variants in KOLF2.1J iPSCs and their potential impact on forebrain organoid differentiation.
best.abstract: The KOLF2.1J human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) line was created as a reference for neurological disease modeling. Previous genotyping efforts identified several large structural variants (SVs), raising questions about their potential impact on neuronal differentiation. Here, we identified 37 additional SVs using long-read sequencing and optical genome mapping. Additionally, we found that one of the known SVs contained a previously undetected overlap with RYBP, a neurodevelopmental gene. To assess the functional consequences of these SVs, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing of day 90 forebrain organoids derived from KOLF2.1J and two independent control iPSC lines. While cell-type composition was preserved, multiple SV-affected genes were differentially expressed and cell-cell adhesion and synapse-related processes were enriched in KOLF2.1J organoids. These findings highlight the importance of robust genetic characterization and multi-line validation for reliable iPSC-based modeling.

best.title: Neuronal cell-cycle re-entry stratifies clinical trajectories in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
best.abstract: The clinical heterogeneity of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) remains a fundamental barrier to effective therapy. While cell cycle re-entry in post-mitotic neurons is a known precursor to neurodegeneration, its role in defining patient-specific outcomes has never been established. Here, we integrate large-scale transcriptomic profiling from the AnswerALS cohort with mechanistic studies in human iPSC-derived spinal motor neurons to define how cell-cycle re-entry shapes disease heterogeneity in ALS. We identify a transcriptionally distinct patient subgroup with the highest expression of G1 or G2-phase cyclins that exhibit significantly slower functional decline (ALSFRS-R), whereas the engagement of S-phase markers correlates with accelerated disease progression. Nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction, a hallmark of ALS and related disorders, disrupts the spatial distribution of key regulatory proteins and may contribute to maladaptive cell-cycle activation. Our recent evidence suggests that impaired nuclear import may initiate, rather than merely accompany, neuronal cell-cycle re-entry. Using iPSC-derived motor neurons, we show that impaired nuclear import initiates TDP-43 pathology and global nuclear/cytoplasmic mis-localization of key ALS-related proteins. This nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction triggers a transient wave of cell-cycle activity immediately preceding neuronal cell death. Crucially, we show that DNA-replication initiation is a pathological inflection point of no return, as neurons entering S-phase accumulate replication-associated DNA damage and undergo cell death. Selective inhibition of CDK4/6 prevents S-phase entry and confers potent neuroprotection. Our findings demonstrate that impaired nuclear import drives maladaptive cell-cycle reactivation in ALS and that the depth of cell-cycle engagement stratifies neuronal fate and patient trajectories.

best.title: A coronavirus protease activates sensory neurons via TRPA1 to drive sneeze, cough, and pain.
best.abstract: Sneezing, coughing, and pain are common symptoms of respiratory viral infection. These responses are initiated by airway-innervating nociceptors that detect noxious stimuli, but how SARS-CoV-2 activates these neurons remains unclear. Here, we show that the coronavirus papain-like protease (PLpro) directly activates airway-innervating nociceptors in mice and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived nociceptors. PLpro triggers sneezing, coughing, acute pain, and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) release in the airways. Both the proteolytic activity of PLpro and the host ion channel transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) are required for neuronal activation and sneezing. Infection with the mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 or the murine coronavirus MHV-A59 also induces sneezing in mice, and MHV-A59-evoked sneezing is TRPA1-dependent. SARS-CoV-2 infection of the trigeminal ganglia altered transcriptional programs associated with nociception, including upregulation of the TRPA1-CGRP signaling pathway activated by PLpro. Together, these findings reveal a direct mechanism by which SARS-CoV-2 triggers pain and airway reflexes and identify PLpro and TRPA1 as potential therapeutic targets for COVID-19.

best.title: iPSC-derived RPE and retinal organoids from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients show differences in ABCA4 function.
best.abstract: Stargardt disease is a phenotypically heterogeneous disease caused by bi-allelic mutations in the ABCA4 gene. We generated retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, photoreceptor precursors (PhRPs), and retinal organoids (ROs) from two induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell lines derived from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients. We observed that RPE cells from the patient with peripheral affectation showed reduced ABCA4 expression, reduced phagocytosis and digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POSs), and accumulation of lipid byproducts. ROs from both patients show stunted segments, more rods, caspase-3 activation, and lipofuscin accumulation at week 45 of maturation. Phenotypical differences seen in Stargardt disease patients are caused by their specific ABCA4 variants, but cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the process of photoreceptor degeneration are still poorly understood. Here, we suggest that peripheral phenotypes associated with these macular dystrophies can be linked to poor clearance of POSs by RPE cells, giving these cells a higher role in the pathogenesis of the disease.

best.title: KIF1A-Mediated Axonal Transport of Netrin-1 in iPSC-Derived Human Forebrain Neurons.
best.abstract: Netrin-1 is a secreted laminin-like protein that functions as a guidance cue for axon pathfinding in development. Netrin-1 also modulates synapse formation in developing neurons and long-term potentiation in mature neurons. Netrin-1 is expressed in human neurons; however, its intracellular distribution and trafficking have not been assessed. Moreover, there is a genetic association in Caenorhabditis elegans between UNC-6/netrin-1 and UNC-104/KIF1A, a kinesin-3 motor protein required for axonal transport. We characterized the endogenous expression of netrin-1 via immunocytochemistry and demonstrated it is localized to both the axon and dendrites of induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived human forebrain neurons. Next, live-cell imaging of netrin-1-mRFP revealed rapid, bidirectional axonal transport, comparable to that of other cargos undergoing microtubule-based trafficking in vertebrate neurons. To identify the netrin-1 vesicle population, co-localization analyses demonstrated that netrin-1 puncta overlap with the dense-core vesicle marker Chromogranin A. Netrin-1-mRFP and Chromogranin A-eGFP also undergo co-transport within the axon. Finally, we demonstrated a role for the kinesin-3 motor protein, KIF1A, in Netrin-1 transport by demonstrating that KIF1A-associated neurological disease (KAND) patient variants significantly reduce netrin-1 axonal transport.

best.title: OGT regulates RNA-binding protein nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, but this fails in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
best.abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

best.title: Restoration of BDNF/TrkB signaling rescues presynaptic dysfunction in GM1 gangliosidosis iPSC-derived neurons.
best.abstract: GM1 gangliosidosis is a lysosomal storage disease characterized by progressive neurodegeneration and severe central nervous system (CNS) dysfunction. Although the abnormal intracellular accumulation of GM1 ganglioside is recognized as a major pathological feature, the molecular mechanisms underlying neuronal dysfunction remain unclear. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) plays essential roles in CNS development and the maintenance of synaptic function and plasticity; however, its contribution to the pathology of lysosomal storage diseases remains unclear. We previously identified a marked impairment of neurotransmitter release in GM1 gangliosidosis neurons, accompanied by reduced expression of synapse-related molecules. In this study, we investigated the potential involvement of endogenous BDNF signaling in synaptic dysfunction using human iPSC-derived neurons. We found that endogenous BDNF expression was significantly reduced in GM1 gangliosidosis neurons, accompanied by a marked decrease in full-length tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), a key mediator of BDNF signaling. Further, the gene expression of synapse-related molecules involved in neurotransmitter release, including SNAP25 and VAMP2, was reduced. Importantly, exogenous BDNF supplementation ameliorated presynaptic dysfunction and substantially restored the expression of synapse-related molecules, which were reduced in disease neurons. Furthermore, 7,8-dihydroxyflavone (7,8-DHF), a selective TrkB agonist, markedly reversed presynaptic dysfunction. These findings suggest that impaired BDNF/TrkB signaling contributes to presynaptic dysfunction in GM1 gangliosidosis and identify the enhancement of this pathway as a potential therapeutic strategy.

best.title: Time-dependent effects of rapid-acting antidepressants in iPSC-derived neurons from treatment-resistant depression and healthy volunteers.
best.abstract: Rapid-acting antidepressants like ketamine and serotonergic psychedelics show promise for treatment-resistant depression (TRD), but the molecular mechanisms that contribute to their therapeutic effects remain unclear. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) offer a platform to model human cortical neurons and investigate drug effects in a human-relevant system. Here, iPSCs from individuals with TRD and healthy volunteers (HVs) were differentiated into mature cortical-like neurons and treated for six and 24 h with agents being investigated as rapid-acting antidepressants, including (2 R,6 R)-hydroxynorketamine (HNK), psilocybin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and 2,5-Dimethoxy-4-iodoamphetamine (DOI). Bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing assessed global and cell-type-specific transcriptomic responses. Synaptic proteins were evaluated via Western blotting and immunocytochemistry. To validate translational relevance, transcriptomic results were compared to CSF proteomics from ketamine-treated HVs. Despite differing initial pharmacological targets, overall gene expression across all compounds was highly correlated at matched timepoints compared to vehicle control, suggesting shared downstream effects. Both glutamatergic and serotonergic drugs converged on pathways involving inflammation, mTORC1 signaling, and cellular growth. At the single-cell level, (2 R,6 R)-HNK showed distinct cell-type specific alterations: upregulation in excitatory neurons and concomitant downregulation of inhibitory neuron populations. Differentially expressed genes from (2 R,6 R)-HNK-treated neurons also overlapped with CSF proteomic signatures from ketamine-treated individuals, supporting the model's translational relevance. This study is the first to assess multiple putative rapid-acting antidepressants in parallel using an iPSC-derived neuron model. Both convergent and drug-specific changes in gene expression and pathway enrichment were observed across diverse compounds, supporting the use of human iPSC-derived neurons in antidepressant drug discovery. best.title: High-resolution genomic architecture of a 1.71-Mb inverted SNCA triplication in a patient-derived PARK4 model.
best.abstract: PARK4, caused by SNCA locus multiplications, is a severe, early-onset form of autosomal dominant parkinsonism. However, the precise structural topography of these massive genomic rearrangements remains inadequately resolved. In this study, we resolved the nucleotide-level architecture of a novel 1.71-Mb PARK4 triplication lineage (PARK4-4) and elucidated its early-stage biochemical consequences in a patient-derived cortical model. By integrating Optical Genome Mapping (OGM) and Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) long-read sequencing, we mapped a complex 1.71-Mb inverted triplication spanning the HERC6 to CCSER1 loci. This rearrangement is organized in a Forward-Inverted-Forward (F-I-F) architecture, punctuated by precisely defined Head-to-Head (H2H) and Tail-to-Tail (T2T) junctions. Using patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) differentiated into forebrain cortical neurons, targeted RT-qPCR and automated capillary western blotting demonstrated SNCA gene-dosage-associated α-synuclein overexpression, with a robust ∼2.3-fold increase. Furthermore, exploratory transcriptomic profiling (RNA-seq) revealed candidate synchronized upregulation of co-triplicated neighboring genes (PIGY, FAM13A, and TIGD2), supporting a regional gene-dosage effect. To our knowledge, this is the first structural characterization of a 1.71-Mb F-I-F inverted SNCA triplication at nucleotide resolution, revealing a complex architecture distinct from previously reported tandem triplications. While future isogenic and functional studies are required to establish mature disease-relevant pathology, this precisely mapped model provides an invaluable platform for studying dosage-dependent early biochemical phenotypes and evaluating targeted therapeutics.

best.title: Convergent neuroimmune signaling underlying rapid antidepressant response to ketamine and psychedelics.
best.abstract: Despite distinct receptor targets, both ketamine and serotonergic psychedelics produce a rapid clinical response and share biological signatures that suggest convergence on common downstream molecular mediators. To identify shared biomarkers of rapid antidepressant response, this study integrated CSF proteomics from healthy volunteers (HVs) who received intravenous ketamine with transcriptomic analyses from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) derived from participants with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) and HVs; iPSCs were treated with ketamine, its metabolite (2 R,6 R)-hydroxynorketamine, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), or psilocybin. Multimodal clinical characterization (transcriptomics (n = 16 TRD; 11 HV), magnetoencephalography (MEG) (n = 30 TRD; 25 HV), and plasma cytokines (n = 39 TRD; 25 HV) were also performed on TRD and HV participants who received a single dose of intravenous ketamine (0.5 mg/kg) or placebo. Conserved immune pathways were identified across CSF and iPSC neurons with interleukin-15 (IL)-15 and monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1) emerging as key regulatory hubs. Transcriptomically, in whole blood, ketamine responders exhibited decreased IL-15 and elevated B-cell signaling pathways at baseline that were reversed post-treatment. At the protein level, plasma IL-7 levels (primary B-cell driver) correlated with baseline MEG gamma power, reaching brain-wide significance across all participants (main effect pFDR < 0.05). The association was most pronounced in the TRD participants across subcortical regions (diagnosis x IL-7 pFDR < 10-14). Post-ketamine, the TRD IL-7-gamma relationship inverted, paralleling widespread gamma power reductions throughout default-mode network regions (session x IL-7 pclc < 0.05). In mixed-effects models, cytokine ratios linked to IL-7/IL-15 signaling predicted antidepressant response (IL-4/interferon gamma (IFN-γ) pFDR < 0.041) and non-response (MCP-1/IL-7 pFDR < 0.009), suggesting that rebalancing within the IL-7/IL-15 axis may contribute to therapeutic efficacy. Clinicaltrials.gov identifier: NCT00088699; NCT02484456.

primary.title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals molecular organization of human and nonhuman primate basal ganglia.
primary.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are interconnected subcortical nuclei with a complex topographical organization that orchestrate goal-directed behaviors and are implicated in neurodegenerative movement disorders. We generated a cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the BG in human, rhesus macaque, and common marmoset, sampling over one million cells in each species. By integrating spatial data with a cross-species consensus single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cell-type taxonomy, this atlas reveals principles of molecular organization within and across structures. Extensive spatial sampling across the rostral-caudal axis illuminates complex, yet highly stereotyped, multi-axis gene expression gradients superimposed onto discrete compartments of the striatum. Additionally, we identify core-shell organization of the internal globus pallidus. This unified, cross-species spatial transcriptomics atlas will be a foundational resource for characterizing the molecular and functional organization of the BG and their roles in health and disease.

primary.title: NeuroBase: A Web-Based Transcriptomic Resource and R Package for Cross-Disorder Analysis of Neurodegenerative and Neuropsychiatric Diseases.
primary.abstract: Neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia, are highly prevalent and biologically complex conditions that remain difficult to diagnose and treat. This study aimed to develop NeuroBase, a web-based transcriptomic resource that supports exploratory comparison of shared and disorder-specific gene expression features across these disorders. Fourteen human brain bulk RNA sequencing datasets (262 total samples) were processed using a standardized pipeline, followed by differential gene expression analysis with DESeq2, edgeR and limma-voom for broad exploratory discovery, complemented by a multi-method sensitivity analysis to define a method-concordant core gene set, protein-protein interaction network analysis using STRING with downstream exploration in Cytoscape, and functional enrichment analysis. Principal component analysis and clustering-based visualizations were used to summarize similarities and differences in transcriptomic patterns among disorders. Differential expression analysis identified dataset-level significant genes within each disorder using DESeq2 for one dataset per disorder (FDR ≤ 0.05), including 38 genes in Alzheimer's disease, 6,704 in autism spectrum disorder, 3,559 in bipolar disorder, 687 in Parkinson's disease, and 2,750 in schizophrenia; a stricter multi-method intersection analysis yielded method-concordant Core Intersection sets in the most informative datasets (983 core DEGs in autism spectrum disorder, 505 in bipolar disorder, 281 in schizophrenia, and 234 and 151 in two Parkinson's disease datasets; only two core genes (SPP1 and CHST3) were found in Alzheimer's disease). A unified strict-threshold reanalysis (FDR ≤ 0.05, |log₂FC|≥ 1) revealed disorder-level DEG burdens ranging from 34 (Alzheimer's disease) to 2,812 (autism) deduplicated genes, but only 24 genes were reproducible across independent cohorts of the same disorder, highlighting the limited cross-cohort reproducibility characteristic of bulk brain transcriptomics. Enrichment analyses identified significantly enriched signaling pathways in autism spectrum disorder and nominally enriched synapse-related pathways in Alzheimer's disease. Representative high-signal genes included SPP1 in Alzheimer's disease, NRGN in one Parkinson's disease dataset, and BEST1 in autism spectrum disorder. Cross-disorder comparison identified 465 differentially expressed genes shared between the neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorder groups, and principal component analysis showed that sample variation was dominated by dataset and tissue of origin. NeuroBase is a publicly accessible, web-based transcriptomic database and companion R package (neurobaseR) that enables standardized, cross-disorder exploration of bulk brain gene expression profiles across neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, supporting comparative analysis, programmatic data access, and hypothesis generation through interactive visualization and pathway-level summaries.

primary.title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain.
primary.abstract: Histone modifications underpin the cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs that drive the remarkable cellular diversity of the mammalian brain. Here, we jointly profiled four histone modifications and the transcriptome in 2.5 million nuclei from the adult mouse brain. By integrating these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and three-dimensional genome organization, we constructed a unified epigenomic atlas spanning over 100 brain cell subclasses and assigned active, primed, and repressive chromatin states across 81% of the genome. Active chromatin states marked by combinatorial histone modifications better nominate candidate enhancers with functional support than chromatin accessibility alone, while H3K27me3- and H3K9me3-marked chromatin states delineate distinct modes of cell-type-specific gene repression. Finally, this multimodal resource enables the development of deep learning models that predict cell-type-specific epigenomic features and gene expression from DNA sequence, providing a comprehensive framework for annotating the brain regulatory genome and interpreting non-coding disease risk variants.

primary.title: A single-cell and spatial 3D multi-omic atlas of developing human basal ganglia.
primary.abstract: Human basal ganglia (BG) neurons and inhibitory interneurons originate in the ganglionic eminences (GEs), transient structures in the ventral prenatal brain. This study delineates the specification and maturation of GEs and GE-derived neurons using single-nucleus methyl-3C sequencing (snm3C-seq), spatial transcriptomics, and single-molecule chromatin + RNA imaging, and we found heterogeneous temporal progression across GE subregions. Spiny projection neurons (SPNs), the principal cells of the BG, acquire distinct subtypes through synchronized 3D-epigenomic remodeling, in contrast to the asynchronous maturation of other neuron types. Oligodendrocyte differentiation involves a transient short-range chromatin state during infancy, showing that the short-range and long-range chromatin conformations previously linked to terminal glial and neuronal fates can also be transient. The temporal cortex matured epigenomically faster than other cortical regions during this period. Lastly, SPNs were enriched in genetic risk for neuropsychiatric disease. Our study extends findings on unique 3D-epigenomic dynamics during human brain development.

primary.title: Human neocortical glutamatergic neurons revealed through multimodal profiling.
primary.abstract: The human neocortex underlies higher cognition, yet our understanding of its neuronal diversity is limited by sparse access to viable tissue, inconsistent cell-type definitions, and limited multimodal data. Although single-cell transcriptomics has transformed our understanding of cell type diversity, transcriptomic data alone cannot explain neuronal function. Here, we introduce a multimodal patch sequencing (patch-seq) resource of human neocortical glutamatergic neurons spanning cortical layers 2-6. Combining morphoelectric features with spatial transcriptomic data to provide laminar context, we sampled 39 of 42 transcriptomically defined glutamatergic neuron types. This systematic approach enabled the identification of unique phenotypes for understudied populations in the human neocortex including L4 intratelencephalic, L5/6 near-projecting, and diverse L6 neurons. Human, macaque, and mouse comparisons of transcriptomically homologous L5 neurons reveal that morphoelectric differences across species were subclass specific. This dataset provides a unified multimodal reference for studying human cortical circuitry and neuronal diversity.

primary.title: Multiscale spatial atlas of human basal ganglia cell types and communities.
primary.abstract: The human basal ganglia comprise functionally varied nuclei, but their cell-type composition and spatial organization have not been comprehensively resolved. We generated a multi-region, subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomic atlas by integrating multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)+ and spatiotemporal enhanced-resolution omics sequencing (Stereo-seq) across four neurotypical donors. The datasets profiled ∼7.9 million cells across the caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, and globus pallidus, resolving 60 transcriptionally distinct cell types. We identify region-selective molecular and spatial diversification of spiny projection neurons and non-neuronal populations. Subcellular RNA localization captures somatic size and projection-inferred signatures, reflecting direct- and indirect-pathway topology. Cellular community analyses reveal astrocyte and oligodendrocyte subclusters enriched at striosome-matrix borders, while primate-expanded interneurons are confined to matrix territories. Cross-species comparisons reveal conserved and species-specialized organization, including orthologous striosome-matrix architecture and conserved dorsolateral-to-ventromedial transcriptional gradients. Together, this multi-centimeter-scale human basal ganglia atlas links cell types, spatial architecture, and subcellular transcript topography across scales.

primary.title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia.
primary.abstract: The basal ganglia are central to motor control, learning, emotion, and reward processing, and their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here, we generated a single-cell multi-omic atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical human donors. This atlas resolved cell-type- and region-specific landscapes of active and repressive candidate cis-regulatory elements and delineated gene regulatory networks underlying cell identity. We found that the combinatorial expression of homeobox transcription factors provides distinctive molecular descriptors of neuronal cell identities in the basal ganglia. Integration with matched MERFISH spatial transcriptomics further uncovered regional heterogeneity in epigenomic and transcriptional programs. Finally, we used this atlas to interpret noncoding risk variants associated with neuropsychiatric disorders and to construct a deep-learning model that predicts gene regulatory activities and variant effects. Together, this work provides a multimodal regulatory framework for understanding human basal ganglia organization, evolution, and disease genetics.

primary.title: Mesoscale molecular architecture of the striatum across cell types and adult aging.
primary.abstract: The human striatum governs diverse motor, cognitive, and affective behaviors yet lacks the obvious cytoarchitectural boundaries defining functional territories elsewhere in the brain. Using Slide-tags single-nucleus spatial transcriptomics, we profiled 1.1 million cells across 19 postmortem donors to uncover the striatum's spatial organization. These data revealed a consistent subdivision of the striatum into six zones, each defined by molecularly distinct populations of spiny projection neurons (SPNs) and featuring spatially coordinated neuron-astrocyte interaction networks. To determine their structural relevance, we generated a companion mouse spatial atlas that identified four homologous zones that aligned with territories defined by brain-wide afferent projections. Finally, imputing zonal identities onto a 131-donor single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cohort revealed that dorsal zones exhibit the greatest age-related transcriptional change and that the expression differences defining zonation attenuate with age. This resource establishes a conserved mesoscale spatial framework for the mammalian striatum, linking single-cell molecular identity to structural connectomics and aging.

primary.title: multiVIB: A unified probabilistic contrastive learning framework for atlas-scale integration of single-cell multi-omics data.
primary.abstract: Integrating heterogeneous single-cell datasets requires aligning shared biological features while preserving meaningful variation across modalities, studies, and species. Here, we present multiVIB, a unified framework combining the variational information bottleneck with probabilistic contrastive learning for horizontal, vertical, and mosaic integration of single-cell multi-omics data. Across diverse benchmarks, multiVIB achieves competitive integration performance while minimizing spurious alignments. Applied to BRAIN Initiative atlas-scale datasets, multiVIB enables incremental integration of nine molecular modalities in the mouse primary motor cortex and cross-species integration of primate basal ganglia transcriptomes, recovering conserved cell identities and species-specific molecular programs. Together, these results establish multiVIB as a versatile framework for scalable, biologically faithful construction and expansion of comprehensive brain cell atlases.

primary.title: Multimodal single-cell epigenomic and 3D genome atlas of the human basal ganglia.
primary.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) underlie motor control, reward processing, and many neurological and psychiatric disorders, yet cell-type-resolved epigenomic and 3D genome maps of the human BG remain limited. Here, we present a multimodal single-cell atlas of DNA methylation (261,331 nuclei) and 3D chromatin conformation (229,286 nuclei) from eight subregions, harmonized under the BG consensus taxonomy and integrated with matched data across multiple regulatory layers. We identify millions of differentially methylated regions across cell types, enriched for distinct transcription factor motifs, and link them to disease-associated heritability. We characterize the POU6F2+ STR D2 SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neuron (SPN) subtype, with concordant signatures across multiple modalities, and reveal region-specific methylation and contact gradients. Integrative gene regulatory networks (GRNs) predict cell-type-resolved enhancer-promoter interactions, nominating candidate regulatory mechanisms for Parkinson's disease (PD) risk variants at SNCA. Finally, multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH) profiling combined with cross-species Patch-seq identifies a neuronal subtype, STR FS PTHLH-PVALB GABA, with electrophysiological differences across the striatal matrix-striosome (MS) boundary.

primary.title: Female iPSC X chromosome inactivation erosion and its transcriptomic effects during CRISPR gene editing and neural differentiation.
primary.abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), together with CRISPR editing, are commonly used for studying neurodevelopmental disorders. Female iPSCs gradually lose the expression of the noncoding X chromosome inactive-specific transcript (XIST), leading to random X chromosome inactivation (XCI) erosion that affects both X-linked and autosomal gene expression. However, the effects of CRISPR editing and neural differentiation on XCI erosion and how this may confound a real-world analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are poorly understood. Here, we analyzed hundreds of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) samples of CRISPR-edited iPSC lines for 66 genes and the matched single-neuron RNA-seq data. We found variable XCI in CRISPR-edited female iPSCs, which was largely preserved in iPSC-derived neurons and predominantly influenced X-linked genes. Mechanistically, XIST mediates allele-specific epigenetic regulation of both X-linked and autosomal genes, with the former showing stronger allele-specific expression (ASE) bias that affects neurodevelopmental genes. These results have significant implications in hiPSC-based modeling of neurodevelopmental disorders.

primary.title: An integrated single-cell and epigenomic resource for comparative analysis of the basal ganglia from BICAN.
primary.abstract: The basal ganglia regulate motor, cognitive, and affective behaviors, and their dysfunction underlies diverse neurological and psychiatric disorders. Comprehensive, accessible multi-omics resources are needed to understand the regulatory mechanisms governing basal ganglia cell types. Here, we present an open, interactive web-based platform for exploring single-cell multi-omics datasets from basal ganglia, generated using 10X Multiome, single-nucleus methylome and chromatin conformation sequencing (snm3C-seq), and Paired-Tag technologies by the BICAN (NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network) consortium. The platform is available at https://basalganglia.epigenomes.net/and enables integrated visualization of gene expression, chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, histone modifications, and chromatin conformation across cell types and human, macaque, marmoset, and mouse species, with direct genome browser support and comparative epigenomic functionality. Representative analyses demonstrate cell-type-specific regulatory landscapes, conserved and species-specific regulatory elements, and links between epigenomic regulation and transcription. This resource provides a scalable, community-oriented foundation for advancing basal ganglia biology and interpreting regulatory mechanisms relevant to brain function and disease.

primary.title: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes.
primary.abstract: Astrocytes shape synapses and circuits, yet their diversity within the human basal ganglia remains poorly defined. Integrating single-nucleus transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with spatial transcriptomics, we identify three anatomically organized astrocyte subgroups-striatal gray matter (GM), extra-striatal GM, and white matter (WM)-distinguished by neurotransmitter transporter expression and synapse-associated programs that reflect afferent input. These molecular distinctions generalize brain-wide, separating telencephalic from non-telencephalic astrocytes, with LHX2 marking telencephalic astrocyte identity across species. Within the striatum (STR), dorsal and ventral populations align with distinct microcircuits; a ventral population maps to the nucleus accumbens mediodorsal shell alongside specialized neuronal subtypes, a pattern conserved in nonhuman primates. A deep learning sequence model identifies subgroup-specific enhancer codes and recovers established transcription factor motif logic from published enhancer-AAV datasets, providing a foundation for targeted viral vector design. These findings define intersecting axes of human astrocyte specialization and offer a framework for cell-type-specific dissection of basal ganglia circuits.

primary.title: Parkinson's disease-linked D620N mutation selectively alters the brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35.
primary.abstract: Mutations in several genes are known to cause familial forms of Parkinson's disease (PD), including mutations in the vacuolar protein sorting 35 ortholog (VPS35) gene linked to late-onset, autosomal dominant PD. VPS35 encodes a core subunit of the retromer complex which functions in endosomal sorting and recycling. It remains unclear how the pathogenic D620N mutation in VPS35 disrupts retromer function to induce neurodegeneration in PD. Using cell- and rodent-based models expressing D620N VPS35, we performed interactome proteomics to identify alterations underlying the pathogenic effects of D620N VPS35 in PD. Using overexpression of VPS35 variants in HEK-293 T cells, we conducted tandem affinity purification (TAP) or co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) with protein chemical crosslinking to determine the native and non-native protein interactomes of wild-type (WT) and D620N VPS35, respectively. Notably, we can confirm the reduced interaction of D620N VPS35 with components of the WASH complex. Additionally, using a viral-mediated gene transfer model of human D620N VPS35 overexpression in adult rat brain, we identify the first brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35. These overexpression models reveal remarkably similar interaction profiles of WT and D620N VPS35, suggesting that the D620N mutation has a subtle effect on the overall VPS35 protein interactome. We also conducted proteomic analysis of brain tissue from a D620N VPS35 knockin (KI) mouse model that expresses VPS35 at endogenous levels. Using co-IP from hemibrain or striatal extracts of WT and D620N VPS35 KI mice, we reveal a high degree of similarity between the brain interactomes of WT and D620N VPS35, further suggesting a subtle effect of the D620N mutation on VPS35 protein interactions. Notably, in both hemibrain and striatum, we find a selective decrease in the interaction of two known interactors, TBC1D5 and VPS29, with D620N VPS35. We also performed global proteomic analysis of striatal tissue from D620N VPS35 KI mice and reveal a high degree of similarity between WT and D620N, further suggesting a subtle effect of this mutation. Together, our study provides a comprehensive evaluation of the VPS35 protein interactome and reveals a selective effect of the PD-linked D620N mutation in mammalian cells and brain. Our study provides key insight into the mechanisms of retromer dysfunction in VPS35-linked PD.

primary.title: Microglial Metabolic Reprogramming Regulated by HIF-1α/HK2 Positive Feedback Inhibits Adult Hippocampal Neurogenesis in Diabetes-Associated Cognitive Dysfunction.
primary.abstract: Diabetes-associated cognitive dysfunction (DACD) is a significant complication with few effective treatments and unclear underlying mechanism. The aim of this study was to investigate how hyperglycemia disrupts adult hippocampal neurogenesis (AHN) through metabolic-immune interactions, seeking to identify potential treatment targets for DACD. DACD models were developed using db/db mice or streptozotocin-induced mice, and their cognitive function was assessed through behavioral tests. Next, we integrated multi-omics analyses (transcriptomic, single-cell, and lactylome profiling) with metabolic studies in BV2 cells exposed to diabetic conditions. Pharmacological modulators (3-BP, C646, TSA) were used to clarify the underlying mechanisms. The mice with DACD demonstrated cognitive deficits, impaired AHN, and activation of hippocampal microglia. Transcriptomic analysis revealed glycolysis as the primary dysregulated pathway. Mechanistically, hyperglycemia/AGEs induced glycolytic reprogramming and increased lactate levels, which promoted HIF-1α lactylation at lysine residues-a modification catalyzed by p300 and opposed by histone deacetylases. This posttranslational modification was associated with HIF-1α stabilisation and with enhanced transcriptional occupancy at the HK2 promoter. This established a self-amplifying feedback loop, perpetuating microglial activation and disrupting the blood-brain barrier via CXCL10 secretion, which led to CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Systemic administration of the glycolytic inhibitor 3-BP disrupted the pathogenic circuit, thereby normalizing metabolism, attenuating neuroinflammation, and restoring cognitive function. HIF-1α lactylation is associated with HIF-1α stabilisation, acting as a potential metabolic-epigenetic mechanism that links glycolytic flux to sustained microglial activation, neuroinflammation and impaired AHN in DACD. Pharmacological inhibition of this axis attenuated neuroinflammation and improved cognitive outcomes in our model, suggesting a candidate therapeutic strategy for DACD.

primary.title: Toward an integrated framework for a human and mammalian brain cell atlas.
primary.abstract: The NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) is developing a standardized, integrated reference framework for classifying and studying brain cell types across human, macaque, marmoset, and mouse. We present a cross-species, multimodal atlas of the basal ganglia, a group of subcortical nuclei central to motor control, adaptive behavior, and neurological disease. Built from large-scale single-cell transcriptomic classification and integrated with epigenomic, spatial genomic, multiomic, and developmental datasets, the atlas provides a curated, data-driven taxonomy with standardized nomenclature, extensive phenotypic characterization, and community-informed annotation. Cell types are mapped into species-specific anatomical reference frameworks and linked across species through structural ontologies. Realizing this resource required coordinated standards for tissue acquisition and processing, harmonized donor metadata, anatomical registration, sequencing pipelines, data infrastructure, visualization, mapping tools, and interoperable metadata. The BICAN basal ganglia atlas demonstrates how pipelines and standards can be implemented, validated, and scaled toward a whole-brain human and mammalian cell-type reference.

primary.title: Lysosomal multi-omics reveals altered sphingolipid catabolism associated with lysosomal dysfunction in the aging brain.
primary.abstract: Lipids dynamically reside in multiple intracellular locations, and their organellar distribution is important for function. During brain aging, lysosomal lipid changes have been noted, but lipid identity, interactions, and functional relevance have not been characterized. We used mass spectrometry to assess longitudinal changes in the lipidome and proteome of lysosomal fractions from the murine cortex, from 3 to 24 months, followed by multi-omics factor analysis (MOFA) to identify factors underlying lysosomal aging. Our data uncover an age-dependent increase in lysosomal abundance of lipid and protein myelin components and suggest altered sphingolipid catabolism favoring degradation of sphingomyelins over glycosphingolipids. We experimentally corroborate MOFA predictions to demonstrate that age-dependent accumulation of myelin-derived glycosphingolipids is associated with lysosomal enlargement and dysfunction and is most pronounced in microglia. Our findings suggest that age-related lysosomal lipidome changes resemble those observed in lysosomal storage diseases and underscore the importance of organelle-specific analyses for elucidating lipid function.

primary.title: PPP1R1B differentially modulates alcohol intake and emotional comorbidity through distinct prefrontal circuits.
primary.abstract: Excessive alcohol consumption frequently co-occurs with anxiety and depression in alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet the specific neural circuits and molecular mechanisms coordinating these comorbid conditions remain poorly defined. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), particularly its prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) subregions, projects to key reward and emotion centers like the nucleus accumbens (Nac) and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but the functional heterogeneity of these projections is unclear. Using chemogenetics, retrograde tracing, electrophysiology, spatial proteomics, and cell-type-specific gene editing in mice subjected to a 4-wk intermittent access to alcohol (IAA) paradigm, we selectively manipulated glutamatergic projections from the PL and IL to the Nac core, Nac shell, and BLA and assessed alcohol intake, anxiety-like, and depression-like behaviors. Chemogenetic activation of PL-Nac core projections reduced short-term alcohol intake, anxiety-, and depression-like behaviors, while IL-BLA activation decreased alcohol consumption and anxiety-like behaviors only. Retrograde tracing revealed mirror-image anatomical segregation of projection-defined neuronal subpopulations within PL/IL linking spatial organization to functional divergence. IAA induced pathway-specific synaptic adaptations. Spatial proteomics nominated protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit 1B (PPP1R1B) as a candidate molecule in PL-Nac core neurons. Independent immunostaining confirmed PPP1R1B downregulation, and circuit-specific knockout recapitulated alcohol-related and affective phenotypes, whereas overexpression reversed them. In IL-BLA neurons, PPP1R1B manipulation modulated alcohol intake and anxiety, but not depression. These findings define a subregion- and projection-specific organizational logic in the mPFC for differentially regulating alcohol consumption and emotional comorbidity, with PPP1R1B as a key molecular determinant. This provides a neural pathway-molecule framework for targeted intervention in AUD.

secondary.title: An Optimized Stem Cell Secretome Proteomics Platform: Application to Progranulin-Deficient iPSCs.
secondary.abstract: Stem cells secrete diverse extracellular proteins that regulate pluripotency, differentiation, and cell-cell communication, making them powerful model systems for studying development, disease mechanisms, and regenerative medicine. However, robust stem cell secretome analysis remains technically challenging. Unlike many other cell types, pluripotent stem cells cannot tolerate serum starvation or growth factor deprivation, while low-abundance secreted proteins are often masked by media-derived proteins and intracellular contamination. Here, we systematically optimized the secretome proteomics workflow in induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) by evaluating culture medium composition, conditioned-media collection time, cell plating density, media harvest and preparation methods, LC-MS acquisition methods, and data analysis strategies. Full-strength Essential 8 medium, 48 h media collection, 80% cell confluency, two-step centrifugation, and data-independent acquisition (DIA)LC-MS/MS provided the optimal secretome proteomics data quality. We then applied the optimized platform to an isogenic iPSC disease model to investigate how progranulin deficiency reshapes the extracellular and intracellular proteomes. Progranulin-deficient iPSCs showed a coordinated reduction of extracellular lysosomal hydrolases despite relatively modest intracellular proteome changes, suggesting altered lysosome trafficking and possible impairment of lysosomal exocytosis. Together, this work establishes a robust and standardized workflow for stem cell secretome proteomics and demonstrates its utility for investigating extracellular proteome remodeling in human disease models.

secondary.title: scMINA: an interpretable workflow for paired scRNA-scATAC multiome integration and regulatory prioritization.
secondary.abstract: Single-cell multiomic technologies that jointly profile transcriptomic and epigenomic states provide unprecedented opportunities to investigate cellular heterogeneity and gene regulatory mechanisms in complex diseases. However, analysis of paired single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) and chromatin accessibility (scATAC-seq) data remains computationally challenging due to modality-specific technical variation, integration complexity, and limited interpretability of downstream regulatory inference. Here, we present scMINA (single-cell Multimodal Integration and Network Attribution), a modular and interpretable analytical workflow for the analysis of paired single-cell multiome datasets. scMINA comprises coordinated modules for multimodal integration, technical covariate correction, and regulatory feature prioritization, enabling systematic characterization of cellular states across transcriptomic and epigenomic modalities. In addition, scMINA incorporates explainable artificial intelligence-based attribution strategies to prioritize candidate genes and transcription factors associated with cell-state heterogeneity and disease-related regulatory alterations. We applied scMINA to the single-cell multiome data from the Seattle Alzheimer's Disease Brain Cell Atlas, where the workflow robustly resolved major glial cell populations and identified regulatory features associated with Alzheimer's disease pathology. By coupling multimodal integration with interpretable regulatory prioritization, scMINA provides a practical workflow for systematic analysis and biological interpretation of paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq datasets.
