best.title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia.
best.abstract: The basal ganglia are central to motor control, learning, emotion, and reward processing, and their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here, we generated a single-cell multi-omic atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical human donors. This atlas resolved cell-type- and region-specific landscapes of active and repressive candidate cis-regulatory elements and delineated gene regulatory networks underlying cell identity. We found that the combinatorial expression of homeobox transcription factors provides distinctive molecular descriptors of neuronal cell identities in the basal ganglia. Integration with matched MERFISH spatial transcriptomics further uncovered regional heterogeneity in epigenomic and transcriptional programs. Finally, we used this atlas to interpret noncoding risk variants associated with neuropsychiatric disorders and to construct a deep-learning model that predicts gene regulatory activities and variant effects. Together, this work provides a multimodal regulatory framework for understanding human basal ganglia organization, evolution, and disease genetics.

best.title: Making smart microscopy deployable in imaging core facilities.
best.abstract: Smart microscopy, in which real-time image analysis enables microscopes to adapt their acquisition dynamically, is becoming central to biological imaging. However, deploying such workflows in imaging facilities remains challenging. The computers that control microscopes in a facility are shared, governed by institutional policies, often offline and run vendor-specific software. As a result, installing custom software environments for the workflow of each user is both unsafe and unsustainable. We argue that smart microscopy requires a practical deployment strategy that links open-source bioimage analysis with commercial acquisition software without turning acquisition computers into development platforms. Using our recently developed tools, NucleiSky and LabConstrictor, as examples, we demonstrate how microscope control and external image analysis can be integrated while keeping the custom Python environment separate from the vendor-managed environment. The deployment strategy might vary - for instance, a USB drive, a facility workstation, a server or a network share - but the underlying principle remains the same: smart-microscopy workflows must be straightforward to approve, launch, reuse, audit and remove. Smart microscopy will become routine only when it is both powerful and deployable.

best.title: Extended depth-of-field reflected-light microscopy with a low-cost robotic microscope and Fiji focus stacking: Workflow integration and baseline evaluation.
best.abstract: Optical reflected-light microscopy is widely used in mechanical and tribological testing laboratories, but its limited depth of field (DOF) restricts imaging of non-planar post-test surfaces when high-NA objectives are needed to resolve fine features. Here we present a low-cost robotic microscopy system (bill of materials around USD 300) that extends depth of field through controlled axial scanning and computational focus stacking. Built on the OpenFlexure platform and using open-source software tools, the system captures z-stacks and reconstructs all-in-focus micrographs in Fiji (ImageJ distribution) using extended-depth-of-field (EDOF) fusion engines. The workflow is demonstrated on mechanically tested surfaces (scratches and indentations), providing all-in-focus visualisation of features such as scratch lips, pile-up, indentation boundaries and microcracks on reflective textured surfaces, with Scanning Electron Microscopy used for cross-checking of feature detectability. Baseline characterisation includes operational DOF and resolving-power measurements, a geometric-distortion assessment using a micrometric grid target, and a time-cost analysis of stack acquisition. Comparative evaluation of three widely used fusion methods (Sobel, variance and complex wavelets) using image-quality metrics and visual inspection indicates that complex-wavelet fusion yields sharper reconstructions and improved edge preservation relative to Sobel and variance, at the expense of higher computation time. Finally, we summarise practical constraints and observed failure modes under representative conditions, providing baseline guidance for routine use, including deployment close to mechanical test stations. LAY DESCRIPTION: Low-cost reflected-light microscopy has shallow depth of field when high-NA objectives image rough surfaces. We demonstrate a fully open (∼USD 300) OpenFlexure-based robotic microscope with an end-to-end Fiji focus-stacking workflow that produces all-in-focus micrographs of scratches and indentations, cross-checked against SEM. Baseline characterisation covers DOF, resolving power, geometric distortion, and acquisition-time effects. Complex-wavelet fusion outperforms Sobel and variance in sharpness at higher computation time. Practical constraints are identified for post-test failure analysis.

best.title: QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath.
best.abstract: Radiomic features provide a quantitative description of tissue organization in histopathology images. QuPath, a widely used open-source platform for whole-slide image analysis, offers morphology, intensity, and Haralick texture measurements but no standardized radiomic feature set such as that of PyRadiomics. Researchers must therefore export data to external Python pipelines, interrupting their QuPath workflow. QuRad extracts radiomic features from cell detections and annotation regions directly inside QuPath. The extension and equivalent Groovy script implement 119 features: 103 two-dimensional features enabled by default and 16 optional legacy shape descriptors. We compared QuRad 0.4 with PyRadiomics 3.0.1 on identical grayscale images and pixel masks. All 103 default features met a 10-9 absolute-or-relative agreement tolerance on a breast-cancer benchmark tile (410 cells). On 20 melanoma tiles (8,644 nuclei), 97 of 103 features met this tolerance and 6 polygon-derived shape features differed from PyRadiomics' raster-derived mesh (minimum concordance correlation coefficient 0.942). The 22 synthetic regions accepted by PyRadiomics reproduced the expected intensity and texture values. A single-threaded server benchmark reached about 1,900 nuclei per second, and processing the 184,242 cells of a whole-slide image took 2.7 min on a laptop. A random forest distinguished tumor cells from lymphocytes in melanoma (pooled macro-F1 0.853) and classified 197 tissue regions of 6 breast-cancer slides into 3 compartments (0.696). QuRad exports the features with object coordinates and extraction settings for use in QuPath or downstream analyses.

best.title: Comparison of manual counting with two rule-based image analysis programs, ImageJ and CellProfiler, for quantitative analysis of c-Fos immunohistochemical positivity in rat brainstem sections.
best.abstract: Quantitative and semiquantitative assessment of biomarker expression using immunohistochemistry (IHC) can be performed using several analytical approaches. Manual counting remains widely used but is inherently subjective and susceptible to observer variability. Rule-based image-analysis platforms may provide accessible alternatives, highlighting the need for direct method-comparison and agreement studies. c-Fos is a well-established marker of neuronal activation commonly quantified by counting IHC-positive cells. This study compared manual counting, ImageJ, and CellProfiler for quantifying c-Fos-positive cells in rat brainstem sections. Of 125 images initially evaluated, one was excluded as an extreme outlier, leaving 124 images for final analysis. Each image was independently analyzed by two trained observers using all three methods. ImageJ and CellProfiler were applied through their standard graphical interfaces and built-in functions using predefined user-guided threshold ranges, without additional plugins, scripts, machine-learning models, or custom code. Agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) and Bland-Altman analysis. No statistically significant difference in c-Fos-positive cell counts was observed among the three methods (Friedman test, P = 0.07). Median (IQR) counts were 6.75 (0.50-13.50) for manual counting, 6.25 (1.00-14.38) for ImageJ, and 6.00 (0.63-14.50) for CellProfiler. Inter-observer agreement was excellent for manual counting (ICC = 0.983), ImageJ (ICC = 0.964), and CellProfiler (ICC = 0.962). Inter-method agreement was also excellent (single-measures ICC = 0.971; 95% CI = 0.961-0.979). Bland-Altman analysis showed small mean biases of 0.33, 0.27, and -0.07 cells, with no significant proportional bias. Manual counting, ImageJ, and CellProfiler produced statistically comparable c-Fos-positive cell counts with excellent agreement. Under the predefined user-guided threshold ranges used, both software platforms closely matched manual counting; however, image-dependent threshold adjustment remains a potential source of observer variability.

best.title: DINOSim: Training-Free Semantic Segmentation on Microscopy Images.
best.abstract: We present DINOSim, a training-free method for segmenting objects in microscopy images without the need for large annotated datasets or additional model training. DINOSim builds on the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder, which captures semantic information from images. By comparing the encoder's features of image patches to those of a user-selected reference, DINOSim generates pseudo-labels that guide semantic segmentation. Subsequently, a k-nearest neighbors framework is used to refine predictions across new images. Our experiments show that DINOSim can effectively segment previously unseen objects in diverse microscopy datasets, offering performance comparable to supervised approaches while avoiding the need for costly manual labeling. We also investigate how different choices of user prompt selection and model size affect accuracy and generalization. To make the method widely accessible, we provide an open-source napari plugin (github.com/AAitorG/napari-DINOSim), enabling researchers to apply DINOSim to their own data easily. Overall, DINOSim offers a fast, flexible and practical solution for bioimage analysis, particularly valuable in resource-constrained settings.

best.title: Benchmarking cell segmentation in two Spatialomics platforms with open-source software.
best.abstract: UNLABELLED: The in situ tissue microenvironment is a complex mixture of different cell types, microanatomic structures, and acellular matrix material. Algorithms utilizing cell membrane and nuclear features demonstrated better performance in both tumor samples. This benchmarking approach is a rapid and effective method to assess performance of cell segmentation methods in different contexts for efficient algorithm selection and iterative model training. best.title: SynapTrack: An automated tool for synapse quantification.
best.abstract: Reliable synapse quantification remains challenging, particularly in high-throughput fluorescence imaging workflows. Here we present SynapTrack, a fully automated FIJI/ImageJ-based tool for quantifying synapses in cultured neurons and brain tissue sections with minimal user intervention. SynapTrack combines channel-specific preprocessing, background subtraction, and SynQuant-based detection of colocalised pre- and postsynaptic puncta. In cultured neurons, it additionally measures cell number and total dendritic length, enabling normalisation of synapse counts per cell and per 10 micrometer of dendrite. Using hippocampal cultures, SynapTrack reliably quantified excitatory and inhibitory synapses, captured the expected predominance of excitatory contacts, and reduced inter-sample variability through structural normalisation. Compared with SynBot, SynapTrack detected more synapses while better preserving biologically meaningful differences between synapse types. For tissue sections, in which cell counting and dendritic segmentation are impractical, we developed SynapTrack_Tissue, an adapted workflow based on presynaptic-postsynaptic colocalisation alone. Despite the lack of cellular normalisation, this approach produced stable measurements across heterogeneous neuropil regions. Because all spatial parameters are defined in micrometres, analysis settings are portable across imaging systems. SynapTrack therefore provides a standardised and scalable framework for synapse quantification in both cultured neurons and tissue sections.

best.title: OrgLine: A versatile pipeline for organoid morphometry using detector-guided prompts.
best.abstract: Patient-derived organoids are increasingly being used in disease modeling, clinical research, drug development, and precision medicine. However, capturing complex organoid behaviors in dense three-dimensional culture environments remains challenging for manual workflows, and bright-field images often contain background artifacts that complicate quantitative analysis. To address this gap, we developed OrgLine, a quantitative analysis pipeline for organoids. Built on a large, curated bright-field image dataset, it couples a detector with a prompt-guided segmentation module. OrgLine recognizes organoids in bright-field images, supports quantitative characterization of morphological phenotypes across developmental stages, and enables accurate instance segmentation for downstream morphometric assessment. Together, these capabilities support more automated and quantitative organoid cultivation workflows.

best.title: A Deep Learning Pipeline for Cell Segmentation and Viability Quantification in 3D Constructs From Fluorescence Microscopy Images.
best.abstract: With the increasing adoption of 3D cell cultures and bioprinting in biomedical research, there is a growing demand for reliable and accurate monitoring methods. While fluorescence microscopy is widely accepted for 2D cell cultures, when introducing the third dimension it often suffers from signal attenuation and out-of-focus interference, making automated image analysis challenging. In this study, a hybrid pipeline that integrates deep learning and traditional image processing techniques is presented with the aim of establishing an automated tool for cell segmentation and viability assessment in 3D from fluorescence microscopy images. A U 2-Net architecture was trained on 2D cell cultures for cell segmentation, while watershed-based separation and intensity-based classification were employed for viability detection. The model demonstrated accurate segmentation with minimal overfitting. Quantitative comparisons with manual counts and ImageJ-based results confirmed its accuracy. We then demonstrated the possibility of extending this model to 3D constructs by tracking cell density and viability during time in the case of human umbilical vein endothelial cells bioprinted in gelatin methacrylate at different seeding densities, taken as case study. Automated counts closely matched manual ones, highlighting the method reliability and minimal invasiveness avoiding the need for sacrificing the construct. Hence, this approach provides a scalable, reproducible, and efficient alternative to manual counting in 3D environments, enabling high-throughput analysis of complex fluorescence microscopy data.

best.title: Unsupervised deep learning enables blur-free resolution enhancement in two-photon microscopy.
best.abstract: Two-photon microscopy enables the non-invasive imaging of deep living tissue. Quantitative three-dimensional analysis is hampered by axial blur and anisotropic resolution in two-photon microscopy. We introduce the two-photon microscopy image enhancement network (TENET), a fully unsupervised framework that simultaneously performs deblurring, up to 12× resolution enhancement, and semantic segmentation on two-photon microscopy volumes in a single pass. TENET embeds a physics-informed blur-generation module with a trainable neural implicit point spread function (PSF), requiring only approximate PSF initialization rather than rigorous experimental measurement, paired "unblurred" images, or isotropy assumptions. On synthetic images, fluorescent beads, and in vivo microglia datasets, TENET surpasses the total-variation-regularized Richardson-Lucy (RLTV) algorithm, CARE, and Neuroclear in image fidelity and segmentation accuracy. Using time-lapse images of microglia surrounding metastatic brain tumors, TENET enables automated 3D morphometry that reveals dynamic microglia-tumor interactions. By converting blur-limited two-photon microscopy data into high-fidelity volumetric reconstructions with ready-to-use masks, TENET streamlines downstream analysis and expands the reach of deep-tissue live imaging.

best.title: BasNet: Attention U-Net-Based Automated Axon Segmentation in Bielschowsky Silver-Stained Histology.
best.abstract: Reliable automatic quantification of axon density in histologic sections is important for both research and clinical neuropathology applications - however, it remains a challenge for silver-impregnation stains, such as Bielschowsky. Classical color-deconvolution approaches perform poorly on silver stains, and manual annotation of densely packed axons is time-consuming and subject to inter-rater variability. We developed an automated axon segmentation pipeline in Bielschowsky silver-stained histological brain sections based on an attention U-Net architecture with attention-gated skip connections, trained using Focal Tversky Loss to handle class imbalance and thin structure recovery. Ground truth was manually annotated on 33 image tiles (covering over 25 million pixels) derived from 26 whole-slide images from varying brain regions of four multiple sclerosis patients. Slides were prepared by different laboratory technicians at different time points to capture realistic staining variability. Model performance was evaluated on a held-out test set of unseen tiles. On the test set (eight held-out tiles) the model achieved a mean pixel-wise F1/Dice of 0.717 and an intersection over union (IoU) of 0.584. A dedicated inter-rater experiment on two representative tiles yielded rater-to-rater F1 scores of 0.637 and 0.671, while model-to-rater agreement (F1: 0.681-0.736) met or exceeded that human ceiling. Generated whole-slide density and orientation visualizations accurately reflected regional axon distributions and provided quantitative readouts suitable for downstream analysis. Our attention U-Net provides an open-source solution for axon segmentation from Bielschowsky-stained sections, reducing manual effort and enabling reproducible, slide-level quantitative metrics. This tool can facilitate studies of axonal pathology across research and clinical settings.

primary.title: Subcellular compartment determines signal dominance: Endosomal cAMP overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation from a single receptor.
primary.abstract: Cells convey information not only via the identity of activated signaling pathways but also through the subcellular location where those signals originate. Whether spatially distinct signals from a single activated receptor compete to determine net cellular output has remained unclear. Here, we demonstrate this principle for a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), showing that endosomal and plasma membrane signals from a single activated receptor are not merely distinct but functionally opposed, with endosomal signaling predominating to reverse the net cellular output. Using the adhesion GPCR GPR64/ADGRG2 as a model system, we show that ligand activation engages two spatially distinct G-protein pathways that are not just additive but functionally opposed: plasma membrane G13/RhoA activation and Gs/cAMP production that persists from endosomes following receptor internalization. The endosomal cAMP pool actively overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation, resulting in net RhoA inactivation, an outcome that is completely reversed by pharmacological blockade of endocytosis or endosomal Gs inactivation. In parathyroid cells, where GPR64 is highly expressed, this endosomal signal dominance suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion independently of extracellular Ca2+ levels. These findings support a model in which the subcellular compartment, rather than pathway identity, determines the dominant signal and the overall cellular response of a single activated receptor, with implications for understanding the complexity of GPCR signaling.

primary.title: VPS35 Regulates Microglial Lipid Droplet Accumulation in Parkinson's Disease via Rab7.
primary.abstract: Microglial dysfunction and aberrant lipid metabolism are emerging as key contributors to Parkinson's disease (PD) pathogenesis. However, the specific role and regulation of lipid droplets (LDs) within microglia remain poorly defined. In this study, we employed MPTP- and LPS-induced PD mouse models and an in vitro system utilizing astrocyte-conditioned medium to model disease-relevant lipid stress and found enhanced LD accumulation in microglia. VPS35 expression was decreased in microglia, correlating with elevated microglial LD levels in PD mouse models. We then performed genetic manipulations (knockdown and overexpression) of VPS35, including the PD-associated D620N mutant, in primary microglia and assessed LD accumulation, phagocytic function, inflammatory responses, and integrated stress pathways. We showed that VPS35 knockdown exacerbated the accumulation of LDs in microglia. Conversely, VPS35 overexpression ameliorated LD formation, improved phagocytic function, and reduced inflammatory and integrated stress responses in microglia. The PD-related VPS35[D620N] mutation abolished these protective effects. We further found that VPS35 interacts with Rab7 to maintain lysosomal function, and the D620N mutation disrupts this interaction, leading to defective LD clearance. Our findings reveal VPS35 dysfunction as a key pathogenic mechanism in PD, where the D620N mutation disrupts microglial lipid handling to promote disease progression, thereby nominating VPS35 restoration as a promising therapeutic strategy.

secondary.title: Spatial mTOR biology: From organelle localization to biomolecular condensates and metabolic control.
secondary.abstract: The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) coordinates cell growth, metabolism, protein synthesis, autophagy, and survival by integrating nutrient availability, growth factors, energy status, mechanical cues, and cellular stress. Beyond classical biochemical cascades, mTOR signaling specificity is fundamentally governed by subcellular localization, temporal recruitment, and microenvironmental context. This review synthesizes current insights into the spatial architecture of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) across lysosomes, endosomes, plasma-membrane microdomains, organelle contact sites, neuronal processes, the nucleus, and biomolecular condensates. We examine how physical principles-including membrane composition and curvature, molecular confinement, macromolecular crowding, scaffold-mediated multivalent interactions, organelle positioning, mechanical tension, and localized translation-dictate signaling outcomes. Furthermore, we contrast membrane-anchored molecular assemblies with three-dimensional biomolecular condensates, detailing their interplay during stress adaptation. Spatial constraints in specialized cell geometries, such as neuronal compartments and developing tissues, illustrate how identical signaling machinery yields divergent functional outputs under altered diffusion environments. We also evaluate how advances in spatial multi-omics and super-resolution imaging extend these subcellular paradigms to tissue-scale heterogeneity. Finally, we highlight major translational hurdles, including the trade-off between spatial resolution and dynamic temporal tracking in current technologies, as well as the inability of conventional pharmacotherapies to selectively target discrete subcellular mTOR pools. Establishing spatial organization as a primary determinant of mTOR signaling clarifies context-dependent physiological outputs and provides a roadmap for developing next-generation spatially targeted therapeutics.

secondary.title: Singapore grouper iridovirus VP018 exploits FTR86 to promote viral replication through Tollip-mediated degradation of the STING-TBK1 axis.
secondary.abstract: Members of the tripartite motif (TRIM) family have been demonstrated to exert crucial roles in immune defense against pathogens. However, functions of the fish-specific TRIM subfamily (FTR), which lacks mammalian orthologues, remains poorly understood. In the current study, we investigated the potential roles of grouper FTR86 (EcFTR86) on innate immune response and its actions during fish virus infection. EcFTR86 was found to localize to lysosomes, and its transcription was significantly up-regulated in grouper spleen cells upon Singapore grouper iridovirus (SGIV) infection. Notably, the exogenous expression of EcFTR86 markedly enhanced SGIV replication, whereas knockdown of endogenous EcFTR86 significantly attenuated viral infection, demonstrating that EcFTR86 functions as a pro-viral factor against virus infection. EcFTR86 negatively regulated type I interferon signaling triggered by STING-TBK1 and interacted with the key molecules of STING-TBKl axis. Mechanistically, EcFTR86 degraded STING or TBK1 via an autophagy-lysosome-dependent pathway. Moreover, autophagic cargo receptor Tollip was identified to interact with EcFTR86, and was involved in EcFTR86-mediated degradation of STING or TBK1. In addition, EcFTR86 was verified to interact with SGIV viral proteins, including VP018 and VP075, whereas only VP018 exploited EcFTR86 to accelerate the degradation effects on STING and TBK1, thereby abrogating the interferon response. Collectively, our findings firstly showed that FTR86 functioned as a negative regulator of interferon response, and was exploited by fish iridoviral proteins to promote viral replication via Tollip-mediated autophagic degradation of the STING-TBK1 axis.

secondary.title: PDE2A is involved in negative emotional behaviors via the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway in the SPS&S model.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by negative affective symptoms, including anxiety, depression, anhedonia, and fear. The molecular mechanisms underlying these symptoms remain poorly understood. Phosphodiesterase 2A (PDE2A), a regulator of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling, has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the role of the PDE2A-cAMP-protein kinase A (PKA) signaling pathway in negative emotional behaviors induced by traumatic stress. METHODS: Transcriptomic datasets were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes and enriched pathways. A rat PTSD model was established using single prolonged stress combined with foot shocks (SPS&S). Behavioral tests were performed, and PDE2A-cAMP-PKA signaling alterations in the amygdala were examined. The effects of PDE2A inhibitor Hcyb1 and the PKA inhibitor H89 were evaluated. RESULTS: Bioinformatics analysis identified PDE2A as a hub gene associated with PTSD, with significant enrichment of the cAMP signaling pathway. SPS&S rats exhibited anxiety-, depression-like behaviors, and anhedonia, accompanied by increased PDE2A expression and reduced cAMP and phosphorylated PKA (p-PKA) levels in the amygdala. Hcyb1 treatment alleviated behavioral deficits, decreased PDE2A expression, and restored cAMP and p-PKA signaling. H89 blocked p-PKA activation and partially reversed the behavioral benefits of Hcyb1. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that amygdala PDE2A-cAMP-PKA signaling is associated with negative emotional behaviors in the SPS&S model. PDE2A inhibition may ameliorate behavioral deficits through PKA-related signaling. However, the peripheral blood transcriptomic data, lack of direct PDE2A activity and cAMP/cGMP measurements, and limited biochemical validation constrain mechanistic interpretation. Further studies using brain-derived datasets and comprehensive biochemical approaches are warranted.

secondary.title: Autophagy- and Ferroptosis-Related Responses and SIRT1/mTOR Signaling in Nucleus Pulposus Cells Under Fluid Shear Stress.
secondary.abstract: INTRODUCTION: To characterize duration-dependent responses of Nucleus Pulposus Cells (NPCs) to Fluid Shear Stress (FSS) and identify candidate pathways associated with autophagy- and ferroptosis-related changes relevant to Intervertebral Disc Degeneration (IVDD). METHODS: Primary NPCs isolated from male Sprague-Dawley rats were exposed to 12 dyn/cm² FSS for 0, 30, 60, 90, or 120 minutes. Cellular morphology, proliferation, apoptosis, mitochondrial function, autophagy-related structures, and protein expression were assessed. Chloroquine, erastin, and ferrostatin-1 were used in pharmacological comparisons. Network pharmacology, Mendelian randomization, transcriptomic analyses, machine learning, human single-cell analysis, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations supported candidate prioritization. RESULTS: Among the conditions tested, 60 min of FSS produced the most favorable cellular response, with improved proliferation and reduced apoptosis. This response was accompanied by increased autophagy-related structures, increased abundance of GPX4 and SLC7A11, and decreased abundance of ACSL4. A longer exposure of 120 minutes produced an adverse response. Network analysis identified 12 candidate hub genes, and integrated transcriptomic screening identified eight IVDD-associated candidates: ACSL1, KDM6B, MAPK14, TLR4, ALOX5, ATG7, PHF21A, and SIRT1. Human single-cell analysis provided their cellular expression context. SIRT1 was the only panel member assessed experimentally by Western blotting under FSS. Its abundance increased, and mTOR phosphorylation decreased after 60 min, with the opposite pattern after 120 minutes. Docking and simulations characterized predicted ligand-protein interactions involving SIRT1/mTOR. DISCUSSION: The cellular and computational findings support SIRT1/mTOR signaling as a candidate pathway linking the observed responses, while functional dependence and autophagy- ferroptosis coupling require validation. CONCLUSION: FSS elicited duration-dependent responses in NPCs, providing a basis for targeted mechanistic investigation and future phenotype-based screening relevant to IVDD.

secondary.title: Preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal cord D2R expression via the PP2A/AKT-dependent NMDA receptor phosphorylation.
secondary.abstract: Preoperative sleep deprivation (SD) is known to exacerbate postoperative pain, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a male mouse model of 48-h continuous SD followed by incisional surgery, we found that SD alone induced transient mechanical hyperalgesia, and when combined with surgery (SI group) it significantly aggravated and prolonged postoperative pain recovery until day 10. On postoperative day 7, SI mice showed marked downregulation of spinal dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) expression and decreased spinal dopamine concentration. D2R was predominantly expressed on spinal glutamatergic neurons. Overexpression of D2R on these neurons via intrathecal AAV injection effectively alleviated the prolonged hyperalgesia, normalizing pain sensitivity by day 7. Mechanistically, D2R downregulation led to increased phosphorylation of NMDA receptor subunits (p-NR1 and p-NR2B) without altering total NMDA receptor levels. Co-immunoprecipitation revealed an interaction between D2R and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A). SI mice exhibited decreased PP2A expression but increased p-AKT, p-GSK3β, and β-catenin, indicating activation of the PP2A/AKT signaling pathway, which were reversed by D2R overexpression. Furthermore, pharmacological activation of PP2A with DT-061 not only downregulated p-AKT, p-GSK3β, β-catenin, p-NR1 and p-NR2B, but also produced significant analgesia in SI mice. Collectively, these results demonstrate that preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal D2R on glutamatergic neurons, which disinhibits the PP2A/AKT pathway and enhances NMDA receptor phosphorylation. Targeting D2R or its downstream PP2A/AKT signaling may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for managing persistent postoperative pain caused by preoperative sleep deprivation in male mice.

secondary.title: A pKa-Guided BBB-Permeable NIR Fluorescent Probe for Tracking Lipid Droplets in Microglia with Neuroinflammation and Alzheimer's Disease.
secondary.abstract: Abnormal accumulation of lipid droplets (LDs), accompanied by altered microenvironmental polarity within the microglia, is closely associated with neuroinflammation and also has been increasingly recognized as an early and dynamic indicator of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Herein, a LD-targeting polarity-sensitive blood-brain barrier (BBB)-permeable near-infrared (NIR) probe, BTDN, was screened by tuning the electron-donating substituents to modulate the pKa values of benzothiadiazole-based derivatives. Endowed with the donor-acceptor-donor (D1-A-D2) architecture and strong intramolecular charge-transfer (ICT) characteristics, the BTDN probe exhibited high sensitivity to polarity change. The BTDN probe displayed suitable physicochemical properties such as a pKa of 7.47 and lipophilicity with a log P of 3.72 for favorable BBB-penetrating efficiency with a permeability percentage of 24.23%. In addition, the BTDN probe showed advantages for fluorescence imaging including NIR emission from 643 to 770 nm with the increased polarity, Stokes shift larger than 308 nm, comparable two-photon absorption capacity with an absorption cross-section of 10 GM at 870 nm, good biocompatibility, and robust photostability. Using this multifunctional BTDN probe, the dynamic fluorescence imaging of accumulation behaviors of LDs in BV2 microglia with neuroinflammation was performed, demonstrating that LD formation may serve as a potential biomarker for neuroinflammation. Furthermore, overproduced LDs within microglia were directly observed in vivo and in tissue sections from the brains of AD mice. This work not only provides an imaging tool for dynamically characterizing LD accumulation in microglia but also provides insights into the relationship between LD accumulation in microglia and AD pathogenesis.

secondary.title: J-Aggregation-Reshaped pKa in a Spirocyclic BODIPY Enables Ratiometric Lysosomal pH Sensing and Super-Resolution Imaging.
secondary.abstract: Ratiometric fluorescent pH probes typically rely on complex intramolecular energy/charge transfer, rendering the design strategies increasingly rigid. We report a conceptually distinct ratiometric probe based on pH-driven J-aggregate disassembly utilizing a spirocyclic BODIPY platform. Strategic installation of β-Cl and α-3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenylvinyl substituents on BODIPY synergistically drives J-aggregate formation via directional X···π, F···H, and π···π interactions. The resulting J-aggregates and the corresponding monomer displayed markedly different pKa values (4.69 vs. 7.54, ΔpKa = 2.85). As pH increases, spirocyclization is triggered, driving the cooperative disassembly of the J-aggregates, while monomer emission remains constant, thereby enabling a robust ratiometric readout (I714/I654) with excellent reversibility. This supramolecular J-aggregate enables quantitative lysosomal pH detection in cells, diagnosis of acute gastritis in mice, and self-blinking super-resolution lysosomal imaging without exogenous additives. This work establishes a new paradigm for ratiometric probe design via aggregation control and stimulus-responsive supramolecular disassembly.

Using the adhesion GPCR GPR64/ADGRG2 as a model system, we show that ligand activation engages two spatially distinct G-protein pathways that are not just additive but functionally opposed: plasma membrane G13/RhoA activation and Gs/cAMP production that persists from endosomes following receptor internalization. The endosomal cAMP pool actively overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation, resulting in net RhoA inactivation, an outcome that is completely reversed by pharmacological blockade of endocytosis or endosomal Gs inactivation. In parathyroid cells, where GPR64 is highly expressed, this endosomal signal dominance suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion independently of extracellular Ca2+ levels. These findings support a model in which the subcellular compartment, rather than pathway identity, determines the dominant signal and the overall cellular response of a single activated receptor, with implications for understanding the complexity of GPCR signaling.

best.title: Spatial mTOR biology: From organelle localization to biomolecular condensates and metabolic control.
best.abstract: The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) coordinates cell growth, metabolism, protein synthesis, autophagy, and survival by integrating nutrient availability, growth factors, energy status, mechanical cues, and cellular stress. Beyond classical biochemical cascades, mTOR signaling specificity is fundamentally governed by subcellular localization, temporal recruitment, and microenvironmental context. This review synthesizes current insights into the spatial architecture of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) across lysosomes, endosomes, plasma-membrane microdomains, organelle contact sites, neuronal processes, the nucleus, and biomolecular condensates. We examine how physical principles-including membrane composition and curvature, molecular confinement, macromolecular crowding, scaffold-mediated multivalent interactions, organelle positioning, mechanical tension, and localized translation-dictate signaling outcomes. Furthermore, we contrast membrane-anchored molecular assemblies with three-dimensional biomolecular condensates, detailing their interplay during stress adaptation. Spatial constraints in specialized cell geometries, such as neuronal compartments and developing tissues, illustrate how identical signaling machinery yields divergent functional outputs under altered diffusion environments. We also evaluate how advances in spatial multi-omics and super-resolution imaging extend these subcellular paradigms to tissue-scale heterogeneity. Finally, we highlight major translational hurdles, including the trade-off between spatial resolution and dynamic temporal tracking in current technologies, as well as the inability of conventional pharmacotherapies to selectively target discrete subcellular mTOR pools. Establishing spatial organization as a primary determinant of mTOR signaling clarifies context-dependent physiological outputs and provides a roadmap for developing next-generation spatially targeted therapeutics.

best.title: Singapore grouper iridovirus VP018 exploits FTR86 to promote viral replication through Tollip-mediated degradation of the STING-TBK1 axis.
best.abstract: Members of the tripartite motif (TRIM) family have been demonstrated to exert crucial roles in immune defense against pathogens. However, functions of the fish-specific TRIM subfamily (FTR), which lacks mammalian orthologues, remains poorly understood. In the current study, we investigated the potential roles of grouper FTR86 (EcFTR86) on innate immune response and its actions during fish virus infection. EcFTR86 was found to localize to lysosomes, and its transcription was significantly up-regulated in grouper spleen cells upon Singapore grouper iridovirus (SGIV) infection. Notably, the exogenous expression of EcFTR86 markedly enhanced SGIV replication, whereas knockdown of endogenous EcFTR86 significantly attenuated viral infection, demonstrating that EcFTR86 functions as a pro-viral factor against virus infection. EcFTR86 negatively regulated type I interferon signaling triggered by STING-TBK1 and interacted with the key molecules of STING-TBKl axis. Mechanistically, EcFTR86 degraded STING or TBK1 via an autophagy-lysosome-dependent pathway. Moreover, autophagic cargo receptor Tollip was identified to interact with EcFTR86, and was involved in EcFTR86-mediated degradation of STING or TBK1. In addition, EcFTR86 was verified to interact with SGIV viral proteins, including VP018 and VP075, whereas only VP018 exploited EcFTR86 to accelerate the degradation effects on STING and TBK1, thereby abrogating the interferon response. Collectively, our findings firstly showed that FTR86 functioned as a negative regulator of interferon response, and was exploited by fish iridoviral proteins to promote viral replication via Tollip-mediated autophagic degradation of the STING-TBK1 axis.

best.title: PDE2A is involved in negative emotional behaviors via the cAMP-PKA signaling pathway in the SPS&S model.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is characterized by negative affective symptoms, including anxiety, depression, anhedonia, and fear. The molecular mechanisms underlying these symptoms remain poorly understood. Phosphodiesterase 2A (PDE2A), a regulator of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) signaling, has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to investigate the role of the PDE2A-cAMP-protein kinase A (PKA) signaling pathway in negative emotional behaviors induced by traumatic stress. METHODS: Transcriptomic datasets were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes and enriched pathways. A rat PTSD model was established using single prolonged stress combined with foot shocks (SPS&S). Behavioral tests were performed, and PDE2A-cAMP-PKA signaling alterations in the amygdala were examined. The effects of PDE2A inhibitor Hcyb1 and the PKA inhibitor H89 were evaluated. RESULTS: Bioinformatics analysis identified PDE2A as a hub gene associated with PTSD, with significant enrichment of the cAMP signaling pathway. SPS&S rats exhibited anxiety-, depression-like behaviors, and anhedonia, accompanied by increased PDE2A expression and reduced cAMP and phosphorylated PKA (p-PKA) levels in the amygdala. Hcyb1 treatment alleviated behavioral deficits, decreased PDE2A expression, and restored cAMP and p-PKA signaling. H89 blocked p-PKA activation and partially reversed the behavioral benefits of Hcyb1. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that amygdala PDE2A-cAMP-PKA signaling is associated with negative emotional behaviors in the SPS&S model. PDE2A inhibition may ameliorate behavioral deficits through PKA-related signaling. However, the peripheral blood transcriptomic data, lack of direct PDE2A activity and cAMP/cGMP measurements, and limited biochemical validation constrain mechanistic interpretation. Further studies using brain-derived datasets and comprehensive biochemical approaches are warranted.

best.title: Autophagy- and Ferroptosis-Related Responses and SIRT1/mTOR Signaling in Nucleus Pulposus Cells Under Fluid Shear Stress.
best.abstract: INTRODUCTION: To characterize duration-dependent responses of Nucleus Pulposus Cells (NPCs) to Fluid Shear Stress (FSS) and identify candidate pathways associated with autophagy- and ferroptosis-related changes relevant to Intervertebral Disc Degeneration (IVDD). METHODS: Primary NPCs isolated from male Sprague-Dawley rats were exposed to 12 dyn/cm² FSS for 0, 30, 60, 90, or 120 minutes. Cellular morphology, proliferation, apoptosis, mitochondrial function, autophagy-related structures, and protein expression were assessed. Chloroquine, erastin, and ferrostatin-1 were used in pharmacological comparisons. Network pharmacology, Mendelian randomization, transcriptomic analyses, machine learning, human single-cell analysis, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations supported candidate prioritization. RESULTS: Among the conditions tested, 60 min of FSS produced the most favorable cellular response, with improved proliferation and reduced apoptosis. This response was accompanied by increased autophagy-related structures, increased abundance of GPX4 and SLC7A11, and decreased abundance of ACSL4. A longer exposure of 120 minutes produced an adverse response. Network analysis identified 12 candidate hub genes, and integrated transcriptomic screening identified eight IVDD-associated candidates: ACSL1, KDM6B, MAPK14, TLR4, ALOX5, ATG7, PHF21A, and SIRT1. Human single-cell analysis provided their cellular expression context. SIRT1 was the only panel member assessed experimentally by Western blotting under FSS. Its abundance increased, and mTOR phosphorylation decreased after 60 min, with the opposite pattern after 120 minutes. Docking and simulations characterized predicted ligand-protein interactions involving SIRT1/mTOR. DISCUSSION: The cellular and computational findings support SIRT1/mTOR signaling as a candidate pathway linking the observed responses, while functional dependence and autophagy- ferroptosis coupling require validation. CONCLUSION: FSS elicited duration-dependent responses in NPCs, providing a basis for targeted mechanistic investigation and future phenotype-based screening relevant to IVDD.

best.title: Preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal cord D2R expression via the PP2A/AKT-dependent NMDA receptor phosphorylation.
best.abstract: Preoperative sleep deprivation (SD) is known to exacerbate postoperative pain, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a male mouse model of 48-h continuous SD followed by incisional surgery, we found that SD alone induced transient mechanical hyperalgesia, and when combined with surgery (SI group) it significantly aggravated and prolonged postoperative pain recovery until day 10. On postoperative day 7, SI mice showed marked downregulation of spinal dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) expression and decreased spinal dopamine concentration. D2R was predominantly expressed on spinal glutamatergic neurons. Overexpression of D2R on these neurons via intrathecal AAV injection effectively alleviated the prolonged hyperalgesia, normalizing pain sensitivity by day 7. Mechanistically, D2R downregulation led to increased phosphorylation of NMDA receptor subunits (p-NR1 and p-NR2B) without altering total NMDA receptor levels. Co-immunoprecipitation revealed an interaction between D2R and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A). SI mice exhibited decreased PP2A expression but increased p-AKT, p-GSK3β, and β-catenin, indicating activation of the PP2A/AKT signaling pathway, which were reversed by D2R overexpression. Furthermore, pharmacological activation of PP2A with DT-061 not only downregulated p-AKT, p-GSK3β, β-catenin, p-NR1 and p-NR2B, but also produced significant analgesia in SI mice. Collectively, these results demonstrate that preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal D2R on glutamatergic neurons, which disinhibits the PP2A/AKT pathway and enhances NMDA receptor phosphorylation. Targeting D2R or its downstream PP2A/AKT signaling may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for managing persistent postoperative pain caused by preoperative sleep deprivation in male mice.

best.title: VPS35 Regulates Microglial Lipid Droplet Accumulation in Parkinson's Disease via Rab7.
best.abstract: Microglial dysfunction and aberrant lipid metabolism are emerging as key contributors to Parkinson's disease (PD) pathogenesis. However, the specific role and regulation of lipid droplets (LDs) within microglia remain poorly defined. In this study, we employed MPTP- and LPS-induced PD mouse models and an in vitro system utilizing astrocyte-conditioned medium to model disease-relevant lipid stress and found enhanced LD accumulation in microglia. VPS35 expression was decreased in microglia, correlating with elevated microglial LD levels in PD mouse models. We then performed genetic manipulations (knockdown and overexpression) of VPS35, including the PD-associated D620N mutant, in primary microglia and assessed LD accumulation, phagocytic function, inflammatory responses, and integrated stress pathways. We showed that VPS35 knockdown exacerbated the accumulation of LDs in microglia. Conversely, VPS35 overexpression ameliorated LD formation, improved phagocytic function, and reduced inflammatory and integrated stress responses in microglia. The PD-related VPS35[D620N] mutation abolished these protective effects. We further found that VPS35 interacts with Rab7 to maintain lysosomal function, and the D620N mutation disrupts this interaction, leading to defective LD clearance. Our findings reveal VPS35 dysfunction as a key pathogenic mechanism in PD, where the D620N mutation disrupts microglial lipid handling to promote disease progression, thereby nominating VPS35 restoration as a promising therapeutic strategy.

best.title: A pKa-Guided BBB-Permeable NIR Fluorescent Probe for Tracking Lipid Droplets in Microglia with Neuroinflammation and Alzheimer's Disease.
best.abstract: Abnormal accumulation of lipid droplets (LDs), accompanied by altered microenvironmental polarity within the microglia, is closely associated with neuroinflammation and also has been increasingly recognized as an early and dynamic indicator of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Herein, a LD-targeting polarity-sensitive blood-brain barrier (BBB)-permeable near-infrared (NIR) probe, BTDN, was screened by tuning the electron-donating substituents to modulate the pKa values of benzothiadiazole-based derivatives. Endowed with the donor-acceptor-donor (D1-A-D2) architecture and strong intramolecular charge-transfer (ICT) characteristics, the BTDN probe exhibited high sensitivity to polarity change. The BTDN probe displayed suitable physicochemical properties such as a pKa of 7.47 and lipophilicity with a log P of 3.72 for favorable BBB-penetrating efficiency with a permeability percentage of 24.23%. In addition, the BTDN probe showed advantages for fluorescence imaging including NIR emission from 643 to 770 nm with the increased polarity, Stokes shift larger than 308 nm, comparable two-photon absorption capacity with an absorption cross-section of 10 GM at 870 nm, good biocompatibility, and robust photostability. Using this multifunctional BTDN probe, the dynamic fluorescence imaging of accumulation behaviors of LDs in BV2 microglia with neuroinflammation was performed, demonstrating that LD formation may serve as a potential biomarker for neuroinflammation. Furthermore, overproduced LDs within microglia were directly observed in vivo and in tissue sections from the brains of AD mice. This work not only provides an imaging tool for dynamically characterizing LD accumulation in microglia but also provides insights into the relationship between LD accumulation in microglia and AD pathogenesis.

best.title: J-Aggregation-Reshaped pKa in a Spirocyclic BODIPY Enables Ratiometric Lysosomal pH Sensing and Super-Resolution Imaging.
best.abstract: Ratiometric fluorescent pH probes typically rely on complex intramolecular energy/charge transfer, rendering the design strategies increasingly rigid. We report a conceptually distinct ratiometric probe based on pH-driven J-aggregate disassembly utilizing a spirocyclic BODIPY platform. Strategic installation of β-Cl and α-3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenylvinyl substituents on BODIPY synergistically drives J-aggregate formation via directional X···π, F···H, and π···π interactions. The resulting J-aggregates and the corresponding monomer displayed markedly different pKa values (4.69 vs. 7.54, ΔpKa = 2.85). As pH increases, spirocyclization is triggered, driving the cooperative disassembly of the J-aggregates, while monomer emission remains constant, thereby enabling a robust ratiometric readout (I714/I654) with excellent reversibility. This supramolecular J-aggregate enables quantitative lysosomal pH detection in cells, diagnosis of acute gastritis in mice, and self-blinking super-resolution lysosomal imaging without exogenous additives. This work establishes a new paradigm for ratiometric probe design via aggregation control and stimulus-responsive supramolecular disassembly.

primary.title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
primary.abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

primary.title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
primary.abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

primary.title: Mechanism of Autophagic Extracellular Vesicles Revealed.
primary.abstract: Recent work by Mao and colleagues identifies a distinct class of small extracellular vesicles, termed autophagic extracellular vesicles (AEVs), generated from amphisomes upon autophagy induction. In this commentary, we discuss how this study provides important mechanistic insight into the coupling between autophagy and secretion. AEVs are molecularly and functionally distinct from canonical exosomes, being enriched in autophagy-related components such as LC3 and p62, and dependent on core ATG machinery for their biogenesis. Notably, their secretion is enhanced by autophagy induction and contributes to intercellular communication, particularly in the context of viral infection. These findings position amphisomes as critical sorting hubs that direct cargo toward either degradation or secretion, thereby integrating autophagic and endolysosomal pathways. We further highlight how these results intersect with prior evidence implicating SNARE-dependent mechanisms, including VAMP7 and stress-responsive regulators such as GRASP55, in unconventional secretion. Finally, we discuss key unresolved questions, particularly the mechanisms underlying the generation of small intraluminal vesicles within amphisomes and the role of ESCRT machinery in this process. Overall, the identification of AEVs adds a new layer of complexity to extracellular vesicle biology and opens new avenues for understanding how autophagy contributes to intercellular signaling in health and disease.

primary.title: Recessive variants in ESCRT-II component VPS25 alter vesicular transport and small extracellular vesicle processing in lethal neonatal encephalopathy.
primary.abstract: BACKGROUND: The role of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), such as exosomes, in cell-to-cell communication is increasingly recognized. Both during development and postnatally, sEVs have been shown to mediate a multitude of essential functions in the central nervous system. While abnormal sEV biogenesis has been observed in a number of neurodevelopmental disorders, a causal link has been largely lacking. METHODS: We clinically evaluated five families in which newborns presented with a novel neonatal-onset encephalopathy. Positional mapping, exome sequencing, and trio exome sequencing were utilized to identify the underlying genetic variants. Additionally, we utilized Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants and performed cellular assays to evaluate ESCRT-II interaction, cellular localization, and sEV secretion and cargo capacities. RESULTS: The observed lethal encephalopathy is characterized by severe hypotonia, brain anomalies, and epilepsy. In families 1, 4, and 5 (multiplex consanguineous), we identified a novel homozygous missense variant in VPS25 as the likely candidate. Family 2 comprises a simplex case with two missense variants in trans in VPS25, one of which impacts the same residue as in the other three families. Family 3 also comprises a simplex case where we revealed a homozygous missense variant. VPS25 is an essential component of ESCRT-II, itself required for sEV biogenesis. We show that Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants recapitulate the developmental brain malformation observed in patients. We also show that mutant VPS25 is associated with abnormal ESCRT-II interaction, abnormal cellular localization, and highly abnormal sEVs. Specifically, mutant cells displayed engorged multivesicular bodies and were significantly defective in their capacity to secrete sEVs such as exosomes, while secreted sEVs contained altered cargo, lacking vital proteins for axon protection and maintenance. CONCLUSIONS: We report a novel neurodevelopmental disorder caused by biallelic hypomorphic variants in VPS25. The consistent impact of these variants on sEV biogenesis suggests a potential pathomechanism. While future cases will further delineate the phenotypic spectrum, these findings offer a new perspective on abnormal sEVs as drivers of human neurodevelopmental disorders.

primary.title: Glycoprotein-induced phase separation drives unconventional secretion of galectin-3.
primary.abstract: The mechanism of unconventional protein secretion remains an unresolved issue. Here, we describe an unconventional protein secretion pathway for galectin-3 that is mediated by phase separation and condensation. Using four lysosomal damage models, we observed a rapid, pronounced release of galectin-3 in large, non-exosomal particles. This secretion is driven by glycoprotein-induced galectin-3 phase separation and is independent of pyroptosis and secretory autophagy. During phase separation, the S-face of galectin-3 carbohydrate recognition domain binds glycoproteins that triggers galectin-3 N-terminal tail release and condensation. These condensates then recruit ALG-2 via the exposed N-terminal tail. ALG-2 directs the condensates to the endoplasmic reticulum-late endosome interface. After translocation into late endosomes, galectin-3 condensates are secreted into the extracellular milieu by SNARE-dependent vesicular transport. This mechanism of exporting phase-separated protein condensates may serve as a clean-up response to membrane damage.

primary.title: A protective role for APP in nuclear waste clearance via lysosomal exocytosis.
primary.abstract: Amyloid precursor protein (APP) is widely known for its role in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis through its proteolytic processing into amyloid-β peptides. However, its physiological functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we uncover a protective role for full-length APP in facilitating the disposal of nuclear-derived debris under genotoxic stress. In both cultured cells and in vivo mouse models, loss of APP leads to nuclear waste accumulation, increased inflammation, and cell death, whereas APP overexpression mitigates these effects. Mechanistically, we show that APP supports the extracellular release of nuclear waste material through lysosomal exocytosis. APP mutants associated with familial AD fail to mediate this process. Consistently, human AD brain tissue exhibits abnormal nuclear morphology, accumulation of nuclear waste in the cytoplasm, and reduced APP levels per neuron. These findings highlight a conserved cellular mechanism by which APP contributes to nuclear and cellular homeostasis, and suggest that impaired nuclear waste clearance may represent an underappreciated contributor to neurodegeneration.

primary.title: GPNMB is a biomarker for lysosomal dysfunction and is secreted via LRRK2-modulated lysosomal exocytosis.
primary.abstract: Genome-wide association studies have identified Glycoprotein Nmb (GPNMB) as a risk factor for Parkinson's disease. The risk allele increases GPNMB transcription and GPNMB protein levels in the CSF highlighting GPMNB as a potential biomarker for Parkinson's disease. However, a lack of knowledge of GPNMB's function and mechanism of secretion has hindered an interpretation of secreted GPNMB levels. In this study, we assessed the mechanism of GPNMB secretion by macrophages, the primary cell type expressing GPNMB in the brain. We show that GPNMB is secreted in response to lysosomal stress via lysosomal exocytosis and highlight the Parkinson's disease risk factor LRRK2 as a strong modulator of GPNMB secretion.

primary.title: Autophagic extracellular vesicles: a distinct secretory route linking autophagy to extracellular communication.
primary.abstract: Macroautophagy/autophagy is classically defined as a degradative pathway that delivers cytoplasmic material to lysosomes. However, accumulating evidence indicates that autophagy can also support unconventional secretion. A recent study identifies a previously unrecognized subtype of small extracellular vesicles termed autophagic extracellular vesicles (AEVs). These vesicles originate from amphisomes formed by the fusion of autophagosomes with multivesicular bodies and are characterized by a size below 100 nm together with the presence of autophagic cargos, ESCRT-III components and RAB13. Importantly, biogenesis of AEVs is distinct from that of classical exosomes, which requires specific components of the ESCRT III complex and the GTPase RAB27A. The further finding that enterovirus can exploit AEVs to infect receptor-negative cells, thereby expanding viral tropism, suggests that secretory autophagy serves as a pivotal mechanism driving pathogen dissemination. This work provides the conceptual framework of extracellular vesicle heterogeneity and positions secretory autophagy as an important contributor to intercellular communication.

primary.title: MYO18B promotes lysosomal exocytosis by facilitating focal adhesion maturation.
primary.abstract: Many cancer cells exhibit increased amounts of paucimannose glycans, which are truncated N-glycan structures rarely found in mammals. Paucimannosidic proteins are proposedly generated within lysosomes and exposed on the cell surface through a yet uncertain mechanism. In this study, we revealed that paucimannosidic proteins are produced by lysosomal glycosidases and secreted via lysosomal exocytosis. Interestingly, lysosomal exocytosis preferentially occurred in the vicinity of focal adhesions, protein complexes connecting the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix. Through genome-wide knockout screening, we identified that MYO18B, an actin crosslinker, is required for focal adhesion maturation, facilitating lysosomal exocytosis and the release of paucimannosidic lysosomal proteins to the extracellular milieu. Moreover, a mechanosensitive cation channel PIEZO1 locally activated at focal adhesions imports Ca2+ necessary for lysosome-plasma membrane fusion. Collectively, our study unveiled an intimate relationship between lysosomal exocytosis and focal adhesion, shedding light on the unexpected interplay between lysosomal activities and cellular mechanosensing.

primary.title: RYR:ATP6V0A1 complexes couple ER-lysosome contact sites to dynamic autophagy control.
primary.abstract: Ryanodine receptors (RYRs) are ER-resident Ca2+-release channels enriched in excitable cells, including neurons. RYR hyperactivity is implicated in early pathogenesis of disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), which is associated with impaired autophagy. We recently uncovered a mechanism linking RYR activity to lysosome availability for autophagy. RYRs localize to ER-lysosome contact sites via direct binding to ATP6V0A1, a V-ATPase subunit that also suppresses RYR-mediated Ca2+ release. In human iPSC-derived cortical neurons, spontaneous RYR activity promotes lysosomal secretion, depleting the intracellular lysosomal pool and inhibiting autophagic flux. RYR inhibition promotes ERlysosome contacts, limits lysosomal secretion, and restores lysosome availability for autophagosome fusion and cargo degradation (including APP). Conversely, disrupting the RYR:ATP6V0A1 interaction using a RYR-derived protein fragment serving as a "decoy" for ATP6V0A1 evokes RYR hyperactivity and stimulates lysosomal secretion. In this Punctum, we discuss how this RYR2:ATP6V0A1 "contact-site hub" may be perturbed in disease and highlight open questions on how lysosomes decode RYR-derived Ca2+ signals.

primary.title: Molecular mechanisms underlying p62-dependent secretion of the Alzheimer-associated ubiquitin variant UBB+1.
primary.abstract: UBB+1, a ubiquitin variant protein resulting from a frameshift in the ubiquitin-B gene, is a pathological hallmark of Alzheimer disease (AD). At the cellular level, UBB+1 disrupts the ubiquitin-proteasome system while inducing autophagy. Notably, UBB+1 itself is secreted via autophagosome-like vesicles. Here, we demonstrate that UBB+1 can be removed from the cell by degradative and secretory autophagy. Sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1)/p62 functions as a pivotal ubiquitin receptor for UBB+1, recognizing its ubiquitin domain and facilitating loading into autophagosomes. Oligomerization of SQSTM1/p62 was critical to isolate UBB+1 in bodies preventing its aggregation. Intriguingly, both gain- and loss-of-function SQSTM1/p62 suppressed UBB+1 secretion, causing intracellular retention: SQSTM1/p62 knockout led to UBB+1 accumulation in insoluble aggregates, while its overexpression promoted the formation of p62-UBB+1 bodies. We further identified distinct roles for SNARE-mediated membrane fusion in secretory autophagy of UBB+1. Specifically, the R-SNARE SEC22B and the Q-SNAREs Syntaxin-4 and SNAP23 participated in UBB+1 exocytosis. Disruption of SEC22B impaired the fusion of UBB+1-containing autophagosomes with the plasma membrane, reducing UBB+1 secretion without affecting its intracellular turnover. Inhibition of lysosomes partially stabilized UBB+1 indicating that degradation and secretion are complementary processes that determine the fate of UBB+1. This study elucidates the dual roles of autophagy in managing neurotoxic proteins, highlighting SQSTM1/p62 as a key mediator of UBB+1 trafficking and secretion. Although ubiquitin typically acts as a degradation signal, our findings reveal a rare instance of a ubiquitin-related protein driving secretory autophagy. These findings advance our understanding of cellular mechanisms underlying the clearance of misfolded proteins in neurodegenerative diseases.

primary.title: Impaired MAPT/tau-secretory lysosomes are linked to cognitive vulnerability in Alzheimer patients.
primary.abstract: MAPT/tau proteins propagate between brain regions in a prion-like manner, driving the onset and progression of dementia in Alzheimer disease (AD). However, the basis for variability in dementia progression among AD patients remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that cognitively resilient AD patients, characterized by reduced MAPT/tau pathology, maintain lysosomal integrity, whereas cognitively vulnerable patients, exhibiting greater MAPT/tau burden, display lysosomal dysfunction. Lysosomes in cognitively vulnerable AD brains contain partially digested, seed-competent MAPT/tau species composed mainly of the amyloidogenic core with degraded peripheral regions. These pathogenic MAPT/tau forms are secreted via lysosomal exocytosis, facilitating MAPT/tau propagation and contributing to cognitive decline. Cognitively vulnerable female AD patients show increased lysosome-mediated MAPT/tau secretion relative to their male counterparts. Our findings suggest that lysosomal dysfunction, marked by altered protein expression, pH dysregulation, and MAPT/tau accumulation, underlies the heterogeneity in dementia severity. Targeting lysosomal exocytosis and the amyloidogenic core of MAPT/tau fibrils offer a promising therapeutic avenue to mitigate MAPT/tau pathology and promote cognitive resilience in AD and related dementias.Abbreviation: AD: Alzheimer disease, LAMP1; lysosomal associated membrane protein 1, NFT: neurofibrillary tangles; MAPT: microtubule associated protein tau; PHF: paired helical filaments; TIRF: total internal reflection fluorescence; TARDBP/TDP-43:TAR DNA binding protein.

primary.title: hucMSC-derived exosomes rescue cognitive impairment and Alzheimer-like pathology in APP/PS1 mice via metabolic remodeling.
primary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder driven by β-amyloid (Aβ) deposition, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress and metabolic dysregulation, with the latter as a central pathological hub. hucMSC-derived exosomes (hucMSC-exosomes) show therapeutic potential for AD, but their metabolic remodeling mechanisms remain unclear. We combined behavioral tests, pathological assays and untargeted metabolomics to investigate the neuroprotective effects and mechanisms of hucMSC-exosomes in APP/PS1 AD mice. Seven-month-old male APP/PS1 mice were randomly divided into AD-vehicle and AD-hucMSC-exosome groups, with age-matched C57BL/6 mice as wild-type controls. All mice received tail vein injections for 6 weeks. Morris Water Maze tests revealed that hucMSC-exosomes significantly improved spatial learning and memory in AD mice. Pathological analyses confirmed that hucMSC-exosomes reduced cerebral Aβ deposition, suppressed hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and restored antioxidant capacity (SOD, GPx, GSH/GSSG). Untargeted metabolomic analysis of brain tissues revealed that 6 primary carbon, 8 primary nitrogen and 3 secondary metabolites were common differential metabolites across the two comparison cohorts (AD-vehicle vs. WT, AD-hucMSC-exosome vs. AD-vehicle), and their aberrant expression in AD mice was all reversed by hucMSC-exosomes. KEGG enrichment analysis showed that hucMSC-exosomes largely reversed dysregulated metabolic pathways in AD, including lipid, amino acid, nucleotide metabolism and autophagy/mitophagy. Collectively, hucMSC-exosomes ameliorate AD pathological phenotypes and cognitive deficits, an effect accompanied by metabolic homeostasis remodeling through cascades of reduced Aβ deposition, suppressed neuroinflammation and alleviated oxidative stress. Metabolic remodeling represents a prominent correlative feature of the neuroprotective effects of hucMSC-exosomes, providing candidate molecular targets for metabolically targeted AD therapy.

primary.title: Inactive ryanodine receptors sustain lysosomal availability for autophagy by promoting ER-lysosomal contact site formation.
primary.abstract: Lysosomal and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ release mutually influence each other's functions. Recent work revealed that ER-located ryanodine receptor(s) (RyR(s)) Ca2+ release channels suppress autophagosome turnover by the lysosomes. In familial Alzheimer's disease, inhibiting RyR hyperactivity restored autophagic flux by normalizing lysosomal vacuolar H+-ATPase (vATPase) levels. However, the mechanisms by which RyRs control lysosomal function and how this involves the vATPase remain unknown. Here, we show that RyRs interact with the ATP6v0a1 subunit of the vATPase, contributing to ER-lysosomal contact site formation. This interaction suppresses RyR-mediated Ca²⁺ release, leading to reduced lysosomal exocytosis. Pharmacological inhibition of RyR activity mimics these effects on lysosomal exocytosis. Retaining lysosomes inside cells via RyR inhibition increases ER-lysosomal contact site formation, rendering lysosomes more available for autophagic flux. In summary, these findings establish RyR/ATP6v0a1 complexes as ER-lysosomal tethers that dynamically and Ca2+ dependently regulate the intracellular availability of lysosomes to participate in autophagic flux.

secondary.title: Serum Exosomes from Subacute Phase Post-cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Promote Microglial Pro-inflammatory Phenotype Polarization and Exacerbate Blood-Brain Barrier Disruption in Mice.
secondary.abstract: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) restores circulation but induces cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury characterized by blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption and microglial-mediated neuroinflammation. Exosomes circulate systemically following CPR, yet their temporal profiles and specific roles remain poorly understood. C57BL/6 mice (n = 5/group) underwent asphyxial cardiac arrest and CPR. BBB permeability was assessed longitudinally (3 h to 14 d) using Evans blue extravasation. Serum exosomes were isolated at 1 d and 3 d post-CPR and characterized. To determine immunomodulatory effects, exosomes were administered via intracerebroventricular injection into recipient mice, and BBB integrity and microglial polarization (CD86, CD206) were evaluated by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry. Additionally, primary cultures of microglia cells isolated from CPR mice were exposed to exosomes in vitro (n = 3/group), and pro-inflammatory phenotype/anti-inflammatory phenotype markers and inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, iNOS, TGF-β, Arg1, IL-10) were quantified. CPR induced transient BBB disruption peaking at 3 d post-resuscitation. Serum exosomes isolated at both 1 d and 3 d exhibited characteristic cup-shaped morphology. Intracerebroventricular administration of post-CPR exosomes significantly exacerbated BBB leakage and skewed microglial polarization toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype (elevated CD86⁺; reduced CD206⁺), with 3-day exosomes eliciting more potent detrimental effects than 1-day exosomes. In vitro, exposure to 3-day exosomes similarly produced stronger pro-inflammatory transcriptional responses and increased nitric oxide (NO) production compared with 1-day exosomes. Serum exosomes derived from post-CPR mice exhibit pro-inflammatory activity, aggravating BBB disruption and promoting microglial pro-inflammatory phenotype polarization upon central delivery. These findings suggest that circulating exosomes may contribute to post-resuscitation neuroinflammatory injury, and highlight exosome-related pathways as candidate targets worthy of further investigation.

secondary.title: Exosomes derived from N2 neutrophils reprogram the immune microenvironment to promote spinal cord injury repair.
secondary.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Spinal cord injury induces irreversible neurological impairments via secondary pathological cascades dominated by excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, and neuronal apoptosis. As the first-responder immune cells following spinal cord trauma, neutrophils can acquire an N2-like reparative phenotype, yet direct neutrophil transplantation is hampered by poor cellular survival. Exosomes, nanoscale cell-secreted vesicles with low immunogenicity and favourable biostability, constitute promising cell-free candidates for regenerative therapy. Nevertheless, the therapeutic potential of exosomes derived from N2-polarized neutrophils remains poorly defined for spinal cord injury repair. METHODS: Murine bone-marrow-derived neutrophils were polarized toward the N2 phenotype using interleukin-6 (IL-6) and granulocyte-colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), with non-polarized neutrophils set as the control group. Exosomes were purified by ultracentrifugation and comprehensively characterized by transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and western blotting. In vitro functional assays were performed to evaluate macrophage phenotypic reprogramming, neuronal axonal regeneration, and neuronal apoptosis. A modified Allen's weight-drop mouse spinal cord injury model was adopted for in vivo intervention. Motor functional recovery was evaluated using the Basso Mouse Scale and gait analysis, while neural tissue repair was assessed via immunofluorescence staining. RESULTS: Exosomes derived from N2-polarized neutrophils (N2-exos) exhibited canonical exosomal hallmarks. In vitro, these exosomes drove lipopolysaccharide-primed macrophages to switch to an anti-inflammatory reparative phenotype, alleviated oxidative-stress-mediated axonal injury, and suppressed neuronal apoptosis. In vivo administration of N2-exos markedly enhanced hind-limb motor performance and gait coordination, and facilitated axonal regeneration across the injury epicenter. CONCLUSIONS: N2-exos remodel the post-traumatic immune microenvironment and confer combined neuroprotective and axon regenerative effects. This cell-free modality represents a promising therapeutic candidate for regenerative interventions against spinal cord injury.
