secondary.title: Evaluation of the effect of p38γ gene delivery using exosomes derived from mesenchymal stem cells on Alzheimer's rat model.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dementia, memory loss, and cognitive decline. This study investigated the therapeutic potential of delivering the p38γ gene via exosomes derived from adipose-derived stem cells (ADSC-Exos) in a rat model of streptozotocin (STZ)-induced AD. METHODS AND RESULTS: After the AD model was established, the rats were administered via intraperitoneal injections of p38γ, Exo, or p38γ-loaded ADSC-Exo (Exo+p38γ). Cognitive and memory assessments were performed via novel object recognition (NOR), passive avoidance, elevated plus-maze (EPM), and the Barnes maze (BM). Histological techniques were used to evaluate cell density and beta-amyloid (Aβ) plaque accumulation, while quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT‒PCR) was used to measure the transcription levels of neuronal nuclei (NeuN), glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), nerve growth factor (NGF), and sex-determining region Y-box 2 (SOX2). Additionally, the expression of GDNF, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), SOX2, and malondialdehyde (MDA) was analyzed via an ELISA kit. The Exo and Exo+p38γ groups demonstrated significant improvements in STZ-induced memory deficits across various assessments. However, no significant differences in the protein expression levels of GDNF, BDNF, SOX2, and MDA or the gene expression levels of SOX2, NeuN, GDNF, and NGF were detected between STZ-treated rats that received Exos+p38γ and those that received Exos alone. CONCLUSIONS: Taken together, this study demonstrates that ADSC-derived exosomes effectively improve cognitive deficits in an AD rat model; Although Exo+p38γ was associated with a significant increase in SOX2 gene expression compared with the AD group, the direct comparison between Exo+p38γ and ADSC-Exos did not demonstrate a statistically significant additional effect.

secondary.title: TRPML3 and TRPML1/3 differentially regulate unconventional MIF secretion through TMED10 and secretory autophagy.
secondary.abstract: The intracellular Ca2+ channel TRPML3 regulates autophagy by multimerization in a phosphoinositide (PIP)-dependent manner; however, its role in other membrane dynamics remains unclear. Here, we report that TRPML3 regulates type III unconventional protein secretion (UcPS) through two distinct pathways: TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy. TRPML3 interacted with TMED10 and macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), a signal sequence-lacking pleiotropic cytokine whose secretion mechanism has remained undefined. We found that cytosolic MIF is transported to membrane-enclosed compartments through TMED10-channeled UcPS. Notably, TRPML3, but not TRPML1 or TRPML1/3, promoted TMED10 oligomerization, thereby enhancing MIF secretion in a Ca2+-independent manner. Furthermore, once translocated into vesicular compartments, MIF colocalized with LC3, and its secretion was dependent on secretory autophagy. Mechanistically, we identified PI(3,4)P2 as a key regulator of secretory autophagy, with TRPML1/3 acting downstream of PI(3,4)P2 to mediate Ca2+-dependent MIF secretion. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that MIF is a novel cargo of type III UcPS, operating through TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy, which are regulated by TRPML3 in a Ca2+-independent manner and by the PI(3,4)P2-TRPML1/3 axis in a Ca2+-dependent manner, respectively.

secondary.title: Extracellular exosome signature links hypertension and Alzheimer's disease.
secondary.abstract: Untreated hypertension is a risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD); however, this association is not well understood. The aim of this study was to reveal protein signatures that bridge the pathophysiological changes in hypertension to AD. Using untargeted proteomics, we analyzed brain samples from aged (30- and 40-week-old) spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHRs, n = 12), and age-matched normotensive Wistar Kyoto (WKY, n = 8) controls, and human AD patients (Braak stages 4-6) (n = 30), cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) (n = 5), non-demented controls (Braak stages 0-3) (n = 37). Differential expression and pathway analyses in SHRs highlighted the 'extracellular exosome' pathway. This pathway also showed significant associations to differentially expressed proteins in AD and CAA patients. Comparison between species identified 24 proteins in SHRs and AD, whose trajectory pattern over the progression of hypertension, aligned with those observed during AD Braak stage progression, compared to respective controls. The proteins were similarly associated with extracellular exosomes. Immunostaining and spatial proteomics support vesicle accumulation and dysregulated exosome protein signatures in the cerebrovasculature of both SHR and AD brains. Additionally, the extracellular exosome pathway-association was not identified in a traditional model of familial AD (5xFAD). Our findings demonstrate cross-species translatability between AD and the SHR and provide novel mechanistic insights into a shared dysregulation of cerebral artery-associated exosomes.

best.title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
best.abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

best.title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
best.abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

best.title: Mechanism of Autophagic Extracellular Vesicles Revealed.
best.abstract: Recent work by Mao and colleagues identifies a distinct class of small extracellular vesicles, termed autophagic extracellular vesicles (AEVs), generated from amphisomes upon autophagy induction. In this commentary, we discuss how this study provides important mechanistic insight into the coupling between autophagy and secretion. AEVs are molecularly and functionally distinct from canonical exosomes, being enriched in autophagy-related components such as LC3 and p62, and dependent on core ATG machinery for their biogenesis. Notably, their secretion is enhanced by autophagy induction and contributes to intercellular communication, particularly in the context of viral infection. These findings position amphisomes as critical sorting hubs that direct cargo toward either degradation or secretion, thereby integrating autophagic and endolysosomal pathways. We further highlight how these results intersect with prior evidence implicating SNARE-dependent mechanisms, including VAMP7 and stress-responsive regulators such as GRASP55, in unconventional secretion. Finally, we discuss key unresolved questions, particularly the mechanisms underlying the generation of small intraluminal vesicles within amphisomes and the role of ESCRT machinery in this process. Overall, the identification of AEVs adds a new layer of complexity to extracellular vesicle biology and opens new avenues for understanding how autophagy contributes to intercellular signaling in health and disease.

best.title: Recessive variants in ESCRT-II component VPS25 alter vesicular transport and small extracellular vesicle processing in lethal neonatal encephalopathy.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: The role of small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), such as exosomes, in cell-to-cell communication is increasingly recognized. Both during development and postnatally, sEVs have been shown to mediate a multitude of essential functions in the central nervous system. While abnormal sEV biogenesis has been observed in a number of neurodevelopmental disorders, a causal link has been largely lacking. METHODS: We clinically evaluated five families in which newborns presented with a novel neonatal-onset encephalopathy. Positional mapping, exome sequencing, and trio exome sequencing were utilized to identify the underlying genetic variants. Additionally, we utilized Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants and performed cellular assays to evaluate ESCRT-II interaction, cellular localization, and sEV secretion and cargo capacities. RESULTS: The observed lethal encephalopathy is characterized by severe hypotonia, brain anomalies, and epilepsy. In families 1, 4, and 5 (multiplex consanguineous), we identified a novel homozygous missense variant in VPS25 as the likely candidate. Family 2 comprises a simplex case with two missense variants in trans in VPS25, one of which impacts the same residue as in the other three families. Family 3 also comprises a simplex case where we revealed a homozygous missense variant. VPS25 is an essential component of ESCRT-II, itself required for sEV biogenesis. We show that Vps25 hypomorphic mouse mutants recapitulate the developmental brain malformation observed in patients. We also show that mutant VPS25 is associated with abnormal ESCRT-II interaction, abnormal cellular localization, and highly abnormal sEVs. Specifically, mutant cells displayed engorged multivesicular bodies and were significantly defective in their capacity to secrete sEVs such as exosomes, while secreted sEVs contained altered cargo, lacking vital proteins for axon protection and maintenance. CONCLUSIONS: We report a novel neurodevelopmental disorder caused by biallelic hypomorphic variants in VPS25. The consistent impact of these variants on sEV biogenesis suggests a potential pathomechanism. While future cases will further delineate the phenotypic spectrum, these findings offer a new perspective on abnormal sEVs as drivers of human neurodevelopmental disorders.

best.title: Serum Exosomes from Subacute Phase Post-cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Promote Microglial Pro-inflammatory Phenotype Polarization and Exacerbate Blood-Brain Barrier Disruption in Mice.
best.abstract: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) restores circulation but induces cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury characterized by blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption and microglial-mediated neuroinflammation. Exosomes circulate systemically following CPR, yet their temporal profiles and specific roles remain poorly understood. C57BL/6 mice (n = 5/group) underwent asphyxial cardiac arrest and CPR. BBB permeability was assessed longitudinally (3 h to 14 d) using Evans blue extravasation. Serum exosomes were isolated at 1 d and 3 d post-CPR and characterized. To determine immunomodulatory effects, exosomes were administered via intracerebroventricular injection into recipient mice, and BBB integrity and microglial polarization (CD86, CD206) were evaluated by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry. Additionally, primary cultures of microglia cells isolated from CPR mice were exposed to exosomes in vitro (n = 3/group), and pro-inflammatory phenotype/anti-inflammatory phenotype markers and inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, iNOS, TGF-β, Arg1, IL-10) were quantified. CPR induced transient BBB disruption peaking at 3 d post-resuscitation. Serum exosomes isolated at both 1 d and 3 d exhibited characteristic cup-shaped morphology. Intracerebroventricular administration of post-CPR exosomes significantly exacerbated BBB leakage and skewed microglial polarization toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype (elevated CD86⁺; reduced CD206⁺), with 3-day exosomes eliciting more potent detrimental effects than 1-day exosomes. In vitro, exposure to 3-day exosomes similarly produced stronger pro-inflammatory transcriptional responses and increased nitric oxide (NO) production compared with 1-day exosomes. Serum exosomes derived from post-CPR mice exhibit pro-inflammatory activity, aggravating BBB disruption and promoting microglial pro-inflammatory phenotype polarization upon central delivery. These findings suggest that circulating exosomes may contribute to post-resuscitation neuroinflammatory injury, and highlight exosome-related pathways as candidate targets worthy of further investigation.

best.title: Glycoprotein-induced phase separation drives unconventional secretion of galectin-3.
best.abstract: The mechanism of unconventional protein secretion remains an unresolved issue. Here, we describe an unconventional protein secretion pathway for galectin-3 that is mediated by phase separation and condensation. Using four lysosomal damage models, we observed a rapid, pronounced release of galectin-3 in large, non-exosomal particles. This secretion is driven by glycoprotein-induced galectin-3 phase separation and is independent of pyroptosis and secretory autophagy. During phase separation, the S-face of galectin-3 carbohydrate recognition domain binds glycoproteins that triggers galectin-3 N-terminal tail release and condensation. These condensates then recruit ALG-2 via the exposed N-terminal tail. ALG-2 directs the condensates to the endoplasmic reticulum-late endosome interface. After translocation into late endosomes, galectin-3 condensates are secreted into the extracellular milieu by SNARE-dependent vesicular transport. This mechanism of exporting phase-separated protein condensates may serve as a clean-up response to membrane damage.

best.title: A protective role for APP in nuclear waste clearance via lysosomal exocytosis.
best.abstract: Amyloid precursor protein (APP) is widely known for its role in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis through its proteolytic processing into amyloid-β peptides. However, its physiological functions remain incompletely understood. Here, we uncover a protective role for full-length APP in facilitating the disposal of nuclear-derived debris under genotoxic stress. In both cultured cells and in vivo mouse models, loss of APP leads to nuclear waste accumulation, increased inflammation, and cell death, whereas APP overexpression mitigates these effects. Mechanistically, we show that APP supports the extracellular release of nuclear waste material through lysosomal exocytosis. APP mutants associated with familial AD fail to mediate this process. Consistently, human AD brain tissue exhibits abnormal nuclear morphology, accumulation of nuclear waste in the cytoplasm, and reduced APP levels per neuron. These findings highlight a conserved cellular mechanism by which APP contributes to nuclear and cellular homeostasis, and suggest that impaired nuclear waste clearance may represent an underappreciated contributor to neurodegeneration.

best.title: Exosomes derived from N2 neutrophils reprogram the immune microenvironment to promote spinal cord injury repair.
best.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Spinal cord injury induces irreversible neurological impairments via secondary pathological cascades dominated by excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, and neuronal apoptosis. As the first-responder immune cells following spinal cord trauma, neutrophils can acquire an N2-like reparative phenotype, yet direct neutrophil transplantation is hampered by poor cellular survival. Exosomes, nanoscale cell-secreted vesicles with low immunogenicity and favourable biostability, constitute promising cell-free candidates for regenerative therapy. Nevertheless, the therapeutic potential of exosomes derived from N2-polarized neutrophils remains poorly defined for spinal cord injury repair. METHODS: Murine bone-marrow-derived neutrophils were polarized toward the N2 phenotype using interleukin-6 (IL-6) and granulocyte-colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), with non-polarized neutrophils set as the control group. Exosomes were purified by ultracentrifugation and comprehensively characterized by transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and western blotting. In vitro functional assays were performed to evaluate macrophage phenotypic reprogramming, neuronal axonal regeneration, and neuronal apoptosis. A modified Allen's weight-drop mouse spinal cord injury model was adopted for in vivo intervention. Motor functional recovery was evaluated using the Basso Mouse Scale and gait analysis, while neural tissue repair was assessed via immunofluorescence staining. RESULTS: Exosomes derived from N2-polarized neutrophils (N2-exos) exhibited canonical exosomal hallmarks. In vitro, these exosomes drove lipopolysaccharide-primed macrophages to switch to an anti-inflammatory reparative phenotype, alleviated oxidative-stress-mediated axonal injury, and suppressed neuronal apoptosis. In vivo administration of N2-exos markedly enhanced hind-limb motor performance and gait coordination, and facilitated axonal regeneration across the injury epicenter. CONCLUSIONS: N2-exos remodel the post-traumatic immune microenvironment and confer combined neuroprotective and axon regenerative effects. This cell-free modality represents a promising therapeutic candidate for regenerative interventions against spinal cord injury.

best.title: Autophagic extracellular vesicles: a distinct secretory route linking autophagy to extracellular communication.
best.abstract: Macroautophagy/autophagy is classically defined as a degradative pathway that delivers cytoplasmic material to lysosomes. However, accumulating evidence indicates that autophagy can also support unconventional secretion. A recent study identifies a previously unrecognized subtype of small extracellular vesicles termed autophagic extracellular vesicles (AEVs). These vesicles originate from amphisomes formed by the fusion of autophagosomes with multivesicular bodies and are characterized by a size below 100 nm together with the presence of autophagic cargos, ESCRT-III components and RAB13. Importantly, biogenesis of AEVs is distinct from that of classical exosomes, which requires specific components of the ESCRT III complex and the GTPase RAB27A. The further finding that enterovirus can exploit AEVs to infect receptor-negative cells, thereby expanding viral tropism, suggests that secretory autophagy serves as a pivotal mechanism driving pathogen dissemination. This work provides the conceptual framework of extracellular vesicle heterogeneity and positions secretory autophagy as an important contributor to intercellular communication.

best.title: Evaluation of the effect of p38γ gene delivery using exosomes derived from mesenchymal stem cells on Alzheimer's rat model.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dementia, memory loss, and cognitive decline. This study investigated the therapeutic potential of delivering the p38γ gene via exosomes derived from adipose-derived stem cells (ADSC-Exos) in a rat model of streptozotocin (STZ)-induced AD. METHODS AND RESULTS: After the AD model was established, the rats were administered via intraperitoneal injections of p38γ, Exo, or p38γ-loaded ADSC-Exo (Exo+p38γ). Cognitive and memory assessments were performed via novel object recognition (NOR), passive avoidance, elevated plus-maze (EPM), and the Barnes maze (BM). Histological techniques were used to evaluate cell density and beta-amyloid (Aβ) plaque accumulation, while quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT‒PCR) was used to measure the transcription levels of neuronal nuclei (NeuN), glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), nerve growth factor (NGF), and sex-determining region Y-box 2 (SOX2). Additionally, the expression of GDNF, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), SOX2, and malondialdehyde (MDA) was analyzed via an ELISA kit. The Exo and Exo+p38γ groups demonstrated significant improvements in STZ-induced memory deficits across various assessments. However, no significant differences in the protein expression levels of GDNF, BDNF, SOX2, and MDA or the gene expression levels of SOX2, NeuN, GDNF, and NGF were detected between STZ-treated rats that received Exos+p38γ and those that received Exos alone. CONCLUSIONS: Taken together, this study demonstrates that ADSC-derived exosomes effectively improve cognitive deficits in an AD rat model; Although Exo+p38γ was associated with a significant increase in SOX2 gene expression compared with the AD group, the direct comparison between Exo+p38γ and ADSC-Exos did not demonstrate a statistically significant additional effect.

best.title: MYO18B promotes lysosomal exocytosis by facilitating focal adhesion maturation.
best.abstract: Many cancer cells exhibit increased amounts of paucimannose glycans, which are truncated N-glycan structures rarely found in mammals. Paucimannosidic proteins are proposedly generated within lysosomes and exposed on the cell surface through a yet uncertain mechanism. In this study, we revealed that paucimannosidic proteins are produced by lysosomal glycosidases and secreted via lysosomal exocytosis. Interestingly, lysosomal exocytosis preferentially occurred in the vicinity of focal adhesions, protein complexes connecting the actin cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix. Through genome-wide knockout screening, we identified that MYO18B, an actin crosslinker, is required for focal adhesion maturation, facilitating lysosomal exocytosis and the release of paucimannosidic lysosomal proteins to the extracellular milieu. Moreover, a mechanosensitive cation channel PIEZO1 locally activated at focal adhesions imports Ca2+ necessary for lysosome-plasma membrane fusion. Collectively, our study unveiled an intimate relationship between lysosomal exocytosis and focal adhesion, shedding light on the unexpected interplay between lysosomal activities and cellular mechanosensing.

best.title: TRPML3 and TRPML1/3 differentially regulate unconventional MIF secretion through TMED10 and secretory autophagy.
best.abstract: The intracellular Ca2+ channel TRPML3 regulates autophagy by multimerization in a phosphoinositide (PIP)-dependent manner; however, its role in other membrane dynamics remains unclear. Here, we report that TRPML3 regulates type III unconventional protein secretion (UcPS) through two distinct pathways: TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy. TRPML3 interacted with TMED10 and macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), a signal sequence-lacking pleiotropic cytokine whose secretion mechanism has remained undefined. We found that cytosolic MIF is transported to membrane-enclosed compartments through TMED10-channeled UcPS. Notably, TRPML3, but not TRPML1 or TRPML1/3, promoted TMED10 oligomerization, thereby enhancing MIF secretion in a Ca2+-independent manner. Furthermore, once translocated into vesicular compartments, MIF colocalized with LC3, and its secretion was dependent on secretory autophagy. Mechanistically, we identified PI(3,4)P2 as a key regulator of secretory autophagy, with TRPML1/3 acting downstream of PI(3,4)P2 to mediate Ca2+-dependent MIF secretion. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that MIF is a novel cargo of type III UcPS, operating through TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy, which are regulated by TRPML3 in a Ca2+-independent manner and by the PI(3,4)P2-TRPML1/3 axis in a Ca2+-dependent manner, respectively.

best.title: RYR:ATP6V0A1 complexes couple ER-lysosome contact sites to dynamic autophagy control.
best.abstract: Ryanodine receptors (RYRs) are ER-resident Ca2+-release channels enriched in excitable cells, including neurons. RYR inhibition promotes ERlysosome contacts, limits lysosomal secretion, and restores lysosome availability for autophagosome fusion and cargo degradation (including APP). Conversely, disrupting the RYR:ATP6V0A1 interaction using a RYR-derived protein fragment serving as a "decoy" for ATP6V0A1 evokes RYR hyperactivity and stimulates lysosomal secretion. best.title: Molecular mechanisms underlying p62-dependent secretion of the Alzheimer-associated ubiquitin variant UBB+1.
best.abstract: UBB+1, a ubiquitin variant protein resulting from a frameshift in the ubiquitin-B gene, is a pathological hallmark of Alzheimer disease (AD). At the cellular level, UBB+1 disrupts the ubiquitin-proteasome system while inducing autophagy. Notably, UBB+1 itself is secreted via autophagosome-like vesicles. Here, we demonstrate that UBB+1 can be removed from the cell by degradative and secretory autophagy. Sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1)/p62 functions as a pivotal ubiquitin receptor for UBB+1, recognizing its ubiquitin domain and facilitating loading into autophagosomes. Oligomerization of SQSTM1/p62 was critical to isolate UBB+1 in bodies preventing its aggregation. Intriguingly, both gain- and loss-of-function SQSTM1/p62 suppressed UBB+1 secretion, causing intracellular retention: SQSTM1/p62 knockout led to UBB+1 accumulation in insoluble aggregates, while its overexpression promoted the formation of p62-UBB+1 bodies. We further identified distinct roles for SNARE-mediated membrane fusion in secretory autophagy of UBB+1. Specifically, the R-SNARE SEC22B and the Q-SNAREs Syntaxin-4 and SNAP23 participated in UBB+1 exocytosis. Disruption of SEC22B impaired the fusion of UBB+1-containing autophagosomes with the plasma membrane, reducing UBB+1 secretion without affecting its intracellular turnover. Inhibition of lysosomes partially stabilized UBB+1 indicating that degradation and secretion are complementary processes that determine the fate of UBB+1. This study elucidates the dual roles of autophagy in managing neurotoxic proteins, highlighting SQSTM1/p62 as a key mediator of UBB+1 trafficking and secretion. Although ubiquitin typically acts as a degradation signal, our findings reveal a rare instance of a ubiquitin-related protein driving secretory autophagy. These findings advance our understanding of cellular mechanisms underlying the clearance of misfolded proteins in neurodegenerative diseases.

best.title: Impaired MAPT/tau-secretory lysosomes are linked to cognitive vulnerability in Alzheimer patients.
best.abstract: MAPT/tau proteins propagate between brain regions in a prion-like manner, driving the onset and progression of dementia in Alzheimer disease (AD). However, the basis for variability in dementia progression among AD patients remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that cognitively resilient AD patients, characterized by reduced MAPT/tau pathology, maintain lysosomal integrity, whereas cognitively vulnerable patients, exhibiting greater MAPT/tau burden, display lysosomal dysfunction. Lysosomes in cognitively vulnerable AD brains contain partially digested, seed-competent MAPT/tau species composed mainly of the amyloidogenic core with degraded peripheral regions. These pathogenic MAPT/tau forms are secreted via lysosomal exocytosis, facilitating MAPT/tau propagation and contributing to cognitive decline. Cognitively vulnerable female AD patients show increased lysosome-mediated MAPT/tau secretion relative to their male counterparts. Our findings suggest that lysosomal dysfunction, marked by altered protein expression, pH dysregulation, and MAPT/tau accumulation, underlies the heterogeneity in dementia severity. best.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder driven by β-amyloid (Aβ) deposition, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress and metabolic dysregulation, with the latter as a central pathological hub. hucMSC-derived exosomes (hucMSC-exosomes) show therapeutic potential for AD, but their metabolic remodeling mechanisms remain unclear. All mice received tail vein injections for 6 weeks. Morris Water Maze tests revealed that hucMSC-exosomes significantly improved spatial learning and memory in AD mice. Pathological analyses confirmed that hucMSC-exosomes reduced cerebral Aβ deposition, suppressed hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and restored antioxidant capacity (SOD, GPx, GSH/GSSG). Untargeted metabolomic analysis of brain tissues revealed that 6 primary carbon, 8 primary nitrogen and 3 secondary metabolites were common differential metabolites across the two comparison cohorts (AD-vehicle vs. WT, AD-hucMSC-exosome vs. AD-vehicle), and their aberrant expression in AD mice was all reversed by hucMSC-exosomes. KEGG enrichment analysis showed that hucMSC-exosomes largely reversed dysregulated metabolic pathways in AD, including lipid, amino acid, nucleotide metabolism and autophagy/mitophagy. Collectively, hucMSC-exosomes ameliorate AD pathological phenotypes and cognitive deficits, an effect accompanied by metabolic homeostasis remodeling through cascades of reduced Aβ deposition, suppressed neuroinflammation and alleviated oxidative stress. Metabolic remodeling represents a prominent correlative feature of the neuroprotective effects of hucMSC-exosomes, providing candidate molecular targets for metabolically targeted AD therapy.

best.title: Extracellular exosome signature links hypertension and Alzheimer's disease.
best.abstract: Untreated hypertension is a risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD); however, this association is not well understood. The aim of this study was to reveal protein signatures that bridge the pathophysiological changes in hypertension to AD. Using untargeted proteomics, we analyzed brain samples from aged (30- and 40-week-old) spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHRs, n = 12), and age-matched normotensive Wistar Kyoto (WKY, n = 8) controls, and human AD patients (Braak stages 4-6) (n = 30), cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) (n = 5), non-demented controls (Braak stages 0-3) (n = 37). Differential expression and pathway analyses in SHRs highlighted the 'extracellular exosome' pathway. This pathway also showed significant associations to differentially expressed proteins in AD and CAA patients. Comparison between species identified 24 proteins in SHRs and AD, whose trajectory pattern over the progression of hypertension, aligned with those observed during AD Braak stage progression, compared to respective controls. The proteins were similarly associated with extracellular exosomes. Immunostaining and spatial proteomics support vesicle accumulation and dysregulated exosome protein signatures in the cerebrovasculature of both SHR and AD brains. Additionally, the extracellular exosome pathway-association was not identified in a traditional model of familial AD (5xFAD). Our findings demonstrate cross-species translatability between AD and the SHR and provide novel mechanistic insights into a shared dysregulation of cerebral artery-associated exosomes.

best.title: Inactive ryanodine receptors sustain lysosomal availability for autophagy by promoting ER-lysosomal contact site formation.
best.abstract: Lysosomal and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ release mutually influence each other's functions. Recent work revealed that ER-located ryanodine receptor(s) (RyR(s)) Ca2+ release channels suppress autophagosome turnover by the lysosomes. In familial Alzheimer's disease, inhibiting RyR hyperactivity restored autophagic flux by normalizing lysosomal vacuolar H+-ATPase (vATPase) levels. However, the mechanisms by which RyRs control lysosomal function and how this involves the vATPase remain unknown. Here, we show that RyRs interact with the ATP6v0a1 subunit of the vATPase, contributing to ER-lysosomal contact site formation. This interaction suppresses RyR-mediated Ca²⁺ release, leading to reduced lysosomal exocytosis. Pharmacological inhibition of RyR activity mimics these effects on lysosomal exocytosis. Retaining lysosomes inside cells via RyR inhibition increases ER-lysosomal contact site formation, rendering lysosomes more available for autophagic flux. In summary, these findings establish RyR/ATP6v0a1 complexes as ER-lysosomal tethers that dynamically and Ca2+ dependently regulate the intracellular availability of lysosomes to participate in autophagic flux.

primary.title: Neuronal cell-cycle re-entry stratifies clinical trajectories in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
primary.abstract: The clinical heterogeneity of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) remains a fundamental barrier to effective therapy. While cell cycle re-entry in post-mitotic neurons is a known precursor to neurodegeneration, its role in defining patient-specific outcomes has never been established. Here, we integrate large-scale transcriptomic profiling from the AnswerALS cohort with mechanistic studies in human iPSC-derived spinal motor neurons to define how cell-cycle re-entry shapes disease heterogeneity in ALS. We identify a transcriptionally distinct patient subgroup with the highest expression of G1 or G2-phase cyclins that exhibit significantly slower functional decline (ALSFRS-R), whereas the engagement of S-phase markers correlates with accelerated disease progression. Nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction, a hallmark of ALS and related disorders, disrupts the spatial distribution of key regulatory proteins and may contribute to maladaptive cell-cycle activation. Our recent evidence suggests that impaired nuclear import may initiate, rather than merely accompany, neuronal cell-cycle re-entry. Using iPSC-derived motor neurons, we show that impaired nuclear import initiates TDP-43 pathology and global nuclear/cytoplasmic mis-localization of key ALS-related proteins. This nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction triggers a transient wave of cell-cycle activity immediately preceding neuronal cell death. Crucially, we show that DNA-replication initiation is a pathological inflection point of no return, as neurons entering S-phase accumulate replication-associated DNA damage and undergo cell death. Selective inhibition of CDK4/6 prevents S-phase entry and confers potent neuroprotection. Our findings demonstrate that impaired nuclear import drives maladaptive cell-cycle reactivation in ALS and that the depth of cell-cycle engagement stratifies neuronal fate and patient trajectories.

primary.title: Cofilin hyperphosphorylation triggers TDP-43 pathology in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
primary.abstract: Pathological forms of TAR-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), involving its aberrant mislocalization to the cytoplasm, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, are present in ∼45%-50% frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease individuals and most (97%) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Hence, identifying mechanisms that induce TDP-43 pathology are central to neurodegeneration and developing new therapeutic targets in these conditions. Cofilin is a multifunctional protein with a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Actin has important neuronal-specific activities in dendritic spines, axonal growth cones and synapses and it is in constant equilibrium between two forms: monomeric globular actin (G-actin) and polymeric filamentous actin (F-actin). Cofilin controls actin dynamics by depolymerizing and severing actin filaments. When cofilin is phosphorylated (at serine-3, Ser3) by LIM kinase1 (LIMK1), it becomes inactive, leading to production of more F-actin. Defects in cofilin are well described in other neurodegenerative disorders, unlike in ALS. We examined phosphorylation of cofilin and actin dynamics in post-mortem spinal cord tissue from sporadic ALS (SALS) patients, the TDP-43 rNLS8 transgenic mouse model and NSC-34 motor neuronal cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. F-actin was pharmacologically stabilized to mimic cofilin hyperphosphorylation and TDP-43 pathology was assessed. Neuronal cells were treated with a non-phosphorylatable cofilin S3A peptide (MAAGVAVSDGVIKVFN) and TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis were evaluated. Here, we show that cofilin is hyperphosphorylated in human ALS and disease models compared to controls. This was detected in spinal motor neurons from SALS patients and a TDP-43 mouse model (rNLS8) displaying key ALS phenotypes, and in motor neuronal NSC-34 cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. Supporting this observation, more F-actin relative to G-actin was present in cortical/spinal cord lysates from SALS patients and TDP-43 rNLS8 mice, and NSC-34 cells expressing TDP-43. We also show that mimicking cofilin hyperphosphorylation by pharmacological stabilization of F-actin induced TDP-43 pathology: cytoplasmic mislocalization, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, and promoted its recruitment into stress granules (SGs). Furthermore, we detected increased levels of LIMK1 phosphorylation and tropomyosin isoforms 4.1 and 4.2 in SALS patients. These findings reveal aberrant cofilin hyperphosphorylation disrupts actin dynamics, triggering TDP-43 pathology and SG recruitment in SALS. They imply that preventing cofilin phosphorylation is a novel therapeutic strategy applicable to most ALS cases. Treatment of neuronal cells with the S3A peptide prevented features of TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis compared to control peptides. These findings thus describe a novel pathogenic mechanism producing TDP-43 pathology, applicable to most ALS cases and other neurodegenerative diseases.

primary.title: Amyloid and tau display distinct patterns across Alzheimer's in anterior caudate.
primary.abstract: The anterior caudate shows a pattern of Alzheimer's disease pathology that differs from the more extensively studied cortex. Across 41 donors, we found mostly diffuse amyloid beta plaques in gray matter and phosphorylated tau threads associated with white matter. Combining digital pathology with single-nucleus and spatial gene expression data, we detected no significant loss or gain in neuronal cell-type abundance with increasing pathology. However, we did observe increases in an FLT1+/IL1B+ microglial population with tau burden. Fast-spiking PTHLH-PVALB interneurons showed changes in genes related to ion channels, cellular trafficking, and phosphorylation. These findings offer a cellular-resolution reference for investigating how Alzheimer's disease affects subcortical brain regions.

primary.title: NeuroBase: A Web-Based Transcriptomic Resource and R Package for Cross-Disorder Analysis of Neurodegenerative and Neuropsychiatric Diseases.
primary.abstract: Neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia, are highly prevalent and biologically complex conditions that remain difficult to diagnose and treat. This study aimed to develop NeuroBase, a web-based transcriptomic resource that supports exploratory comparison of shared and disorder-specific gene expression features across these disorders. Fourteen human brain bulk RNA sequencing datasets (262 total samples) were processed using a standardized pipeline, followed by differential gene expression analysis with DESeq2, edgeR and limma-voom for broad exploratory discovery, complemented by a multi-method sensitivity analysis to define a method-concordant core gene set, protein-protein interaction network analysis using STRING with downstream exploration in Cytoscape, and functional enrichment analysis. Principal component analysis and clustering-based visualizations were used to summarize similarities and differences in transcriptomic patterns among disorders. Differential expression analysis identified dataset-level significant genes within each disorder using DESeq2 for one dataset per disorder (FDR ≤ 0.05), including 38 genes in Alzheimer's disease, 6,704 in autism spectrum disorder, 3,559 in bipolar disorder, 687 in Parkinson's disease, and 2,750 in schizophrenia; a stricter multi-method intersection analysis yielded method-concordant Core Intersection sets in the most informative datasets (983 core DEGs in autism spectrum disorder, 505 in bipolar disorder, 281 in schizophrenia, and 234 and 151 in two Parkinson's disease datasets; only two core genes (SPP1 and CHST3) were found in Alzheimer's disease). A unified strict-threshold reanalysis (FDR ≤ 0.05, |log₂FC|≥ 1) revealed disorder-level DEG burdens ranging from 34 (Alzheimer's disease) to 2,812 (autism) deduplicated genes, but only 24 genes were reproducible across independent cohorts of the same disorder, highlighting the limited cross-cohort reproducibility characteristic of bulk brain transcriptomics. Enrichment analyses identified significantly enriched signaling pathways in autism spectrum disorder and nominally enriched synapse-related pathways in Alzheimer's disease. Representative high-signal genes included SPP1 in Alzheimer's disease, NRGN in one Parkinson's disease dataset, and BEST1 in autism spectrum disorder. Cross-disorder comparison identified 465 differentially expressed genes shared between the neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorder groups, and principal component analysis showed that sample variation was dominated by dataset and tissue of origin. NeuroBase is a publicly accessible, web-based transcriptomic database and companion R package (neurobaseR) that enables standardized, cross-disorder exploration of bulk brain gene expression profiles across neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, supporting comparative analysis, programmatic data access, and hypothesis generation through interactive visualization and pathway-level summaries.

primary.title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
primary.abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

primary.title: Thalamic Reticular Nucleus Excitability and Cholinergic Signaling are Disrupted in a Mouse Model of Alzheimer's Disease Neuropathology.
primary.abstract: The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) forms powerful GABAergic connections with thalamic nuclei that regulate sleep, attention, and sensory processing. TRN neurons receive dense cholinergic innervation from the basal forebrain and brainstem, dynamically shaping TRN function across brain states. We previously showed reduced TRN activity and sleep deficits in amyloid precursor protein transgenic mice (APP mice), implicating TRN dysfunction as an early contributor to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathophysiology. Here, using slice electrophysiology in mice of both sexes, we determined whether changes in intrinsic membrane properties or cholinergic synaptic transmission contribute to TRN hypoactivity in APP mice. We found that TRN neurons located in the inner core and outer shell regions undergo substantial increases in excitability after the first postnatal month. In mature animals, core neurons exhibited higher firing rates and diverse firing patterns, including persistent firing, whereas shell neurons fired at lower rates and displayed more homogeneous firing patterns without persistent activity. Firing diversity in core neurons was mediated in part by low-threshold T-type Ca²⁺ channels. Cholinergic synaptic activation, mediated predominantly by basal forebrain afferents, produced biphasic excitatory-inhibitory postsynaptic responses in both core and shell neurons, with the ratio of postsynaptic excitation and inhibition varying across postsynaptic targets. Overall, cholinergic activation suppressed TRN firing. In APP mice, core neurons showed reduced intrinsic excitability and cholinergic afferents evoked postsynaptic responses with a larger muscarinic receptor-mediated inhibitory component, leading to delayed TRN firing. Together, these findings identify both intrinsic and cholinergic synaptic mechanisms that may contribute to TRN dysfunction during early AD.Significance Statement Alzheimer's disease (AD) is typically diagnosed after cognitive symptoms emerge when treatments are less effective, highlighting the need to understand preclinical disease mechanisms. Cholinergic signaling and slow-wave sleep are disrupted before symptom onset, but the mechanisms underlying these changes remain poorly understood. Because the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) receives strong cholinergic input and mediates sleep-related rhythms, it is well positioned to contribute to early AD pathophysiology. We previously found reduced TRN activity and disrupted sleep in an AD mouse model. Here, we show that intrinsic excitability and cholinergic synaptic signaling are altered in TRN neurons during preclinical AD. These changes may contribute to thalamic dysfunction and sleep disturbances, providing a potential circuit mechanism linking early AD pathology to disease progression.

primary.title: 27-Hydroxycholesterol Modulates Microglial α-Synuclein Handling and Is Associated with AKT1/JAK-STAT/TNF Signaling in Parkinson's Disease Models.
primary.abstract: 27-Hydroxycholesterol (27-OHC) is an oxysterol implicated in neuroinflammation, but its relationship to microglial α-synuclein (α-syn) handling and intracellular signaling in Parkinson's disease (PD) models remains incompletely defined. We combined BV2-cell assays, an rAAV-A53T mouse model, untargeted lipidomics and proteomics, network analyses, molecular docking, pathway immunoblotting, pharmacological AKT inhibition, and a cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA). In BV2 cells, 0.5-2.5 μM 27-OHC did not reduce viability, whereas concentrations ≥ 5 μM were cytotoxic. At 2.5 μM, 27-OHC increased cell-associated α-syn signal after exposure to recombinant α-syn PFFs. Brain lipidomics in the PD model showed accumulation of the broad sterol-lipid class, but did not provide absolute brain 27-OHC concentrations. Network analyses nominated AKT1, IL6, STAT3, and MMP9 as hub genes. In three independent BV2 experiments, PFF and 27-OHC exposure were associated with altered phosphorylation of AKT, STAT3, and NF-κB p65; a PFF × 27-OHC interaction was detected for STAT3 phosphorylation. MK-2206 lowered the cell-associated α-syn/GAPDH signal in the combined-treatment group, although the comparison did not remain significant after adjustment across three pairwise tests. CETSA showed greater soluble AKT1 retention after 27-OHC exposure and a higher thermal-curve area under the curve (paired p = 0.023). These findings support an association between 27-OHC exposure, microglial α-syn handling, and AKT-related signaling in BV2 cells. They do not establish direct 27-OHC-AKT1 binding or an in vivo causal effect of brain 27-OHC on microglia.

primary.title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes.
primary.abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

primary.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss.
primary.abstract: TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts1-8. Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.

primary.title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
primary.abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

primary.title: Hyperactive KIF5A in Neurodegeneration.
primary.abstract: The highly polarised morphology of neurons and the sheer length of their axons make transport of cargoes throughout the cell a formidable task. Decades of evidence obtained from genetic studies on patients and animal models highlight deficits in axonal transport as a recurrent cause, or early contributing factor, in a plethora of neurodegenerative diseases. Axonal transport abnormalities usually manifest as a slowing of cargo trafficked by molecular motors along microtubules; however, hyperactivation of motors can also lead to disease. That is the case for the kinesin-1 protein KIF5A, in which hyperactive mutations are linked to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and neonatal intractable myoclonus (NEIMY). In this Perspective, we summarise the latest insights into the impact of KIF5A hyperactivity, such as loss of autoinhibition, aggregation, altered cargo binding and microtubule damage. We conclude by discussing possible strategies to counteract these disruptions, with an emphasis on the necessity of restoring axonal transport to physiological levels, a key requirement to maintain neuronal homeostasis.

primary.title: The blood-brain barrier imports diverse neuroprotective proteins through pathways impaired early in Alzheimer's disease models.
primary.abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) has been defined primarily by what it excludes, yet the scale and function of physiological blood-to-brain protein transport remain largely unknown. Using bioorthogonal proteomics, we find that the healthy BBB samples 191 plasma proteins and permits 92 into the brain parenchyma. Enriched for carrier and metabolic functions, these proteins home to distinct brain cell types, such as apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1) to astrocytes and alpha-1 antitrypsin (SERPINA1) to microglia. This cell-type tropism relies on a BBB-parenchyma receptor hand-off: APOA1 crosses the BBB via SR-B1 and engages astrocytic ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), a key Alzheimer's risk gene, driving cholesterol efflux that supports synapse integrity. Unlike LPS-induced nonspecific leakage, early-stage 5xFAD mice show selective BBB transport remodeling, with reduced APOA1 and increased SERPINA1 uptake. Hepatic APOA1 overexpression restores APOA1 in the 5xFAD brain, rescuing astrocytic, synaptic, and behavioral deficits. These findings recast the BBB as a selective interface that recruits neuroprotective circulatory proteins for brain health.

primary.title: Alzheimer's disease-associated presenilin 2 N141I mutation impairs neuronal lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial dynamics through selective downregulation of the Golgi exchange factor Gbf1.
primary.abstract: Presenilin 2 (PS2) mutations cause familial Alzheimer's disease, yet their effects beyond amyloid processing remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how PS2 deletion and the N141I mutation affect neuronal lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial dynamics in mouse primary neurons. Both PS2 deletion and N141I mutation reduced neuronal lipid content. However, exogenous lipid supplementation rescued this deficit only in N141I-expressing neurons, indicating a partial loss-of-function effect. N141I neurons also displayed reduced OPA1, a mitochondrial fusion regulator, restored by lipid supplementation. RNA-sequencing identified Gbf1, a Golgi-specific guanine nucleotide exchange factor, as selectively downregulated in N141I but not knockout tissue, which was confirmed at the protein level in mouse brain and primary neurons. Gbf1 knockdown in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) recapitulated the N141I lipid profile. Together, these findings reveal a PS2-GBF1-lipid-mitochondria axis disrupted specifically by the N141I mutation, suggesting an amyloid-independent pathway contributing to neurodegeneration and identifying potential therapeutic targets for familial Alzheimer's disease.

primary.title: VPS35 mutation inhibits PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy via increased LRRK2 kinase activity.
primary.abstract: The p.D620N mutation in VPS35 causes an autosomal dominant form of Parkinson's disease via mechanisms that are poorly understood. PINK1 and parkin, two proteins whose loss-of-function underlies autosomal recessive Parkinson's disease, cooperate to mediate mitophagy, a quality control pathway for selective elimination of damaged mitochondria. PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy is disrupted by LRRK2 mutations, which are the most prevalent cause of autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease. Here, we investigated whether the p.D620N VPS35 mutation has an effect on PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy. We identified a novel family with autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease caused by a p.D620N VPS35 mutation. We cultured skin fibroblasts and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived dopaminergic neurons from the proband and from a second, unrelated Parkinson's disease patient with the p.D620N VPS35 mutation, and compared them with isogenic and non-isogenic control cells. PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy was severely impaired in VPS35 mutant fibroblasts and neurons, while non-selective, starvation-induced autophagy and lysosomal degradative capacity were preserved. siRNA-mediated VPS35 knockdown rescued the mitophagy defect in VPS35 mutant cells, whereas overexpression of wild-type VPS35 did not, suggesting a gain-of-function mechanism of the mutation. The VPS35 mutation did not interfere with activation of PINK1 or parkin after mitochondrial depolarization, but impaired mitochondrial recruitment of the autophagy receptor optineurin. LRRK2 kinase activity was increased in the VPS35 mutant cells, as shown by enhanced levels of the T73-phosphorylated form of the LRRK2 substrate RAB10. The enhanced level of phosphorylated RAB10 in VPS35 mutant cells was decreased by treatment with LRRK2 kinase inhibitors and by VPS35 knockdown. Importantly, the mitophagy defect of VPS35 mutant fibroblasts and neurons was fully rescued by LRRK2 kinase inhibitors as well as by overexpression of PPM1H, a phosphatase that dephosphorylates multiple RAB substrates of LRRK2. Finally, in situ proximity ligation experiments revealed that endogenous VPS35 and LRRK2 are proximity partners in human dopaminergic neurons and that this proximity relationship is enhanced by the VPS35 mutation. In conclusion, the VPS35 mutation impairs PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy via a gain-of-function mechanism that involves stimulation of LRRK2 kinase activity. Thus, a VPS35/LRRK2 axis linked to dominant Parkinson's disease intersects with a pathway mediated by proteins encoded by the recessive Parkinson's disease genes.

primary.title: Parkinson's disease-linked D620N mutation selectively alters the brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35.
primary.abstract: Mutations in several genes are known to cause familial forms of Parkinson's disease (PD), including mutations in the vacuolar protein sorting 35 ortholog (VPS35) gene linked to late-onset, autosomal dominant PD. VPS35 encodes a core subunit of the retromer complex which functions in endosomal sorting and recycling. It remains unclear how the pathogenic D620N mutation in VPS35 disrupts retromer function to induce neurodegeneration in PD. Using cell- and rodent-based models expressing D620N VPS35, we performed interactome proteomics to identify alterations underlying the pathogenic effects of D620N VPS35 in PD. Using overexpression of VPS35 variants in HEK-293 T cells, we conducted tandem affinity purification (TAP) or co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) with protein chemical crosslinking to determine the native and non-native protein interactomes of wild-type (WT) and D620N VPS35, respectively. Notably, we can confirm the reduced interaction of D620N VPS35 with components of the WASH complex. Additionally, using a viral-mediated gene transfer model of human D620N VPS35 overexpression in adult rat brain, we identify the first brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35. These overexpression models reveal remarkably similar interaction profiles of WT and D620N VPS35, suggesting that the D620N mutation has a subtle effect on the overall VPS35 protein interactome. We also conducted proteomic analysis of brain tissue from a D620N VPS35 knockin (KI) mouse model that expresses VPS35 at endogenous levels. Using co-IP from hemibrain or striatal extracts of WT and D620N VPS35 KI mice, we reveal a high degree of similarity between the brain interactomes of WT and D620N VPS35, further suggesting a subtle effect of the D620N mutation on VPS35 protein interactions. Notably, in both hemibrain and striatum, we find a selective decrease in the interaction of two known interactors, TBC1D5 and VPS29, with D620N VPS35. We also performed global proteomic analysis of striatal tissue from D620N VPS35 KI mice and reveal a high degree of similarity between WT and D620N, further suggesting a subtle effect of this mutation. Together, our study provides a comprehensive evaluation of the VPS35 protein interactome and reveals a selective effect of the PD-linked D620N mutation in mammalian cells and brain. Our study provides key insight into the mechanisms of retromer dysfunction in VPS35-linked PD.

primary.title: Dystrophic changes of nigrostriatal axons harboring a SYNJ1 Parkinson's mutation suggest catastrophic failure of endocytic mechanisms.
primary.abstract: Synaptojanin 1 is a brain enriched phosphoinositide phosphatase implicated in endocytosis at the synapse. A mutation (R258Q) that selectively impairs its Sac1 phosphatase domain causes early onset familial Parkinsonism. Neurons of mice with this mutation display synaptic vesicle traffic defects across the brain, but selective dystrophic changes in a subset of dopaminergic axons in the dorsolateral striatum. Using correlative light microscopy-FIB-SEM of mutant mouse striata to visualize in 3D these abnormal structures we show that they represent clusters of focal axonal dilations harboring massive, onion-like DAT enriched plasma membrane infoldings, generally localized next to cell bodies of neighboring cells, often engulfing evaginations of such cells. This dysmorphia was associated with a deficit in dopamine release in the same striatal region. Given the involvement of Synj1 in endocytic mechanisms, these structures may reflect an imbalance between exocytosis and endocytosis. Their occurrence only in a subset of axons suggests a vulnerability threshold of these axons beyond which the expansion of the plasma membrane is not counteracted by compensatory mechanisms.

primary.title: BAG3 coordinates astrocytic proteostasis of Alzheimer's disease-linked proteins via proteasome, autophagy, and retromer interactions.
primary.abstract: Bcl-2-associated athanogene 3 (BAG3) is a mediator of chaperone-assisted selective autophagy, and in the brain, is most highly expressed in astrocytes. However, its role in astrocytes remains poorly defined. Given the genetic and pathological links of BAG3 to proteostasis and neurodegenerative diseases, we investigated how BAG3 contributes to astrocyte function and Alzheimer's disease (AD). To define its function and relevance, we used single-nucleus RNA sequencing to confirm BAG3 enrichment in astrocytes and employed CRISPR/Cas9 editing of human induced pluripotent stem cells followed by proteomic and transcriptomic profiling, which revealed that BAG3 loss caused greater disruption in astrocytes than in neurons. BAG3-deficient astrocytes displayed reduced autophagy, lysosomal abundance and activity, and proteasome function. Coimmunoprecipitation identified BAG3 known binding partners (e.g., HSPB8, proteasome regulators), as well as an interactor in the retromer complex, VPS35. BAG3 deficiency resulted in altered retromer activity as measured by amyloid precursor protein (APP) localization in endosomes. In addition to validating these binding partners, integrative -omics analyses showed that BAG3 regulates AD-relevant proteins (GFAP, BIN1), as well as HSPB8. Functionally, BAG3 knockout astrocytes exhibited impaired amyloid-β proteostasis when cocultured with APP/PSEN1 mutant neurons, directly linking BAG3 to a disease-relevant astrocyte phenotype. Finally, analysis of postmortem human brain revealed that BAG3 expression marks a stress-responsive astrocyte subtype in aged individuals. Together, these findings demonstrate that BAG3 coordinates astrocyte proteostasis through interactions with regulators of autophagy, proteasome activity, and retromer function, positioning it as a potential therapeutic target and central node of astrocytic protein quality control in neurodegeneration.

primary.title: VPS35 Regulates Microglial Lipid Droplet Accumulation in Parkinson's Disease via Rab7.
primary.abstract: Microglial dysfunction and aberrant lipid metabolism are emerging as key contributors to Parkinson's disease (PD) pathogenesis. However, the specific role and regulation of lipid droplets (LDs) within microglia remain poorly defined. In this study, we employed MPTP- and LPS-induced PD mouse models and an in vitro system utilizing astrocyte-conditioned medium to model disease-relevant lipid stress and found enhanced LD accumulation in microglia. VPS35 expression was decreased in microglia, correlating with elevated microglial LD levels in PD mouse models. We then performed genetic manipulations (knockdown and overexpression) of VPS35, including the PD-associated D620N mutant, in primary microglia and assessed LD accumulation, phagocytic function, inflammatory responses, and integrated stress pathways. We showed that VPS35 knockdown exacerbated the accumulation of LDs in microglia. Conversely, VPS35 overexpression ameliorated LD formation, improved phagocytic function, and reduced inflammatory and integrated stress responses in microglia. The PD-related VPS35[D620N] mutation abolished these protective effects. We further found that VPS35 interacts with Rab7 to maintain lysosomal function, and the D620N mutation disrupts this interaction, leading to defective LD clearance. Our findings reveal VPS35 dysfunction as a key pathogenic mechanism in PD, where the D620N mutation disrupts microglial lipid handling to promote disease progression, thereby nominating VPS35 restoration as a promising therapeutic strategy.

primary.title: Early reduction of myelin-associated glycoprotein at myelin membranes in Huntington's disease.
primary.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is marked by progressive neuronal loss and atrophy of grey matter structures, particularly the caudate and putamen. Brain imaging studies reveal that the white matter starts to decay in the brain of individuals bearing the HD mutation many years before symptomatic onset. However, the mechanism by which the HD mutation causes white matter loss remains to be further defined. In this study, we examined white matter pathology and explored the underlying mechanism in the HDQ140 knock-in mouse model of HD. Western blot analysis of proteins localized at different layers of the myelin sheath showed that myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG), which is localized at the innermost myelin layer, was decreased earlier than proteins localized at outer layers of the myelin. The loss of MAG occurred at fully myelinated axons and was progressive with age. In postmortem symptomatic human HD brains, the level of MAG as well as other myelin proteins was also decreased. In HD mouse brains, MAG labeling was reduced at fiber bundles but accumulated in perinuclear structures of cells that expressed breast carcinoma amplified sequence 1, a marker for new oligodendrocytes. While their abundance was normal, new oligodendrocytes in HD brains were impeded in acquiring the expression of MAG. Compared with those in wild-type mouse brains, oligodendrocytes in HD mouse brains had a reduced frequency of MAG-bearing small vesicles and an increased abundance and enlargement of MAG-containing perinuclear structures. Further studies suggest that the MAG-accumulating perinuclear structures were derived from the late endosomal lysosomal compartment. Our study suggests that white matter decay in HD brains involves an early progressive loss of MAG in myelin membranes.

primary.title: Neuropathological and functional impact of astrocyte-derived extracellular vesicles in an aged model of Alzheimer's disease.
primary.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are lipid-bound particles that transfer cargos between cells. While plasma neuronal-derived EVs (NEVs) from individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) have been reported to exhibit high pathogenic potential, this study examined the impact of astrocyte-derived EVs (AEVs) in an aged AD mouse model. Plasma AEVs were isolated from cognitively normal control (CNC), MCI, and AD individuals using GLAST-based immunocapture and AEV size, purity, and tetraspanin were validated by flow cytometry, nanoparticle tracking, and super-resolution microscopy. AEVs pooled by clinical cohort were injected into the hippocampus of 6-month-old female PSAPP mice. Behavioral, biochemical, and neuropathological outcomes were assessed 6 months later. Rotarod assessment revealed significant impairment in motor coordination (p < 0.0001) in mice receiving MCI- and AD-AEVs compared with those receiving CNC-AEVs. While Morris water maze (MWM) also demonstrated that CNC-AEVs injected mice exhibited a trend toward increased target quadrant entries and faster escape latencies, these measures did not reach did not reach statistical significance. No overt changes were observed in the staining of amyloid plaque burden (6E10), and astrogliosis (GFAP). Immunoblotting of 82E1 and 22C11 confirmed Aβ/AAP levels remained similar across all injected mice, whereas increased cortical tau accumulation was observed in MCI- and AD-AEV injected mice. Cerebellar synaptic density (SY-38) remained unchanged. These findings suggest that while human-derived AEVs can precipitate early tau-related changes and motor coordination deficits, they do not significantly alter overall amyloidosis or astrocyte-reactivity at this time point. Further investigation is required to determine the viability of AEVs as biomarkers or therapeutic targets given the subtle nature of the observed structural pathology.

primary.title: hucMSC-derived exosomes rescue cognitive impairment and Alzheimer-like pathology in APP/PS1 mice via metabolic remodeling.
primary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a neurodegenerative disorder driven by β-amyloid (Aβ) deposition, neuroinflammation, oxidative stress and metabolic dysregulation, with the latter as a central pathological hub. hucMSC-derived exosomes (hucMSC-exosomes) show therapeutic potential for AD, but their metabolic remodeling mechanisms remain unclear. We combined behavioral tests, pathological assays and untargeted metabolomics to investigate the neuroprotective effects and mechanisms of hucMSC-exosomes in APP/PS1 AD mice. Seven-month-old male APP/PS1 mice were randomly divided into AD-vehicle and AD-hucMSC-exosome groups, with age-matched C57BL/6 mice as wild-type controls. All mice received tail vein injections for 6 weeks. Morris Water Maze tests revealed that hucMSC-exosomes significantly improved spatial learning and memory in AD mice. Pathological analyses confirmed that hucMSC-exosomes reduced cerebral Aβ deposition, suppressed hippocampal pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and restored antioxidant capacity (SOD, GPx, GSH/GSSG). Untargeted metabolomic analysis of brain tissues revealed that 6 primary carbon, 8 primary nitrogen and 3 secondary metabolites were common differential metabolites across the two comparison cohorts (AD-vehicle vs. WT, AD-hucMSC-exosome vs. AD-vehicle), and their aberrant expression in AD mice was all reversed by hucMSC-exosomes. KEGG enrichment analysis showed that hucMSC-exosomes largely reversed dysregulated metabolic pathways in AD, including lipid, amino acid, nucleotide metabolism and autophagy/mitophagy. Collectively, hucMSC-exosomes ameliorate AD pathological phenotypes and cognitive deficits, an effect accompanied by metabolic homeostasis remodeling through cascades of reduced Aβ deposition, suppressed neuroinflammation and alleviated oxidative stress. Metabolic remodeling represents a prominent correlative feature of the neuroprotective effects of hucMSC-exosomes, providing candidate molecular targets for metabolically targeted AD therapy.

secondary.title: Irosustat and STX140 improve cognitive function and modulate amyloid, oxidative stress, and inflammatory pathways in experimental Alzheimer's disease.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is currently the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder affecting the geriatric population. The pathology of AD has been described as neuronal loss caused by the accumulation of beta-amyloid plaques and the formation of neurofibrillary tangles resulting from tau protein phosphorylation. This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of steroid sulfatase inhibition using two drugs, the clinical steroid sulfatase inhibitor Irosustat and the multi-targeting preclinical candidate STX140, in scopolamine-induced AD in male Wistar rats compared to Donepezil as a standard drug. Behavioral tests such as the Open Field Test, Elevated Plus Maze Test, and Morris Water Maze Test were conducted to confirm the disease state and assess any improvement. At the end of the study, the animals were dissected to collect blood and brain samples for morphological, histological, immunohistochemical, biochemical, quantitative polymerase chain reaction and western blotting analyses. Treatment with Irosustat or STX140 improved learning, memory, and cognitive function compared with the disease group. The treated groups showed lowered brain tissue Aβ-40 & 42 levels, acetylcholinesterase activity, oxidative stress, and inflammatory markers. Morphological assessments showed that the drugs protected against brain atrophy and neuronal loss. Irosustat and STX140 are therefore promising therapeutic candidates for the management of Alzheimer's Disease.

secondary.title: Neuroprotective potential of EGF-treated bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells in trimethyltin-induced neurodegeneration: in vitro and in vivo studies.
secondary.abstract: UNLABELLED: Background: Neurodegenerative diseases are progressive, debilitating, and often life-threatening disorders of the nervous system. Bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells are considered a promising therapeutic strategy for different diseases, including neurodegeneration. EGF has been reported to promote neuron-like characteristics and neurotrophic responses in BM-MSCs. This study was conducted to assess the role of EGF-treated Bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells in a neurodegenerative rat model (a novel approach). Methods: In vitro analysis was performed to evaluate the specific dose and cell viability using MTT and Crystal Violet assays and morphology under a microscope. For the in vivo study, forty rats were randomly allocated into four groups: Control, Injury, injury + Bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells (BM-MSCS), and injury + EGF-treated Bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells (BM-MSCs). A neurodegenerative rat model was developed with the use of trimethyltin chloride. Following TMT induction, BM-MSCs and EGF-treated BM-MSCs were administered via the intrathecal route. Behavioral performance, Histopathological alteration, protein expression, and gene expression were evaluated. The assessed biomarkers included TNF-α (inflammation), NFL (neuronal injury), MAPT (Tau gene expression), the neurotrophic factors BDNF and NGF, together with the progenitor-associated marker Nestin. Findings: In vitro, BM-MSCs treated with 10 ng/mL EGF maintained cell viability comparable to untreated controls, as confirmed by MTT and Crystal Violet assays, while exhibiting pronounced neuron-like morphological characteristics. In vivo, transplantation of EGF-treated BM-MSCs significantly improved spatial learning, memory, and neuromuscular performance compared with both the TMT-induced injury group and the untreated BM-MSC group. Histopathological analysis demonstrated improved preservation of hippocampal architecture following EGF-treated BM-MSC transplantation. Furthermore, EGF-treated BM-MSCs significantly reduced the expression of TNF-α, neurofilament light chain (NFL), and phosphorylated Tau (p-Tau), while significantly increasing the expression of BDNF, NGF, and Nestin at both the protein and gene levels. Overall, EGF preconditioning enhanced the neuroprotective and recovery associated effects of BM-MSCs in the TMT-induced neurodegenerative rat model. Conclusion: EGF-preconditioned BM-MSCs attenuated TMT-induced neurodegenerative changes by improving behavioral performance, reducing neuroinflammatory and neuronal injury-associated responses, preserving hippocampal cellular and tissue integrity, and enhancing neurotrophic support. These findings suggest that EGF preconditioning may potentiate the neuroprotective and immunomodulatory effects of BM-MSCs and may represent a promising strategy for the treatment of neurodegenerative disorders.
