secondary.title: A rare TMEM175 mutation drives Parkinson's disease pathology by disrupting proton gating and lysosomal acidification.
secondary.abstract: Transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175), implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, has been variably proposed to function as a background K+ "leak" channel or a proton-activated proton channel in lysosomes. Here, we identified the rare TMEM175 variant p.L275R in a patient with early onset PD. Electrophysiological analyses revealed that TMEM175-L275R mutant proteins retain normal lysosomal expression and K+ "leak" activity, but specifically lose proton- and agonist-dependent activation gating. In skin fibroblasts isolated from the patient with PD harboring the monoallelic p.L275R mutation (TMEM175+/L275R), and in derived induced pluripotent stem cells and induced dopaminergic neurons, lysosomal H+ flux, acidification, and degradation were impaired. These lysosomal defects were corrected upon genome editing to produce the isogenic WT allele (+/+Cor), but appeared when the mutant allele was introduced onto a WT background (+/L275RMut). Pathological α-synuclein aggregation was facilitated in patient-derived (+/L275R) and mutation-introduced (+/L275RMut) neurons. Consistent with these genetic findings, pharmacological activation of TMEM175 with small-molecule agonists restored lysosomal functions and reduced α-synuclein aggregation in TMEM175+/L275R neurons. In in-vivo studies, equivalent-site-mutation knock-in mice demonstrated synucleinopathy and PD-like motor phenotypes. Collectively, our work provides genetic and pharmacological evidence that severe loss-of-function mutations may contribute causally to the onset age and pathogenesis of PD and identifies lysosomal proton channels and transporters as potential therapeutic targets for PD intervention.

secondary.title: TREM2/IGF-1 signaling axis-induced microglial senescence underlies benzo[a]pyrene-associated Parkinson's disease-like lesions.
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder worldwide. Accumulating evidence has linked environmental polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), with benzo[a]pyrene (B[a]P) as a representative ubiquitous member, to elevated PD risk and disease pathogenesis. The present study aimed to investigate whether B[a]P can trigger typical PD-like lesions in mice, and further dissects the functional role of microglial senescence as well as its underlying regulatory mechanism, using complementary systems in vivo mouse model and in vitro BV2 microglia cell. Behavioral assessments revealed that B[a]P exposure induced significant, dose-dependent impairments in motor coordination and cognitive function compared with the control group. Moreover, the degree of functional impairments measured in the high-dose B[a]P group was comparable to that observed in the MPTP positive-control group. Following B[a]P treatment, brain-resident microglia cells exhibited signs of cell senescence, as evidenced by typical ultrastructural alterations, increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity, and elevated expression of the core senescence markers p16, p21, and p53 proteins. Consistent with these in vivo observations, B[a]P was confirmed to also induce cell cycle arrest in cultured BV2 microglia cells. This pro-senescent effect was significnatly attenuated by Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) overexpression, whereas it was markedly exacerbated following TREM2 knockout. Subsequent experiments further validated that insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), as a direct downstream effector regulated by TREM2, is functionally required for B[a]P-triggered microglial senescence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that B[a]P exposure can induce PD-like lesions and microglial senescence, and which is primarily mediated via the TREM2/IGF-1 signaling axis.

secondary.title: Reduced BNIP1 impairs autophagosome-lysosome fusion in hippocampal neurons and contributes to Alzheimer's disease pathology.
secondary.abstract: BNIP1 (BCL2‑interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N‑ethylmaleimide‑sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting that BNIP1 is a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP‑overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells, screened key interacting proteins of BNIP1 via mass spectrometry, and further performed gain‑ and loss‑of‑function assays using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNA (siRNA) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that, in these experimental models, reduced BNIP1 expression contributes to AD‑related pathological alterations by impairing autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b‑mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. secondary.title: Isolated Axoplasm from Squid and Pathogenic Mechanisms in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
secondary.abstract: The squid giant axon is an experimental model that has been instrumental in providing answers to many fundamental questions in cell biology, including the discovery of the motor protein kinesin and probing molecular mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The giant axon offers scale and ease of access that is not possible in mammalian models. The power of this model stems from the fact that one can introduce reagents and proteins that would not cross a plasma membrane at defined concentrations in a buffer environment that is closely modeled on normal components of the axoplasm. By leveraging the unique biology of the squid axon, early studies were able to define the channels and ion specificities of the action potential. Subsequent studies using video-enhanced contrast- differential Interference contrast microscopy (VEC-DIC) and the isolated axoplasm led to the identification of kinesins, a class of motor proteins responsible for intracellular vesicle trafficking toward the plus end of microtubules. This combination of isolated axoplasm and advanced imaging continues to provide insights into pathogenic mechanisms for adult-onset neurodegeneration, including ALS, and regulation of fast axonal transport, a process disrupted in motor neuron disease. Here, procedures for dissecting the giant axon, isolating axoplasm, and perfusing defined amounts of proteins and/or reagents into the axoplasm are detailed, as well as methods for visualizing and interactively analyzing vesicle traffic in real time. This model represents a singular avenue to understand the critical function of neurons, shedding light on the mechanisms driving ALS pathology and other neurodegenerative diseases. This system also offers a tractable platform for drug testing, where candidate therapeutic compounds can be introduced directly into the axoplasm, and their effects on vesicle trafficking can be assessed in real time, providing a rapid and physiologically relevant means of identifying potential ALS therapeutic targets.

secondary.title: A pKa-Guided BBB-Permeable NIR Fluorescent Probe for Tracking Lipid Droplets in Microglia with Neuroinflammation and Alzheimer's Disease.
secondary.abstract: Abnormal accumulation of lipid droplets (LDs), accompanied by altered microenvironmental polarity within the microglia, is closely associated with neuroinflammation and also has been increasingly recognized as an early and dynamic indicator of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Herein, a LD-targeting polarity-sensitive blood-brain barrier (BBB)-permeable near-infrared (NIR) probe, BTDN, was screened by tuning the electron-donating substituents to modulate the pKa values of benzothiadiazole-based derivatives. Endowed with the donor-acceptor-donor (D1-A-D2) architecture and strong intramolecular charge-transfer (ICT) characteristics, the BTDN probe exhibited high sensitivity to polarity change. The BTDN probe displayed suitable physicochemical properties such as a pKa of 7.47 and lipophilicity with a log P of 3.72 for favorable BBB-penetrating efficiency with a permeability percentage of 24.23%. In addition, the BTDN probe showed advantages for fluorescence imaging including NIR emission from 643 to 770 nm with the increased polarity, Stokes shift larger than 308 nm, comparable two-photon absorption capacity with an absorption cross-section of 10 GM at 870 nm, good biocompatibility, and robust photostability. Using this multifunctional BTDN probe, the dynamic fluorescence imaging of accumulation behaviors of LDs in BV2 microglia with neuroinflammation was performed, demonstrating that LD formation may serve as a potential biomarker for neuroinflammation. Furthermore, overproduced LDs within microglia were directly observed in vivo and in tissue sections from the brains of AD mice. This work not only provides an imaging tool for dynamically characterizing LD accumulation in microglia but also provides insights into the relationship between LD accumulation in microglia and AD pathogenesis.

secondary.title: Alzheimer's genetic risk factor CASS4 controls microglial focal adhesion biology and amyloidosis.
secondary.abstract: Recent genome-wide association studies have identified numerous Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk genes enriched in microglia, including Crk-associated substrate (Cas) scaffold protein family member 4 (CASS4), which encodes the adaptor protein CASS4. Despite its strong genetic association with AD, the role of CASS4 in disease remains poorly understood. Here, we show that full-body Cass4 deletion in 5xFAD mice increases amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition, neuronal dystrophy, and cognitive deficits. Since microglia are the predominant brain-resident cells expressing Cass4, we investigated its role in microglial responses to Aβ pathology. Loss of CASS4 impaired microglial mobilization to Aβ plaques and reduced plaque compaction. Phosphoproteomic analysis of purified microglia revealed marked disruption of focal adhesion signaling following Cass4 deletion. Consistent with this, CASS4 deficiency abrogated in vivo microglial recruitment to injury and in vitro wound healing responses, two processes that are centrally orchestrated by focal adhesion biology. Together, these findings identify CASS4 as a critical regulator of microglial function and focal adhesion biology and suggest that CASS4 may represent a therapeutic target for AD.

secondary.title: Up-regulation of the kinase LRRK2, in enteric glia contributes to mucosal barrier impairment in Parkinson's disease via secretory autophagy.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) show intestinal epithelial barrier (IEB) alterations, enteric gliosis and inflammation that could contribute to gastrointestinal symptoms. Moreover, changes in leucine rich-repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) expression/activity have been associated with PD development and related intestinal inflammation. However, the molecular determinants linking LRRK2, enteric gliosis and IEB impairment remain unclear. Therefore, we investigated the role of LRRK2 in IEB changes associated with PD, focusing on its role in the interplay between enteric glial cells (EGCs) and intestinal epithelial cells (IECs). EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Human A53T α-synuclein transgenic (Tg) mice (9 months old) were provided a model of early PD. Central neuroinflammation was studied by IBA-1 staining. Intestinal motility, colonic α-synuclein and LRRK2 expression were assessed. Enteric gliosis was evaluated by detection of GFAP+ cells co-expressing LRRK2; IEB was tested by mucins detection and quantification of Muc-2, tight junction proteins and secretory autophagy. In vitro co-cultures between EGCs and IECs were performed to investigate glial LRRK2-mediated gut barrier alterations. KEY RESULTS: A53T mice, without central neuroinflammation, showed intestinal disturbances, colonic α-synuclein accumulation and an increase in colonic GFAP+/LRRK2+ glial cells before brain pathology. Moreover, PD animals displayed IEB alterations and increased colonic autophagosomes, suggesting a shift towards secretory autophagy. In co-culture experiments, α-synuclein and lipopolysaccharide promoted enteric gliosis and LRRK2 up-regulation in glial cells, contributing to IEB impairment via secretory autophagy. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: These changes could influence bowel symptoms and central pathology associated with PD, via the gut-brain axis.

secondary.title: Lysosome-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe ROCL enables dynamic hypochlorous acid imaging in living cells and a mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
secondary.abstract: Hypochlorous acid (HClO) plays critical roles in oxidative stress and is strongly implicated in the progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). Here, we report ROCL, a new lysosome-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe for sensitive and selective detection of HClO in living systems. ROCL displays rapid response, excellent selectivity, and a low detection limit of 49 nM, based on an HClO-induced spirolactam ring-opening mechanism. The probe enables real-time imaging of exogenous and endogenous HClO in SH-SY5Y and PC12 cells, exhibits low cytotoxicity, and effectively visualizes elevated HClO levels in MPTP- and rotenone-induced PD models. ROCL also shows favorable blood-brain barrier permeability and allows noninvasive in vivo HClO imaging in PD model mice. These results establish ROCL as a valuable tool for probing HClO-associated oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases.

secondary.title: A2A Receptor Intervention Protects Astrocytes Against 6-Hydroxydopamine-Induced Oxidative and Mitochondrial Stress via the p38 MAPK Axis, Alleviating Inflammation in an In Vivo Model of Parkinson's Disease.
secondary.abstract: INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVE: Astrocytic mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance contribute to Parkinson's Disease (PD) pathogenesis, but the role of adenosine A2A receptor (A2AR) antagonism in maintaining astrocytic homeostasis remains unclear. This study investigated whether the selective non-purine A2AR antagonist IDPU protects against 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA)-induced astrocytic stress and improves behavioural, neurochemical, and inflammatory outcomes in an experimental model of PD. METHODS: Primary cortical astrocytes were exposed to 6-OHDA (100 μM) and subsequently treated with IDPU (0.5-1 μM) or ZM241385. Cell viability, apoptosis, Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS), intracellular Ca²⁺, Mitochondrial Membrane Potential (MMP), BDNF, and p38MAPK/DRP1/Parkin signalling were assessed. In vivo efficacy was evaluated in adult male Sprague-Dawley rats with unilateral 6-OHDA lesions following 14 days of treatment with IDPU (6 or 9 mg/kg) or ZM241385 (5 mg/kg), using behavioural, dopamine, and TNF-α assessments. RESULTS: 6-OHDA reduced astrocyte viability, increased apoptosis, ROS production and intracellular Ca²⁺ levels, and disrupted MMP. IDPU treatment improved cell viability, reduced apoptosis, oxidative stress and Ca²⁺ overload, and partially restored MMP and BDNF levels. These effects were accompanied by reduced phosphorylation of p38MAPK and DRP1 and restoration of Parkin expression. In vivo, IDPU improved motor performance and depressive-like behaviour, partially restored dopamine levels, and reduced TNF-α expression in 6-OHDA-lesioned rats. DISCUSSION: These findings indicate that A2AR antagonism may mitigate astrocytic stress by modulating redox balance, calcium homeostasis, mitochondrial dynamics, and inflammatory signalling. The observed regulation of the p38MAPK-DRP1-Parkin axis supports a potential mechanistic link between astrocytic mitochondrial dysfunction and neuroinflammatory outcomes in PD. CONCLUSION: IDPU-mediated A2AR antagonism demonstrated protective effects against 6-OHDA-induced astrocytic and Parkinsonian alterations, supporting A2AR antagonism as a potential non-dopaminergic, astrocyte-targeted therapeutic approach. Further studies are required to establish its effects on dopaminergic neuronal survival and long-term therapeutic efficacy.

secondary.title: Platelet lysates ameliorate impaired neuronal autophagy in Parkinson's Disease: correlative evidence for ROS/Akt signaling.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder and represents a growing global health challenge. Platelet lysates (PLs) are enriched in growth factors, cytokines, and bioactive proteins with known tissue-regenerative and neurorestorative properties; however, their neuroprotective efficacy and molecular mechanisms in PD remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the neuroprotective effects of PLs in PD models and to explore the underlying mechanisms. METHODS: SH-SY5Y cells exposed to 6-OHDA, MPP⁺, or rotenone were used as in vitro PD models. Cell viability, morphological injury, ROS levels, TH expression, and p-α-syn (Ser129) levels were assessed. Autophagosome formation was evaluated using an Ad-GFP-LC3 transduction assay, and autophagic flux was further verified by bafilomycin A1-mediated lysosomal blockade. Mechanistic studies employed SC79 (Akt activator) and N-acetylcysteine (NAC, ROS scavenger). In vivo, MPTP-induced and A53T transgenic mouse models of PD were used to evaluate nigrostriatal dopaminergic neuronal protection, Nissl body preservation, p-α-syn accumulation, and motor function. RESULTS: PLs ameliorated neurotoxin-induced morphological injury, increased cell viability, reduced intracellular ROS levels, upregulated TH expression, and decreased p-α-syn (Ser129) accumulation in SH-SY5Y cells. Ad-GFP-LC3 assays showed that PLs promoted autophagosome biogenesis, and bafilomycin A1-based flux assays further confirmed that PLs rescued neurotoxin-impaired autophagic flux across all three toxin models. Mechanistically, PLs consistently reduced ROS and enhanced Akt phosphorylation. In MPP⁺- and 6-OHDA-injured cells, this was accompanied by ATG5/LC3-II upregulation and restoration of autophagic degradation; however, in the rotenone model, the toxin-induced ATG5 reduction was not significantly reversed despite effective attenuation of oxidative stress and p62 accumulation, suggesting ATG5-independent protective mechanisms. In vivo, PLs administration protected nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons, preserved Nissl bodies, reduced p-α-syn (Ser129) immunoreactivity, and improved motor function in both MPTP-induced and A53T transgenic mouse models of PD. CONCLUSION: PLs attenuate neurotoxin-induced neuronal injury and improve pathological and behavioral phenotypes in PD models. The ROS/Akt signaling axis appears to be one plausible mechanistic correlate of PLs-mediated neuroprotection, with toxin-specific divergence in downstream autophagy mechanisms. These findings support further investigation of PLs as a potential intervention for PD-related pathological phenotypes.

best.title: Neuronal cell-cycle re-entry stratifies clinical trajectories in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
best.abstract: The clinical heterogeneity of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) remains a fundamental barrier to effective therapy. While cell cycle re-entry in post-mitotic neurons is a known precursor to neurodegeneration, its role in defining patient-specific outcomes has never been established. Here, we integrate large-scale transcriptomic profiling from the AnswerALS cohort with mechanistic studies in human iPSC-derived spinal motor neurons to define how cell-cycle re-entry shapes disease heterogeneity in ALS. We identify a transcriptionally distinct patient subgroup with the highest expression of G1 or G2-phase cyclins that exhibit significantly slower functional decline (ALSFRS-R), whereas the engagement of S-phase markers correlates with accelerated disease progression. Nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction, a hallmark of ALS and related disorders, disrupts the spatial distribution of key regulatory proteins and may contribute to maladaptive cell-cycle activation. Our recent evidence suggests that impaired nuclear import may initiate, rather than merely accompany, neuronal cell-cycle re-entry. Using iPSC-derived motor neurons, we show that impaired nuclear import initiates TDP-43 pathology and global nuclear/cytoplasmic mis-localization of key ALS-related proteins. This nucleocytoplasmic transport dysfunction triggers a transient wave of cell-cycle activity immediately preceding neuronal cell death. Crucially, we show that DNA-replication initiation is a pathological inflection point of no return, as neurons entering S-phase accumulate replication-associated DNA damage and undergo cell death. Selective inhibition of CDK4/6 prevents S-phase entry and confers potent neuroprotection. Our findings demonstrate that impaired nuclear import drives maladaptive cell-cycle reactivation in ALS and that the depth of cell-cycle engagement stratifies neuronal fate and patient trajectories.

best.title: Cofilin hyperphosphorylation triggers TDP-43 pathology in sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
best.abstract: Pathological forms of TAR-binding protein 43 (TDP-43), involving its aberrant mislocalization to the cytoplasm, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, are present in ∼45%-50% frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer's disease individuals and most (97%) amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases. Hence, identifying mechanisms that induce TDP-43 pathology are central to neurodegeneration and developing new therapeutic targets in these conditions. Cofilin is a multifunctional protein with a crucial role in regulating the actin cytoskeleton. Actin has important neuronal-specific activities in dendritic spines, axonal growth cones and synapses and it is in constant equilibrium between two forms: monomeric globular actin (G-actin) and polymeric filamentous actin (F-actin). Cofilin controls actin dynamics by depolymerizing and severing actin filaments. When cofilin is phosphorylated (at serine-3, Ser3) by LIM kinase1 (LIMK1), it becomes inactive, leading to production of more F-actin. Defects in cofilin are well described in other neurodegenerative disorders, unlike in ALS. We examined phosphorylation of cofilin and actin dynamics in post-mortem spinal cord tissue from sporadic ALS (SALS) patients, the TDP-43 rNLS8 transgenic mouse model and NSC-34 motor neuronal cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. F-actin was pharmacologically stabilized to mimic cofilin hyperphosphorylation and TDP-43 pathology was assessed. Neuronal cells were treated with a non-phosphorylatable cofilin S3A peptide (MAAGVAVSDGVIKVFN) and TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis were evaluated. Here, we show that cofilin is hyperphosphorylated in human ALS and disease models compared to controls. This was detected in spinal motor neurons from SALS patients and a TDP-43 mouse model (rNLS8) displaying key ALS phenotypes, and in motor neuronal NSC-34 cells expressing cytoplasmic TDP-43. Supporting this observation, more F-actin relative to G-actin was present in cortical/spinal cord lysates from SALS patients and TDP-43 rNLS8 mice, and NSC-34 cells expressing TDP-43. We also show that mimicking cofilin hyperphosphorylation by pharmacological stabilization of F-actin induced TDP-43 pathology: cytoplasmic mislocalization, inclusion formation, hyperphosphorylation and fragmentation, and promoted its recruitment into stress granules (SGs). Furthermore, we detected increased levels of LIMK1 phosphorylation and tropomyosin isoforms 4.1 and 4.2 in SALS patients. These findings reveal aberrant cofilin hyperphosphorylation disrupts actin dynamics, triggering TDP-43 pathology and SG recruitment in SALS. They imply that preventing cofilin phosphorylation is a novel therapeutic strategy applicable to most ALS cases. Treatment of neuronal cells with the S3A peptide prevented features of TDP-43 pathology and apoptosis compared to control peptides. These findings thus describe a novel pathogenic mechanism producing TDP-43 pathology, applicable to most ALS cases and other neurodegenerative diseases.

best.title: Amyloid and tau display distinct patterns across Alzheimer's in anterior caudate.
best.abstract: The anterior caudate shows a pattern of Alzheimer's disease pathology that differs from the more extensively studied cortex. Across 41 donors, we found mostly diffuse amyloid beta plaques in gray matter and phosphorylated tau threads associated with white matter. Combining digital pathology with single-nucleus and spatial gene expression data, we detected no significant loss or gain in neuronal cell-type abundance with increasing pathology. However, we did observe increases in an FLT1+/IL1B+ microglial population with tau burden. Fast-spiking PTHLH-PVALB interneurons showed changes in genes related to ion channels, cellular trafficking, and phosphorylation. These findings offer a cellular-resolution reference for investigating how Alzheimer's disease affects subcortical brain regions.

best.title: NeuroBase: A Web-Based Transcriptomic Resource and R Package for Cross-Disorder Analysis of Neurodegenerative and Neuropsychiatric Diseases.
best.abstract: Neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia, are highly prevalent and biologically complex conditions that remain difficult to diagnose and treat. This study aimed to develop NeuroBase, a web-based transcriptomic resource that supports exploratory comparison of shared and disorder-specific gene expression features across these disorders. Fourteen human brain bulk RNA sequencing datasets (262 total samples) were processed using a standardized pipeline, followed by differential gene expression analysis with DESeq2, edgeR and limma-voom for broad exploratory discovery, complemented by a multi-method sensitivity analysis to define a method-concordant core gene set, protein-protein interaction network analysis using STRING with downstream exploration in Cytoscape, and functional enrichment analysis. Principal component analysis and clustering-based visualizations were used to summarize similarities and differences in transcriptomic patterns among disorders. Differential expression analysis identified dataset-level significant genes within each disorder using DESeq2 for one dataset per disorder (FDR ≤ 0.05), including 38 genes in Alzheimer's disease, 6,704 in autism spectrum disorder, 3,559 in bipolar disorder, 687 in Parkinson's disease, and 2,750 in schizophrenia; a stricter multi-method intersection analysis yielded method-concordant Core Intersection sets in the most informative datasets (983 core DEGs in autism spectrum disorder, 505 in bipolar disorder, 281 in schizophrenia, and 234 and 151 in two Parkinson's disease datasets; only two core genes (SPP1 and CHST3) were found in Alzheimer's disease). A unified strict-threshold reanalysis (FDR ≤ 0.05, |log₂FC|≥ 1) revealed disorder-level DEG burdens ranging from 34 (Alzheimer's disease) to 2,812 (autism) deduplicated genes, but only 24 genes were reproducible across independent cohorts of the same disorder, highlighting the limited cross-cohort reproducibility characteristic of bulk brain transcriptomics. Enrichment analyses identified significantly enriched signaling pathways in autism spectrum disorder and nominally enriched synapse-related pathways in Alzheimer's disease. Representative high-signal genes included SPP1 in Alzheimer's disease, NRGN in one Parkinson's disease dataset, and BEST1 in autism spectrum disorder. Cross-disorder comparison identified 465 differentially expressed genes shared between the neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorder groups, and principal component analysis showed that sample variation was dominated by dataset and tissue of origin. NeuroBase is a publicly accessible, web-based transcriptomic database and companion R package (neurobaseR) that enables standardized, cross-disorder exploration of bulk brain gene expression profiles across neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, supporting comparative analysis, programmatic data access, and hypothesis generation through interactive visualization and pathway-level summaries.

best.abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

best.title: Thalamic Reticular Nucleus Excitability and Cholinergic Signaling are Disrupted in a Mouse Model of Alzheimer's Disease Neuropathology.
best.abstract: The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) forms powerful GABAergic connections with thalamic nuclei that regulate sleep, attention, and sensory processing. TRN neurons receive dense cholinergic innervation from the basal forebrain and brainstem, dynamically shaping TRN function across brain states. We previously showed reduced TRN activity and sleep deficits in amyloid precursor protein transgenic mice (APP mice), implicating TRN dysfunction as an early contributor to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathophysiology. Here, using slice electrophysiology in mice of both sexes, we determined whether changes in intrinsic membrane properties or cholinergic synaptic transmission contribute to TRN hypoactivity in APP mice. We found that TRN neurons located in the inner core and outer shell regions undergo substantial increases in excitability after the first postnatal month. In mature animals, core neurons exhibited higher firing rates and diverse firing patterns, including persistent firing, whereas shell neurons fired at lower rates and displayed more homogeneous firing patterns without persistent activity. Firing diversity in core neurons was mediated in part by low-threshold T-type Ca²⁺ channels. Cholinergic synaptic activation, mediated predominantly by basal forebrain afferents, produced biphasic excitatory-inhibitory postsynaptic responses in both core and shell neurons, with the ratio of postsynaptic excitation and inhibition varying across postsynaptic targets. Overall, cholinergic activation suppressed TRN firing. In APP mice, core neurons showed reduced intrinsic excitability and cholinergic afferents evoked postsynaptic responses with a larger muscarinic receptor-mediated inhibitory component, leading to delayed TRN firing. Together, these findings identify both intrinsic and cholinergic synaptic mechanisms that may contribute to TRN dysfunction during early AD.Significance Statement Alzheimer's disease (AD) is typically diagnosed after cognitive symptoms emerge when treatments are less effective, highlighting the need to understand preclinical disease mechanisms. Cholinergic signaling and slow-wave sleep are disrupted before symptom onset, but the mechanisms underlying these changes remain poorly understood. Because the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) receives strong cholinergic input and mediates sleep-related rhythms, it is well positioned to contribute to early AD pathophysiology. We previously found reduced TRN activity and disrupted sleep in an AD mouse model. Here, we show that intrinsic excitability and cholinergic synaptic signaling are altered in TRN neurons during preclinical AD. These changes may contribute to thalamic dysfunction and sleep disturbances, providing a potential circuit mechanism linking early AD pathology to disease progression.

best.title: 27-Hydroxycholesterol Modulates Microglial α-Synuclein Handling and Is Associated with AKT1/JAK-STAT/TNF Signaling in Parkinson's Disease Models.
best.abstract: 27-Hydroxycholesterol (27-OHC) is an oxysterol implicated in neuroinflammation, but its relationship to microglial α-synuclein (α-syn) handling and intracellular signaling in Parkinson's disease (PD) models remains incompletely defined. We combined BV2-cell assays, an rAAV-A53T mouse model, untargeted lipidomics and proteomics, network analyses, molecular docking, pathway immunoblotting, pharmacological AKT inhibition, and a cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA). In BV2 cells, 0.5-2.5 μM 27-OHC did not reduce viability, whereas concentrations ≥ 5 μM were cytotoxic. At 2.5 μM, 27-OHC increased cell-associated α-syn signal after exposure to recombinant α-syn PFFs. Brain lipidomics in the PD model showed accumulation of the broad sterol-lipid class, but did not provide absolute brain 27-OHC concentrations. Network analyses nominated AKT1, IL6, STAT3, and MMP9 as hub genes. In three independent BV2 experiments, PFF and 27-OHC exposure were associated with altered phosphorylation of AKT, STAT3, and NF-κB p65; a PFF × 27-OHC interaction was detected for STAT3 phosphorylation. MK-2206 lowered the cell-associated α-syn/GAPDH signal in the combined-treatment group, although the comparison did not remain significant after adjustment across three pairwise tests. CETSA showed greater soluble AKT1 retention after 27-OHC exposure and a higher thermal-curve area under the curve (paired p = 0.023). These findings support an association between 27-OHC exposure, microglial α-syn handling, and AKT-related signaling in BV2 cells. They do not establish direct 27-OHC-AKT1 binding or an in vivo causal effect of brain 27-OHC on microglia.

best.title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes.
best.abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

best.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss.
best.abstract: TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts1-8. Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.

best.title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
best.abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

best.title: Hyperactive KIF5A in Neurodegeneration.
best.abstract: The highly polarised morphology of neurons and the sheer length of their axons make transport of cargoes throughout the cell a formidable task. Decades of evidence obtained from genetic studies on patients and animal models highlight deficits in axonal transport as a recurrent cause, or early contributing factor, in a plethora of neurodegenerative diseases. Axonal transport abnormalities usually manifest as a slowing of cargo trafficked by molecular motors along microtubules; however, hyperactivation of motors can also lead to disease. That is the case for the kinesin-1 protein KIF5A, in which hyperactive mutations are linked to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and neonatal intractable myoclonus (NEIMY). In this Perspective, we summarise the latest insights into the impact of KIF5A hyperactivity, such as loss of autoinhibition, aggregation, altered cargo binding and microtubule damage. We conclude by discussing possible strategies to counteract these disruptions, with an emphasis on the necessity of restoring axonal transport to physiological levels, a key requirement to maintain neuronal homeostasis.

best.title: The blood-brain barrier imports diverse neuroprotective proteins through pathways impaired early in Alzheimer's disease models.
best.abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) has been defined primarily by what it excludes, yet the scale and function of physiological blood-to-brain protein transport remain largely unknown. Using bioorthogonal proteomics, we find that the healthy BBB samples 191 plasma proteins and permits 92 into the brain parenchyma. Enriched for carrier and metabolic functions, these proteins home to distinct brain cell types, such as apolipoprotein A1 (APOA1) to astrocytes and alpha-1 antitrypsin (SERPINA1) to microglia. This cell-type tropism relies on a BBB-parenchyma receptor hand-off: APOA1 crosses the BBB via SR-B1 and engages astrocytic ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), a key Alzheimer's risk gene, driving cholesterol efflux that supports synapse integrity. Unlike LPS-induced nonspecific leakage, early-stage 5xFAD mice show selective BBB transport remodeling, with reduced APOA1 and increased SERPINA1 uptake. Hepatic APOA1 overexpression restores APOA1 in the 5xFAD brain, rescuing astrocytic, synaptic, and behavioral deficits. These findings recast the BBB as a selective interface that recruits neuroprotective circulatory proteins for brain health.

best.title: Alzheimer's disease-associated presenilin 2 N141I mutation impairs neuronal lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial dynamics through selective downregulation of the Golgi exchange factor Gbf1.
best.abstract: Presenilin 2 (PS2) mutations cause familial Alzheimer's disease, yet their effects beyond amyloid processing remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how PS2 deletion and the N141I mutation affect neuronal lipid homeostasis and mitochondrial dynamics in mouse primary neurons. Both PS2 deletion and N141I mutation reduced neuronal lipid content. However, exogenous lipid supplementation rescued this deficit only in N141I-expressing neurons, indicating a partial loss-of-function effect. N141I neurons also displayed reduced OPA1, a mitochondrial fusion regulator, restored by lipid supplementation. RNA-sequencing identified Gbf1, a Golgi-specific guanine nucleotide exchange factor, as selectively downregulated in N141I but not knockout tissue, which was confirmed at the protein level in mouse brain and primary neurons. Gbf1 knockdown in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) recapitulated the N141I lipid profile. Together, these findings reveal a PS2-GBF1-lipid-mitochondria axis disrupted specifically by the N141I mutation, suggesting an amyloid-independent pathway contributing to neurodegeneration and identifying potential therapeutic targets for familial Alzheimer's disease.

best.title: VPS35 mutation inhibits PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy via increased LRRK2 kinase activity.
best.abstract: The p.D620N mutation in VPS35 causes an autosomal dominant form of Parkinson's disease via mechanisms that are poorly understood. PINK1 and parkin, two proteins whose loss-of-function underlies autosomal recessive Parkinson's disease, cooperate to mediate mitophagy, a quality control pathway for selective elimination of damaged mitochondria. PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy is disrupted by LRRK2 mutations, which are the most prevalent cause of autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease. Here, we investigated whether the p.D620N VPS35 mutation has an effect on PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy. We identified a novel family with autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease caused by a p.D620N VPS35 mutation. We cultured skin fibroblasts and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived dopaminergic neurons from the proband and from a second, unrelated Parkinson's disease patient with the p.D620N VPS35 mutation, and compared them with isogenic and non-isogenic control cells. PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy was severely impaired in VPS35 mutant fibroblasts and neurons, while non-selective, starvation-induced autophagy and lysosomal degradative capacity were preserved. siRNA-mediated VPS35 knockdown rescued the mitophagy defect in VPS35 mutant cells, whereas overexpression of wild-type VPS35 did not, suggesting a gain-of-function mechanism of the mutation. The VPS35 mutation did not interfere with activation of PINK1 or parkin after mitochondrial depolarization, but impaired mitochondrial recruitment of the autophagy receptor optineurin. LRRK2 kinase activity was increased in the VPS35 mutant cells, as shown by enhanced levels of the T73-phosphorylated form of the LRRK2 substrate RAB10. The enhanced level of phosphorylated RAB10 in VPS35 mutant cells was decreased by treatment with LRRK2 kinase inhibitors and by VPS35 knockdown. Importantly, the mitophagy defect of VPS35 mutant fibroblasts and neurons was fully rescued by LRRK2 kinase inhibitors as well as by overexpression of PPM1H, a phosphatase that dephosphorylates multiple RAB substrates of LRRK2. Finally, in situ proximity ligation experiments revealed that endogenous VPS35 and LRRK2 are proximity partners in human dopaminergic neurons and that this proximity relationship is enhanced by the VPS35 mutation. In conclusion, the VPS35 mutation impairs PINK1/parkin-mediated mitophagy via a gain-of-function mechanism that involves stimulation of LRRK2 kinase activity. Thus, a VPS35/LRRK2 axis linked to dominant Parkinson's disease intersects with a pathway mediated by proteins encoded by the recessive Parkinson's disease genes.

best.title: Parkinson's disease-linked D620N mutation selectively alters the brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35.
best.abstract: Mutations in several genes are known to cause familial forms of Parkinson's disease (PD), including mutations in the vacuolar protein sorting 35 ortholog (VPS35) gene linked to late-onset, autosomal dominant PD. VPS35 encodes a core subunit of the retromer complex which functions in endosomal sorting and recycling. It remains unclear how the pathogenic D620N mutation in VPS35 disrupts retromer function to induce neurodegeneration in PD. Using cell- and rodent-based models expressing D620N VPS35, we performed interactome proteomics to identify alterations underlying the pathogenic effects of D620N VPS35 in PD. Using overexpression of VPS35 variants in HEK-293 T cells, we conducted tandem affinity purification (TAP) or co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) with protein chemical crosslinking to determine the native and non-native protein interactomes of wild-type (WT) and D620N VPS35, respectively. Notably, we can confirm the reduced interaction of D620N VPS35 with components of the WASH complex. Additionally, using a viral-mediated gene transfer model of human D620N VPS35 overexpression in adult rat brain, we identify the first brain-specific protein interactome of VPS35. These overexpression models reveal remarkably similar interaction profiles of WT and D620N VPS35, suggesting that the D620N mutation has a subtle effect on the overall VPS35 protein interactome. We also conducted proteomic analysis of brain tissue from a D620N VPS35 knockin (KI) mouse model that expresses VPS35 at endogenous levels. Using co-IP from hemibrain or striatal extracts of WT and D620N VPS35 KI mice, we reveal a high degree of similarity between the brain interactomes of WT and D620N VPS35, further suggesting a subtle effect of the D620N mutation on VPS35 protein interactions. Notably, in both hemibrain and striatum, we find a selective decrease in the interaction of two known interactors, TBC1D5 and VPS29, with D620N VPS35. We also performed global proteomic analysis of striatal tissue from D620N VPS35 KI mice and reveal a high degree of similarity between WT and D620N, further suggesting a subtle effect of this mutation. Together, our study provides a comprehensive evaluation of the VPS35 protein interactome and reveals a selective effect of the PD-linked D620N mutation in mammalian cells and brain. Our study provides key insight into the mechanisms of retromer dysfunction in VPS35-linked PD.

best.title: Dystrophic changes of nigrostriatal axons harboring a SYNJ1 Parkinson's mutation suggest catastrophic failure of endocytic mechanisms.
best.abstract: Synaptojanin 1 is a brain enriched phosphoinositide phosphatase implicated in endocytosis at the synapse. A mutation (R258Q) that selectively impairs its Sac1 phosphatase domain causes early onset familial Parkinsonism. Neurons of mice with this mutation display synaptic vesicle traffic defects across the brain, but selective dystrophic changes in a subset of dopaminergic axons in the dorsolateral striatum. Using correlative light microscopy-FIB-SEM of mutant mouse striata to visualize in 3D these abnormal structures we show that they represent clusters of focal axonal dilations harboring massive, onion-like DAT enriched plasma membrane infoldings, generally localized next to cell bodies of neighboring cells, often engulfing evaginations of such cells. This dysmorphia was associated with a deficit in dopamine release in the same striatal region. Given the involvement of Synj1 in endocytic mechanisms, these structures may reflect an imbalance between exocytosis and endocytosis. Their occurrence only in a subset of axons suggests a vulnerability threshold of these axons beyond which the expansion of the plasma membrane is not counteracted by compensatory mechanisms.

best.title: BAG3 coordinates astrocytic proteostasis of Alzheimer's disease-linked proteins via proteasome, autophagy, and retromer interactions.
best.abstract: Bcl-2-associated athanogene 3 (BAG3) is a mediator of chaperone-assisted selective autophagy, and in the brain, is most highly expressed in astrocytes. However, its role in astrocytes remains poorly defined. Given the genetic and pathological links of BAG3 to proteostasis and neurodegenerative diseases, we investigated how BAG3 contributes to astrocyte function and Alzheimer's disease (AD). To define its function and relevance, we used single-nucleus RNA sequencing to confirm BAG3 enrichment in astrocytes and employed CRISPR/Cas9 editing of human induced pluripotent stem cells followed by proteomic and transcriptomic profiling, which revealed that BAG3 loss caused greater disruption in astrocytes than in neurons. BAG3-deficient astrocytes displayed reduced autophagy, lysosomal abundance and activity, and proteasome function. Coimmunoprecipitation identified BAG3 known binding partners (e.g., HSPB8, proteasome regulators), as well as an interactor in the retromer complex, VPS35. BAG3 deficiency resulted in altered retromer activity as measured by amyloid precursor protein (APP) localization in endosomes. In addition to validating these binding partners, integrative -omics analyses showed that BAG3 regulates AD-relevant proteins (GFAP, BIN1), as well as HSPB8. Functionally, BAG3 knockout astrocytes exhibited impaired amyloid-β proteostasis when cocultured with APP/PSEN1 mutant neurons, directly linking BAG3 to a disease-relevant astrocyte phenotype. Finally, analysis of postmortem human brain revealed that BAG3 expression marks a stress-responsive astrocyte subtype in aged individuals. Together, these findings demonstrate that BAG3 coordinates astrocyte proteostasis through interactions with regulators of autophagy, proteasome activity, and retromer function, positioning it as a potential therapeutic target and central node of astrocytic protein quality control in neurodegeneration.

best.title: VPS35 Regulates Microglial Lipid Droplet Accumulation in Parkinson's Disease via Rab7.
best.abstract: Microglial dysfunction and aberrant lipid metabolism are emerging as key contributors to Parkinson's disease (PD) pathogenesis. However, the specific role and regulation of lipid droplets (LDs) within microglia remain poorly defined. In this study, we employed MPTP- and LPS-induced PD mouse models and an in vitro system utilizing astrocyte-conditioned medium to model disease-relevant lipid stress and found enhanced LD accumulation in microglia. VPS35 expression was decreased in microglia, correlating with elevated microglial LD levels in PD mouse models. We then performed genetic manipulations (knockdown and overexpression) of VPS35, including the PD-associated D620N mutant, in primary microglia and assessed LD accumulation, phagocytic function, inflammatory responses, and integrated stress pathways. We showed that VPS35 knockdown exacerbated the accumulation of LDs in microglia. Conversely, VPS35 overexpression ameliorated LD formation, improved phagocytic function, and reduced inflammatory and integrated stress responses in microglia. The PD-related VPS35[D620N] mutation abolished these protective effects. We further found that VPS35 interacts with Rab7 to maintain lysosomal function, and the D620N mutation disrupts this interaction, leading to defective LD clearance. Our findings reveal VPS35 dysfunction as a key pathogenic mechanism in PD, where the D620N mutation disrupts microglial lipid handling to promote disease progression, thereby nominating VPS35 restoration as a promising therapeutic strategy.

best.title: Early reduction of myelin-associated glycoprotein at myelin membranes in Huntington's disease.
best.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is marked by progressive neuronal loss and atrophy of grey matter structures, particularly the caudate and putamen. Brain imaging studies reveal that the white matter starts to decay in the brain of individuals bearing the HD mutation many years before symptomatic onset. However, the mechanism by which the HD mutation causes white matter loss remains to be further defined. In this study, we examined white matter pathology and explored the underlying mechanism in the HDQ140 knock-in mouse model of HD. Western blot analysis of proteins localized at different layers of the myelin sheath showed that myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG), which is localized at the innermost myelin layer, was decreased earlier than proteins localized at outer layers of the myelin. The loss of MAG occurred at fully myelinated axons and was progressive with age. In postmortem symptomatic human HD brains, the level of MAG as well as other myelin proteins was also decreased. In HD mouse brains, MAG labeling was reduced at fiber bundles but accumulated in perinuclear structures of cells that expressed breast carcinoma amplified sequence 1, a marker for new oligodendrocytes. While their abundance was normal, new oligodendrocytes in HD brains were impeded in acquiring the expression of MAG. Compared with those in wild-type mouse brains, oligodendrocytes in HD mouse brains had a reduced frequency of MAG-bearing small vesicles and an increased abundance and enlargement of MAG-containing perinuclear structures. Further studies suggest that the MAG-accumulating perinuclear structures were derived from the late endosomal lysosomal compartment. Our study suggests that white matter decay in HD brains involves an early progressive loss of MAG in myelin membranes.

best.title: Irosustat and STX140 improve cognitive function and modulate amyloid, oxidative stress, and inflammatory pathways in experimental Alzheimer's disease.
best.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is currently the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder affecting the geriatric population. The pathology of AD has been described as neuronal loss caused by the accumulation of beta-amyloid plaques and the formation of neurofibrillary tangles resulting from tau protein phosphorylation. This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of steroid sulfatase inhibition using two drugs, the clinical steroid sulfatase inhibitor Irosustat and the multi-targeting preclinical candidate STX140, in scopolamine-induced AD in male Wistar rats compared to Donepezil as a standard drug. Behavioral tests such as the Open Field Test, Elevated Plus Maze Test, and Morris Water Maze Test were conducted to confirm the disease state and assess any improvement. At the end of the study, the animals were dissected to collect blood and brain samples for morphological, histological, immunohistochemical, biochemical, quantitative polymerase chain reaction and western blotting analyses. Treatment with Irosustat or STX140 improved learning, memory, and cognitive function compared with the disease group. The treated groups showed lowered brain tissue Aβ-40 & 42 levels, acetylcholinesterase activity, oxidative stress, and inflammatory markers. Morphological assessments showed that the drugs protected against brain atrophy and neuronal loss. Irosustat and STX140 are therefore promising therapeutic candidates for the management of Alzheimer's Disease.

best.title: Neuroprotective potential of EGF-treated bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells in trimethyltin-induced neurodegeneration: in vitro and in vivo studies.
best.abstract: UNLABELLED: Background: Neurodegenerative diseases are progressive, debilitating, and often life-threatening disorders of the nervous system. Bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells are considered a promising therapeutic strategy for different diseases, including neurodegeneration. EGF has been reported to promote neuron-like characteristics and neurotrophic responses in BM-MSCs. This study was conducted to assess the role of EGF-treated Bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells in a neurodegenerative rat model (a novel approach). Methods: In vitro analysis was performed to evaluate the specific dose and cell viability using MTT and Crystal Violet assays and morphology under a microscope. For the in vivo study, forty rats were randomly allocated into four groups: Control, Injury, injury + Bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells (BM-MSCS), and injury + EGF-treated Bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cells (BM-MSCs). A neurodegenerative rat model was developed with the use of trimethyltin chloride. Following TMT induction, BM-MSCs and EGF-treated BM-MSCs were administered via the intrathecal route. Behavioral performance, Histopathological alteration, protein expression, and gene expression were evaluated. The assessed biomarkers included TNF-α (inflammation), NFL (neuronal injury), MAPT (Tau gene expression), the neurotrophic factors BDNF and NGF, together with the progenitor-associated marker Nestin. Findings: In vitro, BM-MSCs treated with 10 ng/mL EGF maintained cell viability comparable to untreated controls, as confirmed by MTT and Crystal Violet assays, while exhibiting pronounced neuron-like morphological characteristics. In vivo, transplantation of EGF-treated BM-MSCs significantly improved spatial learning, memory, and neuromuscular performance compared with both the TMT-induced injury group and the untreated BM-MSC group. Histopathological analysis demonstrated improved preservation of hippocampal architecture following EGF-treated BM-MSC transplantation. Furthermore, EGF-treated BM-MSCs significantly reduced the expression of TNF-α, neurofilament light chain (NFL), and phosphorylated Tau (p-Tau), while significantly increasing the expression of BDNF, NGF, and Nestin at both the protein and gene levels. Overall, EGF preconditioning enhanced the neuroprotective and recovery associated effects of BM-MSCs in the TMT-induced neurodegenerative rat model. Conclusion: EGF-preconditioned BM-MSCs attenuated TMT-induced neurodegenerative changes by improving behavioral performance, reducing neuroinflammatory and neuronal injury-associated responses, preserving hippocampal cellular and tissue integrity, and enhancing neurotrophic support. These findings suggest that EGF preconditioning may potentiate the neuroprotective and immunomodulatory effects of BM-MSCs and may represent a promising strategy for the treatment of neurodegenerative disorders. best.title: A rare TMEM175 mutation drives Parkinson's disease pathology by disrupting proton gating and lysosomal acidification.
best.abstract: Transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175), implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, has been variably proposed to function as a background K+ "leak" channel or a proton-activated proton channel in lysosomes. Here, we identified the rare TMEM175 variant p.L275R in a patient with early onset PD. Electrophysiological analyses revealed that TMEM175-L275R mutant proteins retain normal lysosomal expression and K+ "leak" activity, but specifically lose proton- and agonist-dependent activation gating. In skin fibroblasts isolated from the patient with PD harboring the monoallelic p.L275R mutation (TMEM175+/L275R), and in derived induced pluripotent stem cells and induced dopaminergic neurons, lysosomal H+ flux, acidification, and degradation were impaired. These lysosomal defects were corrected upon genome editing to produce the isogenic WT allele (+/+Cor), but appeared when the mutant allele was introduced onto a WT background (+/L275RMut). Pathological α-synuclein aggregation was facilitated in patient-derived (+/L275R) and mutation-introduced (+/L275RMut) neurons. Consistent with these genetic findings, pharmacological activation of TMEM175 with small-molecule agonists restored lysosomal functions and reduced α-synuclein aggregation in TMEM175+/L275R neurons. In in-vivo studies, equivalent-site-mutation knock-in mice demonstrated synucleinopathy and PD-like motor phenotypes. Collectively, our work provides genetic and pharmacological evidence that severe loss-of-function mutations may contribute causally to the onset age and pathogenesis of PD and identifies lysosomal proton channels and transporters as potential therapeutic targets for PD intervention.

best.title: TREM2/IGF-1 signaling axis-induced microglial senescence underlies benzo[a]pyrene-associated Parkinson's disease-like lesions.
best.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder worldwide. Accumulating evidence has linked environmental polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), with benzo[a]pyrene (B[a]P) as a representative ubiquitous member, to elevated PD risk and disease pathogenesis. The present study aimed to investigate whether B[a]P can trigger typical PD-like lesions in mice, and further dissects the functional role of microglial senescence as well as its underlying regulatory mechanism, using complementary systems in vivo mouse model and in vitro BV2 microglia cell. Behavioral assessments revealed that B[a]P exposure induced significant, dose-dependent impairments in motor coordination and cognitive function compared with the control group. Moreover, the degree of functional impairments measured in the high-dose B[a]P group was comparable to that observed in the MPTP positive-control group. Following B[a]P treatment, brain-resident microglia cells exhibited signs of cell senescence, as evidenced by typical ultrastructural alterations, increased senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity, and elevated expression of the core senescence markers p16, p21, and p53 proteins. Consistent with these in vivo observations, B[a]P was confirmed to also induce cell cycle arrest in cultured BV2 microglia cells. This pro-senescent effect was significnatly attenuated by Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) overexpression, whereas it was markedly exacerbated following TREM2 knockout. Subsequent experiments further validated that insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), as a direct downstream effector regulated by TREM2, is functionally required for B[a]P-triggered microglial senescence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that B[a]P exposure can induce PD-like lesions and microglial senescence, and which is primarily mediated via the TREM2/IGF-1 signaling axis.

best.title: Reduced BNIP1 impairs autophagosome-lysosome fusion in hippocampal neurons and contributes to Alzheimer's disease pathology.
best.abstract: BNIP1 (BCL2‑interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N‑ethylmaleimide‑sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting that BNIP1 is a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP‑overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells, screened key interacting proteins of BNIP1 via mass spectrometry, and further performed gain‑ and loss‑of‑function assays using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNA (siRNA) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that, in these experimental models, reduced BNIP1 expression contributes to AD‑related pathological alterations by impairing autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b‑mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. best.title: Isolated Axoplasm from Squid and Pathogenic Mechanisms in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
best.abstract: The squid giant axon is an experimental model that has been instrumental in providing answers to many fundamental questions in cell biology, including the discovery of the motor protein kinesin and probing molecular mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The giant axon offers scale and ease of access that is not possible in mammalian models. The power of this model stems from the fact that one can introduce reagents and proteins that would not cross a plasma membrane at defined concentrations in a buffer environment that is closely modeled on normal components of the axoplasm. By leveraging the unique biology of the squid axon, early studies were able to define the channels and ion specificities of the action potential. Subsequent studies using video-enhanced contrast- differential Interference contrast microscopy (VEC-DIC) and the isolated axoplasm led to the identification of kinesins, a class of motor proteins responsible for intracellular vesicle trafficking toward the plus end of microtubules. This combination of isolated axoplasm and advanced imaging continues to provide insights into pathogenic mechanisms for adult-onset neurodegeneration, including ALS, and regulation of fast axonal transport, a process disrupted in motor neuron disease. Here, procedures for dissecting the giant axon, isolating axoplasm, and perfusing defined amounts of proteins and/or reagents into the axoplasm are detailed, as well as methods for visualizing and interactively analyzing vesicle traffic in real time. This model represents a singular avenue to understand the critical function of neurons, shedding light on the mechanisms driving ALS pathology and other neurodegenerative diseases. This system also offers a tractable platform for drug testing, where candidate therapeutic compounds can be introduced directly into the axoplasm, and their effects on vesicle trafficking can be assessed in real time, providing a rapid and physiologically relevant means of identifying potential ALS therapeutic targets.

best.title: A pKa-Guided BBB-Permeable NIR Fluorescent Probe for Tracking Lipid Droplets in Microglia with Neuroinflammation and Alzheimer's Disease.
best.abstract: Abnormal accumulation of lipid droplets (LDs), accompanied by altered microenvironmental polarity within the microglia, is closely associated with neuroinflammation and also has been increasingly recognized as an early and dynamic indicator of Alzheimer's disease (AD). Herein, a LD-targeting polarity-sensitive blood-brain barrier (BBB)-permeable near-infrared (NIR) probe, BTDN, was screened by tuning the electron-donating substituents to modulate the pKa values of benzothiadiazole-based derivatives. Endowed with the donor-acceptor-donor (D1-A-D2) architecture and strong intramolecular charge-transfer (ICT) characteristics, the BTDN probe exhibited high sensitivity to polarity change. The BTDN probe displayed suitable physicochemical properties such as a pKa of 7.47 and lipophilicity with a log P of 3.72 for favorable BBB-penetrating efficiency with a permeability percentage of 24.23%. In addition, the BTDN probe showed advantages for fluorescence imaging including NIR emission from 643 to 770 nm with the increased polarity, Stokes shift larger than 308 nm, comparable two-photon absorption capacity with an absorption cross-section of 10 GM at 870 nm, good biocompatibility, and robust photostability. Using this multifunctional BTDN probe, the dynamic fluorescence imaging of accumulation behaviors of LDs in BV2 microglia with neuroinflammation was performed, demonstrating that LD formation may serve as a potential biomarker for neuroinflammation. Furthermore, overproduced LDs within microglia were directly observed in vivo and in tissue sections from the brains of AD mice. This work not only provides an imaging tool for dynamically characterizing LD accumulation in microglia but also provides insights into the relationship between LD accumulation in microglia and AD pathogenesis.

best.title: Alzheimer's genetic risk factor CASS4 controls microglial focal adhesion biology and amyloidosis.
best.abstract: Recent genome-wide association studies have identified numerous Alzheimer's disease (AD) risk genes enriched in microglia, including Crk-associated substrate (Cas) scaffold protein family member 4 (CASS4), which encodes the adaptor protein CASS4. Despite its strong genetic association with AD, the role of CASS4 in disease remains poorly understood. Here, we show that full-body Cass4 deletion in 5xFAD mice increases amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition, neuronal dystrophy, and cognitive deficits. Since microglia are the predominant brain-resident cells expressing Cass4, we investigated its role in microglial responses to Aβ pathology. Loss of CASS4 impaired microglial mobilization to Aβ plaques and reduced plaque compaction. Phosphoproteomic analysis of purified microglia revealed marked disruption of focal adhesion signaling following Cass4 deletion. Consistent with this, CASS4 deficiency abrogated in vivo microglial recruitment to injury and in vitro wound healing responses, two processes that are centrally orchestrated by focal adhesion biology. Together, these findings identify CASS4 as a critical regulator of microglial function and focal adhesion biology and suggest that CASS4 may represent a therapeutic target for AD.

best.title: Up-regulation of the kinase LRRK2, in enteric glia contributes to mucosal barrier impairment in Parkinson's disease via secretory autophagy.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) show intestinal epithelial barrier (IEB) alterations, enteric gliosis and inflammation that could contribute to gastrointestinal symptoms. Moreover, changes in leucine rich-repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) expression/activity have been associated with PD development and related intestinal inflammation. However, the molecular determinants linking LRRK2, enteric gliosis and IEB impairment remain unclear. Therefore, we investigated the role of LRRK2 in IEB changes associated with PD, focusing on its role in the interplay between enteric glial cells (EGCs) and intestinal epithelial cells (IECs). EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Human A53T α-synuclein transgenic (Tg) mice (9 months old) were provided a model of early PD. Central neuroinflammation was studied by IBA-1 staining. Intestinal motility, colonic α-synuclein and LRRK2 expression were assessed. Enteric gliosis was evaluated by detection of GFAP+ cells co-expressing LRRK2; IEB was tested by mucins detection and quantification of Muc-2, tight junction proteins and secretory autophagy. In vitro co-cultures between EGCs and IECs were performed to investigate glial LRRK2-mediated gut barrier alterations. KEY RESULTS: A53T mice, without central neuroinflammation, showed intestinal disturbances, colonic α-synuclein accumulation and an increase in colonic GFAP+/LRRK2+ glial cells before brain pathology. Moreover, PD animals displayed IEB alterations and increased colonic autophagosomes, suggesting a shift towards secretory autophagy. In co-culture experiments, α-synuclein and lipopolysaccharide promoted enteric gliosis and LRRK2 up-regulation in glial cells, contributing to IEB impairment via secretory autophagy. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: These changes could influence bowel symptoms and central pathology associated with PD, via the gut-brain axis.

best.title: Neuropathological and functional impact of astrocyte-derived extracellular vesicles in an aged model of Alzheimer's disease.
best.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are lipid-bound particles that transfer cargos between cells. While plasma neuronal-derived EVs (NEVs) from individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) have been reported to exhibit high pathogenic potential, this study examined the impact of astrocyte-derived EVs (AEVs) in an aged AD mouse model. Plasma AEVs were isolated from cognitively normal control (CNC), MCI, and AD individuals using GLAST-based immunocapture and AEV size, purity, and tetraspanin were validated by flow cytometry, nanoparticle tracking, and super-resolution microscopy. AEVs pooled by clinical cohort were injected into the hippocampus of 6-month-old female PSAPP mice. Behavioral, biochemical, and neuropathological outcomes were assessed 6 months later. Rotarod assessment revealed significant impairment in motor coordination (p < 0.0001) in mice receiving MCI- and AD-AEVs compared with those receiving CNC-AEVs. While Morris water maze (MWM) also demonstrated that CNC-AEVs injected mice exhibited a trend toward increased target quadrant entries and faster escape latencies, these measures did not reach did not reach statistical significance. No overt changes were observed in the staining of amyloid plaque burden (6E10), and astrogliosis (GFAP). Immunoblotting of 82E1 and 22C11 confirmed Aβ/AAP levels remained similar across all injected mice, whereas increased cortical tau accumulation was observed in MCI- and AD-AEV injected mice. Cerebellar synaptic density (SY-38) remained unchanged. These findings suggest that while human-derived AEVs can precipitate early tau-related changes and motor coordination deficits, they do not significantly alter overall amyloidosis or astrocyte-reactivity at this time point. Further investigation is required to determine the viability of AEVs as biomarkers or therapeutic targets given the subtle nature of the observed structural pathology.

best.title: Lysosome-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe ROCL enables dynamic hypochlorous acid imaging in living cells and a mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
best.abstract: Hypochlorous acid (HClO) plays critical roles in oxidative stress and is strongly implicated in the progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). Here, we report ROCL, a new lysosome-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe for sensitive and selective detection of HClO in living systems. ROCL displays rapid response, excellent selectivity, and a low detection limit of 49 nM, based on an HClO-induced spirolactam ring-opening mechanism. The probe enables real-time imaging of exogenous and endogenous HClO in SH-SY5Y and PC12 cells, exhibits low cytotoxicity, and effectively visualizes elevated HClO levels in MPTP- and rotenone-induced PD models. ROCL also shows favorable blood-brain barrier permeability and allows noninvasive in vivo HClO imaging in PD model mice. These results establish ROCL as a valuable tool for probing HClO-associated oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases.

primary.title: Brain organoids: Experimental access to human-specific brain development.
primary.abstract: Human cerebral cortical development includes species-divergent cellular programs and unusually prolonged trajectories that remain difficult to investigate experimentally. These processes support human-specific cognitive abilities and are thought to be associated with vulnerability to neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. Human brain organoids provide a tractable system for studying these processes across developmental time and under controlled perturbation. Here, we review how cortical organoids model human-specific features of progenitor biology and cell diversification, as well as progressive cellular maturation and circuit formation. We consider the limitations that constrain later-stage maturation and how approaches including the addition of missing cell types, the use of assembloids, and transplantation can extend the developmental processes accessible to study. Finally, we examine how patient-derived, isogenic, chimeric, and perturbation-based organoid systems are being used to investigate neurodevelopmental disorders and, in turn, reveal mechanisms of typical human development.

primary.title: Integrating Cytoskeletal Systems in Neurons and Glia: Dynamic Orchestration of Structure and Function.
primary.abstract: Neurons and glia form the circuitry of our nervous system, allowing nerve cells to communicate with each other and other cell types throughout the body in a highly specific manner to integrate sensory, motor, and cognitive functions. The ability of these cells to do this is profoundly dependent on an elaborate and dynamic cytoskeleton which allows these cells to adopt complex shapes and specialized structures such as myelin sheaths, the blood-brain barrier, axonal growth cones, dendritic spines, nodes of Ranvier, synapses, and elaborate sensory organs. The cytoskeleton is also critical for morphogenetic movements, the migration of neuronal precursors, and axon growth, which together establish the organization and wiring pattern of the central and peripheral nervous system during development. This review provides a primer on our current understanding of the cytoskeleton of neurons and glia, with an emphasis on how the protein polymers of the cytoskeleton-microtubules, actin filaments, intermediate filaments, and septins-work together to orchestrate the remarkable shapes and functions of these cells. We also highlight key questions and challenges for the field and technological advances that may help address them.

primary.title: Beyond Transcriptomes and Dissociated Cells: Spatial Proteomics for Mechanistic Neurobiology.
primary.abstract: Single-cell transcriptomic studies have revealed remarkable molecular heterogeneity across neuronal and glial populations during development, aging, and disease. However, dissociation-based approaches disrupt tissue architecture, and RNA measures alone incompletely capture cellular function. These limitations are particularly relevant in neurodegenerative diseases, where pathology develops within cellular microenvironments and diseased cells progressively lose canonical cell-state identity markers. Spatial proteomic approaches are beginning to address this critical gap by enabling high-dimensional molecular profiling within the intact tissue, preserving the spatial relationships between vulnerable cells and their surrounding cellular environments across scales ranging from subcellular single-cell imaging to large-volume three-dimensional mapping. Here, we discuss emerging spatial proteomic technologies and their applications in aging and neurodegeneration, emphasizing how integration with complementary modalities, including transcriptomics, glycomics, three-dimensional genome architecture, and quantitative neuropathology, is providing new insight into disease biology. We further highlight how these approaches are beginning to accelerate therapeutic target validation, biomarker discovery, and treatment response monitoring. Realizing the full potential of spatial proteomics will require continued advances in cross-platform harmonization, analytical standardization, and computational methods capable of integrating increasingly complex, multimodal datasets.
