primary.title: Kinesin-12 (Kif15) in Neurons: From Mitotic Motor to Activity-Dependent Regulator of Dendritic Spines.
primary.abstract: Kinesin-12 (Kif15) is a canonical mitotic kinesin that crosslinks parallel microtubules and suppresses microtubule catastrophe. It exists in both dimeric and tetrameric oligomerization states that are regulated by ionic conditions and binding partners. Its persistent expression in postmitotic neurons indicates that this ancestral microtubule-organizing activity has been repurposed for neuronal functions, yet the dendritic role of Kif15 has remained poorly defined. Here, we review and hypothesize KIF15 acting as a dendritic regulator. We propose that in the dendritic shaft, Kif15 exists predominantly as a tetramer crosslinker to organize the mixed-polarity antiparallel microtubule array. At the neck of the dendritic spines, perhaps due to the electrical signals, the compartmental ion concentration has changed. The dimeric Kif15 transports PSD95 along microtubule plus ends that invade dendritic spines and unloads PSD95 at the postsynaptic sites. There, synaptic activity triggers Ca2+ influx and CaMKII activation to promote Kif15 association with Myosin IIb (Myh10), forming a Kif15-Myh10 hetero-complex, which reorganizes the microtubule-actin network to facilitate mushroom-like dendritic spine formation. This framework explains why Kif15 loss impairs spine complexity, synaptic development, and mood-related behaviors without causing catastrophic disassembly of dendritic microtubules. It further links KIF15 mutations to cognitive disorders and suggests that mechanistic insights from a mitotic motor to its synaptic functions.

primary.title: The role of ZC3H14 (MSUT2) in neurodevelopment and tauopathies.
primary.abstract: The processes of neurodevelopment and neuropathology can be influenced by RNA binding proteins. The RNA binding protein ZC3H14 (also referred to as MSUT2) is of particular interest for two reasons. First, homozygous loss-of-function alleles in ZC3H14 are associated with an inherited form of intellectual disability. Second, in model systems, loss of ZC3H14 can suppress the toxicity of tau aggregates, which are hallmark diagnostic features of Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative diseases referred to as 'tauopathies'. In this review, we discuss both the normal functions of ZC3H14 and how alterations in these functions may affect cognitive function or tau pathology. Although not fully understood, an emerging theme is that alterations in RNA regulation attributable to ZC3H14 loss can affect neuronal function.

primary.title: Cytoskeletal alterations underlying dendritic and synaptic plasticity in epilepsy.
primary.abstract: Aberrant dendritic changes in epilepsy, morphologically measured by the complexity and length of dendrite, as well as the density of dendritic spines, are dynamic and various considering disease course, developmental stages, and various neuronal type across different brain regions. Correspondingly, imbalanced excitatory and inhibitory synapses in epilepsy, quantitatively measured by the expression level and location of synaptic proteins, still vary considering etiology, disease course, and brain regions. And, various mechanisms involved in synaptic pruning add to the complexity of synaptic alterations in epilepsy. Still, sharing mechanisms underlying aberrant dendritic and synaptic plasticity in epilepsy exist, and cytoskeletal alterations can serve as a tool to decipher alterations of dendritic morphology and synaptic plasticity in epilepsy. Evidences supporting aberrant microtubule dynamics and post-translational modifications of tubulin in epilepsy emerge, combined with their involvement in dendritic morphology and synaptic plasticity. In conclusion, this review respectively summarizes the characteristics of dendritic pathology, synaptic alterations, microtubule dynamics, and tubulin's post-translational modifications in epilepsy, and discusses their interplay and correlation in epilepsy, providing insight into how cytoskeletal organization contributes to macroscopic changes in epilepsy.

primary.title: Prenatal origins of neurodegeneration: The role of maternal immune activation in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's pathobiology.
primary.abstract: Recent evidence suggests that prenatal environmental factors, particularly maternal infection or maternal immune activation (MIA), may influence the progression of brain aging and lifetime risk for neurodegenerative disorders. The hypothesis is that even a short-lived inflammatory event during pregnancy may leave a lasting imprint on the developing brain and immune system of the fetus, such that aging or subsequent insults may later unmask neurodegenerative disorders. Support for this hypothesis comes largely from animal studies, where gestational inflammation has been shown to potentiate the onset of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases (AD/PD), by increasing amyloid/tau pathology, reducing synaptic connections, and damaging nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons. We review convergent mechanisms, including microglial priming, chronic cytokine excess, oxidative stress, epigenetic marks and proteostatic deficits, through which maternal immune activation may embed a latent "hit" that synergizes with aging to precipitate AD or PD. Furthermore, we appraise experimental models and available human data linking MIA to AD versus PD, noting shared and distinct pathways. Despite growing preclinical evidence, translation to human cohorts remains limited by heterogeneity in MIA exposure timing and outcome measures. An understanding of MIA's impact on neurodegeneration could suggest preventive strategies and interventions for early diagnosis and treatment.

primary.title: Protein Quality Control Systems in Neurodegeneration-Chaperones, Cytoskeleton, and the Pathogenic Transition of Tau.
primary.abstract: Maintenance of protein homeostasis is essential for neuronal survival, and its disruption is a defining feature of neurodegenerative diseases. Neurons are particularly vulnerable to proteostatic stress due to their post-mitotic nature, long lifespan, and dependence on cytoskeletal integrity for structural stability, intracellular transport, and synaptic function. In tauopathies and related neurodegenerative disorders, misfolded proteins and aggregation-prone proteins burden the cellular quality-control systems, leading to cytoskeletal destabilization, synaptic dysfunction, and progressive neuronal loss. This review is organized around a central question: for a given tau species, defined by its isoform, post-translational modifications, and assembly state, what determines its fate? We examine how molecular chaperone networks, including HSP100, HSP90, HSP70, J-domain proteins (JDPs), small heat shock proteins (sHSPs), and the Prefoldin-CCT pathway, regulate the folding, disaggregation, sequestration, and degradation of pathogenic tau. We highlight how these chaperone networks influence key proteostasis checkpoints, determine whether tau refolds, is degraded, or is redirected toward toxic aggregation, and how these outcomes impact microtubule stability and neuronal function. Drawing on studies in yeast, Drosophila, mammalian models, and human tissues, we develop two key conclusions. First, chaperone activity is not uniformly protective against tauopathies; its effects depend on the tau species, cellular context, and disease stage. Second, because the cytoskeleton is both a chaperone client and an essential component of intracellular clearance pathways, tau pathology and proteostasis failure can reinforce one another. Finally, we discuss emerging therapeutic strategies and challenges in targeting chaperone networks to restore proteostasis while avoiding unintended neurotoxic consequences.

primary.title: Dynamic contributions of astrocytes in Alzheimer's disease.
primary.abstract: In Alzheimer's disease, pathological stimuli reshape astrocyte functions, which in turn act on neurons, making astrocytes critical modulators of disease progression. A comprehensive understanding of how astrocytes dynamically shift from physiology to pathology across multiple functional domains remains to be established. This review synthesizes recent findings across four key domains: proteostasis, gliotransmission/synapse regulation, blood-brain barrier integrity and metabolism, and microglial crosstalk. For each domain, we compare homeostatic and pathological functions, analyze how supportive roles turn detrimental, and discuss effects on neuronal fate. We also examine signaling pathways that govern astrocyte reactivity and the potential of astrocyte-derived biomarkers. By tracing these dynamic transitions, we aim to refine Alzheimer's disease mechanisms and identify state-targeted therapeutic opportunities.

primary.title: Midbrain organoids as next-generation models for Parkinson's disease: From pathogenesis to therapeutic discovery.
primary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by selective degeneration of dopaminergic (DA) neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) and pathological aggregation of α-synuclein. Traditional two-dimensional (2D) cell cultures and animal models have provided valuable insights but fail to recapitulate the cellular architecture and pathophysiology of the human midbrain. Three-dimensional (3D) midbrain organoids self-organize into neural structures that mimic key aspects of human midbrain development and disease pathology. This review examines midbrain organoid-based PD modeling through a concept-driven lens, addressing five questions: (i) Which aspects of PD can organoids model? (ii) How are technological advances reshaping the field? (iii) How do organoids complement existing model systems? (iv) What are the current limitations, and how can they be addressed? (v) What is the path toward clinical translation? Organoids reliably reproduce mitochondrial and lysosomal dysfunction and, in SNCA triplication models, α-synuclein accumulation, but seldom progressive neurodegeneration or mature Lewy pathology. By distinguishing established findings from emerging technologies and providing a realistic assessment of current limitations, this review offers a framework for prioritizing organoid applications in PD research and translation.

primary.title: Roles of autophagy in brain homeostasis and disease.
primary.abstract: Macroautophagy (autophagy) is a lysosome-dependent degradative pathway that encapsulates proteins and organelles within double-membraned vesicles and recycles the contents back into the cell. The interplay of autophagy with various membrane trafficking pathways is crucial for maintaining cellular homeostasis both under basal conditions and in response to environmental stress. In the CNS, neurons and glial cells rely on a spectrum of quality-control and recycling pathways, notably autophagy, to sustain the intricate functions of the brain. Genetic variants in autophagy genes are known to cause Mendelian disorders primarily affecting the human nervous system, underscoring the critical role of autophagy in brain function. We review the latest research delineating the landscape and network of autophagy in developing and mature neurons, elucidating how conserved autophagy pathways regulate neuronal homeostasis and functions at different ages. We examine the increasing evidence of dysfunctional autophagy that contributes to neurodevelopmental disorders, neurodegenerative diseases and psychiatric conditions. Recent insights into the dysregulation of autophagy provide valuable avenues for biomarker identification and therapeutic development, particularly targeting autophagy-lysosome pathways for neurological disorders.

primary.title: New insights on microglial lysosomal acidification: A therapeutic target of neurodegenerative diseases.
primary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system (CNS), maintain brain homeostasis and respond to pathological insults. Microglial dysfunction has been implicated in the pathogenesis of several neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis. Impaired lysosomal function, particularly defective lysosomal acidification, leads to the accumulation of undegraded material, thereby promoting neuroinflammation and neuronal damage. PURPOSE: This review examines the mechanisms governing lysosomal acidification in microglia and evaluates its potential as both a therapeutic target and a prognostic biomarker in neurodegenerative diseases. METHODS: The literature on microglial lysosomal acidification, lysosomal pH regulation, autophagy, and neurodegeneration was searched in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. Relevant mechanistic, preclinical, and translational studies were critically appraised and synthesized. RESULTS: Lysosomal acidification is increasingly recognized as a key regulator of microglial function and homeostasis. Defective acidification, driven by dysregulation of the vacuolar H+-ATPase (V-ATPase) proton pump, TFEB/TFE3 signaling pathways, and lysosomal ion channels such as TRPML1 and TMEM175, impairs autophagic flux and substrate degradation, facilitating the accumulation of neurotoxic aggregates including amyloid-β and α-synuclein. Emerging evidence suggests that the degree of microglial lysosomal acidification may serve as a prognostic biomarker for disease progression and therapeutic response. Restoration or enhancement of lysosomal acidification through pharmacological modulation of lysosomal pH, activation of autophagy, or targeting of key regulatory pathways has been shown to re-establish microglial homeostasis, attenuate neuroinflammation, and confer neuroprotection in preclinical models. CONCLUSION: Restoration of microglial lysosomal acidification represents a promising therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative diseases. A deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating lysosomal acidification in microglia may facilitate the identification of novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets, ultimately contributing to the development of innovative interventions for neurodegenerative disorders.

primary.title: Analysis of multidimensional molecular mechanisms in Parkinson's disease and precise therapeutic strategies.
primary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most common neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, is characterized by progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and striatal dopamine deficiency, leading to motor dysfunction. The complex pathogenesis involves impaired protein homeostasis with α-synuclein aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation, including NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Newly identified regulated cell death pathways - including ferroptosis, cuproptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis - have further expanded current understanding of PD pathology, while gut-brain axis interactions may contribute to peripheral-central communication and disease progression. These mechanistic insights inspire targeted therapeutic strategies comprising α-synuclein inhibitors, mitochondrial protectants, anti-inflammatory agents, and novel cell death pathway blockers, alongside gut-brain axis interventions. However, these approaches face substantial challenges including limited blood-brain barrier penetration, insufficient target specificity, and individual genetic heterogeneity. Future research should prioritize developing multi-target combination therapies, integrating multi-omics and computational approaches for biomarker identification and patient stratification, while advancing clinical translation of gene- and cell-based therapies. Through interdisciplinary collaboration and precision medicine implementation, disease-modifying treatments for PD may become increasingly feasible.

primary.title: Convergent molecular mechanisms of chronic heavy metal exposure and repetitive mild traumatic brain injury in neurodegenerative processes.
primary.abstract: Repetitive mild traumatic brain injury (rmTBI) and chronic environmental exposure to heavy metals represent widespread contributors to neurological dysfunction that are typically studied independently. However, emerging evidence indicates that these insults converge on overlapping cellular pathways that disrupt neuronal homeostasis, redox balance, genomic stability and proteostasis, including tau regulation. Notably, environmental metals including mercury, lead, arsenic, cadmium, and hexavalent chromium induce oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroinflammatory signaling, processes that are also central to rmTBI pathophysiology. In this review, we synthesize mechanistic and clinical evidence linking chronic heavy metal exposure and rmTBI and examine how their interaction may influence long-term vulnerability to neurodegeneration. To our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate these two domains within a unified mechanistic framework. We first summarize shared and metal-specific mechanisms of heavy metal neurotoxicity and integrate these findings with the cellular and systemic consequences of rmTBI. Attention is given to higher-order convergent processes, including disruption of the blood-brain barrier, dysregulation of the gut-brain axis, protein misfolding and tau pathology, ferroptosis, and impairment of proteostatic and autophagic pathways. We also discuss emerging biomarker signatures and therapeutic targets relevant to combined environmental and traumatic exposures. Collectively, current evidence supports a model in which chronic heavy metal burden may diminish neural resilience and could increase vulnerability to the cumulative effects of rmTBI. Although direct evidence of their interaction remains limited, the substantial mechanistic overlap provides a framework for future studies investigating environmental contributions to post-traumatic neurodegeneration, biomarker discovery, and potential therapeutic strategies.

secondary.title: Rab GTPases and the Rabopathy framework: from synaptic trafficking to neurodegeneration via LRRK2-driven pathology.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and Huntington's disease (HD) show significant differences in their clinical manifestations, but they all seem to share a common upstream problem: malfunction in the membrane transport controlled by Rab GTPases. This review introduces the concept of Rabopathy, a framework that connects developmental synaptic maturation defects with late-onset protein aggregation. The LRRK2-Rab phosphorylation axis is emerging as a potential common amplifying mechanism across these disorders, with the strongest mechanistic support in PD and growing implications in AD and HD. When Rab substrates are excessively phosphorylated at specific sites, vesicular transport is impaired or arrested, leading to progressive depletion of the reserve pool of synaptic vesicles and the surface pool of receptors, and severe compromise of the autophagy-lysosome flux. The failure of distinct Rab sub-networks also produces disease-specific signatures, including Rab5-driven endosomal congestion in AD, Rab35-mediated α-synuclein secretion in PD, and Rab11/Rab7 trafficking collapse in HD. Restoration of Rab flux may be a therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative diseases, which can be achieved through calibration of LRRK2 activity, modulation of selective Rab subtypes, and rescue of the trafficking network at the systems level.

secondary.title: Effects of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus on the Offspring's Neurodevelopment.
secondary.abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a major global health concern that affects up to 14% of pregnancies. Traditionally, it has been characterized by hyperglycemia and insulin resistance. However, GDM can also lead to long-term health consequences in offspring, particularly affecting neurodevelopment. It has been associated with an increased risk of cognitive deficits, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and emotional dysregulation in GDM-exposed offspring. Findings from human and experimental studies suggest that GDM disrupts cortical and hippocampal architecture, impairs synaptic plasticity, and induces epigenetic alterations in key neurodevelopmental genes. These mechanistic pathways include oxidative stress, inflammation, apoptosis, and altered neurotrophin expression and receptor signaling. Maternal metabolism, diet, and genetic background may negatively affect neurotrophin expression, which could impact fetal brain development. Lower levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and nerve growth factor (NGF) in maternal blood, placental tissue, and cord blood have been linked to poor neurodevelopmental outcomes. This suggests that neurotrophins could be considered potential biomarkers. This narrative review compiles the latest evidence on the effects of GDM on fetal brain development, emphasizing the role of neurotrophins, especially BDNF and NGF, as critical mediators in this process. Emerging data also suggest that glycemic control during pregnancy may partially restore neurotrophin levels and improve neurodevelopmental outcomes. Understanding the interaction between maternal glucose metabolism and fetal brain signaling pathways is essential for pregnancy care and the design of neuroprotective strategies.

secondary.title: Lysosomal dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease.
secondary.abstract: Examination of genetic risk factors associated with neurodegenerative diseases has provided important mechanistic insights into the pathophysiology of these disorders, and it has implicated defects in lysosomal function as a key component of the neurodegenerative process. The lysosome has a primary role in mediating degradation of both intracellular contents and endocytosed material from the extracellular space. Aggregation of misfolded proteins is a pathological mechanism that is observed across neurodegenerative disorders, and aberrant lysosomal degradation of such proteins plays a pivotal part in driving neuronal dysfunction and cell loss. In addition to the crucial role of the endolysosomal system in degradation of intracellular constituents, lysosomes also serve as important nodes for intracellular signalling, participating in nutrient sensing, lipid metabolism, membrane repair and neuroinflammation. In this Review, we provide an overview of mechanisms of lysosomal dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease, with a particular focus on Parkinson disease, Alzheimer disease, frontotemporal dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

secondary.title: PINK1‑regulated mitophagy dysfunction in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease (Review).
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and the accumulation of misfolded α‑synuclein forming Lewy bodies. Emerging evidence highlights mitochondrial dysfunction as an important and early event in PD pathogenesis. Among the key regulators of mitochondrial quality control, PTEN‑induced kinase 1 (PINK1) plays a pivotal role by initiating mitophagy, the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria. Under physiological conditions, PINK1 is rapidly degraded, whereas mitochondrial depolarization stabilizes PINK1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane, where it recruits and activates Parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, to promote mitophagy. Loss‑of‑function mutations in PINK1 also disrupt this process, leading to the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria, oxidative stress, abnormal calcium homeostasis and neuronal apoptosis. Furthermore, PINK1 deficiency has been shown to exacerbate α‑synuclein aggregation, impair synaptic transmission and activate neuroinflammatory pathways, collectively accelerating dopaminergic neurodegeneration. Therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring or enhancing PINK1‑mediated mitophagy through pharmacological activation, gene delivery or modulation of parallel pathways‑represent a promising avenue for PD intervention. Continued elucidation of the molecular functions of PINK1 will provide critical insights into mitochondrial homeostasis and novel therapeutic targets for PD.

secondary.title: STMN2: Membrane-Binding Microtubule Regulator or Tubulin Effector?
secondary.abstract: STMN2, a protein implicated in motor neuron degeneration, is widely viewed as a membrane-associated microtubule inhibitor, but emerging evidence challenges whether this activity defined its cellular function. Three alternative models integrates available evidence to offer perspectives beyond microtubule regulation. The vesicle cargo adaptor model proposes that STMN2 recruits diverse cargos to transport vesicles for axonal delivery. The membrane-bound signaling messenger model links STMN2 turnover to local signaling, effector, degradation, or effector release. The traffic director model proposes that STMN2 regulates cargo routing between delivery and degradative pathways. These models are not mutually exclusive and position tubulin binding as a regulator of STMN2 function rather than its defining activity.

secondary.title: Spontaneous Neuronal Activity in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Insights from Human and Animal Studies.
secondary.abstract: Developmental spontaneous neuronal activity (SNA) plays an instrumental role in the generation of precise brain circuits. Spontaneous activity patterns guide neuronal differentiation, synaptic refinement, and circuit formation; consequently, perturbations in these activity patterns can profoundly influence brain network organization. Growing evidence suggests that mutations in autism-associated genes lead to alterations of the SNA pattern during early brain development, thereby giving rise to the behavioral features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This review integrates findings from neuroimaging studies, which reveal widespread alterations in neuronal excitability in individuals with ASD. Regional homogeneity and functional connectivity analyses consistently demonstrate region-specific abnormalities, including hyperactivity in higher-order cortical regions, hypoactivity in sensorimotor areas, and disrupted long-range connectivity. These functional alterations are closely linked to the underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms such as excitation-inhibition (E/I) imbalance, impaired GABAergic signaling, glutamatergic dysregulation, and abnormalities in calcium-dependent signaling pathways. Identification of activity-based biomarkers, together with advanced neuroimaging techniques and computational and machine learning (ML) approaches, may facilitate early diagnosis of ASD. Understanding the origin and consequences of alterations in SNA provides a unifying framework for identifying novel targets for designing pharmacological intervention strategies.

secondary.title: The pathological roles of intrinsically disordered proteins in lysosomal acidification dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and Parkinson's disease (PD) are characterized by the accumulation of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), including amyloid-β (Aβ), tau, and α-synuclein (αSyn). These proteins disrupt neuronal homeostasis through toxic aggregation, impaired proteostasis, and progressive neurodegeneration, in part via dysfunction of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway (ALP). A central feature of this impairment is defective vacuolar-type (H+)-ATPase (V-ATPase) function, leading to lysosomal deacidification and reduced degradative capacity. Pathological IDP species converge on V-ATPase through direct interactions with its subunits or by perturbing its assembly, while also exerting protein-specific effects, including lysosomal membrane destabilization, impaired hydrolase activity, and disrupted endolysosomal trafficking. These combined mechanisms create a reciprocal relationship between lysosomal dysfunction and IDP accumulation, in which impaired lysosomal degradation further promotes the persistence and aggregation of pathological IDP species. This review synthesizes current insights into the molecular interplay between IDPs and lysosomal acidification across AD, FTD, and PD, and highlights how these processes contribute to disease progression. We further discuss emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring lysosomal function. These findings underscore lysosomal dysfunction as a common feature of IDP-driven neurodegeneration and a potential therapeutic target across these disorders.

secondary.title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic insights into neural substrates of behavioural dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease.
secondary.abstract: The transition from bulk-tissue profiling to single-cell and spatially resolved transcriptomics has reshaped our understanding of Alzheimer's disease (AD) from a passive proteinopathy to a coordinated multicellular process spanning the neurovascular unit. However, translating these molecular catalogues into disease-modifying therapies requires a framework that links cellular transitions to neural circuit dysfunction and behavioural abnormalities. This review synthesizes the multicellular landscape of AD, tracing how cell-state-specific remodelling drives network collapse and cognitive decline. Neuronally, selective vulnerability targets projection networks and subclass-specific inhibitory interneurons. Their transcriptional silencing compromises projection pathways, including the entorhinal-hippocampal perforant path, disrupts cortical microcircuits, and underlies episodic memory impairment, hyperexcitability, and executive control failure. This neuronal degeneration is dynamically coupled to reactive glial and vascular remodelling across distinct spatial niches. We examine the non-linear transition of homeostatic astrocytes and microglia into specialized, plaque-associated reactive sub-states, as well as paracrine signalling decay at the neurovascular interface. Compromised capillary tight junctions and the shedding of pericytic survival receptors are proposed to promote blood-brain barrier disintegrity, triggering a feed-forward neuroinflammatory cascade of complement-mediated synaptic pruning. Crucially, we establish a three-tiered hierarchy of evidence, rigorously distinguishing cross-sectional, associative human postmortem findings from inferred functional trajectories in human cellular platforms, and causal, perturbation-based validations in transgenic rodent models. We review how contemporary multi-scale integration-combining single-nucleus transcriptomics with functional electrophysiological platforms and biophysical connectomic modelling-bridges the gap between terminal postmortem signatures and living brain dynamics. Finally, we outline a coordinated translational roadmap illustrating how spatially resolved cell-state networks can guide the development of fluid and imaging biomarkers, support biologically informed patient stratification, enrich clinical trials, and accelerate the development of circuit-restoring precision therapies, thereby providing a mechanistic framework that links cell-state transitions to neural circuit dysfunction, behavioural impairment, and precision medicine in Alzheimer's disease.

secondary.title: The Red Nucleus in Motor Control and Autism Spectrum Disorder.
secondary.abstract: Neuromotor differences of motor coordination, timing, postural regulation, and prospective motor control are common and emerge early in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, their underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood, with existing research emphasising cortical and cerebellar systems. This review re-examines the red nucleus (RN), a midbrain structure embedded within cortical, cerebellar, and olivary motor pathways, as an underexplored component of distributed sensorimotor networks. We synthesise evidence from comparative neuroanatomy, animal experiments, human neuroimaging, movement disorders, and autism research, distinguishing direct RN findings from broader circuit-level inferences. Neuroimaging studies have reported RN-region susceptibility differences in autistic children, including an exploratory association with fine-motor development, but reproducible links to specific motor processes and RN-related causal mechanisms remain unestablished. We therefore propose a testable hypothesis that differences in RN structure, function, or connectivity may be associated with specific dimensions of motor function in autism. Error-related sensorimotor adaptation provides a primary experimental target, complemented by prospective motor control. Future investigations combining RN-sensitive neuroimaging, quantitative motor assessment, and transdiagnostic comparisons with developmental coordination disorder may determine whether RN-related measures provide explanatory information beyond sensorimotor systems. This framework positions the RN as a candidate component of autism-related motor networks.

secondary.title: Autism spectrum disorder and mild traumatic brain injury in the pediatric population: a scoping review.
secondary.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Concussions (i.e., mild traumatic brain injuries [mTBIs]) commonly produce transient neurocognitive and somatic symptoms that may overlap with baseline characteristics of neurodiverse populations. The relationship between autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and concussion/mTBI remains poorly characterized. This scoping review sought to synthesize existing literature evaluating concussion/mTBI risk, baseline neurocognitive testing, and symptom reporting in individuals with ASD. METHODS: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Embase, Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and CENTRAL databases were searched for studies evaluating ASD and concussion or mTBI. The central research question was the following: What is the current state of knowledge related to concussions/mTBI in patients with ASD? This review sought to evaluate the areas of baseline testing, acute symptomatology, injury characteristics, and recovery. Studies were required to explicitly evaluate ASD in relation to concussion/mTBI outcomes or neurocognitive testing. Studies that did not isolate ASD from other neurodevelopmental disorders, as well as reviews, editorials, and conference abstracts, were excluded. RESULTS: The search identified 374 studies, of which 7 (1.9%) met full inclusion criteria after screening. Most studies evaluated baseline neurocognitive testing using the Immediate Post-Concussion Assessment and Cognitive Testing (ImPACT) platform in pediatric/adolescent athletes. Three studies (42.9%) reported that individuals with ASD were more likely to produce invalid baseline neurocognitive scores and demonstrated differences in certain cognitive composites compared with controls. Two studies (28.6%) evaluated baseline concussion-like symptoms, with one reporting higher symptom endorsement among athletes with ASD and the other finding no statistically significant differences from controls. Epidemiological studies did not demonstrate a clear association between ASD and increased risk of concussion. Notably, no identified studies evaluated acute postinjury symptom trajectories or recovery outcomes following concussion in individuals with ASD. CONCLUSIONS: Existing literature examining ASD and concussion/TBI primarily evaluated baseline neurocognitive testing and suggested potential differences in testing performance and symptom reporting among individuals with ASD. However, the authors identified a critical lack of studies evaluating acute symptoms and recovery trajectories following concussion/mTBI in this population, which represents a significant barrier for clinicians-from athletic trainers to pediatricians to pediatric neurosurgeons-in accurately diagnosing, risk stratifying, and managing these patients in the postinjury setting. Prospective investigations are needed to better define concussion/mTBI presentation, recovery patterns, and optimal management strategies for individuals with ASD.

secondary.title: Lipid homeostasis and cellular metabolism in neurodegenerative diseases: A maturing framework to guide therapeutic development.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and dementia with Lewy bodies have long been viewed through the lens of protein aggregation. Emerging evidence, however, highlights lipid transfer, load, metabolism, and cellular homeostasis as upstream drivers of pathology. This perspective integrates established neurobiological, genetic, and mechanistic evidence of lipid dysfunction and outlines how these pathways can guide patient stratification, biomarker discovery, and therapeutic development. Of critical importance, lipid transport and lysosomal and trafficking networks are at the center of cholesterol regulation, glycosphingolipid clearance, endolysosomal function, and neuron-glia lipid exchange across genetic and sporadic neurodegenerative diseases. We present an integrated framework where correcting lipid imbalances and metabolic dysregulation may complement or obviate protein-targeted approaches, creating more precise clinical trials and combination strategies. By re-centering the therapeutic focus on lipid and cellular metabolism, we aim to catalyze translational advances in neurodegenerative disease treatment.

secondary.title: TLDc proteins: Stress-responsive nexus regulators of redox signaling, V-ATPase dynamics, and organellar crosstalk in neurodegeneration.
secondary.abstract: Many age-related neurodegenerative disorders are marked by progressive defects in cellular energy metabolism and protein homeostasis that converge on mitochondrial and lysosomal dysfunction. TLDc domain-containing proteins, such as OXR1, NCOA7, and related family members, have emerged as crucial modulators of organellar physiology and cellular stress responses. Growing evidence indicates that TLDc proteins physically interact with vacuolar ATPases (V-ATPases) to modulate their assembly and catalytic activity, linking TLDc function directly to the maintenance of lysosomal and Golgi lumen pH. This organellar pH homeostasis, in turn, is fundamental to intracellular iron handling and metabolic regulation, processes essential for mitochondrial bioenergetics, lysosomal functions, and cellular viability. Lysosomes maintain an acidic lumen via V-ATPase proton pumping, counterbalanced by specific ion channels, including TMEM175. This acidic environment is required for ferric iron reduction and subsequent release into the cytosol; when acidification fails, cells develop cytosolic iron deficiency, mitochondrial defects, pseudohypoxia via HIF-1α activation, and inflammation. Conversely, iron flux from lysosomes to mitochondria depends on acidic conditions and direct organelle contact, as exemplified by BDH2-driven siderophore transport, a V-ATPase-dependent but not TLDc-regulated process, which supports mitochondrial bioenergetics and sustains lysosomal acidity. Iron and pH dysregulation synergize to drive ferroptosis, lipid peroxidation, and neurotoxicity. Emerging studies link lysosomal deacidification and iron dyshomeostasis to the pathogenesis of major neurodegenerative diseases. These mechanisms collectively shape neuronal resilience, survival, and aging trajectories. This review integrates recent insights into how TLDc proteins coordinate organellar pH regulation and iron homeostasis and discusses how disruption of these interconnected pathways contributes to age-related neurodegeneration.

secondary.title: Maternal circulating cytokine and chemokine levels during pregnancy and risk of autism spectrum disorder in offspring: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Maternal immune activation (MIA) during pregnancy has been implicated in offspring neurodevelopment, but evidence linking maternal gestational immune mediators with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains heterogeneous. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether maternal circulating cytokine and chemokine levels during pregnancy are associated with autism in offspring. METHODS: Five databases were searched for human observational studies measuring maternal blood cytokines or chemokines during pregnancy and reporting autism outcomes in offspring. Eligible studies included autism versus control comparisons using maternal serum or plasma samples. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted using odds ratios (ORs) as the primary effect measure. Standardised mean differences (SMDs) were also analysed where group-level concentration data were available. Heterogeneity was assessed using I² statistics, and small-study effects were explored using Egger's test where estimable. RESULTS: Seven studies met the eligibility criteria. In OR-based analyses, nominal associations with autism were observed for IL-10 (OR 1.34, 95% CI 1.06-1.69), CXCL10 (OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.24-2.11), IL-1α (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.23-1.65), IL-5 (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.18-1.89), and IL-17A (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.70-0.94). CCL4 showed a borderline association. Supportive SMD analyses indicated higher IL-6 and lower IL-1β concentrations in autism-associated pregnancies. Heterogeneity varied across analytes and was substantial for IL-10 and CCL4. CONCLUSION: Maternal gestational immune profiles may differ in pregnancies later associated with autism, but current evidence does not support a single robust cytokine biomarker. Progress requires larger prospective cohorts with repeated sampling, harmonised assays, pathway-level analyses, and integrated placental-foetal neurodevelopmental phenotyping.

secondary.title: Nanoplastics as disruptors of microtubule dynamics and intracellular trafficking: implications for cellular senescence and ageing.
secondary.abstract: Nanoplastics (NPs) are increasingly recognized as persistent intracellular cargoes whose long-term effects may depend not only on chemical reactivity, oxidative stress, and inflammation, but also on how particle-containing vesicles are transported, positioned, and cleared. Because the positioning and movement of endosomes, lysosomes, autophagosomes, mitochondria, and NP-containing vesicles are extensively regulated by microtubule-based transport, prolonged NP retention has the potential to disrupt intracellular trafficking and organelle homeostasis. Here, we examine how NPs may influence microtubule dynamics, tubulin post-translational modifications, motor-dependent trafficking, and organelle positioning, with particular emphasis on their relationships to cellular senescence and ageing. We first summarize evidence that senescence and ageing are associated with alterations in microtubule organization, stability, acetylation, intracellular transport capacity, cytoplasmic physical properties, and neuronal microtubule integrity. We then evaluate emerging evidence linking NP exposure to altered microtubule states and trafficking-related dysfunction, while considering particle size, shape, surface chemistry, aggregation, exposure duration, and intracellular burden as important determinants of particle fate and cellular response. We propose microtubule-dependent trafficking congestion as a testable framework in which persistent NP-containing cargo progressively reduces intracellular transport efficiency, while distinguishing this state from simple particle retention or generalized organelle dysfunction. Potential mechanisms include increased cargo loading, altered kinesin-dynein balance, perinuclear lysosomal retention, changes in cytoplasmic crowding or viscosity, and dysregulation of tubulin-modifying enzymes. Direct evidence for NP-induced trafficking congestion remains limited, highlighting the need for quantitative live-cell measurements of vesicle mobility, velocity, run length, pausing, directionality, and recovery after exposure withdrawal. Finally, we discuss human biomonitoring and tissue-distribution evidence and emphasize the distinction between detection of plastic particles in human tissues and demonstration of pathological causality.

secondary.title: Exploring shared genetic pathways and gene interplay in major neurodegenerative diseases: a comprehensive review.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are progressive disorders that involve the loss and dysfunction of neurons. Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, Frontotemporal dementia are examples of diseases. While different clinically, these disorders have a common genetic, molecular and cellular basis. This review examines the common genetic pathways, along with the interactions between genes of major neurodegenerative diseases, with a focus on the key genes, such as APOE, SNCA, MAPT, TARDBP, LRRK2 and HTT. The common pathogenic mechanisms considered to play a major role in disease progression include protein misfolding and aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, diminished autophagy, and impaired lysosomal function, as well as synaptic degeneration. The review also emphasizes the role of systems biology strategies, such as genome-wide association studies, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, interactome analysis, and multi-omics integration, to unveiling complex molecular networks in neurodegeneration. Furthermore, the emerging biomarker strategies and therapeutic strategies targeting convergence signaling pathways including NF-κB, PI3K-Akt-mTOR, MAPK and Wnt/β-catenin are summarized. The common genetic basis and the cross-connecting molecular mechanisms of the various neurodegenerative diseases could help in the discovery of new biomarkers and pan-therapeutic targets. Further advances in molecular genetics, computational biology and precision medicine are needed to enhance early detection and the creation of effective disease-modifying treatments.

secondary.title: AKAP12 as a signal-compartmentalizing Hub across diseases: Context-dependent functions and translational potential.
secondary.abstract: A-kinase anchoring protein 12 (AKAP12; Gravin/SSeCKS) is a multidomain scaffold that coordinates spatially restricted signaling rather than acting as a single linear effector. By organizing protein kinase A (PKA), protein kinase C (PKC), phosphodiesterases (PDEs), proto-oncogenic non-receptor tyrosine kinase (Src)-related modules, and cytoskeleton- or adhesion-associated proteins within local signaling microdomains, AKAP12 regulates kinase output, PDE-dependent cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) gradients, cytoskeletal remodeling, cell migration, barrier integrity, inflammatory activation, fibrosis, and tissue repair. However, AKAP12-related evidence remains dispersed across oncology, cardiovascular biology, neurovascular research, and inflammatory disease. Its apparent protective or pathogenic roles are often interpreted without sufficient attention to cell type, isoform usage, post-translational modification, disease stage, or microenvironmental stress. This review integrates mechanistic and translational evidence for AKAP12 across cancer, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, neurological disorders, and inflammation-related conditions. In malignant tumors, AKAP12 most often acts as a tumor suppressor by restraining oncogenic signaling, invasion, cytoskeletal reorganization, and metastatic niche formation; however, emerging studies also reveal pro-tumor functions in hypoxia-adapted melanoma, drug-resistant ovarian cancer, and AKAP12-positive cancer-associated fibroblast niches that drive macrophage-mediated immunosuppression. In the cardiovascular and neurovascular systems, AKAP12 shapes beta-adrenergic cAMP microdomains, PDE-dependent contractile responses, endothelial migration, blood-brain barrier stability, oligodendrocyte differentiation, and injury repair. In inflammatory and fibrotic disorders, AKAP12 links immune polarization, stromal remodeling, metabolic homeostasis, and organ repair. We propose that AKAP12 should be viewed as a dynamic signaling-interface module whose functional output depends on cellular origin, isoform context, and microenvironmental state. Future studies integrating single-cell and spatial omics, interactome proteomics, isoform-specific perturbation, organoid models, and precision delivery strategies will be essential to define when AKAP12 is protective, pathogenic, or therapeutically targetable.

secondary.title: Human Brain Organoid-Enabling Discoveries Reach the Clinic: A Translational Inflection Point.
secondary.abstract: Human brain organoids have evolved from early neurodevelopmental models into platforms for therapeutic discovery. Here, we highlight two cases in which organoid-derived findings enabled FDA-approved clinical trials. Patient-derived organoids modeling Pitt-Hopkins syndrome revealed human-specific, TCF4-dependent abnormalities and supported the development of a regulated AAV gene therapy. In parallel, Rett syndrome organoids cultured aboard the International Space Station uncovered space-induced neural senescence, characterized by retroelement-associated neuroinflammation, prompting evaluation of antiretroviral therapy. These examples illustrate how organoids can reveal disease mechanisms that are inaccessible or incompletely reproduced in animal models, while animal studies remain essential for validation and safety assessment. As the field advances, matching model complexity to experimental purpose-and ensuring reproducibility, scalability, and accessibility-will be critical. Human brain organoids are crossing a translational threshold, emerging as engines of therapeutic discovery and gateways to clinical intervention.

secondary.title: Emerging role of cGAS-STING in the pathogenesis of allergic diseases.
secondary.abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) signaling pathway, classically recognized as a crucial cytosolic DNA-sensing mechanism in innate antiviral immunity, is now emerging as a pivotal regulator of sterile inflammation and immune dysregulation. Recent evidence has shifted the paradigm, revealing its significant involvement in the pathogenesis of various allergic diseases, including asthma, atopic dermatitis, and allergic rhinitis. Beyond its canonical role in infection, aberrant activation of cGAS by endogenous DNA from mitochondrial stress, cellular damage, or neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) can drive pro-inflammatory cytokine responses and, depending on context, type I interferon responses; however, stimulus-induced type I interferon production is impaired in asthmatic airway epithelium and is further suppressed by type 2 inflammatory mediators. This review synthesizes current findings on how dysregulated cGAS-STING signaling contributes to allergic inflammation by amplifying Th2 responses, promoting airway remodeling, enhancing epithelial barrier dysfunction, and modulating the activity of key immune cells such as eosinophils, macrophages, mast cells, dendritic cells, and fibroblasts. We further explore the interplay between this pathway and other allergic signaling cascades, highlighting its role as an innate immune amplifier of allergic sensitization and chronicity Finally, we discuss the translational potential of targeting the cGAS-STING axis as an emerging therapeutic strategy for managing severe, steroid-resistant, or type-2-low allergic endotypes, while emphasizing the need for further validation, particularly in settings where type I interferon responses are impaired and where direct evidence for type-2-low endotypes remains limited.Understanding the emerging role of cGAS-STING provides critical insights into the complex immunobiology of allergic diseases and opens new avenues for intervention.

secondary.title: Pathogenesis and therapeutic targets of neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease mediated by microglia lysosomal dysfunction.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by two core pathological features: senile plaques formed by amyloid-β protein (Aβ) deposits and neurofibrillary tangles formed by hyperphosphorylated tau protein. In recent years, neuroinflammation has been recognized as a key driver in the pathogenesis of AD, and microglia, as innate immune cells of the central nervous system, play a central role in regulating the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Lysosomes are key organelles within microglia responsible for degrading pathological proteins and regulating inflammatory signaling; dysfunction of lysosomes in microglia severely impairs their ability to clear Aβ, damaged proteins, and cellular debris, thereby promoting inflammatory responses. This manuscript summarizes upstream mechanisms that may influence microglial lysosomal dysfunction from four perspectives: pathological proteins, genetic factors, lipid metabolism disorders, and proinflammatory cytokines. Pathological proteins can impair lysosomal acidification and biogenesis by interfering with key pathways such as the TFEB-v-ATPase axis; various genetic factors exacerbate functional dysregulation by influencing the expression of lysosome-related genes and lipid metabolism; lipid metabolism disorders promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization, block the autophagy cascade and activate the inflammasome; proinflammatory cytokines can exert varying effects on the clearance of pathological substrates and by regulating lysosomal function. The aforementioned factors can influence microglial lysosomal function through various mechanisms, thereby contributing to impaired clearance of pathological substrates and the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Intervention strategies targeting microglial lysosomal dysfunction, including enhancing lysosomal degradation capacity, regulating autophagy related pathways, correcting cellular metabolic dysregulation and suppressing excessive neuroinflammation, may offer new avenues for AD treatment.

secondary.title: Dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier and neurovascular unit in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis - From advanced human models to treatments.
secondary.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by the degeneration of motor neurons, resulting in progressive and eventually complete loss of motor function. The phenotypical heterogeneity of ALS poses a challenge to early diagnosis and treatment, with currently available therapeutics only capable of relieving symptoms and slowing progression. While ALS is classified as a motor neuron disease (MND), research has identified significant impairment to the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and neurovascular unit (NVU) of ALS patients. The BBB along with supporting cells of the NVU selectively control the entry of substances into the central nervous system (CNS) and maintain brain homeostasis, with its many cellular components demonstrating impaired function, specifically relating to inflammation, oxidative stress and TDP-43 proteinopathy. The advent of more advanced in vitro techniques as well as use of patient-derived BBB cells has presented a promising alternative to recreate the in vivo structure of the BBB/NVU in a highly controlled platform. Such approaches have ranged from simple 2-dimensional (2D) cell culture to intricate 3-dimensional (3D) co-culture systems, as well as microfluidic systems and organoids, with a potential to investigate ALS associated BBB/NVU dysfunction and drug discovery. This review provides a comprehensive assessment of known BBB/NVU dysfunction in ALS and methods of investigating this using in vitro and in vivo platforms with a focus on inflammation, oxidative stress and pathological TDP-43 expression. This review also presents a future perspective to overcoming barriers to treatment of ALS using new patient-derived BBB/NVU model systems.

secondary.title: The early MALDI years and how "microscopy-grade" transmission-mode MALDI-2 mass spectrometry imaging was realized after a long delay: a personal retrospective and review.
secondary.abstract: Since its invention in the mid-1980s, matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization (MALDI) mass spectrometry (MS) has developed into a key bioanalytical technique for numerous research areas in the life sciences. One remarkable application shift that began in the mid-1990s is the increasing use of the label-free MALDI technique as a molecular microscope. One holy grail of MALDI-MS Imaging (MALDI-MSI) is to reach a true single-cell or even a sub-cellular resolution to visualize the molecular content of individual cells and organelles thereof. This requires pixel sizes in the low to sub-micrometer range. These are difficult to achieve, such that new irradiation concepts are needed. Another contemporary research focus is on the advancement of multimodal imaging, especially in the combination of immunofluorescence (IF) microscopy and highly-resolved MALDI-MSI. Drawing upon four decades of active research in the MALDI field, I structured this review to offer both a personal (retro-)perspective and a comprehensive exploration of both historical and contemporary aspects. The initial chapter provides a historical overview of the development of the first laser microprobe mass analyzer (LAMMA 500), while the subsequent chapter chronicles the discovery of the MALDI technique and its initial applications in biological research. The third and fourth sections then direct the reader's attention to selected recent advancements in MALDI-imaging, highlighting pioneering contributions from both in-house and external laboratories. These developments include the utilization of laser postionization for MALDI-2 and the resurgence of the LAMMA 500 concept in the form of transmission (t-) mode MALDI-2. The recently introduced direct coupling of t-MALDI-2 with IF microscopy holds significant promise in unveiling novel avenues for cell biology research.

secondary.title: TMEM175: lysosomal ion channel physiology, therapeutic potential, and emerging pharmacology.
secondary.abstract: Transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175) is a lysosomal cation channel that has emerged as a promising drug target for Parkinson's disease (PD). Genetic and functional studies linking TMEM175 loss-of-function variants to increased PD risk, lysosomal dysfunction, and α-synuclein accumulation have generated considerable interest in developing pharmacological approaches to enhance channel activity. As a lysosomal cation channel with reported K+ and H+ permeability, TMEM175 regulates lysosomal membrane potential, pH stability, autophagic flux, and degradative capacity, placing it at a critical control point for cellular proteostasis. Recent advances in high-throughput screening, automated and lysosomal patch clamp electrophysiology, cryoelectron microscopy, and structure-guided medicinal chemistry have transformed TMEM175 from a relatively obscure lysosomal ion channel into a tractable drug target. These approaches have enabled the discovery of multiple classes of TMEM175 modulators while providing new insights into channel gating and mechanisms of activation. In this review, we summarize current progress in TMEM175 pharmacology, including advances in functional assay development and the emerging landscape of tool compounds used to study channel function. We discuss TMEM175 physiology and structure-function relationships, the growing evidence supporting therapeutic intervention, and recent discoveries revealing multiple mechanisms of channel activation. Finally, we highlight key challenges that remain for the field, including the development of potent and selective modulators, opportunities afforded by synergistic channel activation, and the potential application of TMEM175-directed therapeutics beyond Parkinson's disease in a broader range of neurodegenerative and lysosome-associated disorders.

secondary.title: Patient-derived 3d cell models as new approach methodologies: Applications, advances, and challenges for increased-throughput assays.
secondary.abstract: Patient-derived three-dimensional (3D) cell models are new approach methodologies (NAMs) that bridge the gap between traditional 2D cell cultures and in vivo models, making them attractive for increased-throughput screening (ITS) and secondary assays. In this review, we outline screening applications implementing patient-derived 3D cell models, with an emphasis on patient-derived organoid (PDO) based assays, across oncology, toxicity testing, and rare disease drug discovery. We summarize how tumor and non-tumor organoids are used to discover new drug vulnerabilities, prioritize standard-of-care regimens, and model dynamic pathophysiologic processes in 96 to 1536-well formats. We then highlight advances in plating strategies, assay design, and advanced assay outputs that have enabled semi-automated and fully automated pipelines. Finally, we discuss persistent challenges, including heterogeneity, assay standardization, and limited publicly available protocols, and propose future directions such as integration with immune and stromal compartments, and national standardization efforts to increase reproducibility and translational impact.

secondary.title: Effects of PPAR modulation on cognitive function and oxidative stress in experimental Alzheimer's disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
secondary.abstract: Oxidative stress is a key pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD), characterized by increased levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), malondialdehyde (MDA), 4-hydroxynonenal, and protein carbonyls, alongside impaired antioxidant defenses such as superoxide dismutase (SOD). These alterations contribute to endoplasmic reticulum stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, neuronal apoptosis, and cognitive decline. Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs) have been recognized for their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties; however, their effects on oxidative stress in AD have not been systematically evaluated. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, with an updated search performed in February 2026. Twenty-nine eligible studies were included. Standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for outcomes reported in at least three studies. Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q and I² statistics, and random-effects models were applied when necessary. PPAR agonists significantly improved cognitive performance in the Morris water maze, reducing escape latency (p = 0.02). Protein and gene expression levels of PPARs were significantly increased compared to controls (p < 0.001). Experimental studies showed enhanced antioxidant capacity, including increased SOD levels and reduced MDA and ROS production. PPAR activation also decreased BAX expression, suggesting reduced apoptosis and improved cell viability. In addition, PPAR agonists attenuated amyloid-β deposition and improved neuronal morphology, whereas receptor antagonists largely reversed these beneficial effects. Current preclinical evidence suggests that PPAR modulation exerts beneficial effects on cognition, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammatory pathways in experimental AD. Nevertheless, substantial methodological heterogeneity and the absence of clinical evidence warrant cautious interpretation and further translational studies.

secondary.title: Nitric oxide signaling and mitophagy in Parkinson's disease: implications for aerobic exercise-related neuroprotection.
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease is strongly associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitochondrial quality control, including defective mitophagy. Aerobic exercise is increasingly recognized as a safe and accessible intervention that can improve motor and non-motor outcomes in Parkinson's disease and may also engage mechanisms relevant to disease modification. In this review, we propose a context-dependent framework in which aerobic exercise reshapes nitric oxide signaling toward a more adaptive profile, characterized by relatively moderate, transient, and spatially restricted nitric oxide bioactivity, and we discuss how this shift may influence mitochondrial biogenesis, mitophagy initiation, and autophagic flux regulation. Rather than treating nitric oxide as uniformly protective or deleterious, we argue that its biological effects in Parkinson's disease depend on source, concentration, duration, subcellular localization, cellular target, and surrounding redox milieu. However, direct evidence that exercise-derived nitric oxide activates these pathways in Parkinson's disease-relevant neural tissue is still limited. We further highlight major translational gaps, including cell-type and brain-region heterogeneity, incomplete definition of exercise dose-response relationships, and the lack of validated in vivo biomarkers of neuronal mitophagy and nitric oxide dynamics in patients with Parkinson's disease. Overall, aerobic exercise is a plausible modulator of mitophagy-related pathways in Parkinson's disease, and nitric oxide is a credible contributor to this effect; however, the current evidence supports a multi-node, context-dependent model rather than a simple linear mechanism.

secondary.title: Neuroprotective roles of Klotho signaling in Huntington's disease: From molecular insights to clinical translation.
secondary.abstract: Huntington's Disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by CAG repeat expansion in the HTT gene, producing toxic mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein. This leads to progressive motor dysfunction, cognitive decline, and psychiatric disturbances. Despite advances in understanding mHTT toxicity, potentially disease-modifying therapies remain scarce, underscoring the need for novel approaches targeting core pathophysiological mechanisms. Klotho, a multifunctional anti-aging protein, regulates several pathways relevant to neuronal survival and may have relevance to HD pathophysiology. Klotho is a co-receptor with a membrane and is a soluble co-receptor that regulates synaptic and metabolic homeostasis. Although direct experimental evidence in HD remains limited, emerging findings from aging and neurodegeneration research suggest that Klotho-mediated pathways may influence mechanisms relevant to HD pathogenesis. It suppresses fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) signaling and major pathways such as PI3K/Akt-FOXO, Wnt/ -catenin and insulin/IGF-1 pathways, which oppose the hallmarks of HD, namely excitotoxicity, calcium dysregulation, impaired neuroprotection, and peripheral neuroinflammation. There is growing evidence of the involvement of Klotho in mitochondrial health and biogenesis, mitophagy coordination, and oxidative stress resistance - direct mitigating cellular toxicity caused by mHTT. These mechanistic overlaps suggest that Klotho signaling may represent a potential area for investigation in HD. It deals with oxidative stress, excitotoxicity, inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation, and compares it to other diseases of the neurodegenerative type in which Klotho deficits contribute to pathology. Such a structure encourages Klotho-based interventions as a new, mechanism-based approach to HD. Further experimental studies are required to determine whether modulation of Klotho signaling could influence disease progression in HD.

secondary.title: VPS13C-mediated endoplasmic reticulum-lysosome tethering in neuronal stress responses.
secondary.abstract: Organelle contact sites are increasingly recognized as regulatory interfaces that coordinate lipid transfer, ion signaling, and metabolic adaptation. In neurons, communication among the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), lysosomes, and mitochondria is essential for cellular homeostasis. Recent studies have identified vacuolar protein sorting 13 homolog C (VPS13C), a lipid transport protein, as a key mediator of ER-lysosome tethering and as an important component of the response to lysosomal stress. Structural analyses show that VPS13 family proteins form elongated lipid transport channels that are proposed to facilitate phospholipid transfer between adjacent membranes. Following lysosomal damage, VPS13C is recruited to ER-lysosome contact interfaces, where it forms tethering bridges that may support membrane repair by enabling high-capacity lipid transfer from the ER to lysosomal membranes. Beyond membrane repair, these contact interfaces may also participate in broader organelle communication networks. ER-lysosome contacts can occur in proximity to ER-mitochondria junctions, potentially forming multi organelle signaling hubs that coordinate lipid redistribution, calcium signaling, and mitochondrial adaptation. These signals may influence downstream responses, including activation of TFEB and TFE3, which regulate lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. Disruption of this contact site network has emerged as a potential contributor to Parkinson's disease. Loss of VPS13C function is associated with altered lysosomal homeostasis and intersects with pathogenic pathways involving α-synuclein aggregation, PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, and LRRK2 signaling. This review presents a framework in which ER-lysosome tethering is considered part of a staged cellular damage response linking membrane repair, metabolic coordination, and transcriptional adaptation.

secondary.title: Axonemal dynein gene dysfunction as a cause of male infertility: insights from DNAH family mutations.
secondary.abstract: Male infertility is a complex disorder and defective sperm motility is one of the most common reasons for impaired fertility. The dynein axonemal heavy chain (DNAH) gene family encode molecular motors that form the structure of cilia and sperm flagella. Abnormalities in several DNAH genes have already been confirmed to be causative factors responsible for male infertility conditions, mainly including asthenozoospermia, multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF), and reproductive failure related to primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD). Here, this review illustrates the current evidence regarding the involvement of members of the DNAH family in male infertility, along with summarizing their biological functions, genotypic and phenotypic correlations and clinical significance. Due to the breakthroughs of the technologies of whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing along with research with animal models and functional investigations, the diversity of reported causative DNAH mutations and their implications for the organization and function of sperm axonemes are currently better understood. DNAH1, DNAH8 and DNAH17 are the DNAH genes most frequently described as being involved in male infertility, though growing evidence also indicated that DNAH3, DNAH11, DNAH12 and DNAH14 also contribute to the male reproductive disorders. Implementation of testing DNAH genes into molecular diagnostics enhances the assessment of genes causing severe sperm motility disorders and aids genetic counseling of the affected families. Together with the genomic and functional data, further research will elucidate additional details for disease mechanisms and will bring benefit to more precise diagnosis and treatments of DNAH-associated male infertility.

secondary.title: UBE3A Dosage Imbalance as a Molecular Framework Linking Angelman Syndrome and Dup15q-Associated Autism Phenotypes.
secondary.abstract: UBE3A is a dosage-sensitive HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase whose neuronal expression is shaped by genomic imprinting at the 15q11.2-q13 locus. Opposite directions of UBE3A dosage imbalance contribute to distinct neurodevelopmental phenotypes: loss of maternal UBE3A underlies Angelman syndrome, whereas maternally derived 15q11.2-q13 copy-number gains, including interstitial duplications and isodicentric inv. dup(15)/idic(15) rearrangements, contribute to Dup15q-associated syndromic autism phenotypes. This review synthesizes evidence across molecular architecture, isoform biology, neuronal imprinting, synaptic regulation, circuit excitability, and therapeutic development. The central argument is that UBE3A should not be interpreted as a general explanation for autism, but as a mechanistically informative model for a defined subset of neurodevelopmental disorders in which parent-of-origin effects and copy-number state are central. In Angelman syndrome, UBE3A loss disrupts proteostasis, synaptic plasticity, inhibitory circuit function, and neuronal excitability through distributed rather than single-pathway mechanisms. In the maternally derived Dup15q spectrum, increased UBE3A dosage is strongly implicated in neuronal and synaptic abnormalities, although interval-wide dosage effects also contribute. Therapeutically, the direction of dosage change creates opposite translational requirements: restoration or paternal reactivation in Angelman syndrome versus dosage normalization in Dup15q-associated overdosage states. A dosage-directionality framework may therefore clarify how UBE3A biology connects molecular mechanism, developmental timing, and precision therapeutic design.

secondary.title: Cortical transcriptomic dysregulation in Autism spectrum disorder: A conceptual synthesis.
secondary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition in which human post-mortem cortical transcriptomic studies have identified recurrent but context-sensitive molecular abnormalities. This narrative review synthesises RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) evidence from ASD cortex and organises recurrent findings into three interacting cortical domains: synaptic/neuronal programmes, immune-glial programmes, and RNA-regulatory processes. Across bulk cortical datasets, the most reproducible signals include relative downregulation of neuronal and synaptic expression programmes together with upregulation of glial-associated and neuroimmune signatures, whereas transcript-level analyses further implicate alternative splicing, microexon dysregulation, differential transcript usage, and isoform-level perturbation. Single-nucleus and related cell-resolved approaches localise these abnormalities to defined neuronal and glial populations, while long-read strategies strengthen inference on transcript structure and isoform complexity. Within this framework, mitochondrial-related findings are best interpreted as a linked bioenergetic component rather than an equally established standalone transcriptomic domain. The review also summarise the principal interpretive constraints of cortical ASD transcriptomics, including region specificity, developmental stage, cohort heterogeneity, cell-type composition, post-mortem tissue quality, and cross-platform comparability.

secondary.title: Advancing early detection of Alzheimer's disease: from established biomarkers to future innovations.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a major form of dementia, imposes an escalating global burden on public health and social care. Pathological changes in AD occur years before clinical symptoms, defining a prolonged preclinical phase. Currently, there is no effective treatment exist for late-stage AD, making early diagnosis and intervention indispensable, in which biomarkers play a pivotal role. While cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and positron emission tomography (PET) biomarkers improved AD diagnostic accuracy, their clinical application is limited by invasiveness, high costs. Advances in ultrasensitive immunoassay technologies has rendered peripheral blood biomarkers easily accessible, cost-effective, minimally invasive, and suitable for continuous monitoring, offering noval opportunities for AD screening, diagnosis and progression tracking. Additionally, non-invasive body fluids including saliva, urine and tears are being explored as potential biomarkers. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven multimodal fusion, integrated with large-scale multimodal computing frameworks, significantly improve the accuracy of early AD diagnosis. Recent studies have identified a series of promising synaptic and neuronal biomarkers, such as neurofilament light chain (NFL), neurogranin (Ng), β-secretase 1 (BACE1) and synaptosomal-associated protein 25 (SNAP-25). Inflammatory mediators and genetic factors also contribute to AD pathological evaluation. This review systematically characterizes biomarker profiles of emerging non-invasive carriers (saliva, urine and tears). It further synthesizes cohort-derived quantitative diagnostic metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity) of multimodal AD biomarkers and conducts head-to-head comparison to clarify their respective strengths and translational limitations, aiming to provide evidence-based insights for optimizing early AD screening and diagnostic strategies.

secondary.title: Disruptions in axonal lysosome transport and its contribution to neurological disease.
secondary.abstract: Lysosomes are central to the maintenance of protein and organelle homeostasis in cells. Optimal lysosome function is particularly critical for neurons which are long-lived, non-dividing and highly polarized with specialized compartments such as axons and dendrites with distinct architecture, cargo, and turnover requirements. In recent years, there has been a growing appreciation for the role played by axonal lysosome transport in regulating neuronal development, its maintenance and functioning. Perturbations to optimal axonal lysosome abundance leading to either strong accumulations or dearth of lysosomes are both linked to altered neuronal health and functioning. In this review we highlight how two critical regulators of axonal lysosome transport and abundance, the small GTPase Arl8 and the adaptor protein JIP3, aid in maintaining axonal lysosome homeostasis and how alterations to their levels and activity could contribute to neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases.

secondary.title: Targeting Nrf2 signaling in Parkinson's disease: Mechanisms, strategies, and therapeutic perspectives.
secondary.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the selective loss of dopaminergic neurons and the accumulation of α-synuclein. Disease progression is driven by a complex interplay of chronic oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired proteostasis. As a central regulator of the cellular antioxidant response, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) protects against these cellular insults by driving the expression of various cytoprotective genes. In this review, we summarize the regulatory mechanisms of the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway and evaluate how its activation counteracts core PD pathologies. We also highlight the extensive crosstalk between Nrf2 and other major signaling networks that collectively determine dopaminergic neuronal survival. Finally, we examine the therapeutic potential of current Nrf2 modulators, including natural phytochemicals, clinical-stage candidates, and repurposed drugs, and critically discuss the pharmacokinetic barriers, electrophilic off-target toxicities, and the Nrf2 paradox that must be overcome to successfully translate these compounds into disease-modifying therapies for PD, highlighting the transition toward non-covalent PPI inhibitors.
