secondary.title: From exercise-associated lactate to the tubulin code: α-tubulin lactylation as a candidate mechanism for poststroke neural remodeling.
secondary.abstract: Aerobic exercise promotes functional recovery after ischemic stroke, but the proposed link between an exercise-associated lactate pulse and durable neural remodeling remains unproven. The metabolite relevant to the hypothesis is L-lactate generated by skeletal-muscle glycolysis. In the principal mouse study, moderate treadmill exercise begun on poststroke day 6 (10 m/min, 30 min/day for 14 days) increased circulating and brain lactate together with α-tubulin lysine 40 (K40) lactylation and recovery; this regimen cannot be assumed feasible in patients with acute or severe disability. Electrically evoked skeletal-muscle contraction offers a preclinical exercise-mimetic option for nonambulatory subjects and increased circulating lactate in stroke mice, but it has not established a therapeutic lactate target, brain K40 lactylation, or clinical efficacy. Mechanistically, concurrent changes in L-lactate, K40 lactylation, and recovery show association rather than causal mediation. Exogenous L-lactate and dichloroacetate broadly alter metabolism and signaling, while substrate oxidation, HCAR1/VEGF signaling, BDNF/NMDAR-related plasticity, and lactylation of other proteins remain parallel explanations. The in vivo role of K40 lactylation has not been tested by a selective blockade. Moreover, the LacAVC phase IIa intravenous lactate trial was terminated after 28 enrollments for recruitment and protocol-related reasons. Although no results have been posted in the trial registry, a 2026 conference abstract reported preliminary safety and cerebral-bioavailability findings without establishing clinical efficacy or α-tubulin K40 target engagement.

secondary.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease: mechanisms, pathogenic interplay, and therapeutic opportunities.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains a major cause of dementia, yet effective disease-modifying therapies are still limited. Although amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau pathology remain core features of AD pathogenesis, they do not fully explain how these pathological alterations drive progressive cellular dysfunction. Increasing evidence suggests that mitochondria are involved at this critical interface. In AD, mitochondrial abnormalities impair energy production, compromise organelle quality control, disrupt calcium (Ca2+) homeostasis, and alter communication with the endoplasmic reticulum and glial cells. As these defects accumulate, neurons and glia become less able to maintain metabolic stability, redox balance, and synaptic function. Mitochondrial dysfunction is therefore relevant to AD not as a single isolated lesion, but as a convergent process through which metabolic failure, oxidative stress, mitochondrial DNA damage, inflammatory signaling, and defective cellular maintenance reinforce one another. This perspective also helps explain why disease progression is difficult to reverse once mitochondrial homeostasis has been broadly compromised. At the same time, this framework also points to therapeutic opportunities, as the mechanisms driving the development and progression of mitochondrial dysfunction may be amenable to intervention. However, many mitochondria-centered strategies remain preclinical or have yielded inconsistent clinical benefit. Current evidence supports mitochondrial dysfunction as both a useful mechanistic basis for understanding AD progression and a biologically meaningful, though challenging, therapeutic target.

secondary.title: Intermittent fasting as a therapeutic strategy in Alzheimer's disease: Understanding of brain-derived neurotrophic factor modulation.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques, tau tangles, neuroinflammation, and oxidative stress, and it causes cognitive impairment and neuronal loss. The pharmacological treatment is of limited effectiveness, therefore the interest in novel approaches such as intermittent fasting (IF). IF, a nutritional regimen of periodic caloric restriction, has shown a potential to modulate neurodegenerative alterations by metabolic and molecular mechanisms. This review presents the implications of IF in the etiopathogenesis of AD, specifically in controlling brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). BDNF is a major neurotrophin that plays a key role in synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival, and cognition. Evidence indicates that BDNF is drastically decreased in AD, therefore enhancing disease progression. IF enhances BDNF expression via mechanisms such as improved mitochondrial function, increased ketone body production, and reduced systemic inflammation. Preclinical studies indicate that IF not only upregulates BDNF but also alleviates key AD pathologies, including Aβ deposition and tau hyperphosphorylation. Additionally, clinical data highlight the cognitive benefits of IF and its role in modulating metabolic health, although studies specifically linking IF, BDNF and AD in humans remain limited. This review underscores the need for further research to determine optimal IF protocols and clarify its long-term impact on AD progression. IF's ability to modulate BDNF and other neuroprotective pathways positions it as a promising non-pharmacological intervention for AD management. By bridging metabolic health and neuroprotection, IF offers potential therapeutic synergy for mitigating AD's complex etiopathogenesis.

secondary.title: From iPSC disease modeling to epigenome editing: Toward therapeutic reversal of genomic imprinting disorders.
secondary.abstract: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and organoids are increasingly important components of new approach methodologies because they provide experimentally accessible human systems that preserve patient-specific genetic backgrounds and can be differentiated into disease-relevant cell types. Genomic imprinting disorders are particularly attractive targets for this approach because their pathogenesis depends not only on DNA sequence but also on parent-of-origin-specific epigenetic regulation. Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS) and Angelman syndrome (AS), which arise from distinct disruptions within the same imprinted domain on chromosome 15q11.2-q13, illustrate both the opportunities and the complexity of therapeutic epigenetic manipulation. Recent studies using PWS patient-derived iPSCs have shown that disease-associated imprinting states are largely retained after reprogramming and can be experimentally reversed by locus-specific epigenome editing. Targeted demethylation of the PWS imprinting control region restored multiple paternally expressed genes, and the corrected state persisted after differentiation into hypothalamic organoids, partially normalizing disease-associated transcriptomic and functional phenotypes. Here, we discuss how iPSC-based disease modeling is evolving from a platform for mechanism discovery toward a test bed for therapeutic epigenome engineering and outline the major challenges that must be addressed before epigenome editing can be translated to patients with imprinting disorders.

secondary.title: Oxidative stress in neurodegeneration: from a simple insult to a dynamic regulator.
secondary.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the central role of oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases, and to explore its dynamic regulatory features, underlying signaling pathways, and molecular mechanisms, as well as advanced technological strategies for antioxidant intervention. METHODS: This review comprehensively evaluated existing literature on oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases. It analyzed key regulatory pathways (Nrf2, Keap1, AMPK, mTOR) and molecular processes, including ferroptosis, NETosis, and mitochondrial quality control systems, along with oxidative damage to DNA, lipids, and proteins. The review also assessed advanced technological approaches such as subcellular organelle targeting, nanocarrier delivery systems (e.g. gold nanoparticles, liposomes for glutathione delivery), and single-cell/spatial omics technologies (e.g. single-cell redoxomics, spatial transcriptomics). RESULTS: Oxidative stress exhibits dynamic features, generating protective signals in early stages but transitioning into destructive factors later. A major obstacle for current antioxidant therapies is the blood-brain barrier. Breakthrough strategies identified include precision targeting at the subcellular level, functionalized nanoparticles for efficient antioxidant delivery, and the integration of single-cell redoxomics with spatial transcriptomics to identify specific biomarkers and enable personalized treatments. DISCUSSION: By integrating novel molecular mechanisms and advanced technological resources, this review redefines oxidative stress not as a singular event but as a complex, dynamically regulated system in neurodegenerative diseases. This reconceptualization provides new perspectives for developing targeted and personalized therapeutic interventions.

secondary.title: Multi-omics integration deciphers arsenic-induced multi-organ toxicity and the novel ferroptosis axis.
secondary.abstract: Chronic arsenic exposure threatens over 200 million people worldwide and induces multi-organ injury, yet the panoramic molecular reprogramming across organs remains incompletely understood, and traditional single-omics approaches fail to capture cross-level and cross-organ regulatory associations. This review systematically integrates evidence from global epidemiology to single-cell spatial omics, tracing the evolution of multi-omics technologies-from single-platform profiling to data fusion strategies such as coupled matrix factorization (CMF) and the DIABLO framework, two complementary multi-omics integration approaches-and to cutting-edge spatial transcriptomics. We highlight ferroptosis as a common mechanism in arsenic-induced multi-organ injury. At the molecular level, we propose a mechanistic model wherein arsenic (AsIII) disrupts selenium metabolism by inhibiting Sec-tRNASec synthesis, thereby impairing selenoprotein (especially GPX4) biosynthesis, a paradigm distinct from the traditional "ROS burst → lipid peroxidation" theory. Supporting evidence includes reduced 75Se incorporation into cellular RNA, genetic deletion of PRDX6 exacerbating ferroptosis, and rescue by selenium supplementation via Nrf2 activation. At the organ level, we compare toxicity features and propose that tissue-intrinsic ferroptosis thresholds-determined by iron content, PUFA-phospholipid composition, GSH reserves, GPX4 redundancy, and selenium availability-govern differential organ susceptibility; the brain shows extreme vulnerability, whereas the liver exhibits relative resistance. Emerging spatial omics further reveals elevated arsenic-responsive gene expression in tumor-adjacent regions. This systems toxicology paradigm offers mechanistic grounding for combinatorial biomarker panels and genotype-guided precision selenium supplementation, although definitive causal validation through tissue-specific Gpx4 knockout or Sec-tRNASec rescue experiments remains a critical next step. We also discuss prospects for AI-driven toxicity prediction models.

secondary.title: From pathogenesis to non-medical therapy: A review of exploring sensory and multi-sensory stimulation as a non-invasive treatment approach for Alzheimer's disease.
secondary.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, marked by the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, tau pathology, and synaptic dysfunction, ultimately leading to memory loss, cognitive decline, neuropsychiatric symptoms and neuronal degeneration that impairs daily functioning. Despite the availability of pharmacological treatments developed to slow down symptom progression, their clinical efficacy remains uncertain, and they are frequently associated with adverse side effects, underscoring the urgent demand for safer and more effective therapeutic alternatives. Non-pharmacological approaches, therefore, have been investigated and are considered promising alternative therapeutic strategies for AD. This paper outlines the pathological features and neural network changes that occur across the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD), reviews the effects of different sensory stimulation approaches on reducing these AD-associated changes, and discusses the potential mechanisms underlying various sensory and multisensory stimulation interventions in mitigating AD-related symptoms. These sensory stimulation interventions, including 40 Hz Gamma Entrainment Using Sensory Stimulation [GENUS], Photobiomodulation, Bright Light Therapy, Music Therapy, Aromatherapy, Tactile Stimulation, and Multisensory Stimulation, are found to slow down the progression of AD by ameliorating multiple AD pathologies, enhancing cognitive function, promoting neuroplasticity, regulating sleep patterns, and reducing behavioural or neuropsychiatric symptoms. Crucially, this present work integrates both human and animal studies, aligning clinical outcomes with mechanistic insights derived from animal studies, thereby bridging preclinical and clinical research to promote the translation of sensory interventions into effective treatments for patients with AD.

papers.title: Pathogenic MAPK8IP3 variants drive distinct motor and behavioral phenotypes in humans and mice
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Pathogenic variants in MAPK8IP3 (JIP3) cause Neurodevelopmental Disorder with or without variable Brain Abnormalities (NEDBA), characterized by cognitive impairment, global developmental delay, motor dysfunction, abnormal muscle tone, behavioral dysregulation including autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), seizures, and structural brain abnormalities. While more than 30 largely de novo MAPK8IP3 variants have been reported, the functional impact of variants across JIP3 protein structural domains is poorly defined. To address this knowledge gap, we compare clinical features of individuals with a truncating (p.E27X) or one of two missense (p.R578C and p.R1146C) variants from distinct JIP3 functional protein domains to corresponding knock-in mouse models. Our findings showed that all individuals, regardless of variant type, exhibited delays in language and gross motor function, but individual variants were associated with distinct motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms. Corresponding homozygous p.E27X and p.R1147C variant mice resulted in embryonic lethality, consistent with essential roles for JIP3 in early neurodevelopment. Behavioral characterization of viable heterozygous mice revealed variant-specific locomotor, motor coordination, and hindlimb clasping defects that closely recapitulate clinical observations. Heterozygous p.R579C mice exhibited reduced locomotion, impaired motor performance, and hypertonia-like clasping, mirroring human motor deficits. In contrast, p.R1147C mice displayed hyperactivity, hindlimb clasping, and decreased brain weight, paralleling human clinical features. Together, our findings demonstrate that while distinct MAPK8IP3 variants lead to some shared phenotypes, they are also associated with distinct phenotypes that could reveal domain-specific aspects of JIP3 function. This work establishes the first domain-resolved in vivo rodent models of NEDBA and provides a validated translational platform for mechanistic investigation and preclinical therapeutic testing.

papers.title: Phenotype-genotype spectrum in CTNND2-related neurodevelopmental disease
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Heterozygous variants in CTNND2 , encoding the brain-specific protein δ-catenin, are associated with a broad spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders, including dyslexia, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, intellectual disability, and autism. Despite its clinical significance, the full phenotypic spectrum of CTNND2 -associated disorders and the neurodevelopmental role of δ-catenin, a key component of the cadherin-catenin cell adhesion complex, remain poorly defined. Methods Through international collaboration, we assembled the phenotypic and molecular information for 57 individuals, 42 previously unpublished, carrying heterozygous CTNND2 variants. All individuals were evaluated by local clinicians, and the variants were identified through exome or genome sequencing, clinical microarray, or karyotyping. To investigate the effects of δ-catenin loss on early neurogenesis, we performed neural induction and transcriptomic profiling in three patient-derived neuroepithelial stem cell (NESC) lines and three isogenic CRISPR-Cas9-edited CTNND2 knockout lines. Transcriptomic changes were assessed across the patient-derived and CRISPR-edited models to identify shared and distinct transcriptional alterations, with particular focus on genes within the CTNND2 interactome and WNT- and cadherin-associated networks. Results We identified 41 distinct CTNND2 variants, including 28 novel variants comprising 18 predicted loss-of-function and 10 protein-altering variants. Among cases with parental testing, eight variants occurred de novo and 12 were inherited from an affected parent. The most common clinical features were developmental delay (90%), intellectual disability (74%), and behavioral abnormalities (79%). Neural induction revealed delayed neural rosette formation in one of the three patient-derived lines, whereas the remaining patient-derived and knockout lines showed apparently normal neural induction. Transcriptomic profiling revealed variable but partly convergent alterations across the patient-derived and knockout models, involving the CTNND2 interactome and WNT and cadherin signaling networks at both developmental time points. Conclusions This study defines CTNND2 -related neurodevelopmental disorders as a clinically recognizable but highly variable phenotype overlapping with other intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorders. Across cellular models, transcriptomic analysis identified variable and partly convergent changes involving interconnected networks associated with CTNND2, WNT, and cadherin signaling. The variability observed across both individuals and cellular models further highlights the influence of genetic background and other modifying factors on the consequences of CTNND2 disruption. These findings expand the clinical and molecular spectrum of CTNND2 -associated disorders and provide a framework for further investigation of the molecular consequences of CTNND2 disruption during early human neural development.

papers.title: Inactivating mutations in polyadenylation factor CSTF2 disrupt intronic polyadenylation patterns and are associated with intellectual disability.
papers.abstract: Alternative polyadenylation contributes extensively to transcript diversification and is particularly prominent during neuronal differentiation; however, its contribution to monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders remains incompletely understood. CSTF2 encodes an RNA-binding subunit of the cleavage stimulation factor complex and has previously been associated with X-linked intellectual disability through a single Asp50Ala missense variant with increased RNA-binding activity. Here, we identify seven rare CSTF2 variants in ten hemizygous male probands with intellectual disability, global developmental delay and/or autism spectrum disorder, including missense, nonsense, splice-site, and frameshift variants. Functional analysis of selected variants using RNA sequencing and 3′-end-proximal sequencing in CSTF2–depleted cells identified Phe19Leu, Gln543ter, Leu555Ser as strongly functionally impairing variants. These variants predominantly reduced usage of intronic polyadenylation sites while increasing usage of downstream sites within terminal 3′UTRs. Suppressed intronic sites were enriched for GU-rich sequence elements, were more evolutionarily conserved, and showed higher predicted polyadenylation–site strength, consistent with preferential impairment of CSTF2-dependent polyadenylation. In contrast, the previously reported Asp50Ala variant produced an opposing pattern, with preferential activation of intronic polyadenylation sites, consistent with its increased RNA-binding activity. These findings indicate that both reduced and increased CSTF2 activity disrupt the balance of polyadenylation–site usage and can result in neurodevelopmental disorder. Our data provide genetic and functional support for CSTF2 as an X–linked neurodevelopmental disorder gene, identify inactivating CSTF2 variants as a disease mechanism, and implicate dysregulation of intronic polyadenylation in human intellectual disability.

papers.title: Stathmin-2 regulates microtubule dynamics and axonal resilience in human motor neurons
papers.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is characterized by the selective degeneration of motor neurons, yet the mechanisms that either induce neurodegeneration or confer neuronal resilience remain poorly understood. Loss of the microtubule-associated protein Stathmin-2 (STMN2) is a downstream consequence of TDP-43 pathology present in nearly all cases of ALS and has emerged as a central feature of disease. However, the mechanisms by which STMN2 maintains homeostasis in motor neurons remain incompletely defined. Here, we investigated the role of STMN2 in regulating cytoskeletal organization and axonal function. Using TIRF microscopy, we quantified STMN2-dependent changes in microtubule growth and catastrophe at single-microtubule resolution. In human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons, STMN2 depletion increased baseline rates of microtubule polymerization. However, STMN2 depletion impaired recovery of axonal microtubules following transient nocodazole-induced depolymerization, indicating that STMN2 is required for efficient cytoskeletal remodeling after stress. Consistent with these findings, STMN2-depleted neurons exhibited impaired microtubule recovery following acute depolymerization and reduced axonal recoil after optically induced local microtubule severing. Finally, STMN2 depletion disrupted the formation of neuromuscular junction-like contacts in human motor neuron-myocyte co-cultures, linking impaired cytoskeletal homeostasis to loss of distal neuronal connectivity. Together, these findings identify STMN2 as a key regulator of cytoskeletal resilience that coordinates microtubule remodeling, mitochondrial transport, and maintenance of neuromuscular junctions. We propose that impaired resilience of the axonal cytoskeleton represents a critical point of vulnerability in motor neurons in patients with ALS, establishing cytoskeletal resilience as a potential therapeutic target downstream of TDP-43 pathology.

papers.title: Dual kinase inhibition provides early clues to restoration of neuroimmune homeostasis in an AAV-haSyn model of Parkinsons disease
papers.abstract: Background: Previous studies of drugs targeting mixed linage kinase type 3 (MLK3) and/or leucine rich repeat kinase type 2 (LRRK2) in sporadic Parkinsons disease (PD) have failed to meet clinical endpoints despite multiple lines of evidence implicating these kinases in pathogenesis. This has reduced enthusiasm for MLK3 and LRRK2 as druggable targets. Largely overlooked is the evidence that these targets remain valid but must be considered in combination to achieve a therapeutic outcome. This provides the rationale for this study. Methods We conducted a pilot study modeling early, pre-symptomatic PD with subsequent evaluation of therapeutic potential of a multi-kinase inhibitor (URMC-099) in alleviating disease pathology. Sprague Dawley rats received unilateral intranigral injections of low dose AAV-haSyn. After a two-week recovery period, all animals were administered either once-daily intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of URMC-099 or its vehicle control until their terminal endpoint. Induction of early PD, and its alleviation with URMC-099, was evaluated by lateralized motor impairment using the cylinder test and immunohistochemical analysis of neuropathology in the substantia nigra (SN) and striatum. Finally, an in vitro microglial PD model exposed to aSyn pre-formed fibrils and treated with URMC-099 was used to further evaluate the mechanism underlying therapeutic activity. Results A unilateral model of early and progressive AAV-haSyn model for PD was used to demonstrate the therapeutic potential of a targeted multi-kinase inhibitor to attenuate PD-associated neuropathology and prevent the manifestation of lateral motor deficits. Immunohistochemical analysis revealed protection of neuronal cellular integrity along the nigral-striatal pathway with once-daily i.p. URMC-099. The mitigation of degenerative neuropathology was linked to targeted inhibition of MLK3 and LRRK2 and complemented by reduced levels of gliosis in astrocytes and microglia in the SN. Single-microglia segmentation analysis suggested URMC-099 treatment preserved dynamic effector state switching in microglia to enhance autophagic flux to reduce the overall burden of pathologic aSyn. Transcriptomic analysis of a complementary in vitro microglia model corroborated the retention of a homeostatic-like effector state with URMC-099 treatment that was unique to MLK3/LRRK2 dual inhibition. Conclusions Unilateral injection of low dose AAV-haSyn successfully resulted in a lateralized model of early, progressive PD. Dual inhibition of aberrant MLK3 and LRRK2 activity with once-daily i.p. URMC-099 therapy significantly mitigated the development of PD pathology and progression in an early manifest phenotype. Our results present a potential mechanism of therapeutic action dependent on the dual inhibition of MLK3 and LRRK2. This presents a novel therapeutic modality that may be beneficial to a broad population of etiologic PD patients.

papers.title: Temperature-dependent Fano resonance in Microtubules and Tubulin investigated with Spontaneous Raman Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Microtubules are self-assembled biological hollow nanotubes composed by protein tubulin. They are essential for many biological functions, including cell motility, cell division, and act as intracellular track for organelle transport. In turn, through dynamic assembly and disassembly, they form spindle fibers for chromosome segregation during mitosis and meiosis. In this paper, we have measured the Raman spectra of microtubules and their constituent protein tubulin in dry powder form for a range of temperatures, from nitrogen liquid T =77 K up to room and physiological temperature T =310 K, to determine if molecular bond vibrations present potential Fano resonance asymmetry. We have found nontrivial persistence of Fano resonances, q <5, at room and physiological temperatures for some specific vibrational modes.

papers.title: Rab10 and Arhgef7 interact to promote axon extension by linking vesicle supply and exocytosis
papers.abstract: The formation of functional neural circuits begins with the extension of a single axon by immature neurons. Axon elongation requires an expansion of the plasma membrane that depends on the polarization of vesicle trafficking and exocytosis. It is not completely understood how the increased transport of vesicles into the growing axon is linked to their subsequent insertion into the plasma membrane. An analysis of early stages of neuronal differentiation indicates that an asymmetry in neurite length precedes axon specification and the accumulation of PPVs in the nascent axon. We show that increasing the transport of vesicles in unpolarized neurons is sufficient to promote the extension of additional axons. This effect indicates that an increased supply of vesicles stimulates their subsequent insertion into the membrane to allow neurite growth. The link between vesicle transport and exocytosis is mediated by the interaction of Rab10 with Arhgef7. Rab10 stimulates Arhgef7 activity on PPVs as a GEF for Cdc42b to promote axon extension through exocyst-dependent exocytosis, suggesting that their interaction links the increased supply of PPVs to their exocytosis.

papers.title: Disrupted mannosidase enzymes in C9orf72 ALS/FTD
papers.abstract: Summary Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is an age-related neurodegenerative disorder resulting from the loss of motor neurons in the brain and spinal cord. Neuroinflammation, induced by glial cells including microglia (MG) and astrocytes, is an acknowledged aspect of this neurodegeneration. Generating induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) neuroinflammatory models of ALS may help elucidate non-neuronal mechanisms of disease. Here, we analyze human postmortem tissue and an iPSC derived glia-crosstalk model identifying a reduction in Golgi enzymes MAN1A1 and MAN1A2 in addition to other glycan enzymes from ALS-associated microglia and astrocytes. Impaired Golgi and glycan metabolism is linked to inflammation and other related ALS disease mechanisms including impaired lysosomal proteostasis, altered extracellular matrix, disrupted secretion, and altered cell-cell signaling.

papers.title: Disrupting SORL1-retromer endosomal recycling in mice drives the age-dependent neurodegenerative signature of Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: MRI studies have mapped the atrophic signature that distinguishes Alzheimer's disease (AD), isolating regions differentially vulnerable to its age-dependent neurodegenerative process. An endosomal recycling pathway regulated by the interaction of SORL1 with retromer is pathogenically disrupted in AD. Here we test the hypothesis, that the pathway might drive the neurodegenerative process, via multiple yearlong studies in over 140 wildtype and SORL1 deficient mice, modeling SORL1's causative mutations. MRI studies revealed that SORL1 deficiency induced an age-dependent AD-pattern of atrophy, centered on the trans-entorhinal cortex, and that atrophy was prevented by SORL1 restoration, secondary to overexpressing the retromer protein VPS26b. Postmortem studies validated that the atrophy reflects neuronal loss. Proteomic profiling revealed that the atrophy is associated with reductions in cell death suppressors, one of which was then found deficient in the trans-entorhinal cortex of AD patients. Besides supporting the hypothesis, when taken together with other findings the results suggest that SORL1-retromer disruptions represent a therapeutically-amenable common 'neurodegeneration pathway' in AD.

papers.title: KIF1A-driven entry of degradative lysosomes into the axon is developmentally regulated by the microtubule environment at the axon initial segment.
papers.abstract: Neuronal function requires precise transport of lysosomal vesicles along highly polarized processes, yet how this trafficking is spatially and developmentally regulated remains poorly understood. Here, we show that the neuronally enriched kinesin-3 motor KIF1A is required for dendritic and axonal localization of lysosomal vesicles in both immature and mature rat hippocampal neurons. Remarkably, the specialized microtubule environment of the axon initial segment (AIS) restricts KIF1A-driven transport of degradative, cathepsin D-positive lysosomal vesicles while permitting less degradative lysosomal vesicles to enter axons in mature neurons. Disrupting the AIS microtubule environment or expressing a hereditary spastic paraplegia type 30-associated KIF1A variant with increased affinity for GTP-tubulin bypasses this restriction, enabling degradative lysosomal vesicles to enter mature axons. In human iPSC-derived neurons, KIF1A depletion similarly disrupts axonal lysosomal vesicle transport, causes autophagic vesicle accumulation, and triggers axonal degeneration. Together, our findings reveal a developmentally regulated AIS gate that selectively controls KIF1A-driven lysosomal vesicle transport into axons and link its subversion to KIF1A-associated neurological disease.

papers.title: Parkinson’s disease genetic risk converges on Lewy body pathology-associated microglial states
papers.abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) and related α-synucleinopathies are defined by the spread of Lewy body (LB) pathology across vulnerable brain regions, yet how substantia nigra (SN) myeloid cells respond remains unresolved. Using SOX10-based oligodendrocyte depletion and CD11b-based myeloid enrichment, we profiled 169,799 brain myeloid cells and nuclei from 96 donors spanning the LB continuum, including 86,427 from the SN, and integrated them with AMP PD for a total of 298,592 profiles. Across eight conserved states, α-synucleinopathy is associated with a bidirectional signature: upregulated glycolytic and proteostatic-stress programs alongside downregulated lysosomal and mitochondrial pathways. Microglia shift from P2RY12-high sensome cells toward an HSP90AA1-high proteostatic stress state, a transition that intensifies at late Braak LB stages. Immunohistochemistry confirmed that HSP60 + proteostatic microglia state proportions increase with SN neuron loss. A rare NUCKS1-high state (∼1% of myeloid cells), more abundant in late-stage disease, carried the strongest PD polygenic-risk loading. The PD-protective rs3732765-A allele, a microglial cis-eQTL that lowers P2RY12 expression, was nominally associated with a higher proportion of P2RY12-high microglia and higher lysosomal program activity. These findings frame microglial involvement as structured and genetically tractable, nominating the P2RY12 genetic axis and NUCKS1-high microglia for mechanistic studies.

papers.title: A novel mouse model recapitulates features of the neurodevelopmental disorder 3p25.3 microdeletion syndrome
papers.abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders globally affect approximately 15% of children and adolescents, but many disorders do not have mouse models, thus limiting our ability to further understand them and ultimately develop treatments. In our study, we developed a novel mouse line to model 3p25.3 microdeletion syndrome ( 6qE3 del/+ ) that reliably recapitulates key features of the syndrome. 6qE3 del/+ mice display congenital heart defects, craniofacial defects, skeletal anomalies and subtle brain changes. We also generated another neurodevelopmental disorder model for a gene often included in the deleted region, Brpf1 , and found that congenital heart defects and craniofacial defects may be partly attributable to the heterozygous loss of Brpf1 in 6qE3 del/+ mice. Together our work offers new neurodevelopment models, and provides evidence that treatments developed for Brpf1 haploinsufficiency may also benefit 3p25.3 microdeletion syndrome.

papers.title: Plasma phosphorylated tau species across neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases: An ONDRI study
papers.abstract: Elevated plasma phosphorylated tau (p-tau) species are proposed as specific biomarkers of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology but have also been reported in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Their profile across neurodegenerative and cerebrovascular diseases, as well as their discriminatory value when combined with other plasma biomarkers, remain uncertain. We studied 551 participants (ages 40.1 to 87.1 years; 207 women), comprising 506 patients from the Ontario Neurodegenerative Disease Research Initiative (ONDRI) multi-site cohort and 45 amyloid-β (Aβ) PET-negative cognitively unimpaired controls from the Brain-Eye Amyloid Memory study. Ten diagnostic groups were studied: mild cognitive impairment (MCI), AD, Parkinson’s disease subdivided into cognitively unimpaired (CU), MCI, and dementia, frontotemporal dementia (FTD), cerebrovascular disease (CVD) subdivided into cognitively unimpaired (CU) and cognitively impaired (CI), ALS, and the control group. Baseline visit plasma measurements included p-tau217, p-tau181, Aβ42/40, neurofilament light chain (NfL), and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). Cross-sectional analyses compared biomarker levels as well as p-tau217-based inference of amyloid positivity status across diagnostic groups. Receiver operating characteristic-area under the curve (ROC-AUC) analyses ascertained the discriminatory capacity of these biomarkers and ratio combinations. Within the ALS group, baseline biomarker measures were also tested for association against baseline clinical features as well as longitudinal measures of neuropsychological change. P-tau217, p-tau181, GFAP, and NfL differed across groups (all P < 0.001). Compared to controls, p-tau217 was elevated in AD and ALS, p-tau181 and GFAP only in AD, and NfL in ALS and FTD. Inferred amyloid-β positivity was more probable in MCI, AD, ALS, and cognitively impaired CVD groups compared to controls (all P < 0.05). The p-tau217 to NfL ratio discriminated ALS from AD with an ROC-AUC of 0.92 (95% CI 0.85-0.97) compared to p-tau217 alone at 0.65 (95% CI 0.52-0.76). No ALS clinical or longitudinal association survived correction for multiple comparisons. Elevated p-tau217 and inferred amyloid-β positivity in ALS provide further evidence that the assay signal is not necessarily specific for AD pathology. However, the use of p-tau217 in combination with NfL provides improved discriminatory power between ALS and AD, supporting the use of plasma biomarker combinations rather than sole reliance on individual plasma biomarkers. Inferred amyloid-β positivity in cognitively impaired CVD may indicate AD and/or cerebral amyloid angiopathy co-pathology. Currently available plasma biomarkers should therefore be used as diagnostic complements and interpreted within clinical context rather than as standalone molecular diagnoses.

papers.title: Beyond organ age gaps: comparing plasma proteomic metrics of organ biology in relation to brain structure and neurodegenerative disease.
papers.abstract: Biological aging is heterogeneous across organ systems, and brain health may be influenced by biological processes extending beyond the central nervous system (CNS). This can be investigated using biological age measures that are increasingly used to estimate how biological systems deviate from chronological aging. However, organ level plasma proteomic metrics may capture different forms of biological variation depending on how they are defined. Here, we compared three complementary organ level proteomic metrics across 15 organ systems (and two global systems) in relation to age, organ-relevant physiological phenotypes, brain morphometry, and incident neurodegenerative disease, using plasma proteomics from 52,667 UK Biobank participants and brain MRI data from 5,078 of those individuals. We derived i) supervised age gap metrics using XGBoost models trained to predict chronological age, ii) unsupervised PC1 metrics capturing dominant organ-associated proteomic variation, and iii) phenotype guided PLS metrics linking plasma proteins to organ-relevant physiological traits. The three metric classes were related but not interchangeable. Global all-protein and all-organ-protein models showed strong age-related proteomic structure. However, organ-specific PC analyses showed that age was often but not always the dominant source of variation in protein signal across organs. Age gap metrics showed the most consistent associations with subsequent ICD-10-based neurodegenerative and vascular diagnoses, whereas all three metric classes showed distinct associations with brain structure and organ-relevant physiological phenotypes. Brain structure analyses revealed heterogeneous organ-brain association patterns across organs, suggesting that proteomic variation relates to brain structure in both a systemic and an organ-specific manner. Several systemic and organ-specific signals partially mediated the associations between disease specific genetic risk and incident diagnoses of Alzheimer's disease and stroke, albeit with small effect sizes (1-8%). Similarly, organ metrics provided modest incremental predictive improvement over baseline demographic models, with the largest increase in ROC-AUC observed for Alzheimer's disease when all organ age gap metrics were added jointly (delta ROC-AUC = 0.037). These results link brain related outcomes to proteomic variation across both CNS and non-CNS systems. Our work suggests that proteomic organ metrics capture complementary dimensions of biological variation rather than a single construct of organ aging. Although these measures may provide informative biological and potentially predictive signals, their incremental predictive value in the present analyses was modest.

papers.title: Structure-Based Discovery of GTP-Enhanced Rab10 Modulators and Their Effects on Alzheimer’s Disease-Relevant Cellular Phenotypes
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Rab10-mediated membrane trafficking has been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but pharmacological tools for investigating its function remain limited. Here, we screened more than 80 million compounds using structure-based virtual screening and prioritized five candidate Rab10 modulators ( R1-R5 ). These compounds exhibited favorable docking scores, stable modeled protein-ligand complexes in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and predicted acceptable ADME/toxicity profiles. Comparative docking against Rab5, Rab8, and Rab11 predicted preferential interactions with GTP-associated Rab10. R1 and R2 yielded the most favorable Rab10 scores, whereas R3 showed the largest differences between GTP-associated, GDP-containing, and nucleotide-free Rab10 models. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) revealed micromolar apparent affinities of R1-R4 without added GTP and nanomolar apparent affinities under GTP-containing conditions, generally favoring GTP-bound Rab10 over Rab5. In a cell-based GTP quantification assay, R1 , R2 , R3 , and R5 reduced GTP-bound Rab10, whereas R4 increased it. R3 produced dose- and time-dependent reductions in GTP-bound Rab10 and was selected for functional studies. R3 altered endosomal organization and reduced EEA1 and LAMP1 expressions. In amyloid precursor protein (APP)/presenilin-1-expressing CHO cells, R3 redistributed intracellular APP, reduced APP carboxyl-terminal fragments (APP-CTFs), and decreased enlarged endosome-like structures. In neuronal differentiated PC12 cells, R1 - R3 attenuated NGF withdrawal-induced cytoskeletal disruption and cell death, accompanied by reduced APP-CTF accumulation and tau phosphorylation. These studies highlight novel Rab10 modulators and support their further validation as candidate pharmacological probes for investigating Rab10-associated trafficking and AD-relevant cellular phenotypes.

papers.title: Rare protein-disrupting variants in NPY5R, DLGAP1 and MAPK8IP3 segregate with OCD in two multiplex pedigrees.
papers.abstract: Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) is significantly heritable, but only a fraction of the contributory genetic variation has been identified, and the molecular etiology involved remains obscure. Identifying rare contributory variants of large effect would be an important milestone in helping to elucidate the mechanisms involved. Analysis of densely affected pedigrees is a potentially useful strategy to bypass the sample size challenges of standard case-control approaches. Here we performed whole genome sequencing (WGS) of 25 individuals across two multiplex OCD pedigrees. We prioritised rare variants using a Bayesian inference approach which incorporates variant pathogenicity and co-segregation with OCD. In the first pedigree, we identified a highly deleterious missense variant in NPY5R, carried by the majority of affected individuals. This gene is brain-expressed and has previously been implicated in panic disorder and internet addiction GWAS studies. In the second pedigree, we identified a large deletion of DLGAP1 and a missense variant in MAPK8IP3, that perfectly co-segregated in a specific branch of the family: both genes have previously been implicated in OCD and autism. Both genes contribute to a protein interaction network including ERBB4 and RAPGEF1 which we had previously identified in a large Tourette Syndrome pedigree. Our analysis suggests that both energy homeostasis and downstream signalling from the post-synaptic density may both be important avenues for future research.

papers.title: Anti-Parkinsonian Drugs Rescue Locomotor Deficits in JIP3 Knockout Zebrafish: Implications for Treating Patients with MAPK8IP3 -related Neurodevelopmental Disorders
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT MAPK8IP3- related neurodevelopmental disorders are a spectrum of rare conditions caused by de novo mutations in the MAPK8IP3 gene that encodes the JIP3 protein. These disorders are associated with a spectrum of neurodevelopmental symptoms that manifest in children and cause brain abnormalities, profound intellectual disabilities, movement disorders, and developmental delays. JIP3 is required for axonal transport of proteins and organelles between the soma and the synaptic terminal of neurons, a process critical for normal brain development and function. Homozygous loss-of-function mutations in JIP3 lead to impaired axonal transport and aggregation of cargo, which result in axonal swelling and stunted elongation. Despite these severe outcomes, disease mechanisms are poorly understood, and no current treatments are available. Here we conduct thorough morphological, behavioral, and motility phenotyping in the JIP3 knockout zebrafish and identify locomotor deficits and morphological abnormalities. To identify treatment options, we used insights from expert clinicians and the artificial intelligence tool, mediKanren, to identify drug candidates hypothesized to improve patient symptoms or compensate for the loss of JIP3 at the molecular level. We then prioritized drugs that are FDA-approved, safe for children, and readily available. These collective efforts identified amantadine and levodopa as candidate therapies and rescued motor phenotypes associated with JIP3 loss-of-function in zebrafish.

papers.title: Red fluorescent sensor for intensity-and lifetime imaging of cAMP in living cells
papers.abstract: cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) is a crucial intracellular messenger involved in neuromodulation and plasticity, but more information on its spatiotemporal regulation is desirable. Here we constructed a red fluorescent indicator based on a truncated cAMP binding site derived from a regulatory PKA subunit of protozoan origin. It contains a single binding site for cAMP highly specific for cAMP over cGMP. chILI ( c AMP h ighly-responsive I ntensity and L ifetime I ndicator) can be imaged as an intensity-based probe, but alternatively also offers options for fluorescence lifetime imaging. When expressed in the mouse brain using AAV-vector mediated gene transfer, it reports spontaneous and evoked cAMP transients from CA1 neurons in the hippocampus of awake mice. chILI will add valuable options for monitoring cAMP in vitro and in vivo.

papers.title: Autophagy activator AA-20 engages CDK5 to promote lipophagy and improve neurodegeneration-associated phenotypes
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Lipophagy, the selective degradation of lipid droplets (LDs) by autophagy, has the potential to ameliorate neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s (PD) and Alzheimer’s (AD), wherein LD accumulation has been linked to the exacerbation of the proteinopathy component of neurodegeneration. Pharmacological lipophagy inducers remain scarce. We previously identified AA-20 as a novel autophagy activator that acts independently of mTORC1 inhibition, thereby providing a means of stimulating autophagy while avoiding the immunosuppressive side effects associated with direct mTORC1 inhibition. Prior work also showed that AA-20 treatment reduces PolyQ aggregate levels in several C. elegans tissues. Here, we demonstrate that AA-20 enhances LD recruitment to autophagosomes and promotes LD degradation via lysosomal acid lipase activation in murine hippocampal neuronal cells, consistent with lipophagy activation. In human Swedish Amyloid Precursor Protein mutated cerebral organoids, two weeks of AA-20 treatment normalized aberrant lipidomic profiles by selectively reducing various disease-associated lipids, while also correcting the AD-associated electrical hyperexcitability phenotype. Moreover, we identified cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5), a neuronal kinase linked to AD hyperexcitability and PD pathology, as a target of AA-20. AA-20-induced autophagy and lipid clearance in HT22 cells require CDK5. In a neuronal seeding model of α-synuclein pathology, AA-20 reduced pS129-α-synuclein levels. Collectively, these findings indicate AA-20 can promote lipophagic clearance of LDs and mitigate multiple cellular phenotypes associated with lipidopathy and proteinopathy in neurodegenerative disease models. SIGNIFICANCE Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s are associated with impaired autophagy and abnormal lipid droplet (LD) accumulation. Few small molecules enhance neuronal lipid clearance without inhibiting mTORC1, but chronic blockade of which is associated with immunosuppressive and metabolic side effects. This study shows that AA-20, an mTORC1-independent autophagy activator, promotes lipophagic LD clearance in neuronal cells and reduces selected disease-associated lipids in human Alzheimer’s cerebral organoids in a lysosomal acid lipase-dependent manner. AA-20 binds CDK5 and appears to modulate, rather than classically inhibit, this neuron-enriched kinase. In an exploratory Parkinson’s neuron model, AA-20 also reduced pathological α-synuclein phosphorylation. These findings support further investigation of AA-20 as a tool to probe neuronal lipid clearance and neurodegeneration-associated phenotypes.

papers.title: AKAP-CaN-NFATc3 signaling drives persistent inhibitory long-term potentiation
papers.abstract: GABAergic inhibitory synaptic plasticity has critical roles in neuronal function, synaptic plasticity, and cognition. Activity-dependent alterations in gene expression are essential for generating long-term changes in inhibitory postsynaptic strength, yet the signaling mechanisms that drive inhibitory postsynaptic plasticity are not well understood. During an important form of inhibitory long-term potentiation (iLTP), NMDA receptor (NMDAR) activity promotes de novo synthesis of GABAA receptors (GABAARs) and the inhibitory scaffold, gephyrin, leading to persistent strengthening of inhibition. However, it remains unclear what activity-dependent signaling mechanisms control these changes in gene expression to maintain iLTP. In this study, we identify that activation of the transcription factor, nuclear-factor of activated T-cells (NFAT), and anchoring of the phosphatase, calcineurin (CaN), to A-kinase anchoring protein (AKAP79/150) are crucial in regulating long-term structural and functional GABAergic postsynaptic plasticity. Using short hairpin RNA (shRNA) to knock-down hippocampal NFAT isoform, NFATc3, we demonstrate its requirement for the synthesis of new inhibitory synaptic proteins, inhibitory synapse growth, and strengthening of synaptic currents during persistent iLTP. Additionally, using a knock-in mouse line containing a mutation in the CaN binding region of AKAP, we find that AKAP-CaN signaling lies upstream of NFATc3 activation and is required for increased inhibitory synapse clustering and synapse strengthening during iLTP via regulation of miRNA transcriptional activity and protein synthesis. Thus, we have identified an excitation-transcription coupling pathway that rapidly controls the synthesis of new inhibitory synaptic proteins and maintains persistent inhibitory synaptic plasticity, an essential process for memory formation and cognition in the brain.

papers.title: Developmentally-regulated splice remodeling shapes functional CACNA1C channel diversity during human neurodevelopment
papers.abstract: CACNA1C encodes the pore-forming subunit of the Ca V 1.2 L-type voltage-gated calcium channel, a major regulator of neuronal calcium signaling and one of the strongest genetic risk loci for bipolar disorder and other psychiatric disorders. Although extensive alternative splicing of CACNA1C has been described in the adult human brain, how alternative splicing of CACNA1C is regulated during early human neurodevelopment remains largely unknown. Here, we used long-read RNA sequencing to characterize full-length CACNA1C transcripts during differentiation of human induced pluripotent stem cells, from healthy controls and patients with bipolar disorder homozygous for either the A or G allele at rs1006737, into cortical glutamatergic neurons. We identified 60 putative isoforms, including ten annotated transcripts and 23 previously reported in adult human brain. We also demonstrate that CACNA1C undergoes developmentally-regulated remodeling of isoform composition during neuronal differentiation. This remodeling was characterized by an exon-switching program involving mutually exclusive exon pairs and alternative splice site usage, including prominent developmental transitions between exon pairs 8/8a, 21/22, and 31/32. Neither rs1006737 genotype, diagnosis, sex nor age significantly affected splicing profiles. The developmental splice trajectories were recapitulated in dorsal forebrain organoids, showing that CACNA1C splice remodeling is conserved across independent human neural differentiation models. Electrophysiological characterization of the two most abundant neuronal isoforms found that exon 31/32 switching alters channel inactivation properties. Together, our findings demonstrate that developmentally-regulated alternative splicing of CACNA1C transcripts contributes to the functional diversity of Ca V 1.2 channels expressed during human neurodevelopment.

papers.title: TMEM55B promotes anterograde transport and distal axonal distribution of LAMP1-positive organelles
papers.abstract: Lysosomal function throughout life is vital for the proper functioning and survival of post-mitotic neurons by mediating cellular signaling, degradation, and recycling processes. Their intracellular transport relies on microtubule-dependent mechanisms involving kinesin and dynein motors. While lysosomes were long thought absent from axons, recent studies have demonstrated the importance of LAMP1-positive endo-/lysosomal organelles in axonal compartments. This study investigates the physiological role of TMEM55B, a lysosomal membrane protein involved in lysosome positioning and motor coupling in neurons. TMEM55B is highly expressed in LAMP1-positive organelles in cortical neurons. We generated viable Tmem55b knockout mice that exhibited altered lysosomal positioning in neurons. Lysosomes clustered abnormally in the pre-axonal exclusion zone and the proximal axon, with many forming elongated tubular structures. Similarly, in primary rat neurons, TMEM55B depletion resulted in lysosomal tubulation and impaired bidirectional lysosomal transport, particularly in distal axon segments, without affecting lysosome velocity in the proximal and mid-axon. These transport defects were consistent with disrupted JIP4 function, a scaffold linking TMEM55B to both dynein and kinesin motors. TMEM55B deficiency did not result in neurodegeneration, behavioral deficits, or reduced lifespan in mice. As an orthogonal approach, we analyzed TMEM55B function in C. elegans . Worms lacking the TMEM55B homolog Y71H2AM.2 showed altered lysosomal dynamics in cholinergic neurons, supporting an evolutionarily conserved role. To test the involvement of TMEM55B’s paralog, TMEM55A, in regulating neuronal lysosome positioning, we generated Tmem55a/b double-knockout mice, which exhibit impaired growth, premature death, and an overall aggravated phenotype. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that both TMEM55B and TMEM55A regulate lysosome distribution in neurons, particularly in axons, by influencing JIP4-dependent retro- and, notably, anterograde motor protein-mediated transport. This function is critical for spatial lysosomal homeostasis. Our study underscores the importance of TMEM55A/TMEM55B in regulating neuronal organelle dynamics and may be a factor considered in neurodegenerative diseases involving lysosomal trafficking defects.

papers.title: Longitudinal single-cell transcriptional profiling identifies dynamic neurodegenerative mechanisms in Christianson Syndrome rat
papers.abstract: Endolysosomal dysfunction is a central feature of many neurodegenerative disorders. Loss-of-function mutations in the endosomal Na+/H+ exchanger NHE6 cause lysosomal dysfunction and the early-onset neurodegenerative disorder Christianson syndrome (CS). CS shares pathological features with more common neurodegenerative diseases; however, the extent of mechanistic overlap remains unclear. Using single-nucleus RNA sequencing across the lifespan in a CS rat model, we define the temporal progression of disease at single-cell resolution in the hippocampus. Neurons exhibit early transcriptional signatures of mitochondrial dysfunction. We investigated mitochondrial function in vitro and ex vivo and discover progressive defects in mitochondrial quality control and bioenergetics in NHE6-null tissue. Furthermore, both transcriptomic and proteomic analyses reveal robust activation of innate immunity, including cGAS-STING signaling which localizes to microglia. Therefore, in CS rat brain, early neuronal endosomal and mitochondrial impairments are followed by pronounced microglial and astrocytic activation, as well as age-dependent decline in oligodendrocyte myelinating capacity. Cross species comparison reveals substantial overlap between single-cell analyses in CS rat and in human postmortem Alzheimers disease hippocampus. Together, our findings define the cellular trajectories of neurodegeneration in CS, and identify convergent endolysosomal, mitochondrial, and inflammatory mechanisms that support a broader role for endolysosomal dysfunction in Alzheimers disease pathogenesis.

papers.title: Dissecting human embryonic patterning during organogenesis reveals a rostral midline progenitor population for mesoendoderm induction
papers.abstract: Understanding how human organogenesis is accomplished via intricate spatiotemporal patterning of organ primordia requires spatial atlases at cellular resolution. However, existing human embryo spatial atlases are built using sequencing-based platforms such as Stereo-seq, which have limited spatial resolution and blurred anatomical boundaries, leading to misclassification across adjacent cells. Here, we integrate in situ imaging-based transcriptomics (Xenium) with transcriptome-wide spatial profiling (Visium-HD) of Carnegie stages 9-12 embryos to delineate the patterning of core embryonic tissues at single-cell resolution, including the brain, spinal cord, somites, neural crest, notochord, heart, and gut tube. A new finding enabled by spatial single-cell resolution is the identification of rostral midline progenitors (RMPs), a cell population co-expressing SOX2, TBXT, and OTX2. Transcriptionally, RMPs are distinct from both neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) and prechordal mesoderm, and in vivo clonal barcoding in mice indicates that RMPs share a common developmental origin with rostral neural ectoderm. To interrogate their functional significance, we leveraged our spatial transcriptome data to recapitulate RMP-like cells from human pluripotent stem cells and showed that these cells can induce epiblast-like cells to acquire mesendodermal and endodermal fates, while themselves adopting an ectodermal fate consistent with their in vivo counterparts. This work provides a 3D, stage-resolved molecular cell atlas of tissue patterning in human embryo that serves as a reference for in vitro models.

papers.title: Early Joint Attention Behaviors in Infants at High Familial Risk for Autism Spectrum Disorder: association with cortical development
papers.abstract: Abstract Joint attention is the ability to follow the gaze of others, which allows infants to share a common focus on individuals or objects. Impairments in initiating and responding to joint attention are some of the earliest indicators of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). Subcortical brain areas are implicated in joint attention, but less is known about cortical regions and joint attention behaviours in infancy. In this longitudinal study, 101 high-risk infants (64% males) with an older biological sibling with ASD underwent MRI scanning at 4 or 6 months of age and were assessed for joint attention behaviours at 2 years of age. Brain volumes were automatically extracted. High-risk infants with ASD demonstrated atypical initiating and responding joint attention behaviours compared to those who did not. When examining cortical regions in relation to initiating and responding to joint attention behaviours, significant associations were found between the left posterior cingulate gyrus and impaired initiating joint attention in infants who developed ASD. Additionally, the right cuneus was associated with impaired initiating joint attention in this group. Better characterization of the neural mechanisms underlying initiating joint attention can help identify biomarkers to assess the efficacy of therapies to promote improved social and behavioural outcomes.

papers.title: High-content imaging of live microglia-containing Alzheimer's disease brain organoids.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common progressive neurodegenerative disease for which there is currently no safe and effective treatment. AD is characterized by the pathological aggregation of amyloid-β (Aβ) in the brain resulting in neuronal dysfunction/death and cognitive decline. Modeling these processes in vitro remains challenging due to the lack of an immune-competent 3D in vitro human model of AD amenable to high-throughput analyses. Conventional cerebral organoids (COs) lack microglia and are optically dense which precludes real-time longitudinal analyses. Here, we employ the fluorescent amyloid probe PyrPeg to selectively monitor Aβ aggregation, and calcein AM and propidium iodide to assess cellular viability within microglia-containing COs (MCOs). We identify age-dependent DS-AD-associated phenotypes within T21 MCOs including Aβ neuropathology, neurodegeneration, and glial cell dysregulation. Our platform supports real-time, multiplexed tracking of disease progression and provides a scalable platform for longitudinal analyses studying disease mechanisms and targeted approaches to treatment. MOTIVATION: High-throughput in vitro drug screening using cerebral organoids (COs) has great potential to accelerate drug discovery efforts for treating Alzheimer's disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative diseases. However, live fluorescence imaging of COs has proved challenging due to their dense, optically opaque tissue. Furthermore, conventional COs lack microglia which are key immunomodulators of pathogenesis in the AD brain. To address these limitations, we developed and optimized a live organoid imaging approach employing the fluorescent amyloid-binding probe PyrPeg to label amyloid-β (Aβ) aggregates within human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived microglia-containing COs (MCOs). We achieved selective labeling and visualization of Aβ neuropathology in intact live MCOs and observed increased age-associated Aβ accumulation in MCOs derived from donors with trisomy 21 (T21) relative to disomy 21 (D21), consistent with the Down syndrome-associated AD (DS-AD) phenotype in the human brain. This method establishes a platform for high-throughput longitudinal drug screening in immunocompetent human COs that will enable the identification of new therapeutic candidates to modulate Aβ aggregation, glial reactivity, and neurodegeneration. HIGHLIGHTS: A platform was developed for high-resolution in vitro visualization of insoluble Aβ aggregates in live MCOs. The approach enables deep tissue imaging of Aβ pathology in intact 3D MCOs, allowing spatial mapping of Aβ aggregate distribution over time.Differences in Aβ burden and viability of neurons, neural progenitors, and astrocytes were quantified, distinguishing T21 COs from D21 control MCOs.The platform is positioned to support high-throughput longitudinal drug screening, providing a scalable tool to identify novel therapeutics targeting Aβ-mediated neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Evaluation of fractalkine and interleukin-6 plasma levels in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
papers.abstract: Abstract Background the etiology of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is multifactorial with a substantial immunological component. Children with ASD show abnormal levels of cytokines which significantly contribute to core features of the disorder such as behavioral and sensory impairments. Interleukin 6 (IL-6) represents a major neuroimmune mediator commonly implicated in ASD. Alternatively, fractalkine (FKN) is a key chemokine that regulates the homeostasis of cytokines and activation of microglia. However, its role in ASD pathophysiology is still understudied. In this pilot study, we evaluated the plasma levels of FKN and interleukin-6 (IL-6) in 40 Egyptian children diagnosed with ASD in comparison to 40 age and sex-matched controls using Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Results both groups showed comparable circulating levels of FKN ( p = 0.22) and IL-6 ( p = 0.65). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves showed poor diagnostic potential for FKN (AUC = 0.56, p = 0.33) and IL-6 (AUC = 0.53, p = 0.65) alike. Amongst the ASD group, FKN availability showed negligible associations with IL-6 levels, age, childhood autism rating scale, receptive expressive Arabic language scores and sensory profile. Conclusion our pilot findings indicate that impact of FKN might affect ASD at the brain level with no changes to the peripheral concentrations. Further studies are warranted to evaluate the implication of both endogenous and circulating FKN in neuroinflammation among larger cohorts of children with ASD.

papers.title: A protocol for cortical and deep-brain calcium imaging in freely moving mice with the Mini2P system.
papers.abstract: Two-photon calcium imaging has transformed our understanding of neuronal circuit function, yet conventional approaches require head fixation, limiting the study of neural activity during natural behavior. Miniaturized two-photon microscopy (Mini2P) overcomes this constraint by enabling calcium imaging in freely moving animals while preserving the optical single-cell resolution of conventional two-photon microscopy. However, its implementation requires the careful integration of multiple technically demanding procedures, presenting substantial challenges for laboratories adopting this approach. Here, we present a comprehensive, step-by-step protocol for implementing Mini2P calcium imaging in freely moving mice, emphasizing procedures that are unique to or particularly critical for successful implementation of this technique. This protocol covers system preparation and performance checks, optical alignment, field-of-view selection, baseplate installation, and strategies for maintaining imaging stability during microscope attachment and reattachment. We also address behavioral habituation, integration with behavioral tasks, imaging acquisition, quality control, and troubleshooting as a part of an integrated experimental workflow. Representative imaging data acquired through cranial windows in the primary visual and somatosensory cortices, and through a gradient-index lens in the medial prefrontal cortex, illustrate the applicability of this workflow across different brain regions and optical preparations. Designed for adaptation across brain regions and behavioral paradigms, the protocol provides practical guidance for identifying technical challenges and verifying successful implementation. By establishing clear decision points, validation criteria, and troubleshooting strategies at each stage, this workflow aims to improve reproducibility and facilitate the adoption of the Mini2P for investigating neuronal circuit dynamics during freely moving behavior.

papers.title: Proteomic profiling of postmortem prefrontal cortex identifies molecular signatures of borderline personality disorder
papers.abstract: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is characterized by a severe pattern of symptoms including emotional instability, impulsivity, and unstable interpersonal relationships. A complex interplay between genetics and environmental factors has been hypothesized to be associated with the development of BPD. While neuroimaging studies have identified structural and functional changes in the brain, and genome-wide association studies described some first genetic risk loci, the neurobiological underpinnings of BPD remain poorly described. To better understand disease processes in BPD, we performed a molecular characterization of the prefrontal cortex (PFC), an important brain region for emotion and impulsivity regulation in BPD. Label-free brain proteomics was performed in postmortem human brain tissue in a sample of n=79, with a case group of n=36 individuals with BPD and a control group of n=43 individuals without BPD. Differential protein expression analysis suggested protein-level dysregulation of mitochondrial, immunological, and neuroplasticity pathways. Network analyses identified a BPD-associated co-expression module enriched for protein secretory and synaptic processes that is druggable with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Additional druggability analyses on protein-protein interaction networks and drug-repositioning analysis suggested VEGF signaling as a potential pharmacologic target in BPD. When we integrated BPD proteomic signatures with genomic and proteomic datasets of common comorbidities such as posttraumatic stress disorder and major depressive disorder, we observed a strong convergent overlap across disorders, with STX7 and RTN4 identified as conserved, differentially expressed proteins. Our study provides first insights into proteomic signatures of BPD in the brain, suggests potential pharmacological targets, and provides evidence for convergent protein signatures across BPD and common comorbidites.

papers.title: COG5-mediated Golgi organization coordinates neural progenitor fate during human brain development
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Apical radial glial cells (aRGs) are highly polarized epithelial cells that drive human cortical development through tightly regulated lineage progression. A distinctive feature of aRGs is their non-canonical Golgi organization, raising the possibility that specialized intracellular trafficking and secretory processes contribute to progenitor behaviour. However, how Golgi architecture contributes to human corticogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate this question in the context of COG5 deficiency, a rare congenital disorder of glycosylation associated with neurodevelopmental defects, using patient-derived fibroblasts and brain organoids, N-glycomics, glycolipidomics, and single-cell transcriptomics. We show that COG5 deficiency disrupts Golgi organization and impairs Golgi-to-ER retrograde trafficking. At the neurodevelopmental level, COG5-deficient organoids display altered ventricular organization and reduced basal progenitor abundance. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis reveals rewired developmental trajectories characterized by premature differentiation from apical progenitors with activation of neuronal pathways. Despite the absence of major abnormalities in plasma glycoproteins glycosylation, glycolipidomic analysis identified marked defects in glycosphingolipid maturation within patient-derived brain organoids, indicating selective impairment of neural lipid glycosylation. Transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of developmental pathways, including reduced Notch signalling and altered localization of both cleaved Notch1 and the Golgi-associated protein ACBD3. Consistent with impaired progenitor maintenance, COG5-deficient organoids displayed altered cleavage plane orientation in apical progenitors. Together, our findings suggest a link between Golgi organization, intracellular trafficking, membrane glycosylation, and lineage progression in human neural progenitors, identifying Golgi architecture as an important regulator of apical radial glial cell biology and cortical development.

papers.title: Generation of human iPSC-derived motor neurons with defined regional identities across the rostrocaudal axis
papers.abstract: This study establishes a unified pipeline for generating human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived motor neurons (iMNs) with defined hindbrain, cervical, and lumbar identities to support anatomically resolved studies of motor neuron development and degeneration. Conventional differentiation methods can efficiently produce iMNs but provide limited control over rostrocaudal identity and frequently generate populations with heterogeneous HOX profiles. We addressed this limitation by optimizing developmental morphogen combinations and treatment windows, establishing three complementary protocols that reproducibly generated hindbrain/rhombomere-associated motor neurons (RiMNs), cervical motor neurons (CiMNs), and lumbar motor neurons (LiMNs) across iPSC lines from six non-diseased donors balanced by sex. Transcriptomic and protein analyses demonstrated graded rostrocaudal specification from RiMNs through CiMNs to LiMNs, together with region-appropriate motor neuron subtype features. These identities showed the expected relationships to human week 9 fetal rostrocaudal HOX programs. High-density multielectrode array analysis further revealed synchronized network firing, electrically active neurite networks, and enhanced axonal signal propagation in the regional iMN populations compared with conventionally differentiated iMNs. Spike-sorted recordings additionally revealed protocol-associated differences in single-neuron electrophysiological profiles. Together, this three-protocol pipeline enables the reproducible generation and comparative analysis of anatomically defined human motor neuron populations and provides region-matched cellular models for investigating motor neuron development, selective degeneration, and therapeutic responses.

papers.title: TMEM55B downregulation promotes neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's disease models.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Lysosomal distribution is critical for numerous biological functions within the cell, including protein degradation in autophagosomes, cholesterol homeostasis, and cell invasion. Changes in the positioning of lysosomes and dysregulation of lysosomal trafficking are known to contribute to different human pathologies, such as lysosomal storage disease, neurodegeneration, and cancer. Here we report the critical role of the lysosomal T ransmembrane P rotein 55B (TMEM55B) in mediating neurodegeneration. Using human clinical-pathological datasets, transgenic flies and iPSC-derived neurons, we demonstrate that loss of function of dTMEM55 potentiates neuronal degeneration. We found that TMEM55B levels are lowered in severe Alzheimer's Disease (AD) cases, validated from microarray, single neuron and total RNA Seq datasets from brain sections of the ROSMAP cohort. Our results demonstrates that loss of function of dTMEM55 results in accumulation of lysosomes in the fly's larval neuronal axons, enhances Tau-mediated retinal degeneration, locomotory dysfunction, lethality, and cell death in the fly AD model. The iPSC-derived AD neurons exhibit reduced TMEM55B levels, autophagic flux defects and increased accumulation of phosphorylated Tau in the lysosomes, confirming the observations in the fly. Overall, our findings indicate that TMEM55B downregulation could contribute to neurodegeneration through defects in lysosomal transport, potentially hindering autophagic clearance of Tau. Our findings have significant relevance in validating the role of lysosomal proteins in normal lysosomal function and maintaining healthy neurons. This work supports continued research into lysosome-mediated neurodegeneration and may provide a basis for exploring potential therapeutic approaches for lysosome-associated neuronal disorders. HIGHLIGHTS: TMEM55B expression is significantly reduced in postmortem brain tissues of patients with severe AD. Genetic loss of TMEM55B enhances Tau-mediated neurodegeneration in Drosophila , indicating a conserved neuroprotective function. TMEM55B regulates neuronal lysosomal positioning across species, and its loss disrupts lysosomal transport.iPSC-derived Alzheimer's disease neurons exhibit late-stage TMEM55B downregulation concomitant with increased accumulation of pathological phosphorylated Tau.Impaired lysosomal trafficking provides a mechanistic link between TMEM55B loss and progressive neurodegeneration.

papers.title: JIP4 deficiency causes a lysosomal storage disease arising from impaired cystine efflux.
papers.abstract: Lysosomes break down macromolecules, clear cellular waste and recycle nutrients such as cystine. We describe a novel mechanism whereby JIP4 regulates lysosomal cystine storage by controlling the abundance of cystinosin (CTNS), the transporter responsible for lysosomal cystine efflux. To this end, JIP4, previously characterized as a motor adaptor and kinase signaling scaffold, suppresses TMEM55B-dependent ubiquitylation of CTNS. Loss of JIP4 reduces CTNS protein levels, leading to lysosomal cystine accumulation and lysosomal storage defects that phenocopy loss of CTNS in both human cells and the renal proximal tubules of JIP4 knockout mice. These phenotypes mirror cystinosis, the lysosomal storage disease caused by CTNS loss-of-function. Our findings thus reveal a fundamental process that controls the efflux of lysosomal cystine and has relevance to understanding human disease arising from JIP4 mutations.
