papers.title: Engineering iPSC-Derived Organoids for Disease Modeling and Regenerative Medicine: Differentiation Strategies, Functional Maturation, and Translational Challenges
papers.abstract: Induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived organoids are three-dimensional in vitro models that recapitulate se-lected structural and functional features of human tissues. They provide useful platforms for studying development and disease, screening drugs, and exploring regenerative medicine. This review examines strategies for generating iPSC-derived organoids across multiple organ systems, with a comparative focus on how differentiation logic and culture design influence organoid development. Specifically, we discuss guided differentiation using developmental signaling cues and unguided approaches that rely on the cells’ intrinsic capacity for self-organization. We also con-sider scaffold-based and scaffold-free culture methods and how these approaches, together with organ-specific proto-cols, affect organoid formation and maturation. In addition, we summarize signaling pathways commonly used to direct differentiation and the biomedical applications of iPSC-derived organoids. Despite their promise, these models may show variability between cell lines, incomplete maturation, and limited oxygen and nutrient delivery to their inner regions, which can contribute to necrotic core formation. Further refinement of differentiation protocols, culture conditions, and characterization standards may improve the reproducibility and physiological relevance of organoids. By comparing differentiation strategies and culture approaches across organ systems, this review provides a framework for understanding how protocol choices shape organoid development and for guiding future studies in disease modeling, drug discovery, and regenerative medicine.

papers.title: Activity-dependent presynaptic proteomics reveals a prefrontal–amygdala release-site programme for remote contextual recall
papers.abstract: Abstract Remote memory retrieval engages distributed neuronal ensembles, yet how these ensembles organise long-range circuit output at the presynaptic molecular level remains poorly understood. Here, we develop Activity-dependent Projection-eXclusive BioID (ActProX-ID), an in vivo proximity-labelling strategy that combines TRAP2-dependent capture of behaviourally activated neurons with presynaptic membrane-targeted TurboID to profile projection-level, presynaptically enriched proteomic states. Application of ActProX-ID to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC)–basolateral amygdala (BLA) pathway during recent and remote fear-memory recall identified overlapping but phase-biased presynaptic programmes. Recent recall was associated with cytoskeletal and synaptic-organisation proteins, whereas remote recall preferentially engaged synaptic vesicle trafficking, transmembrane transport and release-site organisation. Subsequent analyses under remote contextual recall validated TSPAN7 as a remote recall-associated presynaptic component at mPFC–BLA terminals. TSPAN7 loss or expression of the disease-linked P172H variant impaired recall-associated synaptic remodelling, CPLX2 recruitment, SNAP25-positive release-site organisation and presynaptic release efficacy, and disrupted remote contextual fear memory while sparing recent contextual and tone-cued fear memory. These findings link behaviourally recruited prefrontal projection neurons to presynaptic molecular remodelling and reveal a TSPAN7–CPLX2-dependent release-site mechanism that controls remote contextual recall.

papers.title: Donor-Aware Reanalysis of Neuronal Nuclei Supports STMN2 Depletion Associated with Nuclear TDP-43 Loss in FTD and ALS
papers.abstract: Background Nuclear TDP-43 depletion is a central pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD), but donor-to-donor variation can obscure transcriptomic associations in small postmortem cohorts. We reanalyzed public RNA-seq data from FACS-isolated NeuN-positive frontal-cortex neuronal nuclei to quantify gene-expression changes associated with nuclear TDP-43 loss while explicitly accounting for donor structure. Methods The supplied GSE126542-derived matrix contained 62,754 genes across 12 libraries from seven donors, including five complete matched pairs. Source labels “TDP-43 positive” and “TDP-43 negative” were harmonized as nuclear TDP-43 retained and lost, respectively. After validation against featureCounts-assigned read counts, 44,225 genes with at least 10 total counts were analyzed using PyDESeq2. The primary model was ∼ donor + nuclear_status; status-only and diagnosis-adjusted models were sensitivity analyses. The contrast was TDP-43 loss minus retained. Results The donor-aware model identified 3,442 genes at false discovery rate (FDR) Conclusions Donor-aware analysis supports a robust association between nuclear TDP-43 loss and STMN2 depletion in this neuronal-nuclei cohort, alongside extensive but model-dependent transcriptomic variation. Whole-gene UNC13A expression cannot be used to infer UNC13A cryptic-exon inclusion or functional UNC13A depletion. No splice-junction, percent-spliced-in, isoform, or protein measurements were available; mechanistic claims therefore require junction-level and experimental validation.

papers.title: SNX13 and SNX14 interorganelle tethers suppress lysosome membrane damage and neurodegeneration.
papers.abstract: Lysosome membrane permeabilization (LMP) is an emerging signature of neurodegenerative diseases, yet the mechanisms that enable an effective repair are largely undefined, particularly in neurons. Here, we reveal sorting nexin (SNX) proteins SNX13 and SNX14 maintain lysosome membrane lipid composition to support efficient LMP repair and neuronal survival. We identify loss of function mutations in SNX13 in children manifesting a previously unrecognized cerebellar neurodegenerative disorder. Consistently, Snx13 ablation in mice causes cerebellar Purkinje cell death and signatures of ataxia-like motor deficits. We show loss of SNX13 or its ataxia-linked paralog SNX14 perturbs lysosome morphology, positioning, and acidity and causes increased susceptibility to lysosome damage. Using lysosome immunoprecipitation and proteomics, we comprehensively map lysosome proteome remodeling during membrane damage and repair, finding that SNX13 or SNX14 deficiency blunts recruitment of repair machinery, including ESCRTs and PITT pathway proteins, to damaged lysosomes. Mechanistically, we determine SNX13 and SNX14 support lysosome integrity through interorganelle lipid crosstalk. We define SNX13 and SNX14 as lipid binding proteins that localize to ER-lysosome junctions, where they support lysosomal phosphoinositide levels in response to membrane damage. In line with this, loss of SNX13 or SNX14 impairs lysosome PtdIns4P signaling. Altogether, our work reveals a conserved mechanism of interorganelle lipid crosstalk by SNX13/14 family proteins that safeguards lysosome membranes, maintaining them competent for repair, and is defective in cerebellar neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Widespread oscillatory suppression in autism persists in the absence of psychotropic medication.
papers.abstract: Purpose: Investigate the neural oscillatory activity associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) using electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings in children and adolescents. Compare the corresponding oscillatory power between ASD patients taking psychotropic medication with a drug-naive group. Methods: ASD diagnosis was done using DSM-IV and CARS (Childhood Autism Rating Scale). EEG recordings employed 22 scalp electrodes (10/20 system). ASD vs. neurotypical groups were matched for sex and age (5 females; average age: ~10 years old). We analyzed the resting state (eyes open) EEG power spectrum during ~2-minute recordings. The multitaper FFT method was used to estimate spectral power for the delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma frequency bands. We pooled together data from several electrodes to compute comprehensive power spectra and assess the oscillatory behavior of macro brain regions. Results: We observed widespread (~4Hz - 20Hz) oscillatory suppression comprising the theta, alpha and beta frequency bands. The most widespread and robust ASD-associated power suppression was in the high theta and alpha bands. Delta and gamma bands showed no significant power change for any of the brain regions studied. Results from a subgroup of patients (N = 9) who never used psychotropics confirmed these findings, indicating that they are not an artifact of medication. Conclusion: Suppression in theta, alpha and beta oscillations may offer insights into the neurophysiological underpinnings of autism and could be used as an accessible and comprehensive tool in ASD diagnosis, regardless of the patients being or not on medication.

papers.title: STING activation drives pericentrosomal positioning of acidic organelles via the VAIL-LRRK2-Rab35 pathway
papers.abstract: The cGAS-STING pathway is an innate immune system that responds to cytoplasmic double-stranded DNA, but recent studies have highlighted its noncanonical role in facilitating lysosomal stress responses. Specifically, STING activation has been shown to trigger V-ATPase-ATG16L1-induced LC3 lipidation (VAIL) and to activate LRRK2, a Parkinson disease-associated kinase, but the detailed molecular mechanism and the physiological roles of the activation have remained unclear. Here, we found that STING activation in microglia induces the translocation of LRRK2 to the pericentrosomal area, where lysosomes and recycling endosomes (REs) concentrate. This process was VAIL-dependent, and LRRK2 was found to be localized to the organelles. The translocation of LRRK2 required intact microtubule structures and was mediated by LRRK2 kinase activity, its substrate Rab35 and the motor adaptor proteins including JIP4. All these proteins were concentrated at the pericentrosomal area upon STING stimulation. The hyperactivating G2019S mutation of LRRK2 promoted the pericentrosomal translocation of these proteins. Overall, we propose a novel STING-induced noncanonical pathway that involves LRRK2 to facilitate pericentrosomal organelle positioning.

papers.title: Ligilactobacillus salivarius enolase is an oxytocin-like systemic signal and it is reduced in children with autism spectrum disorder
papers.abstract: Abstract Oxytocin (OT) is a peptide hormone promoting social interactions and reducing anxiety, both core behaviors altered in autism spectrum disorder (ASD)1. Current approaches to boost OT signaling in the brain have, however, had little success2. OT is carried in the blood by immunoglobulin G (IgG), suggesting a new therapeutic target for boosting OT, but its antigenic origin and capacity to influence central OT signaling are unknown3. Here we show that Ligilactobacillus salivarius (LS) 48 kDa enolase (ENO) displays a species-unique structural homology with OT underlying both its OT-like antigenic and ligand properties. While LS ENO was naturally present in human plasma, correlating between members of the same family, its levels were reduced in children of both sexes diagnosed with ASD, starting from the disorder’s onset. Using mice, we show that LS ENO was present in both plasma and brain, and that its levels were lower in BTBR mice, a model of ASD. We further show that LS ENO immunization induced OT-binding IgG, which enhanced OT stability in plasma, increased OT receptor activation, and facilitated OT entry into the brain. Accordingly, LS ENO-immunization boosted OT concentrations in the brain and improved social, repetitive and anxiety-like behavior in BTBR mice. Thus, LS ENO is an OT-like protein which enhances OT signaling and boosts brain OT levels via production of OT-carrier IgG. Reduced plasma levels of LS ENO may, hence, contribute to ASD pathophysiology.

papers.title: Trisomy 21 Perturbs Oligodendrocyte Developmental States and Oligo–Neuron Communication in Human Forebrain Assembloids
papers.abstract: Intellectual disability is a hallmark of Down syndrome (DS), caused by the triplication of human chromosome 21. Abnormal neuronal connectivity and impaired myelination are consistently observed in DS, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we used DS-derived isogenic induced pluripotent stem cell-derived forebrain assembloids (FAs) to investigate oligodendrocyte lineage cell (OLLC) development and neuron–glia interactions. Trisomic FAs exhibited an expansion of BCAS1+ pre-myelinating OLLCs, without a corresponding increase in myelin basic protein (MBP) expression. Transcriptomic analyses identified a euploid-enriched, trophic and maturation-supportive state (OLLC_2-TMS) and a trisomy-enriched synaptic interactions and differentiation state (OLLC_3-SID), lacking coordinated enrichment in myelination-promoting programs. Corresponding transcriptional signatures were identified in OLLCs from early postnatal human cortex. Increased excitatory neuronal contacts with pre-myelinating OLLCs accompanied ultrastructural myelin abnormalities in trisomic assembloids. Our findings suggest that trisomy redirects OLLC development toward a pre-myelinating state, uncoupling oligodendrocyte differentiation from productive myelination.

papers.title: Brain and kidney Extracellular Vesicle Morphology and Complementary Brain proteomics after Inflammatory Challenge.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Shape, size variation, and protein composition describe different properties of tissue extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations. We compared brain and kidney EV shape and size using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). We also assessed repeated protein detection and reanalyzed a deposited brain proteomics cohort, with attribution to its original source. The study used intracerebroventricular lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and an intravenous miRNA-associated EV formulation. Each group contained three biological samples, as labelled in the source data. Source morphometry summaries included 385 brain and 101 kidney profiles. Kidney circularity was 0.9225, 0.8977, and 0.9288 in the control, LPS, and treatment groups, respectively. The corresponding values for diameter quartile dispersion, a measure of size variation, were 0.2603, 0.5334, and 0.6018. Thus, near-control outline shape coexisted with persistent size variation. None of the six primary morphology tests remained significant after Holm correction. Independent recalculation confirmed 1,527 eligible rat protein accessions across individual searches. The complete quantitative matrix contained 953 features. The main peptide filter combined unique and razor peptides. A stricter analysis retained 916 features. PTGFRN and LAMB2 remained the only significant treatment-versus-LPS findings. In the main analysis, PTGFRN increased 14.71-fold (q = 0.0365), and LAMB2 increased 6.23-fold (q = 0.00585). Their LPS levels were already close to control values. Exploratory normalization used the geometric mean of four measured EV-associated markers. The resulting treatment-versus-LPS increases were 16.43-fold and 6.96-fold, respectively. These ratios support selective changes in relative protein representation within the recovered mixture. They do not establish protein copies per EV. Analysis of the full protein profile and calibration of the complete selection process did not support an overall return to control. This study compares morphology and composition as separate outcomes. It identifies membrane and matrix associations as priorities for validation. Original TEM measurements were unavailable, sample matching remained unresolved, and kidney proteomics were absent. These limitations prevent causal conclusions and individual-sample comparisons between morphology and protein composition. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: This study contributes to exosome research by integrating particle morphology and proteomic analysis to characterize tissue-derived extracellular vesicle-enriched preparations following inflammation and miRNA-associated vesicle administration. The findings highlight that particle shape, size heterogeneity, and protein composition can follow different treatment-associated patterns, supporting their assessment as complementary features of exosome preparations. Selective enrichment of PTGFRN and LAMB2 prioritizes membrane and extracellular-matrix association for further investigation. This approach strengthens the interpretation of exosome characterization data and defines focused questions about particle identity, protein localization, and functional cargo delivery. It provides a foundation for evaluating how changes in recovered vesicle preparations relate to the biological activity of exosome-based interventions.

papers.title: GPNMB enables lysosomal adaptation required for myelin clearance and nerve regeneration after peripheral nerve injury
papers.abstract: Recovery from peripheral nerve injury involves coordinated axonal and immune repair programs that promote tissue regeneration. However, the mechanisms regulating immune-mediated repair remain incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that glycoprotein non-metastatic melanoma protein B (GPNMB) is a key regulator of repair processes following peripheral nerve injury. In a mouse sciatic nerve crush model, loss of Gpnmb impaired functional recovery after injury. MRI and histological analyses revealed persistent myelin debris accumulation, defective debris clearance, and impaired macrophage lysosomal function within injured nerves. Mechanistic studies showed that GPNMB-deficient human iPSC-derived macrophages exhibited impaired lysosomal adaptation, reduced lysosomal fitness, and defective processing of myelin-associated cargo, resulting in inefficient degradation of injury-associated material. These defects were accompanied by impaired acquisition of repair-associated cellular programs. Together, our findings identify GPNMB as a critical regulator of lysosome-dependent repair programs during nerve regeneration and demonstrate that efficient GPNMB-dependent myelin processing is required for functional recovery following peripheral nerve injury. Graphical abstract GPNMB enables efficient nerve regeneration after injury GPNMB promotes lysosomal adaptation in injury-responsive macrophages and microglia, enabling efficient myelin debris clearance and successful nerve regeneration. GPNMB coordinates injury-responsive myeloid and glial remodeling following peripheral nerve injury. After sciatic nerve crush, GPNMB is induced in macrophages, Schwann cells, and spinal cord microglia, where it promotes lysosomal adaptation and efficient myelin debris processing. By supporting reparative cellular states and sustained debris clearance, GPNMB enables axonal regeneration and functional recovery.

papers.title: Spatial proteomics on repurposed sequencers reveals early astrocytic remodeling in an ALS mouse model
papers.abstract: Spatial proteomics can reveal how disease reshapes cells and their local environments, but extending these measurements across replicated tissue cohorts requires validated antibodies, consistent sample processing and integrated analysis. These requirements are particularly pressing in studies of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), where pathology evolves unevenly across spinal-cord regions and disease stages. Here, we established an end-to-end spatial proteomics workflow linking a validated 28-antibody panel to automated fluorescence decoding and imaging on repurposed high-throughput sequencers, followed by multicycle image processing, cellular profiling and probabilistic spatial-neighborhood analysis. We applied it to 70 lumbar spinal-cord sections from nine SOD1-G93A and nine wild-type mice at presymptomatic, disease-onset and symptomatic stages. Spatial neighborhood analysis revealed that the environments surrounding motor neurons were already remodeled at disease onset. GFAP-high neighborhoods expanded in the ventral gray matter, with 43% of motor neurons embedded in these environments in SOD1-G93A mice, compared with 15% in wild-type mice. This early expansion preceded the later decline of non-reactive gray matter and detectable motor-neuron loss. The regional organization of the protein-defined changes shared features with neuronal and astrocytic patterns mapped by spatial transcriptomics in mouse and human ALS. This work enables spatial proteomics across replicated tissue cohorts and identifies localized remodeling of the environments around surviving motor neurons as an early feature of disease in the SOD1-G93A model.

papers.title: SACHET: seeded contour tracking measures Rab conversion kinetics on individual endosomes in live cells
papers.abstract: Membrane-labeled endosomes appear as hollow rings in a projection; they move, deform and exchange their coat, which population trackers — tools that detect every object of one kind and link the detections across frames — are not designed to follow. Here we introduce SACHET (Seeded Adaptive Contour & Hollow Endosome Tracking), a human-supervised Fiji tool that tracks one endosome at a time. On simulated ground truth it localizes the center to 10 nm, recovers transition time constants and lags without bias and holds the target among touching neighbors; comparisons with tuned TrackMate and Cellpose delineate where each is superior. In crowded spinning-disk projections, TrackMate followed one of seven marked Rab5-to-Rab7 conversions; supervised SACHET followed all 37. SACHET thus provides a stable per-endosome frame in which membrane morphology and protein exchange can be quantified: in five cell lines the conversion toggles like a digital switch within seconds to minutes, differing between lines.

papers.title: Mitochondrial DNA-cGAS-STING-CISD1 axis mediates hypoxia-induced cognitive impairment by driving hippocampal neuronal ferroptosis
papers.abstract: Abstract High-altitude hypoxic cognitive impairment severely compromises the physical and mental health of individuals who rapidly ascend to or reside long-term at high altitude; however, its initiating mechanisms, pathological cascades, and molecular regulatory network remain incompletely understood, leaving a paucity of effective therapeutic targets and preventive strategies. Using a mouse model of simulated 6000 m hypobaric hypoxia and a primary hippocampal neuron hypoxia model, we integrated behavioral testing, transmission electron microscopy, Seahorse metabolic analysis, transcriptomic profiling, co-immunoprecipitation-coupled proteomics, structural prediction, pharmacological intervention, and clinical validation in human cohorts to systematically delineate the molecular mechanisms and core regulatory pathways underlying hypoxia-induced neuronal ferroptosis. Hypoxic exposure time-dependently impaired object recognition and spatial memory in mice and caused hippocampal neuron loss. Mechanistically, mitochondrial damage emerged as a critical initiating event during hypoxic stress, triggering mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release and subsequent activation of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway. Hypoxic hippocampal neurons exhibited canonical features of ferroptosis, including elevated Fe²⁺ and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, decreased GPX4 expression, and enhanced ACSL4 expression and increased mitochondrial C11-BODIPY oxidation. Pharmacological inhibition of STING with C-176 significantly alleviated these ferroptosis phenotypes, neuronal loss, and cognitive impairment. Co-immunoprecipitation combined with proteomics identified CISD1 (mitoNEET), a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, as a STING-interacting partner, and their binding was enhanced under hypoxia and localized to mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contact sites. Moreover, the ferroptosis inhibitor Liproxstatin-1 rescued hypoxic cognitive impairment and partially restored mitochondrial morphology and respiratory function without reversing STING phosphorylation, indicating that ferroptosis functions downstream of STING and constitutes a feed-forward amplification loop by aggravating mitochondrial damage. In human cohorts, levels of serum iron and oxidative damage markers correlated positively with residential altitude. Collectively, these findings establish a self-amplifying pathological axis of mitochondrial damage-mtDNA-cGAS-STING-CISD1-ferroptosis, and targeting this axis may provide novel strategies for the prevention and treatment of high-altitude hypoxic cognitive impairment.

papers.title: Astrocytic sEH–EET signaling regulates microglial lysosomal function and suppresses the STING–Type I interferon pathway in Alzheimer’s disease
papers.abstract: Background The development of β-amyloid (Aβ) pathology in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is accompanied by profound changes in astrocytes and microglia and associated neuroinflammation. Soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH), which degrades anti-inflammatory epoxyeicosatrienoic acids (EETs), is elevated in the AD brain, yet how EETs restrain inflammation remains poorly understood. Methods We performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on brains from wild-type, sEH knockout, 5xFAD, and 5xFAD; sEH knockout mice, and used primary mouse microglia and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived microglia to define the underlying mechanism. To test cell-type-specific contributions, we generated astrocyte- and endothelial-specific she knockout mice and crossed them with 5xFAD mice. Results Genetic disruption of sEH in 5xFAD mice markedly reduced the abundance of a type I interferon (IFN)-responsive microglial subcluster and lowered phospho-STING (pSTING) levels. In primary microglia, supplementation with 11,12-EET attenuated STING activation and IFN target gene expression; blocking lysosomal acidification abolished this effect and caused pSTING to accumulate, identifying lysosomal degradation as a critical route for terminating STING signaling. 11,12-EET also enhanced microglial lysosomal acidification and Aβ phagocytosis. Astrocytic, but not endothelial, disruption of sEH recapitulated the reductions in Aβ pathology and microglial STING activation seen in global sEH-deficient mice, identifying astrocytes as the major cellular source of EETs regulating this pathway. Conclusion We define an astrocyte–microglia axis in which astrocytic sEH limits EET availability and thereby sustains microglial STING signaling. By promoting lysosomal clearance of pSTING, EETs suppress type I IFN signaling and enhance microglial Aβ clearance, highlighting sEH inhibition as a therapeutic strategy targeting both neuroinflammation and lysosomal dysfunction in AD.

papers.title: Using a 3-step semi-automated image analysis pipeline to quantify differences in VE-cadherin junction morphology in lymphatic endothelial cells in vitro.
papers.abstract: Lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) function is strongly tied to transitions between button- and zipper-like junctions that control fluid flow into vessels. Published methods quantifying junction morphology are limited to single cell analysis or use few quantitative metrics to describe junctions across LEC monolayers. Therefore, a novel 3-step image analysis pipeline was developed to identify new metrics that quantify differences in button- and zipper-like junctions in LECs. The pipeline used Cellpose, CellProfiler, and Fiji to analyze VE-cadherin expression across lymphatic vessels within a 3D microfluidic chip and quantify VE-cadherin radial intensity, number of objects, object size, branchpoints, endpoints, and junction thickness. Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α exposure produced button-like junctions, and unexposed cells were zippered. Radial intensity was heightened at the cell membrane in zipper-like junctions while perinuclear intensity increased for button-like junctions. Increased branchpoints, endpoints, objects per cell, and junction thickness were associated with junction buttoning, while increased object size was associated with junction zippering. Principle component analysis results reinforced these trends and identified metric combinations that represented each junctional state. Overall, this semi-automated pipeline quantified differences in VE-cadherin junction morphology across LEC monolayers and generated new quantitative metrics to expand the tools available for studying junction morphology in lymphatic vasculature.

papers.title: Explainable multi-view graph neural networks for prioritizing autism risk genes and identifying transcriptional modules
papers.abstract: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has a heterogeneous genetic architecture in which risk-associated genes may participate in interconnected molecular pathways. We present an graph-explainable multi-view graph neural network (GEM-GNN) for prioritizing ASD-associated genes by integrating protein-protein interaction (PPI) and brain-specific co-expression networks with genomic features. The model uses two GraphSAGE branches to learn representations from the structural and functional network views, combines these representations through a feature bottleneck, and applies an adjusted focal-loss objective to address class imbalance. Permutation feature importance and neighborhood subgraph extraction are used to examine the genomic and network evidence underlying candidate rankings. In experiments covering 19,832 protein-coding genes, the manuscript reports an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.8008, an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.93, an F1 score of 0.74 and a precision at 100 of 76%. An ablation analysis reports an AUPRC of 0.80 for the bottleneck-fusion model, compared with 0.71 for the PPI-only model, 0.69 for the co-expression-only model and 0.75 for simple concatenation. The authors also report that 85 high-ranking candidates overlap with independent de novo mutation evidence and that candidate genes are enriched for RNA polymerase II-mediated transcriptional processes. These results suggest that combining structural and brain-specific functional networks may support ASD gene prioritization and pathway-level interpretation. The reported performance and biological findings require interpretation in light of the dataset construction, evaluation protocol and validation procedures described in the manuscript.

papers.title: Allele-agnostic KCNH1 suppression rescues gain-of-function developmental epileptic encephalopathy
papers.abstract: Gain-of-function variants in KCNH1, which encodes the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv10.1, cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) characterized by seizures, developmental delay and intellectual disability. While pathogenic variants enhance channel activity, loss of KCNH1 is tolerated in humans and mice, suggesting that allele-agnostic gene suppression may represent a viable therapeutic strategy. Here, we developed a gapmer antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) targeting KCNH1 and evaluated its efficacy in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons and a knock-in mouse model of KCNH1-related disorder. Neurons carrying the pathogenic KCNH1 variants I494V or G375R exhibited a shared phenotype characterized by hyperpolarized resting membrane potential and abnormalities in neuronal network activity despite largely preserved intrinsic firing properties. ASOs efficiently reduced KCNH1 expression without disrupting network activity in control neurons. In contrast, ASO treatment normalized network dysfunction across both mutant genotypes, demonstrating that distinct KCNH1 gain-of-function variants converge on a reversible disease state. To assess the efficacy of ASOs in vivo, we generated a new Kcnh1-R357Q knock-in mouse model that exhibited profound seizures and early mortality. A single ASO treatment reduced seizure burden significantly and restored survival to near-normal levels. Together, these findings establish KCNH1 suppression as a precision therapeutic strategy for KCNH1-related DEEs and provide a framework for treating gain-of-function epilepsies in which partial gene reduction is clinically tolerated.
